movements.sigSummary: Henry's first letter home: the 34th New York reaches Washington after a river boat from Albany and a half-mile march through Baltimore, where twenty of his company carried loaded guns "in case of attack" but the city "rather cheered" them. In the depot he counts bullet holes from an earlier row and sees a volunteer accidentally killed by a dropped gun. Mindful of his widowed mother, he declines a costly furlough, trusting she needs the eight dollars he sent more than he needs the visit.
movements.transcription:
June 6th, 1861
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother -

We arrived at Washington Friday eve about ten. We took the boat at Albany and went down the river some ways past New York, were not allowed to go into the City. It seems to me I never got into such a drunken set as I have here, however there are some that don't drink. After we left the boat we took the cars, and then went to Baltimore. Our regiment was cheered all the way from Albany to Washington. We marched half a mile through Baltimore and then took the train for Washington. It is said our regiment was the best looking that came into Washington.

No one attempted to molest us going through Baltimore, but rather cheered us. In the depot I saw several holes in the roof where there had been a row. There was one volunteer accidentally killed by another letting his gun fall when it was loaded. Twenty of our company had their guns loaded going through Baltimore in case of attack, but it was useless. It took thirty cars to carry our regiment and two engines to draw the train. I have not been around the city yet, hope to before long and get my likeness taken. Had not time in Albany.

I hope when you write you will let me know whether you received that money, was eight dollars. You must excuse bad spelling and improper grammar. I am writing where there is a great noise. Going through Mariland I saw some very fine farms and some fine grain. We had three day rations given us from New York to Washington.

I would have been very glad to have gone home for three or four days, and spoke to Brink about it, but he said it would cost me twelve dollars, thought it would not pay. If I had known it would have cost only five dollars I would have gone. However, perhaps it is all for the best. I know you will need the money at home. Several of our company have spent their money for drinking, some have had it stolen from them.

I hope you will write all the news. I find it very heavy to carry the knapsack, but shall get use to it. I shall not write any more just now. Please write soon.

I remain your aff Son

Henry

P.S. I cannot tell definitely how you should direct your letters, but you might write Care of Capt. Reich, Co. D., 34th Regt., Washington. Can tell more definitely when we get into Camp.

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a Union soldier's real-time account of First Bull Run reaching the capital by sound alone. He doesn't yet know whether his regiment will march or hold as city guard, and steadies himself in faith hours after a six o'clock chapel service: wherever he goes, he is ready.
movements.transcription:
July 21st, 1861
Washington D.C.

Dear Mother:

Although I wrote a day or two before I received this letter, I thought I would write a few lines. I am very glad you are going to Charlotte. I hope you will make a long visit. I have received the two papers. Very glad to get them. While I am writing there is a battle going on. Can here cannons firing not over twenty-eight miles from here. Am not certain when our Regt. will go. Did here something about our Regt. being City guard. Am not certain. Wherever we go I am ready. Know I shall not be forsaken if I put my trust in the all seeing power.

I am very glad you have corrected the bad spelling. It is more careless than any thing else.

We had service this morning at six o'clock by the Chaplain reading a portion of scripture and prayer. Shall probably have service again this afternoon. The Capt. is very fond of singing, have it very often. I shall write more next time.

I remain your Aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Washington, Henry fills most of this letter to his sister Frances with the ordinary rhythm of camp — five hours of daily drill, the Colonel's praise drawing three cheers, two newspapers to pass the dull hours, a dollar begged to wash a shirt. Then a postscript breaks the calm: "We are ordered off... There has been a hard battle today." He doesn't yet know it is Bull Run, only to leave by morning — and tells her not to send the money after all.
movements.transcription:
(On same sheet)

Dear Frances:

You must excuse me for writing on the same paper but could not think of sending this without writing a few lines as I received so good a letter from you. I am enjoying comparatively good health thus far. There are several that are sick. I am glad if you are pleased with my picture. Albert thought it was perfect, as did others. I shall get a better one taken when pay day comes around and let you have it.

I suppose you would like to know how I pass my time when not on drill. I find it very dull unless I have something to read. Happy to say I have two papers to read. We drill five hours a day. Rise at five in the morning, retire at nine in the eve. The Colonel told each Capt. last night that the men were improving in drilling. Each camp gave him three cheers. I have written to Nellie and Aunt L. Was a real treat to read their letters. Want me to write often which I intend to do. There is not much of importance going on now. I shall have to go on guard before a great while. They will never find me sleeping while on guard. If you would send me one dollar I should like it. Our letters are franked now and then. I want to get a shirt washed. Please excuse this scribble. My pen is not good. Please write often if possible. Shall have more to write next time.

I remain your Aff. Brother,

Henry

Later - We are ordered off. Shall probably leave in the morning. Ready tonight. May leave before morning. There has been a hard battle today. Have not heard much about it yet. You need not send any money now, till I write.

movements.sigSummary: Filtering letters near Manassas, Henry writes to his mother that the regiment has marched into Virginia and lies in camp three miles from the enemy, with pickets exchanging fire daily. He plays down the danger — he is well, the food is plain but plenty — yet asks her to direct his next letter carefully, as if uncertain where he will be. A son steadies his mother even as the army gathers him in.
movements.transcription:
Aug. 6th, 1861
Camp ?
(While attending West Point)

Dear Frances:

I think it is about time that I answered your letter. I wrote to you and Charles a week ago, but when I came to mail the letters the next morning both were missing. Today I had a general overturning of things in my locker to find my note paper, and up came the letters. I don't know whether to tear them up or send them with those that I am now writing. I think I will send them in order that you may see that I have written.

The locker or chest where we put our clothes, paper, books and everything in general is five feet long, one foot high and one foot broad, and must answer for three persons. Whenever we are in a hurry - which occurs frequently - we jerk out whatever we want, putting everything of course "in a muss". There is a little oil on the corner of my paper; you must excuse it as it is the best I have - my hair oil got upset. It did not get onto my clothes fortunately.

There is a cessation of all business here today on account of Ex President Van Buren's death. A cannon is fired every half hour, the flag hung at half mast, and all the officers have put crape on their right arm, which they are to wear for six months. Thirteen guns were fired this morning before reveille, thirty will be fired tonight at six. This morning, when the third class came in from firing, a little before reveille, they went around to the fourth class' tents and made all the Plebes turn over towards the color line "in honor of Van Buren's death."

If a person wishes to come to West Point "to see the sights", August is the month. There is the most going on at this time. The third class have horses attached to their battery now in drilling. It is a very pretty sight to see them drill. We all drill together during this month in infantry tactics. The fourth class drill by themselves in artillery. The drill is to learn to load and also to mount upon the limber boxes and casions of the piece. It takes seven men to work one piece. After the men understand the duties of the places which they happen to have they change places, so that each person may understand the duties of each number well.

You asked me for my photograph. I cannot conveniently get it taken now, but perhaps I will before long. I think you will get out of patience if I scribble much more, so will close.

Please write soon.

Your aff. brother,

James.

Remember me to Mrs. Brinckerhoff.

movements.sigSummary: From the Washington defenses, Henry reports his regiment posted as Potomac guards against rebel crossings — and the camp talk that it may never see a battle, to which he answers, "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where." Three days too sick to drill, sleeping on wet ground in fever-and-ague country, he still sends his five-dollar gold piece home by the Captain, ordering his sister and mother to spend it: "I put that down as a command."
movements.transcription:
Sept. 5th, 1861
Washington, D.C.

Dear Sister —

I received your letter this morning. Very glad to know that you are all well. As for myself, I have not been well, have not been able to drill for three days, but am some better now. The Dr. gave me medicine. I think it is very unhealthy sleeping on the ground. I have got so now I don't mind it much. This is a great place for fever and ague. I have got to be careful xx or I shall come down with it.

I can hardly realize that it is now fall. The summer has passed quickly away to me. It is nearly three months since I left home. It is now raining — shall probably have a wet day of it. We have a very fine tent to keepout the rain. I suppose you would like to know bout matters and things in our Camp. I shall write a Journal as soon as pay day comes around when I can get paper. When we get paid off again we shall probably have $24 or $26. I have now a five dollar gold piece. I shall send it all home except one or two dollars, by the Capt. as he expects to go to Champlain this month. Now I shall expect, of course, you and Mother will use what money you want. You must not hesitate, I put that down as a command. Times are hard and you will need it bad enough.

Our Regt. is stationed here as guards to keep the rebels from crossing the river. The pickets go out by Co. Ours has been out once. There are ten thousand of our troops three miles from here so that if we are attacked we can fall back and have a strong force. I have heard the opinion expressed that our Regt. may never see a battle, that we will always be stationed here as guards, but we can not tell. I for one am willing to go. I don't care where.

A sad accident happened here last Sabbath morning. A private from Co. H. was shot while on guard by another person. There were playing with their guns when one of them went off. He lived about fifteen minutes after he was shot. This makes three that have lost their lives by carelessness in this Regt.

I have received all the papers that have been sent from home. A short time ago I got two papers from Charles — New York Times. It is some time since I received any Observers. I don't doubt but what they all come, as the direction is correct. I have heard that we will have a band to our Regt. I hope it will be so, heretofore we had fife and drum. We have a very good drummer.

I hope you and Mother will take rides with our horse. He is very gentle if only managed right. I don't suppose he could run away if he should try. I hope the boys will get a chance to go to Middleburg. It is better than soldiering. Please write often.

Your aff Brother

Henry

Please let me know if my old clothes have been received. I sent them in a box with others that live in Champlain. I had mine directed to Mother.

movements.sigSummary: From the Washington defenses after coming off picket with Corporal Kellogg, Henry counsels his mother that Alexander "had better stay at home" rather than join "Ransoms Company" — college or home over war. Word has just reached camp of the fall of Fort Hatteras, "a noble achievement," and he wagers the war can't last two years. His regiment's two brass cannon lobbed shells three miles into Virginia last Sabbath, but the enemy "would not return the favor."
movements.transcription:
Sept. 11, 1861

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of Sept. 5th and also two papers from home day before yesterday. Very glad to know that matters and things are going on well at home. I received two letters from you while in Charlotte, also two or three from home while you were away, and several papers. I don't doubt but what they all came, as the direction is correct. After this I shall acknowledge all that I receive.

I have come off from picket today. There were six of us on one post with Corporal Kellogg, two on guard at a time, as it is more safe. We had a very fine time while on picket, lived very well.

I never heard of the taking of Fort Hatteras and others till you wrote. That was indeed a noble achievement. A few such battles and the South will have to give in. It is my belief that the war can not last two years, still we can not tell. Time can only tell how long it will continue.

You write that Alexander is very anxious to join Ransoms Company. My opinion and advise is he had better stay at home, and I think I am wright. If he can get a good chance to go to College, he had better go. If not he can make himself xxxxxx yousefull at home. I don't know as I have spelt that long word right. At all events Alex can do better than going to war. I hope he will think the matter over the right way.

Sept. 12th
We have not received our pay yet. Expect to have it in a few days. I shall send all I have coming except two or three dollars which I may need. Reich will not go to Champlain till pay day comes around. I have now a five dollar gold piece.

We have two brass cannon with our Regt. Fired some xxxx bomb shells over into Virginia last Sabbath morning. They will carry over three miles, but they would not return the favor by fireing back. I have heard this morning that we shall probably winter in Kentucky. Please write often.

Your aff. Son,

Henry

P.S. I heard the Capt. say the other day that if Ransom went to Albany without a full Company it would probably be scattered as they will not receive part of a Co. I suppose that must be so.
movements.notes: Two-part letter: begun Sept 11, continued Sept 12

movements.sigSummary: Alexander's first letter home, written from the Ogdensburgh barracks: "Here I am safe and sound... How strange it does seem. Ah! what a bedlam!" He marvels at hemlock-board berths stuffed with straw, the parade ground ringed with armed sentinels, and a half-tipsy soldier on the cars who hollered for the fifer and drummer to "strike up." Dinner was soup, boiled pork, and potatoes — but it was the ginger bread from home that "went well."
movements.transcription:
September 20/61
Ogdensburgh

My Dear Mother —

Here I am safe and sound in the barracks. How strange it does seem. Ah! what a bedlam! You said you wished me to tell you everything. We had a very pleasant journey. The cars were very noisy most of the time. We had at last subsided into something like quiet, when a half tipsy fellow sung out "Strike up there forward (the fifer and drummer) or they will think we are all dead". We had it then in good earnest.

The machine shop (a large building) is used as a dining room. Two other large buildings, as sleeping houses. The buildings are provided with tiers of berths (made of hemlock boards and filled with straw). When we came off the cars (the barracks are close to the railroad) we were formed in double file and marched to the parade ground and dismissed. I was surprised to see the ground surrounded with armed sentinels. (There are some fellows above my head singing "Am I a follower of the lamb.") In a short time we were formed in double file and marched to dinner which consisted of soup, bread, boiled pork, cold slum, I potatoes. Very good, I think. That ginger bread went well. I have no more time. You must excuse this, people knocking my elbows and making noise have quite put me out.

Your affectionate son

F. A. Hubbell (Alex)

movements.sigSummary: On picket duty near Washington, Henry watches a Confederate signal rise over Virginia — "somewhat like the evening star, only it was a dark red — looked very fine." Between such glimpses of the enemy he relays the small comforts of camp: a merry supper with Lieutenant Scott, word that a friend from Chazy Village addressed his last letter, and a note for Mother that he already has more clothing than he can carry.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 21, 1861
Near Washington, D.C.

Dear Frances —

I meant to have written before, but was interrupted, expect of course, you will excuse me this time.

We have had very pleasant weather thus far, except last night and today it has rained very fast. It has been so warm that I have been obliged to keep my coat off in the day time, but it gets cold at night. You wished to know who it was that directed my letter to you. It was Edgar Graves from Chazy Village. Is well acquainted with Mrs. Brinkhoff. Wished to be remembered to her, etc., etc. It was his desire to direct it so I let him.

I have not much news to relate except while on Picket I saw what they call a Signal thrown up over in Virginia — looked somewhat like the evening star, only it was a dark red — looked very fine. Only wish you could have seen us while at supper on picket. Lieutenant Scott was with us, had a merry time of it. Tell Mother I will not need any clothing, I have more than I can carry now. Please write all the news. I will write more next time. I have no more room now.

I remain your aff Brother

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Henry takes in the news that his brother Alexander has gone "in for the war," answering it with measured resignation — "Perhaps it is all for the best" — and the quiet conviction it "can't last a great while." From camp near Washington, where bombs are lobbed into Virginia and jittery guards have just fired on a white horse in a false alarm, he wraps twenty-five dollars to send home and prepares to head out two days on picket in the first cold snap of fall.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 22, 1861.

Dear Mother:

As the Captain is expecting to go home in a short time, I though I would write a few lines, although I have not much to relate. I expect Reich wi. go tomorrow or next day. I shall send twentyfive dollars by him.

Our Camp was routed up not long since, but it was a false alarm. Two of the guard fired at a white horse. Some got frightened at nothing some times, but I doubt I should not wonder if we were called up again to night. Bombs have been fired over into Virginia today.

I don't know of anything that I want except paper and ink pens. It is quite cold this morning. Seems more like fall. Our company goes on picket today for two days.

So Alexander is in for the war. Perhaps it is all for the best. I don't think it can last a great while. I can say for one that I would rather be where I am now than to be any place, for I have gone all through the drilling and that I consider the worst of it. I received a week ago four papers besides the Observer — one paper from Aunt L. I have no more time to write.

Your affectionate son,

Henry.

movements.sigSummary: At Camp Wheeler in Ogdensburg, nineteen-year-old Alexander walks his sister through a soldier's full day — reveille at six, drill after breakfast, a twelve-pound brass field piece fired at sunrise and sunset. His company was sworn into state service Saturday after a rigid exam; the surgeon called him "a fine boy." He asks for Henry's overcoat, "tucked up so that it will not be too long for me," a small line that measures the boy inside the uniform.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 23, 1861
Camp Wheeler
Ogdensburg

My Dear Sister:

I am contented and happy, though I long to see you all. Our fare is excellent. We had for breakfast this morning coffee, beefsteak, potatoes and bread. Each man has a quart cup of coffee and the privilege of having it sweetened. This is a specimen of our fare. Reveille beats at six o'clock A.M. We have the Corporal's roll call at seven when we form in double line and march to breakfast. After breakfast comes drill. At one dinner. Drill again at three. Retreat beats at six P.M. Roll call again. Supper at seven. Tattoo at nine. Roll call again when all retire.

Our Company was examined and sworn into the States service on Saturday. The examination was very rigid. The surgeon told me that I was a fine boy. There are now over seven hundred men in the Regt. It will soon be full.

5 P.M. I have just come from drill. Our time is pretty well occupied. You can have no idea how difficult it is to write here. There is a bugle playing not fifty feet from me. Can you send me an overcoat if it is not to much trouble. I have needed one very much. If you send Henrys, please tuck it up so that it will not be too long for me. Will you also send me Charleys wide-awake suit. I shall need it when I stand on guard. If you can get a satchel with a key please send it with said articles. My satchel is xxxx at headquarters and I am obliged to go to the Captain whenever I wish anything. It is very inconvenient.

We have a wash house where all the Regt. wash in long troughs. There is a large twelve pound brass field piece attached to the Regiment, which is discharged at sunrise and sunset. The Captain is very kind to me. We have elected our Capt. and first Lieutenant. Loring E. White, a pious young man, is Lieut. I think we have the best officers of any company in the Regt. Each company thinks they have. I have no more time. The drums are beating for supper. Tell Mother, James and Charles x that this letter is as much for them as you. The band has just truck. Oh how I wish I could see you all. Tell C. I will try to write better next time. Give my love to Mrs. Brink and tell her I want to see her very much.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell.

P.S. Direct your letters to (it is almost dark) Camp Wheeler, Ogdensburgh, New York, care Capt. Ransom.

movements.sigSummary: On guard duty as sentry No. 11 at Camp Wheeler, Alexander Hubbell passed five men through his post in the dark before catching a whispered "is it right" — the watch word had leaked. He called out the Officer of the Guard, the watch was doubled, and the Colonel ordered any man who ran the guard shot through the legs. Off duty, he wrote a letter for a fellow who couldn't, and found unexpected comfort in a Methodist prayer meeting, thirty or forty strong.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 26, 1861
Camp Wheeler
Ogdensburg, New York

My Dear Brother James:

I have at last found time to write you. Today is fastday. We shall probably not drill today. Services will be held here today at four P.M. Our Company stood on guard on Tuesday. I stood from fifteen to twenty hours. The reason why I stood so long was because a great many ran the guard after nightfall and we were obliged to thrible it to prevent this. A watch word is given to the guard at nightfall and no one is allowed to go in or out unless he can give it. During the evening I saw a person coming toward me. When within ten feet of me I chalenged him with "who comes there" (reply) "Friend" "Advance Friend and give the countersign". He advanced until hil abdomen touched my bayonet and then leaning over he gave the word. I immediately passed him. In like manner I had passed another and another until I began to wonder what was in the wind when I heard a fellow say in a half whisper to a man outside the camp "is it right". I then saw what was the matter. (I had passed five). I immediately called out "Officer of the Guard No. 11 (I was sentry No. 11). He came, and I told him the watch word was discovered. The Guards were immediately doubled and the Colonel came around and gave order to run any man through the legs who attempted to run the guard, also to pass no one in or out. No one ran the guard again that night. Last night a great many ran the guard. The Colonel went after them with an officer of the Guard and a squad of about twenty-four men. (I just wrote a letter for a fellow named Wilson.)

Our Colones is a small, smart energetic-looking man, and I think a capital officer. Captain Ransom was elected by an unanimous vote. If anybody asks you how I like soldiering you may tell them I like it very well. The only very hard thing about it is that I am obliged to listen to so much profanity and obscene language. "However" as Henry says, I make the best of it. They do not fire the cannon now.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alex

P.S. Tell Charles I will write him soon.

..... 30 .....

Same Sheet —

My dear Mother:

I can not close this letter without saying a word or two to you. You may consider all this letter yours. I shall write you soon. I received your letter yesterday. Very glad to hear from you. I was beginning to think you had forgotten me. Daily prayer meetings are held in the camp. I attended one last night. Have not spent so pleasant an evening since I have been here. There were from thirty to forty there. They were all Methodists I think. There was plenty of groans and shouting, but I presume I shall get used to it. I just found out last night that they had meetings here. I am very well. Give my respects to Mrs. B.

Your affectionate Son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Alexander, barely a week into camp at Camp Wheeler near Ogdensburgh, writes his mother in genuine distress: offered the office of Adjutant in the "Brother Craftsmen," a mutual-aid society that vows to rescue brothers "if sore pressed in battle," he keeps asking "What shall I do?" Sickened by camp vice, he confesses he has "no friends in the Reg." and begs her to consult Mr. Copeland.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 27, 1861
Ogdensburgh, N.Y.
Camp Wheeler

My dear Mother —

I write to ask your advice. I am in a xxxxxxx dilemma. The office of Adjutant in the Society of the "Brother Craftsmen" has been proffered me. What shall I do? I presume you will not be able to judge until I tell you something about it. Well, the object of the Society is this — to band together a body of men who will care each other as if they were brothers. If one is sick they will see that he is cared for. If sore pressed in battle, they will come to his assistance. If set upon by any person or persons, they will succor him, but if he picked the quarrel they will let him alone. He must suffer for it. If wounded in battle they see that he is properly cared for. If anyone is convicted of licentious conduct, he is dismissed from the Society. The headquarters of the Society are at Watertown. If I accept this office I shall be third officer in the Society. I shall receive a salary of one dollar (perhaps more) per month. Now what do you think about it? I have accepted the office with the privilege of withdrawing if it does not meet your approval.

I attended the prayer meeting last night. I don't no what to do or what to think. One man there began to shout, roar, and bawl, calling on God to "come down now and bless us" until he was exhausted; all the while clapping his hands and swaying his body. He then began to draw his breath between his lips and xxxxx mutter and ejaculate. After he had somewhat recovered he began to shout "The Lord is with us", "He is here", "Glory to God", etc. All this was plentifully interspersed with Amen and ejaculations from the others. The Colonel was in the room below drilling some officers in the use of arms. This must have disturbed him. I felt xxxx ashamed that I was there. Perhaps I feel wrong. What shall I do? I wish to go to meeting, but I do not wish to see such scenes as that.

[page break]

Contd. Sept. 27, 1861

Ask Mr. Copeland what I shall do. I tell you what it is, Mother. If I ever hated vice I hate it ten times worse now. The writing on the first page of this letter was written by the second officer of the Society. I don't like the way he talks about me. It seems to me it would be a good plan to join it as I have no friends in the Reg.

I am well. Hope you all are. Have you heard from Henry? How is he? I shall write him soon.

Your affectionate Son

Alexander F. Hubbell

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your letter last evening. I am getting along pretty well now. I have had the rheumatism very bad, am over it now. The reason I have not written about it before is I could not spell the word...
movements.sigSummary: Writing to brother Charles, Henry corrects an inflated report of an attack across the river — not three companies of Rebels but thirty-five men against twelve — quipping, "I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand." He recounts a bad bout of rheumatism from sleeping on bare ground, eased only after he and two tentmates splurged 95 cents on a tent floor, and admits he held off writing of his illness because he couldn't spell the word.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 27th/61

Dear Charles —

I received your letter last evening. I am getting along pretty well now. I have had the rheumatism very bad, am over it now. The reason I have not written about it before is I could not spell the word. It is a long word to spell. I hope you will always correct all bad spelling.

We have got a floor to our tent. It cost 95 cts. — that would make little over 30 cts for three of us. I should probably have the rheumatism now if we had not got the floor. I had it so bad before that, I could hardly walk, but I am all right now. It is raining quite hard today and it has rained all night. We do not have so much of it here as up North.

So Alexander is off for the war. Well, good luck to him. I rather think he will get sick of it when he comes to go on guard duty, but perhaps he wont. I was cut four hours in the rain on guard last night, but I have got so I don't mind it much. I came off from picket day before yesterday, was on with Lieutenant Scott and H. Cooper and Sergeant H. There were also two privates besides myself to stand guard, three hours and a half at a time. Had a very pleasant time while on picket. Our Regiment has not drilled for some time, but we will have three drills every day after this besides dress parade.

So you have heard about the attack over the river, but you did not hear it quite strait. There were not three Comp. of Rebels, but only thirty-five against twelve. I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand. We fare very well now, have bread every day, have a large oven to bake it in. We get our rations every five days. Each man gives two shillings a month for cooking. We have fresh meat quite often.

[page break]

Contd. Sept. 27, 1861

You wished to know how the men pass the time. Thus far they have played cards, but that is not allowed now. The Col. has forbidden it. There was to much gambling going on, so the boys can not play now.

I have nothing more to write now. Please send me a paper if it is convenient.

I remain your aff Brother

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Nearly broke two weeks into camp, Alexander asks his mother to spare him a three-dollar fare he cannot afford: a railroad pass from Mr. Hoyle so he can come home on furlough the moment his uniform arrives Saturday. Even his postage is rationed — he tucks a letter to Henry inside hers to save the cost, confessing he has barely enough to settle his washing bill until a dollar or two arrives from the State.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 3, 1861
Camp Wheeler
Ogdensburgh

My dear Mother:

Our uniforms will be here Saturday and the Captain has promised me a furlough as soon as I get mine. Will you be so kind as to get a pass for me from Mr. Hoyle as it would cost me three dollars to go and come and I can not afford that. If you can get it please send it immediately. I am enjoying excellent health.

Your affectionate son

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Please to send the enclosed letter to Henry as I have probably hardly enough money to pay my washing bill. I shall soon have a dollar or two from the State.
movements.notes: Short letter; enclosed letter to Henry mentioned

movements.sigSummary: Camp Wheeler, a mile and a half from Ogdensburgh, was filling fast: the regiment counted some 800 men marching toward its full thousand, Alexander's company already 60 or 70 strong of a planned 101. Writing his brother, he confessed he liked soldiering "very well so far" — the fare excellent, the captain kind, a corporal's berth and a furlough both within reach. He'd bathed in the Lawrence the day before and enjoyed it famously. "Don't you envy me."
movements.transcription:
Oct. 3, 1861
Camp Wheeler
Ogdensburgh

My dear Brother:

I presume you will be glad to hear from Camp Wheeler. Well, here I am — been here almost two weeks. I like the life of the soldier very well so far. Our Camp is situated a mile and a half from the town. We use the car factory building as barracks. The fare is excellent, also the sleeping accomodations. Capt. Ransom says th t our uniforms will be here on Saturday. I don't know whether I shall have a Corporals berth or not. I hope I shall. The Captain is very kind to me. I don't believe a better officered company than our has gone to the war.

I had a bath in the Lawrence yesterday. I enjoyed it famously. The Regiment now numbers about eight hundred men and will soon have its thousand. We have now between sixty and seventy men in our Company. Our Company when full will number one hundred and one. We shall soon have it. I must write home to have them get me a pass from Mr. Hoyle. The Captain has promised to give me a furlough as soon as I get my uniform. Don't you envy me. I have enjoyed excellent health ever since I have been here. Write soon.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: A disciplinary crisis grips Henry's company near Washington: a soldier who left his picket early and grew abusive to Lt. Scott had his pay docked, a 30-lb knapsack strapped on, and his hands tied above his head — until a comrade cut the rope, throwing the whole company under arrest. From picket duty, the eighteen-year-old vows he "tries to do what is right," even as card-playing now brings court martial and his brother Charles grows anxious to enlist.
movements.transcription:
October 6th, 61

Dear Mother:

I received your letter last eve. Very glad that you are all well. We are having very warm weather now. Has been quite cold. I came off from picket yesterday. I enjoyed it very much. The pickets are stationed ½ mile and some a whole mile apart. I with three others had to walk three miles from Camp to our picket. The hardest of it is to carry our overcoat and two blankets, but I have got use to it and don't mind it much.

I have bought a frying pan. It cost 50¢. I shall take it home when I go. Our Company are all under arrest so I have heard. It seems one of our boys left his picket before his time, had some high words with Lieut. Scott, was quite abusive to him, when he was put under arrest. Six dollars is taken off his next wages and a knapsack of 30 lbs. for two days, and his hands tide over his head. Well the boys thought that was to much so one of them went and cut the rope that was on his hands. Our whole Co. is under arrest to find out who it is.

I have got all the clothing I want. Since I have been in camp in M. have got a pr. of shoes, pr. socks and one shirt. That will be all I will want for the present.

Oct. 7th

Today is quite cloudy. Looks like rain. There is a guard stationed around our tents and all on account of that occurance yesterday. I am sorry for the man that cut the rope. It will go hard with him. Have not found out who it is yet. There is no card playing permitted now. If any of the boys are found at it they are court martialed and have a knapsack of 30 or 40 lbs. to carry besides a heavy fine which I think is alright. I for one try to do what is right, and know that you would approve of it if I was at home. I could get into a quarrel every day if I should try to, but I keep out of it, and get along very well.

I am very glad that you correct the bad spelling in my letters. I hope in time to become a perfect speller. I neglected it to much at school, or at least the teachers did. We have a prayer meeting every Sabbath evening, had no preaching yesterday as the Chaplain was sick. Had a very dull day of it. I see Charles is anxious to enlist, but I think he is doing very well where he is, but if he intends or makes up his mind to go he must not enlist into another Regt. but come into our Co. It would be very pleasant to have him here. I have no more time to write.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry
movements.notes: Two-part letter: begun Oct 6, continued Oct 7
Left Ogdensburg. Traveled via rail to NYC, then to Baltimore.

movements.sigSummary: Henry relays a daring escape from rebel captivity: a prisoner taken in the same skirmish as Kellogg feigned illness to hoard his daily ration of opium, then drugged his guard's coffee and slipped through three enemy regiments to reach camp — bringing word that Kellogg is held unwounded at Richmond. Henry also notes a man stabbed by a drunk at midnight, dead by morning, and the 34th lately christened "the sharp shooters" in the papers.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 17, 1861

Dear Mother:

I received your letter while on picket. Very glad that you are all well at home. I have dreamt of being at home twice since I have been in Camp, but my dreams are not quite long enough for on wakening in the morning I find that I am not quite there yet. There is not a day that passes but what I think of you all. I know that matters and things can not go on as well at the farm as when I was there, as James is in school, but I shall be home one of these days.

Rich has not returned yet. We expect him tonight.

A sad occurrence happened here the other night about twelve o'clock. A man was stabbed by another person that was drunk. He lived till morning. Rum is not allowed in Camp. If any one is found with it he is severely punished. I don't know how that man came to get it, but the gallows will not be to hard for him.

Brigadier General Gormon was here today to inspect our Regt. of there knapsacks and everything we got from the State. We made a very fine appearance. Our Regt. is thought a good deal of by him. I see in the papers we are called the sharp shooters. Quite flattering, so the boys think.

One of those prisoners that was taken by the rebels in that skirmish when Kellogg was taken, has returned. He had two guards placed over him. He managed his escape very cunningly. He pretended that he was sick for some time. They gave him opium every day. When he got enough of it he drugged the guard's coffee and thus got away. He had to pass through three Regts. of Rebels. Said he was very well treated while prisoner. They told him they were going to put him in a cage and take him around for a show, but he outwited them. He said that Kellogg is safe in Richmond a prisoner, was not wounded. This man that escaped had a ball glance by his face the time he was taken.

The report is now that our Regt. will go to Poolsville for winter, to be there as guards. Shall probably go before a great while. Do not know how soon. There is nothing more to write at present. Please write often.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: I am very much oblige for the portfolio that you sent me, and also for the paper and pens, pen holder and ink. I would not have believed that you made it had you not written about it. Very nicely made...
movements.sigSummary: From the camps around Washington, Henry thanks his sister Frances for a handmade portfolio of writing supplies — so finely made he refused to believe it wasn't store-bought ("I thought it came form the store"), now the envy of the other boys, who have theirs but none to match it. Beneath the gratitude runs a quieter homesickness: he longs for her picture and a chance to sing when she has company. A postscript notes a letter from Nellie, with a photograph promised.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 19, 1861

Dear Francis:

I am very much oblige for the portfolio that you sent me, and also for the paper and pens, pen holder and ink. I would not have believed that you made it had you not written about it. Very nicely made. I thought it came form the store. Was nice as could be. A good many of the boys have them here, but thy won't come up to the one you made. I am writing on it now. Find it very convenient — more so to keep my paper in and letters. I shall enjoy reading the papers very much. I will give Brink that paper as soon as I can get a chance. He has left from where he was formerly. I do not remember the name of the place he has gone to.

I have not much more to write. I hope to get your picture one of these days, the sooner the better. Perhaps I shall get mine taken one of these days better than the other one. I wish I was going to be at home when you have company and could try my voice in singing. I shall be one of these days. Please write often.

Your aff. Brother, Henry.

P.S. I got a letter from Nellie with a promise of her picture.

movements.letterExcerpt: Here I am safe and sound three miles from Baltimore. Our regiment is distributed along the railroad between said place and the Relay House, a distance of nine miles.
movements.sigSummary: At Camp Jackson, three miles from Baltimore, Alexander recounts to his mother a nine-day march from Camp Wheeler to the war: dawn past West Point ("the most beautiful I ever saw"), a flag and bay horse presented in New York, a Philadelphia breakfast of beef and sauerkraut, and five rounds of cartridges issued before marching through Baltimore. A hungry stretch the men dubbed "Starvation Heights" tested them. "I think of all of you often, very, very, often," he closes.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 13, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Mother:

Here I am safe and sound three miles from Baltimore. Our regiment is distributed along the railroad between said place and the Relay House, a distance of nine miles.

Now that you know that I am well and where I am I presume you would like to hear the particulars of my journey. We left Camp Wheeler November the first and arrived at Rouses Point at six. I was very much surprised and very much pleased to F and C there. I was feeling very lonely and seeing them cheered me up wonderfully. I only regret I could not have seen you.

The steamer there could only carry half of the regt. and we (our company) being in the left wing, were oblige to wait an hour for another boat, the United States. Supper was given us on board the boat. I gave that case to Capt. Ransom then. He wishes me to give you his thanks and said that he did not see how you managed to contrive so convenient a thing.

We took the cars at Whitehall for Albany. There we left them and marched down to the river escorted by a company (I think) of artillery. A steamer and two barges carried the regiment to New York. We arrived there Sunday morning. We passed West Point. The scenery on the river is the most beautiful I ever saw. We passed West Point at 3 A.M. It was daylight when we passed through the most beautiful part of the river. I was on deck nearly all night. We lay anchored off New York until Monday evening when we crossed over to Jersey City and took the cars for the South. While at New York we received the rest of our knapsacks and blankets, and each man a beautiful Enfield rifle and sword bayonet.

On Monday afternoon we left the boat and marched into the city. We were drawn into a hollow square on a beautiful square in the center of which stood an equestrian statue of Washington. A star spangled banner was presented to the regiment and a beautiful bay horse to the Colonel. We were again drawn up in line in another street and a banner was presented to us there. We then left the city. It was about 2 oclock A.M. when we reached Philadelphia. An excellent breakfast was given us there. It consisted of beef, sweet potatoes, coffee, cheese, sourcrout and bread and butter. After breakfast we were taken to another room where there was every convenience for washing. I shall always think with pleasure of the Quaker City. At New York they gave us something to look at, but at Philadelphia they gave us something better pleasing to hungry soldiers — something to eat. They both treated us very kindly, but of the two I like the treatment of the latter place the best.

We reached Baltimore between three and four oclock in the afternoon. Before marching through the city five rounds of cartridges were distributed to the men, but no caps. (What the reason was I don't know).

Nov. 14. It was dark when we left Baltimore. We did not reach Washington until between two and three in the morning. We remained there till afternoon when we left for Kalarama Heights, three miles distant. It was dark when we reached there and we were obliged to pitch our tents after we arrived. We all suffered from hunger while there (on account of the Quartermaster's inexperience. The boys have given the place the name of Starvation Heights. Orders were received on Friday (November eighth) for us to leave.

I don't know what to think of our Colonel. He sent our baggage on before and we were obliged to sleep on the ground that night. There was no necessity for it, for they were expecting us in Washington that night, and had supper prepared for us. We left Washington Saturday morning. Five companies were left at the Relay House and the rest distributed between that place and Baltimore. We are stationed three miles from Baltimore as I have told you. Company C is encamped

(Contd.)

with us. We have hired a black cook for our company. Each pays the cook two shillings per month. The business of the regiment is to guard the railroad. I was on guard duty yesterday. I was obliged to walk half a mile every two hours during the night to relieve the pickets. They do not extend so far during the day. The first night we came to this camp was a very hard one to me. The pickets from our Company were entirely under my charge. I was obliged to call out the reliefs and take them around. What made it so hard was we had no guard tent and I was obliged to go around among the tents and hunt out the relief every two hours. Another thing that made it hard was that it was my first experience of picket duty. I think that I gave satisfaction.

Now, my dear Mother, the reason that I haven't written is because I lost my knapsack the first night we came here and I never found it until yesterday (November 13). I wish I could see you all very much. Write me often and send me a paper now and then. I try to keep my promise to you "to do nothing of which you would not approve." I feel that God is very near me. I sometimes feel very lonely, but I think of Him and you fighting for me and I feel better. I think of all of you often, very, very, often.

Your affectionate son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Direct your letters to Washington, D.C., Sixtieth Regt. I do not think you could go two miles in any direction without coming upon some picket or camp. Give my respects to all friends.
movements.notes: Multi-part letter: begun Nov 13, continued Nov 14. **Alexander's regiment confirmed: 60th NY Infantry**

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan in a cold November rain, Henry tells brother Charles his regiment may see a battle before winter — and recounts the night the whole brigade was formed in line of battle and marched toward the river on a false report that the rebels were crossing. Between the soldiering he sends $20 home by express, registers quiet shock at Albert Savage's death, and asks that Mother be told her preserves arrived safely.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 15, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Charles:

As I have a little leisure I thought I would write a few lines. It is cold enough today to wear overcoats. We cannot have much pleasant weather now. It rained all last night. The mud is not so deep here as it is at Champlain when it rains. The soil here is sandy, some of it has a redish color.

I have sent home $20.00 by express. I put it in a letter and directed it to Mother, and then gave it to the Adjutant. He is going to Washington today or tomorrow and will there send it by express. I thought that was the safest way to send it. Please be on the lookout and see that mine is not lost. I suppose the package will be sent either to B. Moore or G. Dunning.

I am glad to know that we own 100 acres near Reiders, as the sugar bush is so far away, 50 acres is enough off there. So Silas and Sid are selling more land. They had better look out or they will want money one of these days.

I cannot tell now where our Regt. will go for winter quarters. We may see a battle before winter. I heard last night that there were five Regts. of the rebels in Georgia that resigned because they could not get their pay and could not get enough to eat. Uncle Sam takes care of his soldiers very well. We have plenty to eat and of the right sort. We have bread every two days. The rest of the time we have crackers. Have very good meta, fresh meat now and then.

The other night our Regt. and the other Regts. were formed in line of battle, and ready to go down to the river, as the e was a report that the rebles were crossing the river, but it was not so. We are liable to be called up any night. We have four in our tent. Pretty well filled up. We have new blankets, very heavy. Sleep quite warm nights.

I am surprised to hear of Albert Savage's death. His father must feel very bad. I have nothing more to write now. When you write, please write all the news. I like to hear of my friends.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

Nov. 16th — I thought I would add a few lines before I seal this up. Last night it froze one or two inches. Quite cold this morning. Very hard wind. My money will not go to Washington till Monday. I suppose it will be about three days going to Champlain from Washington. Tell Mother that those preserves went very well. I fold this letter this way because it is so large. I am going to try and get a pass and go to Poolsville Monday.

movements.sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his brother James of a drunken Confederate deserter who paddled a half-swamped boat across the Potomac to surrender to Henry's twelve-man picket post — cursing the sentries as "sons of biches" when they demanded the countersign, then refusing to go back when the rebels called him the next morning. Henry kept two rebel gun caps as souvenirs; Lt. Scott paid five dollars for the deserter's knife.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 30, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear James:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. I should like it if you would write often. I must tell you what news I can. When our company was on picket a secesh or reble came across the river, near our post. He came over as a deserter, had a very small boat. It was most full of water when he got over. He had a very fine gun and a large knife with him. We heard him paddling the water some time before he came across. There were twelve of us on post. We all had our guns loaded and our bayonets fixed for we did not know but what there was a large force of them. When he was nearly over we halted him and demanded the countersign, but he called us all sons of biches. He had been taking a drop before he came over. The rebles, next morning, wanted him to go back, but he would not. We can see the rebles quite plainly in the day time. They have fires all along the river at night. It is against the orders to talk with the rebles across the river.

I have got two secesh caps, those that they use for "Guns". Lt. Scott bought a large knife that the rebles brought over. He bought it for five dollars. He bought it for a curiosity to show when he goes home what the rebles use in war. No more this time.

I remain, your aff. Brother,

Henry.

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry sketches his brigade's order of battle: three New York regiments including the 2nd, the Minnesota regiment, and his own 34th NY, all drilling together two or three times a week under General Gorman. He has shaken off a bout of homesickness and gently corrects the rumors reaching home that his company has suffered — "It is not correct" — admitting only one hard stretch in Virginia.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 30th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. I have been a little homesick lately, but I have got over it. I see you are forming plans for me when I go home. I hope they will turn out good. I should not wonder but they will, I hope so.

I saw Brink not long since, said he had received a letter from you, seemed to be in good humor. I have not continued my Journals. Have not had much time. Shall continue them next week. Our Company have all got new blankets, very heavy and good.

In regard to our Company suffering so mucy. It is not correct. There was one time in Virginia we had a pretty hard time, but that was all. We have a brigade drill two or three times a week, three Regts. of New York 2d and the Minnesota, besides ours. Gorman is General. I have nothing more to write at present. Write often.

I remain your aff. brother,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan in cold so sharp he can scarcely hold his pen, Henry begs his worrying mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease," reports he stands third or fourth in the furlough queue, and came off picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock. He confesses he sometimes thinks he "did wrong to leave home" with the farm needing him that winter, yet pledges that "when I do get home I shall stay."
movements.transcription:
Nov. 30, 1861

Dear Mother:

I received your letter last eve. It is so cold now that I can not write very good, but I shall do the best I can. I am sorry to know that you have been worrying about me. You must not. If I am sick I shall let you know, you must let your mind rest at perfect ease about me. I admit we suffer with the cold some, but that cannot be helped. Some of the boys have fireplaces in their tents and others have stoves. Have not any in our tent. The stoves cost between three and four dollars. When we go into winter quarters we shall probably have log houses, but we shall have to build them.

I received two papers from home, one was the Observer and the other, New York Times. Very glad to receive them. In regard to my having a furlough to go home. I do not think I can get one at present. There are three or four before me now. I understand that two can only go at one time. I should like to go home if I could. The war may be over before I go. I hope it may. I came off from picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock in the afternoon.

I am, of course, perfectly willing to pay my portion in regard to the taxes, or anything else. Very glad to do so. I had my picture taken, but could not get it standing. It cost me a dollar, the case and all. You wrote about sending me some mittens, but if I had a pair of woolen gloves they would be very acceptable. I bought a pr. of buckskin, but they are not very warm.

I sometimes think that I did wrong to leave home, knowing that you will need me this winter, but when I do get home I shall stay. I think that you got along very well last summer in regard to farming. That is, I think the boys worked it very well although the crops did not turn out very well.

I have no more time to write now. More next time. Write often.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Alexander's first army pay reaches Camp Jackson — and he sends fifteen of his seventeen dollars home, half-joking he'll have his Mother "courtmartialed" if she won't buy herself a warm winter cloak. He recounts a sentry's rifle going off on the picket bridge, taking off a man's thumb, and now cautions his own reliefs to carry their arms with care. He clings to the verse Frances wrote in his Bible — "God is our refuge and strength."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 8, 1861
Camp Jackson

My Dear Mother:

Don't you think I was glad to hear from home, eh? Why when I received those four letters I hardly knew whether I was on my head or feet. You wish me to acknowledge all the letters that I receive. I have received one mailed Nov. 18, another Nov. 6th. (I believe the figures are not very plain.) Another Dec. 3 and one from Henry mailed Dec. 4. I have not received any papers as yet. I never enjoyed anything more than the reading of those letters.

We received our pay last Friday morning up to the first of November. I received seventeen dollars and thirty-three cents. I have sent home fifteen dollars. The Capt. sends it for me. He sends it to George Dunning. Dunning will pay it over to you as soon as he received it. Now, my dear Mother, I give it all to you. This is the first time that I have been able to make my Mother a present and I want you to take it. If you do not I shall feel very, very bad. I want you to buy you a nice warm cloak for winter or else a warm woolen dress and a warm pair of gaiters. Now if you disobey my orders I shall feel very much like having you courtmartialed. It is rather a bad thing to fall into the hands of such a court. You had not better disobey. I give you fair warning.

Quite a sad accident happened night before last. (Luther and I were on guard duty). David Dava[?]way, one of the pickets on a bridge a little below the camp, while stepping off from a wall, in some way stumbled and dropt his rifle. He endeavored to catch the piece with his right hand, but before he could do so it struck against a stone and went off. The ball passed through his right thumb between the first and second joints and almost graised his head. His thumb was taken off. He will be discharged. When I go out with my reliefs, I am oblige to caution the men with "men be careful how you carry your rifles". They sometimes carry them very carelessly. Tell Frances I shall never forget the text she wrote in my bible, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." He is such indeed to me. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

Dec. 9 — We are now having very warm weather. The weather today promises to be quite sultry. I was really uncomfortable yesterday on account of the heat. Luther and I are on guard duty today. Send me papers as often as you can. We have nothing to read here. Tell Frances I will write her soon. I shall give you the direction again for fear that you will forget them. Direct to Baltimore, Md. Sixtieth Regt. N.Y. S. A. Co. H, care of Capt. Ransom.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P.S. You ask me in one of your letters "how I like soldiering" and to be candid xxxx about it, I like it very well. Mother, I am dependent on no one. That is a great comfort to me. I shall try and get a pass tomorrow to go to Baltimore and have my miniature taken.
movements.notes: Two-part: Dec 8, continued Dec 9. **Confirms Alexander in Co. H, 60th NY**

movements.letterExcerpt: I have at length heard from home. Four letters all in a bunch. Doing pretty well — don't you think so? I feel about five hundred per cent better. You have no idea how much good they have done me. It t...
movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from Camp Jackson, near Baltimore, having finally received four home letters in a bunch — "I feel about five hundred per cent better" — after a lost knapsack swallowed his earlier letter and writing materials. At Charley's request he sketches camp life minute by minute, from the half-past-five reveille to the day's rations of bread, beef, and green coffee. Then he turns urgent: James must never give up the idea of an education — "Never — never, never."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 8, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Brother:

I have at length heard from home. Four letters all in a bunch. Doing pretty well — don't you think so? I feel about five hundred per cent better. You have no idea how much good they have done me. It took me nearly two hours to read them all. It seems to me that I never spent that space of time so pleasantly before.

So you thought I had forgotten you all at home. Well, well, well, I thought you knew me better than that, but then I don't wonder at it. It was no fault of mine that you did not hear from me sooner. You may be sure of that. I began a letter when we were at Kalarama Heights. When we arrived at Camp Jackson it was quite late in the evening. We were obliged to stack our arms and knapsacks prior to pitching our tents. I was detailed for guard duty that night, and Luther as one of an escort to the Major as he was oblige to go back to the Relay House on business — so that I had no one to look after my knapsack. A sergeant in Company C took it by mistake and I did not find it until quite a number of days afterward. The letter and my writing materials were in it. Now you see that I was not to blame.

Charley in his letter (how I should like to see him) asks me to "write all the minute details of my life" in Camp. I will do my best. Reveille beats at half-past five. As soon as I hear the drum (almost the first tap wakes me) I spring up, put my cap, jacket and shoes on (I generally sleep with them off) turn out and fall into line. We are allowed only five minutes to do all this in. At the expiration of the five minutes the Orderly proceeds to call the roll. If any are absent they are placed on guard duty with their knapsacks on. It is no small thing to carry a knapsack for seventy-four hours.

After roll call one of the men from our tent goes to the Commissaries and draws the ration for the tent. (one loaf of bread, one and a fourth pounds of beef or three fourths of a pound of pork or bacon per each man, and a certain amount of sugar and rice or hominy or potatoes and some tea. We also have coffee, but as it is green it is not served out to the company. We then set to work to get breakfast (except the Commissary (he tents with us) and those on guard duty.) Some get the water, another cooks the meat, another makes the tea, etc., etc., etc. We get along "first rate". At half past eight comes guard mounting. It would take up too much room to tell you how it is done. I will finish the synopsys of the day in another letter as I have not much more room.

I am very glad to hear that you are to attend Mr. Partridges convention. Improve your time. Learn all you can. Now James, don't you never give up the idea of getting an education. Never — never, never. Don't be discouraged. You CAN do it if you have health. Now you must not be vexed at me for saying what I have, a little fellow like me. I feel very anxious that you should do well. If my life is spared, when I return won't I put in, eh?

I understand from one of the letters that you could have had the position of Orderly Sergeant if you could have got five men. I was almost sorry at first that you did not accept of it, but on reflection I think you have done well. You now stand a chance of getting into West Point, whereas if you had enlisted that is forever done for besides to take three or even two years out of your life now, would make it useless to try to get an education. There I am talking like an old man, well, well, well, what next.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: His furious sketch of a Baltimore swindle: Alexander tells Mother two "pictures" cost thirteen shillings, lamenting "that which is dearly bought is apt to be prized." The first portrait so enraged him he "felt like making a bayonet charge upon the one who took it," vowing a better likeness "if it costs me fifty dollars." The joint photograph with Luther he asks her to hide away and show no one — "a memorial of our soldiering together."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 11th, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Mother:

Here is my "picture." Luther and I were at Baltimore yesterday and had them taken. I was badly cheated on account of my inexperience in such things. Those two "pictures" cost thirteen shillings. That which id dearly bought is apt to be prized. I shall profit by this experience. The picture in which Luther and I are taken cost ten shillings. When that picture was given to me I felt like making a bayonet charge upon the one who took it. I said to myself "I cannot and will not send home that picture. I will have another taken if it costs me fifty dollars." I went to another gallery and had the other taken which cost three shillings. If you think it is worth it you had better have it put in a case as it is easily spoilt. The other picture I want you to put safely away in some drawer and show it to no one. The only reason why I send it is I want to keep it as a memorial of our soldiering together.

My dear Mother, will you be so kind as to send me some postage stamps. I will refund the money to you next pay day. I feel bad to think I have spent so much money. I want to be very economical. I am enjoying excellent health. The weather has been very warm and pleasant. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander.

movements.letterExcerpt: I wonder what sort of weather you are having up there. Pretty cold I guess, eh? The weather here is warm and sunshiney — very much like our September weather.
movements.sigSummary: Capt. Ransom climbs aboard a passing freight train during the "Grand Rounds" near Camp Jackson — and survives a boiler explosion that kills everyone else on the engine. Alexander gives his sister Frances a harrowing, almost forensic account: the engineer hurled hundreds of feet through a tree, the iron dome flung thirty rods, the fireman left burning in a ditch until Ransom puts out the flames with his bare hands. Not even a scratch on him.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 16, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Sister:

I wonder what sort of weather you are having up there. Pretty cold I guess, eh? The weather here is warm and sunshiney — very much like our September weather.

We came very near losing our Captain the other night but then "an inch of a miss", you know, "is as good as a mile." I feel very, very thankful that his life was spared to the Company. I hardly think his place could have been filled. The Major paid him quite a compliment the other day. He said to the Company "You have a good Capt." and that was a great deal for him.

Now I suppose you would like to hear how Capt. Ransom came so near losing his life. It was about as narrow an escape as I ever heard of. The only marvel is that he is now living. I can almost hear you say, "Out with it you provoking boy." Well, "here goes". The Capt. was going the "Grand Rounds". One of the officers is obliged to go over the line every night between the hours of one and six to see that the sentries are awake on their posts doing their duty and are properly instructed. This is called the "Grand Rounds". A freight train just then passed and as it was going slow he jumped on to ride out to one of the pickets about a quarter of a mile distant. (The freight engines on this road are different from those up North. They are fed with coal. The cabin is directly over the boiler which extends back so that the fireman standing upon a platform of the tender (which is open in front) is able to shovel coal into it. The Capt. stood upon the platform with the fireman. He (the fireman) had just commenced "firing up" when the boiler burst blowing the engineer, I presume, two or three hundred feet into the air. In his descent he fell through a tree breaking a limb about three inches in thickness, and on xxxx striking the ground he bounded and fell some fifteen or twenty feet from where he first struck. The Capt. stood still for a moment "thunder struck" I suppose when it occurred to him that the cars might come pileing one upon another, as they had been under some headway. He stepped off and started to go up the bank (about twenty feet in heighth.) When about half way up the body of a soldier (Haine, I believe) fell close beside him and pieces of the wreck all around him. If some of those large pieces had struck him they would have killed him instantly. The dome (weighing I should judge a ton perhaps, two, three or four) was thrown some thirty rods from the engine. The engineer was thrown about twenty-five rods. You can have some idea how high the men were thrown from the time it took them to fall.

The Capt. soon heard some one calling for help and immediately went in search of him. He found the fireman on fire and extinguished the fire by throwing water upon him from the ditch with his hands. The fireman died a day or two after. The Capt. is the only one that escaped alive of those upon the engine. He did not receive even a scratch. The fireman was so badly burned that he died, and Capt. Ransom standing beside him not even scratched. We certainly have great reason to be thankful.

Now, Miss Fannie, I want you to write me often — very often — once a week certainly. You tell James and Charles if they don't write me more often I will pull their ears for them when I get home. I certainly shall and they may look out for their noses, too. I have received four papers and letter dated Dec. 9 since I last wrote. You would never neglect writing me if you knew how much good that letter did me. Do not forget to send me some postage stamps to frank our letters. The ladies of Chazy are making up a box to send to those in the Company who came from there. I wish the ladies of Champlain would follow their example. Some warm woolen gloves would be very acceptable indeed.

Mr. Luther wrote Amos for a list of the names of those who came from Chaney. I do not have many idle moments. I am on guard duty tomorrow if all is well. I was up to Baltimore yesterday to church. I will tell you about it in another letter. I have sent my "picture" home. I will let you and Mother settle which shall have it. Capt. Ransom was very, very, very, very kind to me when I was sick. He came often to see me and brought me toast and tea a number of times. I wish Mother would write him a note. It would please him. Love to all.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander.

P.S. I see by the papers that there is danger of war with England. Let her come, I am as ready to fight Britons as Southerners. If she does interfere I hope my brothers and every other able bodied man will turn out and help us fight. I hope our regiment will be sent up the frontier.
movements.notes: Two-page letter with P.S. referencing Trent Affair

movements.sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, two days before Christmas, Henry expects the 34th New York to settle into winter quarters guarding the Potomac — the Minnesota regiments are raising log houses and his own regiment is building a hospital, signs enough that "this looks somewhat like staying." He watches discipline tighten: the old sutler drummed out for selling liquor, gamblers made to stand on a barrel six hours without food. Still unable to reach his brother Alexander, he confesses he gets very lonesome now and then.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 19th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Chas:

I received a letter from you and also two papers. We are having very fine weather for this time of the year. Our Co. came off from picket yesterday. The probability is now that our Regt. will stay here for winter quarters to guard the Potomac. That is what I heard. The Minnesota Regts. are fixing up for winter, building log houses. Our Regt. is also building a hospital. This looks somewhat like staying.

You wished to know who tents with me. They ar strangers to me. E. Graves from Chasy and John Green and A. Perkins. Pleasant fellows, but I would rather tent with some of the Champlain boys, but the tents are all full. I get very lonesome now and then. I go on line guard every week. We have three drills every day besides dress parade. We have also three Brigade drills every week. Three Regts. besides our march in line of battle, etc., etc. The old sutler was drumed out of Camp yesterday for selling licor, good for him, but some of the boys don't like it. We have one sutler in our Camp now. I have not got any tickets from him since pay day nor do I intend to. He charges to much. The boys cannot get anything to drink but cider now.

I am much oblige to you for sending me some of my money. I am not shure that I will get a pr. of boots. If I do not I think I will not use the money. In regard to sending money home — I paid 31 cts. freight. After this I shall send home my money in a letter. It is about as safe. I have not heard from Alexander yet. I have written him, but it seems that the direction is not correct. I shall write him soon. So far as I know the boys from Champlain like soldiering very well. Col. L--- has resigned so I have heard. Good many of the boys thought he was a coward. He has a very good voice. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx A good many of the boys pass away there time by playing cards, but I have not learned yet. If they are caught at it they are severely punished. Some of our Regt. were caught gambling the other night. They will have to stand on a barrel six hours without any food and four dollars taken off their wages. Write often. I am your aff. Brother,

Henry
