movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry reports eight rebels crossing the lines as deserters with word that the enemy "have nothing to eat" — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac. With little else to tell in the sameness of winter quarters, he confesses the cold has stopped his journal, a thing he'll be sorry for if he gets home, and admits he'd give much to be back for the village sing school.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 20th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

I send this letter by B. Miner. He starts tomorrow morning for Champlain. I gave him my other letter also. The reason why I did not write to you before is because I had nothing to write about. Everything goes on here about the same from day to day. I have got an accordian. Bill Robers offered to learn me how to play on it. I have not made much progress yet, but I will after a while. You know how I play the violin. I have not continued my journal any since it has been so cold. That is one thing I shall be sorry for if I ever get home. I heard through one of the boys from Champlain that they had a sing school there, I should like to attend if I was at home. Albert has been home and had a fine time sleigh riding as I heard. To day eight rebels came across to our side as deserters. They say the rebels have nothing to eat. We went to church today — Capt. Rich preached. Poolesville is about three miles from our camp. Write often.

I am your aff. Brother,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: We have had a Brigade drill today. Gen. Gorman told our Regiment that they did the best of them all. We felt quite proud, I tell you. I have found a dictionary here. Some of the boys bought one in Was...
movements.sigSummary: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry writes home with a soldier's pride: at brigade drill, Gen. Gorman told the regiment "they did the best of them all" — "we felt quite proud, I tell you." Yet he still cannot reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington on a direction now proving wrong: "It seems bad that we cannot correspond." Unsettled by the swearing and gambling around him, Henry insists a man keeps good morals in camp only if "very strict and firm."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 20th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

We have had a Brigade drill today. Gen. Gorman told our Regiment that they did the best of them all. We felt quite proud, I tell you. I have found a dictionary here. Some of the boys bought one in Washington. I think I shall buy one and send home. It is a very good one. I have written to Alex, but directed to Washington, that was the direction he gave me. I have not heard from him. We hear that Washington is the wrong direction. I do not know his Regt. I shall write again soon. It seems bad that we cannot correspond. A man cannot live in Camp and maintain good morals unless he is very strict and firm. There is so much swearing and gambling that it is enough to ruin any young man. Four men in our company were caught playing cards the other night. They will have to stand on a barrel six hours and two or four dollars taken from their wages. A man in the Minnesota Regt. shot himself through the arm the other day accidentally. How it was done I have not learned. I am well and hope this will find you the same. Write often.

I am your aff. son,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: You perceive by the heading of my letter that we have moved camp. Colonel Hayward being dissatisfied with the conduct of Company C and as Company H had the reputation of being the best, or at least on...
movements.sigSummary: Company H, singled out as one of the best in the regiment, is pulled by Colonel Hayward into Baltimore to replace Company C guarding Camden Station, the Baltimore & Ohio depot. Alexander writes from a three-story brick building where five tentmates sing and brew tea on the Captain's stove. Promoted from seventh to fourth Corporal in three months, he still grumbles, playfully: a soldier who writes twice to their once, and feels neglected.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 22, 1861
Baltimore

My dear Brother:

You perceive by the heading of my letter that we have moved camp. Colonel Hayward being dissatisfied with the conduct of Company C and as Company H had the reputation of being the best, or at least one of the best "companies" in the Regt. he ordered us to take their place. We are quartered in a three story brick building on the outskirts of the City and are guarding a branch railway about three miles in length running from the main road (Baltimore and Ohio) to another end of the city. The depot is called the Camden Station. Luther and I have a first rate room. Five others "tent" with us. One of us are singing — others writing. We make music. It is almost time to get supper. Now I suppose you would like to know how we will go to work to "get it". Well, in the first place we fill our "mess pan" with water. In the next place we put it on the stove (we have the Captains), in the third we put some tea or coffe in it and let it boil, and in the fourth place we put in some sugar and drink it. We sometimes cook beef or port. One of our men says he will get some cabbage tonight for soup tomorrow.

Now, Master James, you must excuse this wandering, disconnected letter. We have been singing and sometimes when I was in the midst of a sentence I would "pitch in". You know that two things can not be done at once and be done well. Don't you think my excuse good — eh? I have been holding an indignation meeting with myself. Why don't you all write me more often. I — a solider — with barely any conveniences write twice to your once. Now — I feel really neglected — yes, neglected. Ask Mother and Frances and Charles and yourself if you have forgotten me. I received two papers yesterday. Don't forget to send some postage stamps. I have risen three grades. When I left the North I was seventh Corporal. I am now fourth. Luther has also risen three grades. He was eighth and is now fifth. Love to all.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alexander

P.S. Has Mother received that fifteen dollars I sent her and my miniature?

movements.letterExcerpt: I have received a letter from you today and very glad I was to hear that you are all so well. Your letter contains some strange news — very strange. Champlain again to be occupied by United States tro...
movements.sigSummary: Preston King is in Baltimore, Alexander reports, "trying to have the Regiment sent North to guard the frontiers" — and so, the corporal hints, he may be home sooner than expected. Yet his Christmas turns wistful: "I a soldier hundreds of miles from home! How funny, eh?" He delights that the white cow has a new "bossy," marches seven men out to relieve the pickets, and adds that Mason and "Stidell" have reportedly been released.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 23, 1861
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

I have received a letter from you today and very glad I was to hear that you are all so well. Your letter contains some strange news — very strange. Champlain again to be occupied by United States troops — well — well — well. What next? "Stranger things have happened." I will not tell you something about as strange. I may be home a little sooner than you expected. Preston King is here it is said trying to have the Regiment sent North to guard the frontiers.

Dec. 25. Christmas is it? So it is. I a soldier hundreds of miles from home! How funny, eh? Luther and I were out in the City yesterday. Baltimore is quite a city. There is no lack of "darkies" here. I wonder what you are doing up there today! How I should like to be with you all today, but then there is no use in wishing. It cannot be. I feel rather lonely today. You have no idea how much good your letters did me. I was particularly pleased to hear that the "white cow" had a little "bossy". I should indeed like to be at home to enjoy the "new milk cow". I should like to return and see you all, nevertheless I am very well contented where I am.

Dec. 23, 1861 — Contd.

You tell James that I do not doubt his good intentions, but if he waits until vacation to write I am afraid that letter never will be forthcoming.

Dec. 26. Luther, Orderly Dickinson, I and three others were out in the city. We went into an eating saloon and got dinner. It cost me a quarter. I find the only place to get a Christmas dinner is at home. I also find that it does not pay to get dinner in these eating saloons. I am on guard duty today. At one oclock I have a relief of seven men to take out to relieve the pickets along the line (about two miles.) Now you have some idea of the duties of a Corporal.

Love to all. Give my respects to Mr. Copeland. I have written grandmother McNiel.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander.

P.S. It is reported that Mason and Stidell have been released.
movements.notes: Multi-part: Dec 23, continued Dec 25, continued Dec 26

movements.letterExcerpt: I received a letter from you Christmas Eve. Glad to know that you are all well. We are having cold weather, but no snow. Our Co. came off from picket this morning, was on for twenty-four hours. Went o...
movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from his brother Alexander — the letter found him despite a direction "not quite correct" — and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between buying a $3.50 sheet-iron stove against the cold and a promise to send $25 home next pay day, Henry sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 26, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you Christmas Eve. Glad to know that you are all well. We are having cold weather, but no snow. Our Co. came off from picket this morning, was on for twenty-four hours. Went on Christmas morning.

Dec. 27th. Today is quite warm from what it has been. I have bought a stove for our tent. It cost $3.50. I advanced the money. It was so cold that I could not get along without it. The stove is made of sheet iron. There will be twenty-one shillings coming to me for the stove next pay day. It cost seven shillings apiece for four of us. I shall try to send home next pay day $25.00. We get paid off by the 15th of Jan. We are having barracks built for our Regt. There are so many men detailed for making them, but I have not been yet. They get extra pay for it. The soldiers do all the wood cutting. The teamsters draw it. It takes a great quantity to supply the Regt.

We have the same Chaplain now that we had at first. Have a prayer meeting every Sunday evening, but I have not been yet, for it so happened, that most every Sabbath I have been on guard. There is not much of any Sabbath here.

I find our stove very comfortable. You need have no fear but what I shall get my money back. I have received a letter from Alex. He seems to like soldiering very well. He has received that letter I wrote him although the direction was not quite correct. He wrote that Capt. Ransom had a narrow escape. I suppose he has written you all about it. I have not much of news to write you. You get it up North faster than we do. I hope Silas will get that accordian. I shall be very careful of it.

I have nothing more to write. I shall be more careful after this and not have so much bad spelling. Sometimes I have to write in a hurry and do not take so much pains as I might or as I should. We have in our Camp a man who takes pictures. He has got the whole rigging.

I do my own washing every week and try to keep myself as clean as I can. Most all the soldiers do their washing. Last summer I washed in cold water, but now I have it warmed.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry
movements.notes: Two-part: Dec 26, continued Dec 27

movements.letterExcerpt: You tell Frances that I shall not write her again until she writes me. That I am really provoked with her. I have received two letters from home within a few days and not a word or message did she wri...
movements.sigSummary: At Camp Jackson the sentinel's challenge ran word for word — "Number ### — Advance" — and after three unheeded halts at night, each guard fired his piece to alarm the camp. Writing from Baltimore, Alexander sets down a corporal's day with an ethnographer's care: two-hour relief rotations, a king's-worthy kettle of beef, pared potatoes and cabbage, his own long vigils by the fire. On New Year's morning he pictures James reading the January Harper's at home.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 29, 1861
Baltimore

My dear Brother:

You tell Frances that I shall not write her again until she writes me. That I am really provoked with her. I have received two letters from home within a few days and not a word or message did she write or send. You are nearly — yes — just as bad. Now do you both "mend your ways". I shall have you both "hauled up" before a "Court of Inquiry" if you dont look out.

I began a "Synopsis of a day in Camp" in a letter to James. I shall now try and finish it in this. I believe I left off at "Guard Mounting". That interesting ceremony sometimes comes off (always at half past eight, before some of the men have finished or even began breakfast. If they are on the "first relief" they are immediately marched off to their posts and are obliged to stand there until eleven. You see this has a tendency to make the men prompt and smart "right up the handle" as the soldiers say. (Whenever this is the case the men usually before going out catch up a piece of bread and run).

I shall try and get a pass and attend service this evening. I have attended once today.

Dec. 30. I attended service again last evening. It seemed like old times. I enjoyed the singing very much. This love of singing seems to be a perfect passion with the soldiers. The church has a very fine organ. I am wandering from my story.

If I am on guard duty I am obliged to take out a part of the relief guard in one direction and the other Corporal in another and the Sergeant places the remainder around the Camp. (I am now speaking as though I were at Camp Jackson.) (I presume you would like to know what orders the sentinels have.) When within six paces of a sentinel I halt the "relief" and command "Number ### — Advance". He advances up to the sentinel and both stand at "arms apart". The sentinel then proceeds to give his orders "I am ordered to guard this road from — to —, to let no one meddle in anyway with the track or wires except those working on the road, and keep a sharp lookout on them. Halt every soldier that comes along and demand a pass. If he has none, take him prisoner and hand him over to the next sentinel. (Thus you see that he could be passed down to Camp without the sentinel leaving his post. "Arrest any person that you may think suspicious. You need not (a sentinel is now "calling" Corporal of the No. 1) stop commissioned officers". The relieved sentinel then falls in the rear and the relief proceeds. The night is the hardest part of the guard duty. At night the orders to the sentinels are the same as in the day time with the exception that they halt every one the comes along when within gun shot. If any one does not stop after being halted three times by the sentinel, he is fired upon. Each sentinel in succession discharges his piece and thus the Camp is alarmed. The Guard is immediately drawn up at a distance from the fire and a reconnoitering party is then sent out to ascertain what is the matter.

As I have said above, the night is the hardest part of it. All the shelter we have is a small tent capable of holding four or five men. The remainder of the Guard "camped down" around the fire. I generally sat up by the fire all night. Sometimes I would take my blanket and stretch out on the ground. Many a night when you have been sleeping comfortably in your bed have I been keeping my vigils by the guard fire. Every two hours the relief is called out. I take my men go out and relieve the sentinel, return and sit by the fire until the next two hours and thus it continues through the night.

At nine A.M the old Guard is marched out to discharge their guns. We sometimes fire in a volley, sometimes by file, and sometimes at a target. Those not on guard cook for those on.

(I will now take a day when I am not on guard and try and give you an account of how I spend my time. I have already in a former letter described how the morning is passed. I believe I omitted one thing. Before (sometimes not till after) breakfast I take a towel and soap and go down to the brook which runs through our Camp and have a "good wash". It is really refreshing. I feel like taking half-a-dozen "somersets" after it. After breakfast I usually take out my rifle (these tents are a great place to rest them) clean and oil it up nicely. If I did not do this it would soon get so rusty that there would be no doing anything with it.

I will now suppose that beef was served out in our days rations and that we had cut all the meat off down to the bone and cooked it for breakfast. I now take a "camp kettle". Fill it two thirds full of water, hang it over the fire, put in the beef, potatoes (pared) and cabbage (if I can get it) and let it boil about an hour. I then season it with salt and pepper if it is to be had. That is soup fit for a king to eat. At least you would think so from the way we all pitched into it. For supper we usually make some tea and sometimes cook a little hominy or rice. Sometimes Luther and I would get a pass and go up town. Sometimes I would stretch out in my tent and go to sleep (after I had been all night and the previous day on guard duty.

At 4 P.M. all not on guard duty are obliged to go out and drill. If any are absent they are placed on guard duty next day with a knapsack of twenty-five, thirty and thirty-five pounds weight. As I have said before I do not have many idle moments. I hate a lazy man. I have quite a number of letters generally to write. It is now late and I have no more time to write. You must excuse this disconnected letter.

Well, my man, you have just saved yourself from the clutches of the law. I have received a letter from you today. So Frances is really going to Canada. I am glad for her sake and sorry for Mothers. How pleasant it must be at home this winter. As quiet up there as though there were no war. Cars are passing here continually loaded with cannon gun carriages, hay, flour, pork, beef, etc, etc, etc. Large numbers of troops pass almost every day though not so large as when we first came on the road. We are, I understand, to be mustered in for pay tomorrow. We are to be inspected I believe at the same time by the Inspector General. New clothes will soon be given us.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander.

P.S. I have received three letters from home within the last few days and one from Jerseyville. I have also received two papers, one Evangelist and one New York Times. Love to al and especially to Mother.

Dec. 31, 1861. 6½ A.M. You mention in your letter that on going home you "found James reading the January Harper and Mother and Frances talking". How pleasant and cozy that must have been. How I should like to be at home one of these long winter evenings. Wouldn't I have a jolly time, eh? In case of Englands interference I hardly ever expect to see home. I shall never lay down my arms until peace is restored. I hope you and James will show your "pluck" by joining the army, if there be a necessity. I have no more time.

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from Baltimore on New Year's Day, 1862, exhausted from a night's guard duty as the city's revelers "made quite a racket" — but proud to report his warrant as a non-commissioned officer, a corporal's equivalent of an officer's commission. He quotes its grand opening verbatim: "Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence... in Alexander F. Hubbell." Tired and "really ashamed" of the brief note, he still thanks the family for the welcome postage stamps.
movements.transcription:
January 1st, 1862
Baltimore

A happy New Year to you all:

The holidays are great days down here. The Baltimoreans made quite a racket last night. I was on guard duty and heard it all. I just write this to let you know that I am in the land of the living. I am enjoying excellent health and spirits. I received my warrant today. Each non-commissioned is obliged to have one of these. It is the same to them as a commissioned officers Commission. Mine runs in this wise "Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence in the patriotism, valor, fidelity and abilities of Alexander F. Hubbell I do hereby appoint him, etc."

I Have received all the letters and papers you have sent me I think. Those postage stamps were especially welcome. Now you must excuse this note. I feel really ashamed of it.

I again wish you a happy New Year. I do not feel very bright after my yesterdays guard duty. Ask Mr. Copeland to write me. I feel almost afraid to write him first. I promise I will answer promptly. I should like to hear from my Minister very much. Please excuse this.

Yours affectionately,

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan after a New Year's of beer "from the Capt." and a few boys gone too drunk, Henry tells his mother his company has presented Capt. Reich a $125 sword — he gave a dollar on a private's pay, "some gave more and some less." The Minnesota band played most all night before the Colonel's tent. He longs for a furlough, but only married men may go, so he waits — lonesome for letters and the box of socks still stuck in Washington.
movements.transcription:
January 9th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. Glad to know that you are all well. If you are sick I want you should write and let me know. Brink said he had a very pleasant visit in Champlain, only his visit was not long enough. I should like to get a furlough and make a visit home, but I do not think I could, for I understand that only the married men can go at present. I shall have to make up my mind to wait another time.

We are having very pleasant weather now. We had some snow, but it is all off. New Years was quite a merry time with some of the boys. We all received a good glass of beer from the Capt. Some of the boys got drunk, or drank a little more than was necessary. Our Company has presented Capt. Reich with a very nice sword. I gave a dollar towards it. Some gave more and some less. The sword cost $125. It is a very handsome sword.

The Minnesota band played most all night New Years. They came over into our Camp and played some very good tunes before the Colonel's tent. The box of socks has not arrived yet. I expect the box is in Washington.

I have nothing more to write at present. Write often. I get very lonesome if I do not get a paper or something else to read. Excuse this writing.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

P.S. Capt. Reich brother is in as sutler for this Regt.

movements.sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, Henry adds a few lines to his sister Frances and admits he has burned every letter he received from home: they took up too much room in his knapsack, and he did not want them on him "if I should go over into Virginia." Then his postscript turns the request around — "Please burn all my letters." He closes glad, for her sake, that she is going to teach in Montreal this winter — a quiet aside beside a plea that, obeyed, would have erased this entire correspondence.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 9th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

As I was writing to Mother I though I would add a few lines to you. Jan. 10th: It is very warm and pleasant today and very (??). It can not last long. I burnt all the letters that I received from home. They took up to much room in my knap-sack. Besides if I should go over into Virginia I should not want all of those letters with me. I received a letter from Nellie and Aunt Laura. I am glad for your sake that you are going to teach in Montreal this winter.

Please excuse this writing and all mistakes. I have forgot all about the Journal. I do not think I can make it very interesting. I hope to write another and a longer letter next time.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

P.S. Please burn all my letters.
movements.notes: Two-part: Jan 9, continued Jan 10

movements.letterExcerpt: The mail has arrived and no letter. What is the matter? The last letter I received from you is dated "Dec. 20". I received one from Charles dated "Dec. 22". That is the last I have received from home....
movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes home from Baltimore, frantic that no letter has come since December 20 — "Are you all sick or are you dead?" Then the harder news: a picket from his own Company was killed on the ninth, and he helped bring in the body, "a sight that but few of our Company could bear." He quotes Henry's New Year letter — "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living" — glad his brother "had not forgotten his God."
movements.transcription:
Jan. 13, 1862
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

The mail has arrived and no letter. What is the matter? The last letter I received from you is dated "Dec. 20". I received one from Charles dated "Dec. 22". That is the last I have received from home. What can be the reason? Are you all sick or are you dead? Something must be the matter for I know you would not forget me. What can be the matter? I am afraid you are sick. Do not keep me in suspense any longer. Let some one of the family write. Why don't Frances write and James, and Charles. Well — well — it certainly is strange. I have a great deal of news to write, but "shant" write a word until I hear from home.

One of our pickets (from our Company) was killed on the ninth of this month. I went out and helped to bring him in and saw a sight that but few of our Company could bear (I have my courage "screwed up" to almost anything). Now, my dear mother, if you want me to describe the affair, funeral and all, you must write me. (I hope to get a letter in this way). I have my letters filed, and they will show whether my friends are faithful in writing or not. I received a letter from Henry mailed on the sixth and was very glad to hear from him. He says, speaking of the New Year "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living. It matters not when we leave this world if we are only right in the sight of God." I was very glad to have him say this for it showed me he had not forgotten his God, as most in the camp seem to have done.

I have not much spirit to write. Please write soon. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: Lonely at Camden Station, Baltimore, Alexander hasn't heard from home since December 22 and conjures Champlain swept off by the Chazy River or buried in snow until "the Sixtieth" digs them out. Ordered to replace the ailing Corporal Myers, he writes now from "head quarters" in the first platoon, wonders whether to buy a revolver for hauling off armed drunken soldiers, and signs himself "Corporal A. F. Hubbell" — a precious Bible his one comfort.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 15, 1862
Camden Station
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

You have no idea how lonely I am. I have not heard from home since the twenty-second of Dec. I am imagining almost everything. Are you all sick or are you dead. Perhaps the Chay River has overflowed its banks and swept Champlain into oblivion. It may be that the earth has opened and swallowed it up. But I think the most probable thing is that you are completely buried up in the snow. If that is the case you (if such a thing be possible) had better send us a message and "the Sixtieth" will come and dig you out. But what is the use of my talking in this way. I feel very — very anxious about you all. I hope you do not suffer for want of money. I hope you will not scruple to use my money. Every cent is yours. I shall soon receive my pay (twenty six dollars.) You perceive by the heading of my letter that I have again changed my quarters. Corporal Myers was taken sick and I was ordered to take his place. So that I am now in the first platoon or in other words "at head quarters". We take our meals at the "Union Relief."

I will tell oh! so much, if you will only write. What do you think about my getting a revolver. What do you think about my getting a revolver. There is a great demand for "Corporal of the Guard with a file of men" to take drunken soldiers to the guard or station house. These soldiers often carry knives or pistols. Perhaps my bayonet will be enough. You can see what it is in my "picture."

Will you be so kind as to send me some postage stamps. I am out. I shall try and get one from the Capt. to send this letter. Perhaps the reason you do not write is that you are so busy getting Frances off that you have not time to write. My greatest fear is that you are sick. Take good care of yourself. I have no notion of coming home and not finding you there. I have got a "precious Bible" from the Clinton County Bible Society. It is a great comfort to me.

Please write soon and do not forget the stamps.

Your affectionate son,

Corporal A. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Porter has been killed upon the track. Roused from a mattress at a sick mess-mate's side, Alexander joined the squad that found him three-quarters of a mile out, "literally cut in two." Writing from Camden Station, Baltimore, he records the inquest and the funeral with a soldier's exactness — corporal and eight men, arms reversed, three volleys over the vault — then turns, stung, to defend why he enlisted: not "for the novelty," but to fight for his native land.
movements.transcription:
Jan 17, 1862.
Camden Station — Baltimore

My Dear Brother:

I received a letter from home yesterday and no one who has not been from home can imagine how glad I was to hear from there. I thought you had all forgotten me. So Frances has really gone. You must be very lonely there this winter. How I envy your long quiet pleasant evenings. What are you studying at school this winter? How do Mr. and Mrs. Dobbin get along. Any more "hair pulls" yet, eh? So Dobbin did not want his wife to eat "nasty orange peel picked off from the floor", eh? How I wish I had been there. I should have had a regular ha ha. I suppose old Dobbin would have taken my head off. How I should like to see him and Mrs. D. get into a "squabble". I should enjoy it up to ninety-nine. What am I talking about. Write me all about home matters. I feel much more interested in matters concerning the "pig", old white cow and calf, and the pony than in anything else.

Have you drawn any more beach logs this winter. Rather unprofitable business with that little "pony" I think. How has Plummer fulfilled his contract? I am afraid you will get shaved. Keep a sharp lookout on him. He will lookout for No. 1, never fear.

(Contd.)

Jan. 17, 1862 — (Contd.

Now I suppose you would like to hear about that "sad accident" that happened here some days since. I had just thrown myself down on a mattress to "snoose" a few moments (I was helping to take care of a sick mess mate) when Sergeant Finch came to the door of the Lieutenants room and roared out Lieutenant, Lieutenant, Porter has been killed upon the track. Shall I take some men and bring him in? I immediately jumped up, put on my overcoat, went down and joined the squad. We had gone about three quarters of a mile when we came upon the body. It was a heart rending sight. He lay partly under the cars and was I might say, literally cut in two as the body only hung together by the cords and muscles of the back. A large piece of his back bone was torn out and lay some distance away. A large piece of flesh lay all around. His liver and entrails were also torn out and pieces of flesh lay all around.

Jan. 21 — I will finish this narrative in another letter. I am enjoying excellent health though I have had a severe cough and cold and am not entirely over them yet. I try to obey your injunctions "to take care of my health". When I read in your letter what Brink Miner said I felt just mad enough to kick him. (Excuse me for saying it.) I wonder if he thinks every one is like him, not two seconds content in one place. I did not enlist only for the novelty of the thing as he did, but to try and take care of myself and to fight for my native land. I don't like to see a young man able to care for himself sit at home with his hands in his lap, or when he is employed to grumble, growl and fret about it, and wish himself out of it. I believe in making the best of everything. (at least I try to.) A man is a great deal happier for doing so.

I have changed my mind and think I will finish my "narrative" in this letter. It was as I have said before — a heartrending sight. The dim lantern light made it doubly so. We made a litter of boards and brought him down to camp. It was pretty tough work, as he was a very large man. We were obliged to be very careful when we lifted him on the litter he was so crushed. His body was completely crushed from the breast down, also his left arm and right leg. There was an ugly gash on his left temple. As soon as we arrived at the camp the Capt. was sent for. A room was immediately prepared and the Capt. laid him out as well as it could be done. An inquest was held next day and a verdict returned of accidental death by being run over by the cars. He was buried the day after the inquest.

Perhaps you would like to hear something about the funeral. First went a Corporal and eight men with arms reversed, next the Chaplain, next the hearse, and last the Company. The band for some reason was no there. When we arrived at the cemetery the coffin was placed in a vault and three volleys fired over it.

Good night. It is now late. Luther is snoring away like a good fellow. Write soon. Love to all. I will write about the Union Relief Association in another letter.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alexander

To James Hubbell esq.
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Multi-part: Jan 17, continued Jan 21. Lt. Porter death narrative.

movements.sigSummary: At Camden Station's Union Relief Association — sustained by private gift and government, with seats for eight hundred men and sleeping room for a regiment — Alexander Hubbell found meals that "saved the soldiers from a great deal of suffering," and writes "God bless the Association," for he had boarded there himself. Hearing brother James may win an appointment, his joy breaks loose: "Hurrah! Hurrah!" He sends home twenty dollars to fit James off.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 24, 1862
Baltimore

My dear Mother:

Wouldn't I like to be at home in your nice cozy sitting room this cold blustering evening. How pleasant it would be, wouldn't it? But here I am and here I must be. Nevertheless I am well content. Didn't you know that I am taking care of myself, eh? Luther insists on my going to bed. He says "it is bad for the health to sit up so late." Rather think so too. Good night.

Jan. 25th: I experienced this morning one of the keenest disappointments that it has ever been my lot to experience. Messrs. Hoyle and Finley left this morning without my seeing them. (Next few lines cut out.) .....

This morning our little drummer said they wished me to come up (this was near eight o'clock). I immediately went up and met the Capt. a short distance from the "quarters." He said they left in the "seven train". I felt all things. "All things" — that don't express half what I felt. I hope my dear Mother, you will tell Messrs H and F the reason why I did not see them. I am afraid they will not think I am very prompt. Luther saw them both up in the city yesterday. Well, well, "disappointment is the common lot of man." I might as well make the best of it.

I said in my last letter "I would tell you something about the 'Union Relief Association'" in my next. This Association is sustained partly by private contribution and partly by Government. Its object is to feed soldiers passing through Baltimore. I boarded there while I was at "Camden Station." They have room to seat over eight hundred men at one time and sleeping room enough for a regiment. God bless the Association. It has saved the soldiers from a great deal of suffering. I wish we had had such a place to go to when we passed through Baltimore.

Your plast two letters filled me with pleasure and anxiety. So you think James will get an appointment. Oh! I hope — I trust. I know he will pass examination. How kind Mr. Wheeler is. I should like to give him three cheers. Hurrah! Hurrah! Hur-- I shall have to wait until I get out doors.

I have not taken a glass of malt or spiritour liquor since I came in the army. I try to keep my promise to you. The Capt. sends home for me twenty dollars. Take it and fix James off with it. If he does not need it, use it yourself. You are welcome to it.

I think our Regt. will leave Baltimore soon. We are doing hard service, very hard service. Please to send me stamps (postage) from home. It is no use to get them here. They all go in no time. Don't forget to send them. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Mrs. F. A. Hubbell                Alexander.

P.S. I have bought myself a dictionary. I am very much obliged to you for your correction. I wish you would write and tell me my mistakes. Keep me posted concerning all the doings of the "Adelphic Debating Club". Tell the boys to persevere. Those meetings in the old Academy I love to think of. I am glad that "Slavery Question" has for once been rightly decided. How I should like to stand up in that old Chapel and hold forth on that subject again. How much did your pig weigh? How does the little bosey get along? How many of the hens died this winter. Now, dear Mother, don't give up housekeeping. Hire a boy. I will pay him. I expect to be home next fall if I am alive. Write often. Oh! how good it does seem to get a letter from home. I charge you again write often, write often, often.

movements.sigSummary: Paid off at Camp McClellan, Henry sends $15 home and itemizes a soldier's whole economy from $13-a-month pay — sutler, boots, a $1 sword installment, fifty cents each to the band and the cook. He turns down requests to lend money in camp: "I would rather send it home." Buoyed by the "glorious victory in Kentucky," he predicts the war will end before July, even as the unhealthy barracks are burned for firewood, leaving the men in tents for the rest of winter.
movements.transcription:
January 24th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

We have been paid off and I shall send home $15.00 this time. I should like to send more but can not very well do so. My bill to the sutler was $5.20. I bought a pr. of boots which came to $4.50 and other necessary's. Then I owe 50 cts. to the band and 50 cts. to the cook and $1.00 for the sword, so that I could not send home as much as I should like to. Next time I shall send home more. In regard to the stove, I shall have to wait till next pay day before I can get paid. I have had several applications to lend money, but I would rather send it home.

We have had pretty warm weather for the last ten days. It is beginning to grow colder now. The mud has been very deep. I hope it will freeze up.

In my last letter I wrote about getting a discharge, but I think this war will be all over before next July from what I have read in the papers and from what I have heard. It seems that we have had a glorious victory in Kentucky. With many such victory's the war can not last long. My health is pretty good now. The barracks have been taken and burnt for fire wood as it was not thought healthy to live in them. We will therefore live in our tents the rest of the winter. I do not know of naything more to write at present. McDonel is in as Corporal.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your unfinished but welcomed letter some days since and you may be sure I was glad to hear that you had not forgotten me. How do you like your new situation. I am glad you have obtained wha...
movements.sigSummary: Alexander, guarding the rails at Baltimore, looks back to see a passenger train "hardly ten feet from me" — "I gave one jump. Jump — that don't half express it." Days earlier the same cars had killed a comrade, Edwin Porter. Writing his sister in Canada, he charges her to defend the Union with her tongue if not arms: "I charge you be valiant." A near-miss told with grin and grief in the same breath.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 25, 1862
Baltimore, Md.

My dearest Sister:

I received your unfinished but welcomed letter some days since and you may be sure I was glad to hear that you had not forgotten me. How do you like your new situation. I am glad you have obtained what you have so long wished for — a situation in Canada where you may perfect yourself in the French language. How lonely, very lonely, Mother must be this winter in that great castle of a house with no one to speak to all day long, not even the old cat for company for I had her shot before I left home. I hope you will write her often. I shall try to. We must not neglect this, for she writes me .... (a portion of this letter cut out at this point.) .......

...... I heard a great roaring and rushing behind me. I looked back and saw a passenger train coming with great velocity hardly ten feet from me. The engineer just at that moment whistled an alarm. I gave one jump — Jump — that don't half express it. It was a half-down all into one. I had so little time to get out of the way that I verily believe it would almost have brushed my coat tails, if I had had them. One of our men, Edwin Porter, was killed some nights since by the cars. Mother will tell you about it.

I think our Regiment will leave Baltimore soon. I am not at all sorry. I wish we could go on some of the "naval expeditions." If we leave here I think we will be sent to Washington to garrison some of the fortifications left vacant when the grand army moves forward.

Now, Miss Fannie, you are in a land where they are not very friendly to the United States. Stand up for your country. You can use your tongue for that country if you can not take up arms in her defense. I charge you be valiant. I believe the hate towards England of 1776 has sprung up in my bosom. Please write often and do not forget to write Mother.

Your affectionate Brother

Alexander F.

Addressed to: Miss Fannie Hubbell
Longale, Canada

movements.sigSummary: Colonel Hayward's resignation has left the 60th NY styled the "Orphan Regiment," though Alexander tells his brother Charles they may be better off without a colonel, hoping new Colonel Green proves "smart and brave." Writing a little each day from Baltimore, he reports measles thinning the ranks — one man so low at the hospital he "was rolled over twice to ascertain whether he was dead or alive" — but none lost from his own well-tended Company.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 28, 1862,
Baltimore

My Dear Brother:

You seem to be the next man in the "docket" to write to. I have "come to the conclusion" that I had better try. Mothers plan to write a little every day. In that way I shall have a letter done "before I know it".

I came off guard duty this morning. When I went on yesterday morning I was what some people would say, down sick with a cold. I feel much better this morning, and it is "my experience" that the best way is, to do your duty and whole duty, and you will feel a great deal better both in mind and body. At least I do.

I think our Regt. will leave here soon. I hope it will. Where we will go to, I do not know. All sorts of rumors are afloat. I presume you must have heard of the resignation of our Colonel (Hayward) long before this. Well may we be styled the "Orphan Regiment". But then I think we are quite as well off and a little better than when we had a Colonel. It is said that we have another Colonel (Green). I hope he will show himself a smart and brave man.

It is raining quite hard today. We have had no very very cold weather this winter, and very little snow. Just enough to make the roads muddy.

Feb. 4: I came off duty again this morning. I am now on every third day. We had quite a heavy fall of snow yesterday from the north-east. It made it very uncomfortable for me with my shoes, as every time I went out with the relief I filled them with snow and consequently went with wet feet. However, I feel quite well this morning. I like the snow and cold weather. It reminds me of home. I don't believe I could get along very well without frost and snow. The "South" is no home for me. Give me the North with its pleasant summers and fall and old winter.

I received two letters and a paper day before yesterday. One letter and paper from home and the other (letter) from Aunt Laurie and Cousin Nellie. You can imagine the pleasure they gave me. (I just received a letter from Willis Savage. I wrote him some time since. I now have five letters to answer.)

You ask me "what is the health of our Company". There was a time when there was quite a number on the sick list although it was not quite so bad as Mrs. Upton represents it. There has not been one case of the black measles in the Co. and I do not think in the Regt. though there has been quite a number of the red measles. The measles, I think, have had their run. Quite a number have died out of the Regt., but none from our Company. The reason I think is that we gave them better care. The hospital is no place to send sick men. They are not properly taken care of. One of our men (sick with the measles) was sent there. At one time he was so low that he was rolled over twice to ascertain whether he was dead or alive. You must not believe all Mrs. Upton or any other person tells you. My health is good. Luther gets along pretty well. He bought him a six shooter and sold it again with three dollars profit.

The boys say I am getting fat. Trudell is in the hospital. Lablue is getting along very well. We are doing hard service. I think I shall have a chance to smell powder before the war is over. I wish I was at home to enjoy the singing school, but then I am content here. How do you like Mr. Partridge?

I return you many thanks for your kindness in sending me the stamps. I feel anxious, very anxious, about James. I hope and think he will pass his examination. That examination will be very important in his life.

Our quarters are excellent. The entire Regt. is now in barracks. So it is decreed, is it, that the calf shall die. I am sorry that I am not there to raise it. I should indeed like to get a taste of the veal, but then we have plenty of fresh beef and I must console myself on that.

(Contd.)

Contd. Jan. 28, 1862

Drunkenness did prevail to a great extent, but it has been greatly checked since the Capt. has prevailed upon most of the Company to sign a pledge of total abstinence during their term of enlistment. You ask me how the men and I agree. Well, we agree pretty well, very well. The men generally obey orders very well. Trudell and I had a few words once. I was taking out the nine o'clock relief and having one man less than the required quota I was obliged to lengthen the beats. Trudell declared he would not walk the beat. I gave him and began to be quite noisy as Frenchmen usually do. I told him he would do as I thought best and that it would be good policy to have no more words about it. No, he would not walk it. No man could make him. Said I, "You can take your choice either to walk that beat or I will get a file of men and bring you to the guard house a prisoner." It was amusing to see how quick he "wopsid" around. He didn't care a --- how far he walked. --- I was the best corporal in the lot, etc. If I had reported him he would have been in a bad fix.

Give my love to Mother and James and Frances. Give my respects to Mr. Holcomb and the rest.

Your affectionate Brother

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan in a thaw he hopes has "broke" the heart of winter, Henry tallies two desertions from his company: one man drank himself into the guard house and bolted, another vanished to cut wood while the Captain was home in Champlain. Amid gambling and watch lotteries he won't touch, the young soldier guards his pay and his pledge not to drink, and sits twice for photographs beside his tent-mate Graves.
movements.transcription:
February 4th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you, brought by Mr. Hoyle. We are having very pleasant weather now. We have had a slight fall of snow, but it is almost all off. I think the heart of the winter is broke here. Wood is very scarce in and around our camp.

I have collected most of the money for the stove, all except $1.00. I shall get that next pay day. In regard to the Sutler's: I mean to keep clear of them the next two months and come out with $26.00 on next pay day. I can get any quantity of beer or Cider, but as I have promised not to drink I shall not touch it unless it is a glass of cider now and then for my health. I have had my picture taken twice. I do not know as you will call the one that is taken standing very good. The other one you may wish to know who it is that is with me. It is one of my tent-mates. His name is Graves. The two pictures cost $2.25. I think it would be a good plan to have them framed if it would not cost to much.

Feb. 6th: I have delayed mailing this letter, expecting to receive an answer from the money that I sent, $15.00. I have nothing more to write at present. One of our Co. has deserted. He got into a drunken scrape and was put into the guard house and from there ran away. This makes two that has deserted. I forgot to mention that one ran away when the Capt. was in Champlain. He went out to cut wood, and has not returned yet. There is a good deal of gambling going on in this Regt., and some in our Co. but I keep away from it. I have not learned how to play cards yet. There is also lottery going on in our Co. for watches, but I keep away from them all.

Today is quite mild, but muddy. We shall not probably move till the roads are better. Nothing more at present. Please excuse this writing, as I have lost all my pens. Write often.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp Gorman, two miles from Harpers Ferry, Henry recounts his regiment's hard march to the front: twenty miles the first day, a freezing night under only blankets and sky, up at three for coffee and a hard cracker. A freight train carried them to a town he finds "a perfect wreck" — buildings burnt to their walls, the bridge gone, a locomotive in the river, all the rebels' work. Crossing the Potomac on a bridge of boats, the 34th was called the best-looking regiment to pass over.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 5th, 1862
Camp Gormon — Bolivor Heights

Dear Frances:

You will no doubt be a little surprised when you receive this letter to know that our Regt. and Brigade are now in Camp two miles from Harpers Ferry, but so it is, and here we are. Shall not probably remain long. We left Camp McClellan on the 25th of Feb. very early in the morning with our knapsacks and two days rations with us. The first day we marched about twenty miles. You may be sure that I felt tired at night and was thankful to get a hard cracker and cold water, salt junk, for that was all we could have.

The first night we camped out with nothing but the sky for a covering except our blankets. Sleep was of course out of the question for it was very cold. I was up next morning at three, had cup of coffee and hard cracker, and was off at day light. This is what I call soldier life, but we may see hard times yet. We marched till about noon when we arrived at Adams Town. We took the cars there for Harpers Ferry, a ride of thirty miles in a freight train. Anything will do for soldiers you know. That is what I think.

Harpers Ferry is a perfect wreck. In some places large splendid buildings burnt, nothing but the walls remain. Also the bridge that was burnt by the rebels. They have about ruined the place. I saw a large locomotive in the river which was the work of the rebels. Harpers Ferry is a large place, but not as large as Montreal is. There is one thing very evident. The Rebels will never have the chance to go into that place again and do what damage or as much more as they have done without a little skirmishing. That is as long as the 3rd remains anywhere *(34th) around. When this Regt. crossed over the River on a bridge of boats, or a floating bridge, it was called the best looking Regt. that passed over. The Rebels must look out for the 34th. I have become so accustomed to it now that I can march 19 or 20 miles a day with my knapsack and not be the worst for it the next day. Nothing like getting used to anything.

(Contd.)

Feb. 5th 1862 — Contd.

I received a letter from home last night with yours. They are all well at home. I hope you will excuse this miserable scrall. I have to write the best way I can. I have not seen Albert or Miner for some time. Write as often as you can.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

Feb. 6th: I saw Miner and Cook this morn. Only had time to shake hands with them. They have gone on to Charleston for signal core. It is very mild today. I would mail this dirrect to Montreal but I have no postage stamps. Albert is very anxious to know who it was that shed tears or felt so bad among the young ladys when he left home last. He is very anxious to know.

movements.sigSummary: Writing to his brother Charles from Camp Bolivar Heights, Henry recounts the 34th's sudden march on "very short notice" — out at three a.m. on coffee, hard crackers, and salt junk, through Barnesville to Adamstown, then thirty miles by freight car into Harpers Ferry behind Col. Ladue. Billeted in a cotton factory, the men ground its stored wheat through the floors until Gen. Gorman laughed he "did not know what to do with them." Crammed seventeen to a bell tent, Henry would rather be home to make sugar this spring, "but that is out of the question."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 5th, 1862
Camp Bolivar Heights
Harpers Ferry

Dear Charles:

I was very much pleased to receive a letter from you. You must excuse this bad writing as I have no bench or table to write on. Have to write just as I can.

You will no doubt be a little surprised to know that our Regt. and brigade are in Harpers Ferry, but for all that it is so. Our Regt. had a very shot notice to pack up and be ready at a moments warning. Col. Ladue has returned to our Regt. We marched very early in the morn on the 27th or 28th, I am not sure which, for Adams Town. The first day we marched about 20 miles. Passed through Barnesville. Camped out the first night. Next morn I rose at three o'clock, had cup of coffee of hard crackers and salt junk. That is all a soldier can expect to get on a march. Glad enough to get that when we are hungry. We left at daylight for Adamstown. Arrived at twelve. Every white man or darkey we would meet we would ask how far it was to Adams Town. They would always reply one mile, when it would be perhaps two or three. I do not doubt but what they were strong seseesh. We took the cars at Adamstown for Harpers Ferry. Not only our Regt., but the whole brigade. We arrived about four in the afternoon, a ride of thirty miles in freight cars. Had seats of course. The remark was made by several as our Regt. passed over the pontoon bridge, that it was the best looking that passed. That has got to be an old story, however. The first night we went into a large brick building which used to be a cotton factory. We stayed there three days. There was several bushels of wheat in the first story. There are four stories to the building. The soldiers got to running the wheat through the floors. Someone asked Gen. Gorman what he intended to do with the 34th. He laughingly said he did not know what to do with them as they had got to grinding wheat the first day.

We are now two miles from Harpers Ferry in large bell tents — 17 in one tent, rather crowded but can not be helped. I have just been to dinner. Had rice, soup and fresh beef. We have tin cups for soup, coffee and tea. Sometimes tin plates but I have not. I think I shall buy one next pay day. We have a stove for the tent furnished by Uncle Sam. We had to leave our stove and tents. The day after our Regt. came into Camp you would have laughed to see the chickens and sheep and fresh beef come in. I did not go into that business. There has a stop been put to it now. I do not know how long we shall remain here, probably not a great while. I shall be very glad to receive the New York Observer, but the New York Times I don't care much for as it is all old news. I should like to be home to make sugar this spring, but that is out of the question. Write as often as you can.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

Scott was arrested not for communicating with the rebels but for falling asleep as officer of the guard. Some in the company dislike Scott; Henry says he likes him very well himself. movements.transcription:
Feb. 5th, 1862
Camp Gorman
Bolivar Heights

Dear Mother:

I received your letter last evening and was very glad to hear from you. Nothing gives me greater pleasure than to receive a letter from home, although I wrote a short time ago I know you will be anxious to hear from me often. You must excuse this writing as I have no bench or table to write on, have to write the best way I can.

I received the Observer last night. Very glad to get that any time it is convenient to send it. Our Regt. are now in large bell tents. I do not know how long we shall remain here, probably not a great while.

You wished to know if I had written about Lieut. Scott having been put under arrest. I have not for I did not think it worth while. In regard to him having communicated with the rebels, it is not so. Some one must have written that that did not like him very well. He was put under arrest for being asleep when he was officer of the guard. There are some in the Co. that do not like him. I like him very well myself. Each of our Co. have had a present of Testament and Psalms. I prize it very much.

It is very mild today. I am very glad if you like the picture that I have had taken, the one taken standing. I hope you will put it away off upstairs. I have nothing more to write this time. Direct your letters the same as before except the Camp.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

P.S. I left home the first of June, I think. Swore in to the United States Service on the 15th of June. Have been in the service a little over nine months.

Ransom paid out of his own pocket for the company's fifteen-cent photographs rather than let his men cover it — a small act of officer kindness Alexander, writing his mother from Baltimore on Feb. 7, 1862, thought worth reporting home. He swaps news of letters to Charles, Henry, and Frances, laughs off a Poolesville "Valentine" mocking him as a "raw recruit," and turns anxious over James: "It will not be him alone that will suffer if he fails."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 7th, 1862
Baltimore, Md.

My Dear Mother:

Enclosed I send Capt. Ransom's photograph. The men (most all) were determined to have them and volunteered to pay fifteen cents for each one (the price of them.) The Capt. would not allow this, but very generously gave us enough to supply nearly all the Company. Please keep it carefully for me.

I received a letter from home and one from Poolesville this morning. What do you think I found in my 'Poolesville letter'? Whay 'A Valentine' with a 'raw recruit' represented on it. I need not tell you that I had not much reason to be flattered. I'll show them that Baltimore can do as much as the '34th'.

I wrote Charles a day or two since, also Henry. I have written Henry again today. I feel very anxious about James. It will not be him alone that will suffer if he fails. The whole family will spur him up, encourage him. Tell him to persevere. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P./S. I shall write Frances soon.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander's reply lands with brotherly thunder: word has reached Baltimore that James has won an appointment to West Point. "How proud I shall feel of you," he writes, "Why, man, I shan't see my boots for a week" — urging James to study hard and "put your best foot forward," since the academy would spare him years of toil. Between fresh-issued blue pants and dish-washing, Alexander promises he'll come home "quite a cook."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 11, 1862
Baltimore

My Dear Brother: (James)

I have just finished dinner. Have been busy all the forenoon washing dishes, sweeping, etc. and getting dinner. I think I shall be quite a cook when I return home, entirely independent of the feminine gender. It is my turn today to see to these things.

So, my man, you have had an appointment to go to West Point, have you? Well, that's good news certainly. You must study hard, very hard, James. How proud I shall feel of you if you get into West Point. Why, man, I shan't see my boots for a week. James, you must put 'your best foot forward.' Now is the time for you to exert yourself if there ever was a time. If you get into W.P. you will save yourself a great many years of toil in getting your education. It is well worth a grand effort. Do you remember, James, what little Doolittle once said to me concerning you. Oh! how mad I was. I could use my bayonet upon him now with every good ground. Exert yourself, James, if it be only for my sake. I should like to 'square up accounts' with little Doolittle one of these days, but then I must 'forgive and forget'. You must have a sweet time at the Academy this winter, I think. I hope your debating society prospers. Be punctual in your attendance. Speaking there once does a man more good than six months of 'Friday afternoon speaking' to my mind. Why don't the trustees 'oust' Dobbin? The scholars can have no respect for the man. What a misfortune it must be to have a 'scolding wife', eh? Look out Master James for yourself.

We have received new pants (blue). We shall probably have our 'dress suit' soon. The pants we have received are the same as those we received at Camp Wheeler. The jackets we received there are still good but the pants are worn out. My health is good. Please acknowledge all letters received. Love to all.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander

P.S. James, you must write longer letters. 'As you sow', you know, 'so you must reap.'

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry answers Charles's question about soldiers allotting pay home with an unvarnished ledger of camp life: many in his company blow their wages at the sutler's, including George Dodds, now borrowing — though Henry asks Charles not to repeat it. He details the ration cycle and the indignity of eating "dog fashion" without tin plates, joking that "a pound or two of dirt" is "good enough for soldiers."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 11th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Charles:

I was very glad to receive a letter from you. It has been a very mild winter thus far, not any snow worth mentioning, but it has been very muddy. It freezes very hard nights. Tonight we are having quite a snow storm, but it will not last long.

There was quite a row in our Co. tonight about six o'clock, all from the cause of getting drunk. One of our Co. drank a little to much of the good thing. I think it was beer, and was making a good deal of disturbance when the Officer of the day came along and ordered him to the guard house, but he would not go. He said unless two of the guard and a Corporal went with him. He was perfectly right there, for he has been through the Mexican war, and the war in India, and of course knows all about the rules of war. Not long since another of our Co. got to fighting, and was completely covered with mud.

You wished to know if I had heard about the soldiers alloting part of their pay to their families. I have heard or at least I have read about it, but there is a great many in this Regt. and in our Co. that spend most of their pay to the Sutlers. George Dodds, for instance, has used up all his wages thus far and is now borrowing, but I would not mention it. There are several others in our Co. in the same way. I have received my pay for the floor and stove. The floor we had to leave in Since. We live quite comfortable with our stove. I have bought a pocket diary. It cost me 50 cts. It will be very convenient to

(Continuation of Feb. 11, 1862.)

note down everything. I must tell you how we live. We do not have tin plates, but eat dog fashion. That just expresses it. We do not mind now and then to eat a pound or two of dirt. Good enough for soldiers, don't you think so. We have fresh meat every two or three days and bread. Have boiled pork or salt junk every morning and hot coffee and hard bread. Soup every noon, and tea every night. We receive our rations every ten days. We have sugar of course. None of our Co. save their rations as I know of, but I think as a general thing they are used up. I am sure if I cooked my own rations I should save a good deal, but as it is, can not.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Writing to his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, Henry passes the night's electric news: word of "the glorious victory in South Carolina" by the Burnside Expedition, two thousand prisoners taken, met with "great cheering" through the camp. Eager and untested, he boasts that once the 34th New York goes into action "the rebels will have to run" — then notes, plainly, that the farms in this country are "all worked by slaves."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 12th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

I was very glad to receive a letter from you. I had about or almost given you up, but I take it for granted that you are perfectly excusable this time. I am very glad for your sake that you have a School. I hope you will enjoy yourself. I saw Lieut. Miner not long ago. He spoke of you having a school in M.C. He thought it was all very fine, etc., etc. He also spoke of James having an appointment at West Point. The Capt. thought it was the best thing a young man could do.

I suppose you would like to hear all the news, but I have not much of that to write. What I do know you shall have forthwith or immediately. The pickets have been firing across the river at each other, but it is since our Co. came off last. I am not shure whether the rebels commenced first or not. If they keep up that game they will get the worst of it. The pickets go on four days at a time now. I think that will be when the roads are in proper order, but now it is very muddy. The weather has been very mild thus far this winter. For my part I would rather have cold weather, but not for soldiering. I should not like to live in this part of the Country. The work performed on the farms down here is all worked by slaves.

Feb. 13th: News came into our Camp last night of the glorious victory in South Carolina. There was great cheering in our Camp when the news came in. The news came from the Burnside Expedition. It seems that our troops captured two thousand prisoners. Many such victorys, besides the one in Tennessee, and the rebels will in time have to give up. Only let the 34th go into action once and the rebels will have to run. That is what I believe.

I have not much more to write this time. I hope when I write again to have more news. We have a very fine band to our Regt. They are beginning to play pretty well now. I received a letter from Nellie and Aunt Laura a short time ago. I have not answered them yet. If it would not be to much trouble I should be very glad to receive a paper. Excuse this scrawl. Hope to do better next time.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan in mud and unseasonably mild weather, Henry calls guard duty "the hardest of soldiering" — up nearly all night — yet admits he has grown so used to it he hardly minds, and longs to "make a move of some kind." He grieves the heavy drunkenness and fighting in his company but insists he keeps clear of it all, and tells his mother that nothing does a soldier so much good as a letter from home.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 12th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I was very glad to receive a letter from you. We are having very mild weather, but very muddy. I am shure I should not like to live in this part of the country. I would rather have cold weather for my part.

I received two letters from Alex at the same time. I received yours. He seems to be in good spirits. There is nothing that does us so much good as a letter from home. My health is pretty good now. Have a good appetite. Your letter did me a great deal of good. I am sorry to write that there is a great deal of drunkenness in the Company and some fighting, but I keep out of it all. The hardest of soldiering is guard duty. Have to be up about all night, but I have got so I do not mind it much. I will be glad when we make a move of some kind. I have no much to write now as I wrote a short time ago. Nothing more at present.

I remain your most aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Corporal A. F. Hubbell, not quite eighteen, writes home from Baltimore with a chilling tale: a Union picket took a "home made cake" from a woman in a covered carriage and was poisoned near to death, frothing and vomiting green before castor oil and turpentine saved him. Alexander declines his mother's offer of college — better the open air than to "shut myself up" — and reports new dark-blue corporal's stripes as his brigade hopes for South Carolina.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 17, 1862
Baltimore

My dear Mother:

Last night about 12 oclock Commissary Howes came in (he rooms with me) and said he had brought a letter for me and that it was on the table. I had a great mind to get up and read it, but restrained myself. I went to sleep thinking about my letter and expected to dream about it, but did not. I generally sleep very sound, but not more than three or four hours at a time. (I mean that I usually 'wake up' every three or four hours.) Being so much on guard duty has given me the habit. After roll call (six A.M.) I lighted a candle and read my letter. It did me good. I have been watching the mails for the last week anxiously expecting one. I expect that letter will be read and reread before I get another.

You speak about my going to college next fall. I have been considering the subject for some time. I will be eighteen the twenty-eighth of next month. After weighing the subject in all its bearings I have come to the conclusion that it would not be best. In the first place when I go I wish to be well fitted. Secondly. I am young yet and there is no need of my pressing in at a disadvantage. And thirdly. I think I can make enough here to clothe myself and pay my school bill and by cutting the wood, making the fires, milking the cows, taking care of the horse, making the garden, hoeing the corn and the potatoes, etc., etc., I can pay my board. I think this would be the best thing I could do, if you have no other plans. For to shut myself up in college after living in the open air so long would, I think, be worse than having a fever in the army. Perhaps I have come to a wrong conclusion. I am but a boy yet, I realize more and more each day how little I know. I try, Mother, to keep my promise 'to you' to do nothing you 'would not approve'. You speak in your letter about 'Fathers psalm'. I generally read each morning the first and nineteenth psalms. They are beautiful. I can join heartily in the Psalmists prayer, 'Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in thy sight Oh Lord my strength and my redeemer'. I feel that God is near me.

You do right to 'bless me' for writing such short letters. The reason was I was wearied out writing. I had had five letters to answer. One from Aunt Laurie and Cousin Nellie, another from Henry, another from Charlotte, another from Willie Savage, another from home.

(Continuation of Feb. 17th, 1862.)

The report just came that our brigade is going on an expedition to South Carolina. I hope it is so. General Robinson is the commander of the brigade. The 12th Mass., 10th Maine and 16th New York form part of it. It is called the 'railroad brigade'.

In telling me about home matters you said nothing about the hens and heifer and if Plummer fulfilled his contract. When will it be time to pay the taxes? I wish to pay them this year. I shall not be sorry when we leave Baltimore. One of our men was poisoned a few days since and came near dying. Yes poisoned — and by a woman too. He was on picket duty. A covered carriage or wagon came along. A woman looked out and asked him if he would not like a home made cake. He suspected nothing, took and ate it. Not long after he was taken violently ill and vomited up a green substance. A doctor was sent for. He came and gave him castor oil and turpentine to make him vomit. The man frothed at the mouth. He is now nearly well.

When I go out in the city I usually wear my sidearms. The Sergeants and Corporals now wear stripes on their pants. The sergeants wear a stripe an inch and a half in width and the Corporals one a half inch. The stripe is dark blue. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Corporal A. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: At seventeen, on "the holy sabbath" in occupied Baltimore, Alexander writes Mother from the quiet of the quarters, having just heard "a very good discourse on death" at the Sharp St. M.E. church. He cannot answer Henry's letter or Corporal Perkins's for want of a single postage stamp — and gently proposes setting aside part of his next pay so Mother can buy stamps too, recalling she once went silent for lack of them. He teases that Aunt Laurie has "turned rebel."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 23, 1862
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

Today is the holy sabbath. An unusual quiet prevails throughout the quarters. I attended divine service this morning at the Sharp St. M.E. church. Heard a very good discourse on death. Was there before service had commenced and went into the sabbath school. I enjoyed this part of the service very much.

I received a letter from Henry today. He seems to be in pretty good spirits. Also one from Corporal Perkins of the same Co: a messmate of Henrys. I should like to answer these letters, but cannot for want of a postage stamp. When I received those stamps Charles sent I was indebted for quite a number of letters and 'used up' my stamps pretty fast.

I feel some delicacy in sending home for more for I remember when I came home on furlough you said the reason you did not write me oftener was because you had no stamps. The next time I send home money I shall appropriate a certain sum for you to purchase stamps for you and myself. Be a good plan, won't it?

I wish Mother, you would write Aunt Laurie and Cousin Nellie and tell them for me that she says in her first letter to me 'I most sincerely hope you will be punctual and Nellie and I will do our part. Try us Alex.' I have tried them and 'found them wanting'. They generally wait four — five — six weeks after they have received my letters before they answer them. When they write, they write good long letters and apologize plentifully and promise to do better in future. You tell Aunt Laurie I have been holding an 'indignation meeting' with myself for some time, but have finally concluded that she has 'turned rebel' and will no longer own her 'soldier nephew'. I am afraid that nose of hers (you know she says it is crooked — I never could see it) has led her astray.

My dear Mother, you complain of the shortness of my letters. I hardly know what to write. I wish you would ask questions for I hardly know what would interest you. Let some of the questions be standing ones; and I will report concerning them every time I write. I wonder if Charley could send me a Plattsburgh paper now and then.

If I had stamps I could send him Baltimore papers very often. All of you at home please write me often. Mother, if such a thing be possible, can you send me some stamps. I am sorry to ask it.

So Albert Savage is dead is he? I never was more astonished when I read in your letter that Henry had thought a great deal on Albert Savages death. When did he die? I received a letter from Willie a few days since and he said nothing about it. Nelhinch wishes to write and as I can think of nothing more of interest to write I will close.

Your affectionate son, Alexander.

P.S. Love to all. I will write Frances soon. Sent "blos up" Aunt L. too hard. She might get vexed and never write me again. Luther sends his respects to you all. I am enjoying excellent health. Luther says I am getting fat.

movements.sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother the order has come: read at dress parade, the men are to pack knapsacks and stand ready to march at a moment's notice, surplus clothes boxed off to Poolesville. The night before, the chaplain preached on "the Duty of Patriotism" and doubted they'd see another Sabbath in camp — heavy firing already sounding across the river. Henry closes, as always, urging his mother not to worry: he has good health now.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 24th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you two or three days ago. Was very glad to hear that you were all well. The reason I have not answered before I thought I would wait and know what news there is to write. The probability is now that we shall make a move before another week goes by or transpires. Orders were read on dress parade last night to have our knapsacks packed and ready to leave at a moments notice. What clothes we could not carry, we are to send to Poolsville in a box. I have mine marked. When we go into camp again we can have them. I can not carry all of the clothes I have now.

The roads are very bad now. We may not move this week, and yet we may. I was over to meeting last night. We had speaking. The text was the Duty of Patriotism. Very good. The Chaplain in his remarks said he thought we would not be here another Sabbath, but that we can not tell for certain. Feris left for the fleet week ago today. He is probably sailing before this time. He got into a fight with some of the boys and was broke from his office. He felt so bad that he left, with the Capt. permission. If he had staid he would have been court martialed and it would have went hard with him.

We came off from picket yesterday, was on reserve, heavy firing has been going on across the river lately. It is raining today. Colonel Ladue has returned into our Regt. again. I heard that he has been promoted to Brigadier Gen. Nothing more this time. I may write again before we move. Do not worry about me, I have good health now.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry
