movements.sigSummary: Henry writes from Harpers Ferry that the regiment "Left Camp McClellan on the 26th," marching through Poolesville, Barnesville, and Adamstown, then taking the cars to a pontoon bridge of boats into the gutted town. He counts perhaps 60,000 troops massed here and, eager for what's coming, confesses he doesn't care how soon they "see some fun." Yet the burnt bridge, brick walls standing over ashes, and wrecked arsenal leave him feeling "bad" at the rebels' destruction.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 28, 1862
Harpers Ferry

Dear Mother:

Our Regt. Left Camp McClellan on the 26th. We marched through Poolesville and from there to Bainsville and from there to Adamstown. We took the cars then to Harpers Ferry. We arrived about three in the afternoon. After a couple of hours we crossed over the river to Harpers Ferry. We went over on a floating bridge of boats. You no doubt remember of the rebles burning the bridge. Nothing but the stone piers remain. It really made me feel bad to see what distruction the rebles have done in this place. Several buildings burnt. Nothing but the brick walls remain. I also saw the Arsenal that was burnt by our boys, four or five thousand stand of Arms distroyed, so that the rebles could not get them I suppose.

The first day we marched 20 miles with our knapsacks. Felt rather tired at night. Next morning we started at seven and marched about five miles to Adams-Town. It is about 30 miles from there to Harpers Ferry. Our Regt. is now in a brick building to recruit for a while. I should judge there was about 60 thousand troops in this place. We may see some fun before long. I do not care how soon, sooner the better. I have got so now I don't mind marching 20 or 30 miles with my knapsack, but of course I get very tired. Some of the boys have thrown away their blankets, but I mean to keep all I have.

When our Regt. crossed the river I heard several remark that our Regt. was the best looking that crossed over. We have a good band to our Regt. I have not been around town much yet, for there are guards posted all around. I am on today. Gen McClellan and staff are here, but I have not seen him yet.

I have nothing more to write at present. I shall write as often as I can. Please excuse all mistakes as I write this in a hurry. Do not feel anxious.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Henry writes from a large brick building that once served as a grist mill — a place, he notes wryly, where the rebels seized so much wheat "they will never have the same chance again." On a cold but pleasant March day, kept from roaming the town and from mailing his letter, he apologizes for falling short of the longer letter he'd hoped to send and promises more when he can.
movements.transcription:
March 1st, 1862

Dear Mother:

I intended to have mailed this letter before but could not get a chance. I shall mail this as soon as I can. Today is rather cold but pleasant. We are now in a large brick building which used to be a grist mill. Some place where the rebles took so much wheat they will never have the same chance again. U gave not been around town and of course cannot write as long a letter as I should like. When I write again I may have something more to write. Write soon.

Your Aff.

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Corporal A. F. Hubbell writes his sister Frances a tale of soldiers gone duck hunting with rifles in Baltimore — so much fog they couldn't find their kills, in a leaking boat with a broken oarlock. The next day Lt. Fitch and Corporal Luther nearly "got ducked" themselves when a gale swamped their boat; they leapt to a pier and lost the boat, Luther's share five dollars. He waves off a wild rumor that Gen. Banks's division — Henry's — was cut to pieces.
movements.transcription:
March 3, 1862

My Dear Sister:

I received your very welcome letter today. It was not much of a letter I must confess, but then I take the will for the deed. I hope in future you will write longer — a little longer letters. You say in the first letter you wrote me from Long — (how do you spell it) that you were very busy and had but little time and little inclination to write. Now Miss Fannie — I — Corporal A. F. Hubbell, do hereby charge you that you take care of yourself, and do you, what Mr. Bass said, "he learned to do" after six years of teaching, — "favor yourself". It will not pay to learn French at the expense of health. Therefore, Miss Fannie, if you find the place too hard, I would counsel you (and so would every other sensible person like myself) to "resign your commission" and return home to comfort your "old Mama" as Mother styles herself.

How does Miss B. get along. Wonder if she has recovered the use of her tongue yet. She seems to be an exception to the sex, for they usually have all the talking to do. You tell Miss Mix the next time you see her that I have not forgotten that of her yet.

We have very pleasant times down here in Baltimore. A party of us "boys" went out duck hunting with our rifles the other day (the ducks are very plentiful in the bay.) I expect we made great slaughter among them, but then the fog was so thick we could not see to pick them up. Our old boat leaked pretty fast. We landed twice to dip the water out. During the last half mile the water increased upon us quite fast and to add to our enjoyment, when we had passed over about quarter of the distance one of the oarlocks broke. After considerable exertion we reached the shore in safety with our boat about quarter full of water. We brought back glowing accounts of the abundance of game (and so there was) etc., etc. The next day the Orderly and another Sergeant and several men went out in one boat and Lieut Fitch and Corporal Luther in another after "ducks", and came pretty near getting "ducked" themselves. While out a heavy gale sprung up, which rendered the small boats perfectly unmanageable. The one in which the Lieut and Luther were in swung round and "gave its sides to the waves". They sat one in each end of the boat casting very doleful looks at one another expecting each moment to be consigned to Neptunes care. But they were disappointed. The boat struck a pier right side up and both hopped on dry land without more ceremony. The boat was never seen again. It either sunk or was carried away by the waves. They were obliged to pay for it. (Luther's share was five dollars.)

The Army of the Potomac is reported to be on the move. Nearly every engine and box car were in use the other day transporting troops. Not one word of all this has been suffered to be published as yet. It was reported here the other day that Gen. Banks division (the one Henry is in) was entirely cut to pieces and that the rebels had been crossing the river all day and that they would be in Baltimore the next day. The latter part of the report was perfectly foolish for it would be impossible for the rebels to penetrate as far as Baltimore on account of the great number of troops we have on the Potomac. When the rebels come to Baltimore we will turn out and "present arms" to them. After which we will "Charge Bayonet". It is said they do not like cold steel. The "Sixtieth" can give them plenty of that. McClellan is in great favor. The latest news is that Columbus has been evacuated. We may now safely say the rebels are routed out of the West. I shall try and send you some papers.

Your affectionate Brother

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: James's appointment from the War Department has come through, and Alexander, newly mustered in at Baltimore and watching cavalry drill swords "till their wrists fairly ache," only wishes he could raise the $60 to send his brother. He delights in news of the hens, the heifer, and eight pounds of butter a week. A postscript reports the 34th at Harpers Ferry as "the van of the advancing army," and a Co. C picket struck by a train, his leg broken and head terribly wounded.
movements.transcription:
Mch. 6th, 1861 [*sic* — 1862]
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

I received your very welcome letter day before yesterday. I have been watching the mails for the last fortnight and had just about dispaired of hearing from you when Luther came in and handed me two letters, one from Charles and Frances and one from Mr. Copeland. You may be sure I had a jolly time reading them. I am very happy to hear from the hens and heifer and "old whity". So you make eight pounds of butter per week, eh? That is doing well — certainly. You must have enough and to spare. I am glad that the hens are doing so well. Where do you keep and what do you feed them. I am very particularly glad that you have allowed me to help pay the taxes. Charles says there is a pew tax of eight dollars and a half. I will pay it and am only to glad to do it. This is something I have longed to do for a good many years and am very glad that I am now able to do it. We have been "mustered in" and will have our pay soon.

So James has had his appointment from the "War Department", has he? I think studying under Everest will be a first rate thing for him. I wish I could raise that 60 dollars. He is welcome ten times over to all the money I have. We shall be paid off again in May. I will try and send him twenty dollars then.

You tell Dodds Beaumont and Bowen that all the poetry will be taken out of them and their uniforms when they come down here and begin to drill through the mud and water as I saw some cavalry doing yesterday. They will have to swing those swords till their wrists fairly ache. How strange it will seem to them to come down here and sleep in a building with several hundred others, and to cook their own provisions, take care of their horses, etc., etc. But then I respect a young man for doing it. They will probably like it after awhile.

Now, dear Mother, don't worry about Mrs. Webb. She is a miserable old hag and beneath your notice. Do you remember when she use to come to our house to have a "talk" — a talk. How sanctimonious she used to look! "Well, now I know Lellies abilities are good, and — I don't see why — etc. etc. etc." Isn't that it, eh? Mr. Kellogg is an "old sputterer". Let things take their course. Don't worry.

You tell Charles that our Regt. is indeed as brave as a lion and eager for fight. Is Dobbin going to remain another term. So you have as much snow as we had last winter. Fairly blocked in, eh?

I have nothing more of importance to write.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P.S. The 34th is now or was the last I heard from them, at Harpers Ferry. They form a part of the van of the advancing army. I saw a fellow from the Regt. yesterday. He carried a letter for me to Henry. One of the pickets of Co. C was nearly killed an hour or two since. He was standing looking at a train loaded with mules and did not see the one coming from the opposite direction. The engine struck him and knocked him off the track, breaking his leg and inflicting terrible wounds on the head. Please write oftener. Do not let so long a time elapse again without writing.

movements.sigSummary: Massive troop movements funnel through Baltimore: three or four thousand soldiers on Sunday alone, with thirty steamers and sixty boats waiting to ferry New York regiments to Fortress Monroe. On guard duty, Corporal Alexander confides darker scenes — drawing his sabre on a drunken runaway, a man seizing him by the hair — then begs his mother to tell no one: the boys hold it a point of honor.
movements.transcription:
March 11, 1862
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

I received your very welcome letter this morning. By each mail we hear long accounts of the "snow blockade". Have you supplies enough in the "old castle" to last you a month or two. I do not think "the blockade" will last much over that time. If it does write and let me know and I will send up several regiments of our sunshine, on the approach of whom I think "old Winter" will withdraw his forces.

I am on guard duty today. Among other duties I generally have to see to the wood chopping (for the guard house. The guards are obliged to do this). One of the men was handcuffed for refusing to do his share of this work the other day. I am not obliged to chop, but only to see that it is done. We are making some pea soup for dinner. It will be the first I have had since I left home. We generally have very good appetites, very good, very good.

Thousands of troops have passed here during the last week, (three of four thousand on Sunday) and thousands more will probably pass. Nearly all the troops are from N.Y. Two Regts. are now at the "Union Relief." They will probably be sent to Fortress Monroe by water. It is said that as many as thirty steamers arrived here the other day for troops. I suppose the reason is they can not transport them fast enough by railway. The Malone and Potsdam Regts. passed through here the other day. A large number of the "Sixtieth" were there to see them. All the N.Y. troops have the Enfield rifle. It was reported last night that four hundred thousand Union troops were on the move yesterday for Manassas and Richmond. I expect some hard fighting will be done. I wish our Regt. was there. I do not like the notion of Henrys fighting there alone. Not at all, at all!

I received the long expected letter from Aunt Laura and Cousin Nellie day before yesterday. I am very, very, very, very, very much obliged to you for those postage stamps.

Mch. 12th: You told me, Mother, to keep at a safe distance from drunken soldiers. That I cannot do and do my duty as Corporal. I have not much fear of my being hurt. Yesterday one of the men ran the guard (he was a little sprung). The Sergeant ordered me to take a file of men and bring him in. After him I went on double quick. The fellow ran towards the glass works and jumped in a door and found himself covered. He started to run back and came "hat upon me". (immediately drew my sabre.) He came to the conclusion that it was best for him to stop, but refused to "budge" an inch. A thrust or two in his stern from my weapon brought him to terms. When we reached the guard house he refused to go in. Myself and men immediately seized him and gave him "a shove" that sent him in "in a trice." He threatened all things. It gave me very little concern. I suppose he can go home now and say he has shed at least a little blood in his countrys cause.

The other day the Sergeant ordered me to take hold of him of a drunken fellow. The fellow seized me by the hair, but nevertheless he went in. One of the men some time since (he was "tight") seized a rifle and snapped it at the guard. Fortunately it was not loaded. Such things as these do not happen very often. I hope you will never mention these events as the boys hold it as a point of honor not to mention anything disparaging to men or company and it would make me trouble should it be known that I wrote any such thing.

Our Company is one of the most orderly in the Regt. A Corporal with a file of armed men is comparatively safe. I think I shall get a revolver. I do not know what may happen. I do not apprehend ever being seriously harmed — if ever. The men are afraid to touch a Corporal as they know it would be a sore job for them should they be courtmartialed. I charge you never to say anything concerning these things.

I understand that there is upward of sixty boats here awaiting troops. I suppose you will hear ere this reaches you of the wonderful display of Southern chivalry at Manassas. They have evacuated the place without firing a gun. The combined armies of the rebel generals Price McCulloch and another Major General (I have forgotten his name) have been defeated by our troops.

I expect to be home soon. I will not get the revolver if you need the money at home. Keep a boy by all means. I will pay him. Please write soon. Tell James I shall write him soon and Charles too. I received an Observer also yesterday. It seems good to get hold of a home paper. I wonder if Charley could send a county paper to send occasionally without too much trouble. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P.S. I am very very very sorry to hear of Mr. T. Hoyles illness. I hope he will recover soon. He has been a good friend to us.

movements.sigSummary: Henry's regiment and two brigades marched some thirty miles on foot from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester to drive out the rebels, only to learn three miles short of the town that 25,000 Union troops already held it and the Confederates had fled "probably for good." Henry pulled picket and skirmish duty after twenty miles and owns to "a good many hardships" — yet nine months from home, he still hopes the rebellion will be over by next summer.
movements.transcription:
March 16th, 1862
Harpers Ferry

Dear Mother:

I know you will be very anxious to hear from me. Our Regt. and two brigades besides ours left Harpers Ferry some time ago for Winchester, with the expectation of driving the rebles away from that place, but after we had marched within three miles of Winchester we heard that twenty-five thousand of our troops were there, and of course we were not needed. The rebles have left that place probably for good. The distance from Harpers Ferry to Winchester is about thirty miles. All that distance we marched on foot with our knap-sacks and, back again, but I have become use to marching now and do not mind it much.

We camped out two nights on the way. We had our tents. A regt. of Cavalry went before us and tore down a reble flag at Berryville, ten miles from Winchester. Our Co., after marching twenty miles, went on picket and also out skirmishing. I was very much fatigued that night. To tell the truth I have gone through a good many hardships since I have left Camp McClellan, but I am none the worse for it. We expect to leave Harpers Ferry very soon, probably for Washington. I do not know where we will go then. The report is now that we leave in the morning at eight. We are having very mild weather now. The roads between here and Winchester are very good.

It is now nine months since I left home. I think this rebellion will be over by next summer, at least I hope so. I received a letter from Uncle John last evening. He is in Mich Genesee Co. He is not well he writes. I have answered his letter.

Please excuse this writing and all mistakes. Take good care of your health. Dirrect your letters the same as before. Write often.

I remain, your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: "God is my refuge and strength: a very present help in trouble."
movements.sigSummary: Alexander, writing his mother from Baltimore on March 17, 1862, refuses her plea to burn his letters — "No — no — I cannot do that" — having kept nearly every one since enlisting. He describes guard duty in a fierce storm, a rubber blanket sluicing water until a gallon pooled in each pant leg, and confesses he was "gulled" out of five dollars by an Excelsior Brigade sergeant who vanished. Of his country he loves it now "ten times ten times."
movements.transcription:
March 17, 1862
Baltimore

"God is my refuge and strength: a very present help in trouble."

My dear Mother:

I received your very welcome letter on the 14th inst. You request me to burn the letter. No — no — I cannot do that. I have all the letters I have received since I have been in the army except a few of those I received while at Ogdensburg. This package will bear record of faithfulness of my friends in writing me.

We are to have our dress coats soon and with them I understand a leather stock and dress hat and plumes and a pair of brass epauletts. Several companies in the Regt. now have the coats. They are very good and quite fine cloth.

Relative to the movements. I know nothing, only that our Colonel is very anxious to get the Regt. off the road. A great many rumors have been afloat concerning us. When I get my knapsack packed and the Colonel gives the command "forward march" then I shall believe that we are to move.

You say Mother, that you sometimes regret letting me come. No — no — you cannot. I do not at all regret coming. It seems to me that I love my country ten times better than ever. Ten times? No, not ten times, but ten times ten times.

So Plummer has proved himself "a great scamp", eh? I was afraid of it. I never had any great opinion of him anyway. I saw enough of him when he thrashed for us.

I find the great maxim of the world seems to be "take care of number one". "Every man for himself." I must now tell you how I have been "gulled". While I was at Camden Station a Sergeant in the Excelsior Brigade (Sickles) station at Budds Ferry, while hurrying on to join his Regt. was left in Baltimore without money, it having been stolen from him. The Capt. went with him to the Provost Marshals and then to a Major Belgor, who has the charge of the transportation of the troops, but could do nothing for him. He told him to wait at the Union Relief. He expected the Malone Regt. through soon and would manage to send him through to Washington with them. He, the fellow, was in great distress about it as he should lose a second lieutenancy if he was not there soon. I took pity on him and loaned him five dollars. He promised to return it as soon as he reached his Regt. I heard nothing of him until lately. One of our Co. received a letter from him. Among other things he asked why Corporal Hubbell had not written him. He said that he had written me some time since and had received no answer. I received no letter from him and have written him asking him for the money. (He left me his address.) I have received no answer to the letter. The boy, I understand, received the lieutenancy. I have learned wisdom. It was one of the most foolish things I ever did. I pitied the poor fellow and thought how bad I should feel to be left in a strange city without money. (I have just heard that Capt. Ransom says that our Regt. will have to fight. He has been to Fortress Monroe. He started last Friday. He is now back. The Lieut. Colonel and Adjutant, I understand, went with him. Our Colonel is determined to get the Regt. off the road. I shall not be at all sorry if we are obliged to fight.

You remember that fellow I told you I chased through the city with a file of men, and who was caught by the policemen; well, he ran the guard the other night. A Sergeant and three Corporals went after him and did not succeed in catching him. He is now at headquarters awaiting his courtmartial.

Now for answering your questions: I am enjoying excellent health. I attend church as often as I can. I attended last evening. It sometimes often happens that I am on guard duty Sunday. I often come off guard Sunday morning and am too tired and sleepy to attend the morning service. This was the case yesterday. I retire almost any time. If I am on guard duty I catch a nap the best way I can. Other days I retire at nine or half past. Generally I rise, if I am on guard duty, at one and take a three miles walk; the same at five. Other days at Reveille (six) when we have roll call. When I am on guard duty I take my blanket and spread it on the floor of the guard house and nap a little with one eye open. When I go out with my one oclock relief I often think of you at home. The last night I was on guard was one of the roughest we have had for some time. The very elements seemed to have conspired. I have a rubber blanket I bought of the Capt. (for five shillings) which kept my body dry, but the water ran off into my pants. Why I should think before morning I have at least a gallon of water in each leg. Capt. Ransom is with the first platoon. I am in the second. The first platoon is at Camden Station, about a furlong from us.

The health of the regt. is at present, so far as I know, very good. We in Baltimore think the war will soon be over. What a wonderful display of Southern chivalry we have had at Manassas. That boasted Southern chivalry which was to accomplish so much. There is one thing they do particularly excel in — the rise of their heels.

The McComb Regt. passed through here last Friday. I saw quite a number if knew. Joe Laforrd, the fellow who plowed our buckwheat field for Lumis, I saw. Ask Charley if he remembers my telling him of a fellow that wished to borrow three thousand dollars of Hiram Dudley to buy a farm. I saw him. His name is Hiram Pettice. I did not know that James Sweney was in the Regt. Luther saw him. I am sorry I did not see him. He (Sweney) is a Capt. (The drum is now beating for drill. I must go.) The drum did not beat for drill. The Company turned out without arms. The Capt. then brought the fellow I spoke of in this letter as at headquarters awaiting trial, before the Co. (us) and he (the fellow) made a confession. The Capt. feels bad to have any of his men court-martialed. He saw the Colonel and managed to get him out on condition that he would make a confession before the Company.

This last letter of yours was one of the most interesting you have written me. My dear Mother, I have not written half I wish too. Please write me all about home matters. How many oats, potatoes, peas, buckwheat, etc. did the farm raise. Write about the hens, pony, heifer and old cow and all about home matters. You have done well this last time. I like to read the letter. Please write soon. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Multi-page, major letter

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, Henry tells his brother James the brigade expects to move soon for Washington, and that the Shenandoah railroad bridge is repaired so the cars again run to Winchester over good macadamized roads. Sixteen men share his bell-shaped tent, a bell stove at its center and the top open for smoke. He confesses a long-neglected debt for Mrs. Douglas's flour, asks James to settle it from his money, and adds wearily that he wouldn't object if the war closed next week.
movements.transcription:
March 21st, 1862
Harpers Ferry
Bolivor Heights
Camp Gormon

Dear James:

I received your letter and was very glad to hear from you. I hope you will write as often as you can. We had a slight fall of snow last night, about three inches. We have more rain and high wind than anything else. Last night two tents blew down. There are sixteen in our tent. Have a stove in the middle in the shape of a bell. The tent is also in the shape of a bell, open at the top to let the smoke out. Have a pole in the middle to hold the tent.

It is raining today. The roads between here and Winchester are very good if the weather is ever so bad. They are made of very small stone. Now and then have to cross a brook. The rebles have distroyed the bridges. The bridge across the Shenandoah River is repaired so that the cars can run between here and Winchester.

I expect our brigade will leave before long for Washington. Gen. McClellan praises up the Army of the Potomac very much, thinks we have done good service in picket duty last summer. I don't care how soon this war closes. If it was next week I would not object. I have had my boots tapped and a patch put on for one dollar. Saves me getting a pr. of shoes from the Government. Peter Guyan did the job. That bag of flour I got from Mrs. Douglas I never paid for. This has been neglected to long. Please take some of my money and pay it. I had the money twice to pay it but didn't pay it. I never could find him. His men would not take it.

I have nothing more to write this time. I expect our Brigade will move before long for Washington.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry
movements.notes: Multi-part, continues on next page

movements.sigSummary: After the railroad bridge at Harpers Ferry was finished, Henry's 34th New York rode a freight train eighty-three miles to Washington in twenty-four hours, reaching brick barracks at two in the morning to await pay before an unknown assignment. A Sabbath in the capital, he marvels, feels nothing like one — cars running, soldiers drunk, the provost guard hauling stragglers to the guardhouse — and he vows to keep his pass signed and dodge arrest himself.
movements.transcription:
March 23, 1862
Washington

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you this morning. Nothing does me more good than to have a letter from home. Our Regt. left Harpers Ferry yesterday morning for Washington, a distance of eighty-three miles on a freight train. We came through in twenty-four hours. Arrived last night about two. We left the cars and marched through the City a little over a mile, and are now in brick barracks. Shall probably remain here until we are paid off. I have nothing to pay the sutler this time.

I don't know where our Regt. os destined to go. Will know in a few days. The bridge across the river at Harpers Ferry is finished. The cars run across now. It was a perfect jam coming through on the train, but that is better than marching. I have had enough of that for a while.

Our Regt. goes to mess about half a mile from the barracks. It reminds me very much of Albany, only we do not live quite so well. Have bread, coffee and salt junk. That is better than hard crackers. Today is the Sabbath, but it does not seem much like it. Cars running all the while. A good many of the soldiers got drunk. The provost guard goes around the City picking up all straglers, and those that go out without a pass. The pass has to be signed by the Gen. Two have been taken prisoners today. I mean to look out for one, and not be taken.

I am glad that you have let out the Sugar-bush. Look out and have an honest man. I shall be glad when this war closes, and be at home again. It seems more like fall than winter, no snow, but mud.

I have nothing more of importance to write this time. Henry Cooper and Jacen, I think, will have to get their discharge. Both of them have been sick. Have not been able to do duty for some time. Write often.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from Camp Preston King near Baltimore — a hasty "dispatch," not a letter. The 60th has "struck tents" again, left its Eutaw St. quarters, and may move for Fortress Monroe within ten days. He sketches his Colonel in one stroke: a "savage looking old fellow" with a beard of "wolfish gray," who threatens to resign if the regiment isn't pulled off road duty. Only James stays silent, and Alex vows to pull his ears when he gets home.
movements.transcription:
March 26, 1862
Camp Preston King
near Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

You see by the heading of my letter that we have again "struck tents." Our Company is now at headquarters. We left our quarters on Eutaw St. last Saturday. It is rumored that our Regiment will leave within ten days for Fortress Monroe. Our Colones is now there. He has said, I understand, that if our Regt. is not moved off this road he will resign. He is like very much by all. He is a savage looking old fellow with a moustache and beard of a wolfish gray. He says but little, and what he says he means. I expect the call for drill every moment. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Direct your letters as usual. I am enjoying excellent health and spirits. Please write soon. You need not consider this as a letter, but only a dispatch to let you know that I am well and my whereabouts. I received a letter and paper from home the day we moved and one from Henry Monday. He writes in good spirits. Told me about their marching to Winchester and how the rebels took to their heels. They (the rebels) seem to have been drilling on the "double quick" of late. Why don't James write. I shall pull his ears when I get home, see if I don't.
movements.notes: With P.S. containing Henry's Winchester march news

movements.sigSummary: Alexander spent his eighteenth birthday on a nine-mile march, then wrote home from Relay House on a sheet he labeled "Dispatch No. 2." His regiment had just struck tents again, brigaded as the "Railroad Brigade" and rumored bound for Harpers Ferry to guard the line. "I feel old," he tells his mother. "I have begun life's battle for myself. I am thrown upon my own resources." Surrounded by sin and vice, he writes, he feels strong in the Lord.
movements.transcription:
March 30th, 1862
Relay House

Dispatch No. 2

My Dear Mother:

We have again "struck tents" as you will see by the heading of my dispatch. Last Friday morning about quarter after eight orders came for us to be ready to march by nine. I had been detailed for guard duty that day and was waiting for the bugle to sound for guard mounting. I immediately went to work and "packed up" and was soon ready. I endured the march of nine miles very well.

It is no use for me to try to write there is so much noise and jarring. I am enjoying excellent health. There is a rumor afloat that we are to go to Harpers Ferry to guard railroad. Guarding railroads will probably be our business during the war as our Regt. is brigaded "Railroad Brigade".

I shall try and write you a long letter soon. We are moving about so that I can get but few opportunities of writing. Direct your letters as usual. My eighteenth birthday I shall remember as a day of exceeding hard duty. I feel old. I have begun life's battle for myself. I am thrown upon my own resources. It will probably be an advantage to me. "The secret of the Lord is with them that fear him; and he will show them his covenant". I feel that God is near me. My trust is in him and in him alone. I am surrounded with sin and vice, but I feel strong in the Lord.

Sargeant Ingram of our Company will probably be home soon on furlough. He will call upon you.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander
movements.notes: Labeled "Dispatch No. 2"; Alexander's 18th birthday letter

movements.sigSummary: Beauregard is massing rebels at Corinth, and Alexander watches from Relay House for word of whether Grant or his rival will prove "the greatest general." His day runs from six AM roll call to nine-thirty taps, every hour drilled and inspected. But the heat is personal: a 200-acre swindle near Riders gnaws at him, and of his Confederate kin he writes he could "draw sight with my rifle on Octove or Julio with a very steady hand." Then marching orders arrive — "Joy, joy, joy."
movements.transcription:
April 1st, 1862
Relay House

My dear Mother & Brothers:

Wonder what you are doing this evening? How I should like to be at home with you. Wouldn't I have a jolly time, eh? But that cannot be. Here I am and here I must be. Nevertheless, I am content. I expect the war will soon be over and then hurrah for home. Oh! how good it will seem to see you all.

I see by today's papers that a great battle is expected at Corinth in the northern part of Mississippi (state). That the rebels are concentrating at that point and are commanded by General Beauregard. He and Grant will now have an opportunity to prove which is the greatest general. I wonder if we shall have another display of "Southern Chivalry" like that at Manassas. That "one Southerner is sufficient for five Yankees" has been clearly proved, hasn't it? (vice versa). I wonder if Toombs doesn't think it is time for "every woman and child" to apply the torch. Wonder if Aunt Mary still "pities us". Wonder is she is as ready as ever to go out and assist her valorous husband. Wonder if he has been drilling on the "double quick time too. O Tempora, O Mores. Guess this rebellion will end considerably like the great Catiline conspiracy, only I think Reff instead of perishing in honorable fight as old Cat. did, shall probably take to his heels.

April 2 (11 o'clock) — This is generally the time for our inspection, but our commissioned officers are on duty today and therefore we will have no inspection, much to my gratification as I have been drilling since nine and am rather tired. I have but very little leisure to write our time is so fully occupied. Our boots, belt buckels, rifles and clothes must be faultlessly clean. At six (AM) roll call, (seven) breakfast, (eight) guard mounting, (nine) uncommissioned drill, (ten) squad drill, (11½) inspection, (12½) dinner, (2½) company drill, (4½) dress parade, (6) supper, (9 PM) roll call, (9½) "taps" (when every light must be put out and every tongue still.

Master Charley, you ask me if we eat on tin plates. Well — we eat on tin plates and drink out of tin cups. Eat pork and beans, beef, potatoes, soup, &, &, and have a good time generally. Our old Colonel is very strict. He sent in seven this morning because themselves or accoutrements were not properly cleaned. We soldiers earn our money.

April 5 — Received your very welcome letter yesterday. Had a hearty laugh over your upset in one of those "Cahoes". Don't wonder James felt mortified. Suppose he felt like "charging bayonet" on the laughing occupants of the other sleigh. I should. So Grandmother made a speech, eh? Well, Well, well, what did she have to say? Something about her two "dear lambs". They seem to have been lambs a good while and I think always will be. Wonder if "Sidy" has got over his fear of a gun yet. Wonder how he would like the locks of our sabre bayonets. Guess he would need the "smelling bottle", eh? So he is about to carry on both farms. I verily believe the fellow lacks common judgment. It seems to me it would take a very extraordinarily smart man to do that, and make any profit.

I see by a letter that Fry Clarks daughter wrote a fellow in our Company that Silas and Sid were sold some two hundred acres of land near Riders to Clark, and he (Clark) thinks he has made quite a bargain. He paid them eight hundred dollars and what he had left of the Rogers farm. Eight hundred dollars won't last them long. I feel mad when I see what belongs to me going in this style. Guess Grandmother will find in the end that she made a bad bargain when she cheated us out of our rights. It don't pay to marry widows and orphans or anybody else. There is a just God who regards such things.

April 6 — Wonder what you are doing now. It is now a little after five. Well, guess Charley is reading the Observer, Mother some book from the parish library, and Master James I guess is off in some corner reading Harpers magazine, little scamp. Oh! how I should like to spend this Sabbath evening with you. But I trust I shall soon be home to spend a great many with you. I have heard today that the 34th has gone to New Orleans. Oh! how I curse the fortune that keeps our Regt. Here. It is wrong for me to talk so. It is all for the best.

So Professor Bass is coming back, eh? Well, well. I should like to see the old croaker. Wonder what he thinks of the war now. I believe the old fellow is half rebel. Well — guess the Champlainers can do no better than to get him. He is a pretty good fellow after all, though he does like money pretty well, a little too well. I have just been reading your letter of the 30th inst. Oh! how vividly it brought before me the many pleasant Sabbaths I have spent with you all. You spoke of the dinner table — wonder when I shall be there to take dinner with you again. Soon I hope. I feel anxious — very anxious — about Henry. I don't like the notion of his fighting there alone. I think I could draw sight with my rifle on Octove or Julio with a very steady hand, and I don't think conscience would trouble me much when I pulled the trigger. Oh, how I should like to have our regt. sent to Mobile and have an opportunity given us to charge upon the "Southern Chivalry". These Southerners don't seem to like our "cold steel" very much. I should like to see Uncle Knapp leg it and if Aunt Mary was with him I guess she would leg it too and bless him because he did not run faster, eh? What do you think about it? I don't believe I can every forgive our Southern connections. I shall always be ashamed of them.

I shall try and have my likeness taken as soon as we are paid off. Cousin Nellie has sent me hers. It does me good to look at her. You wish me to have my picture taken with my cap off. Don't believe I can as I have had my hair cut close to my head and don't look remarkably well with my short fur.

I have just heard that our Regt. has received marching orders. Joy, joy, joy.

April 7 — Guess I had better send this off. My health is very good. I think I have received all your letters. Please write often and you, Master James, why can't you write me often. When you do write your letters are short and sweet. Write longer ones.

Yours affectionately,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Multi-day: Apr 1, 2, 5, 6, 7. Major letter.
Arrived at Fort Monroe. Disembarked for Peninsula Campaign.

movements.sigSummary: Henry writes from Hampton, Va., after the 34th New York's two-day steamboat passage from Alexandria to Fortress Monroe — nearly 200 miles down a Chesapeake so wide he saw no land on either side. He finds the town burned to the ground, "worse than Harpers Ferry, every building burnt," the men penned like sheep, sleeping four rubber blankets buttoned into a tent. Hard crackers, no coffee — "but then we are soldiers," he shrugs, "and have to put up with whatever comes."
movements.transcription:
April 2, 1862
Hampton, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received a letter the day before I left Alexandria, eight miles from Washington. We were in camp there two days, left last Sat. morning, and took the steam boat for Fortress Monroe, Va. We were two days coming a distance of nearly two hundred miles. I for one can write that it was anything but a pleasant trip. Hardly had room to lay down at night. In regard to grub, we had hard crackers and no coffee, but then we are soldiers and of course we have to put up with whatever comes in our way.

The Chesapeake Bay is a large body of water. Could not see land on either side of the boat coming through. We are now about four miles from Fortress Monroe. I have not had a chance to see the Fort yet. We are pened up like sheep — cannot get out without a pass signed by the Gen., but then that is all right for a great many go out for the purpose of getting drunk.

The rebels leave their marks everywhere they go. This place, for instance, is worse than Harpers Ferry, every building burnt to the ground. We left our tents at Alexandria, but the Government has supplied us with rubber blankets. By putting four of them together, makes a very good tent. We left our tents at Alexandria, but the Government has supplied us with rubber blankets. By putting four of them together, makes a very good tent. Green grass around here. Very fine weather. Write often. Direct your letters the same as before.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry.

I received a letter from Aunt Laura and Nellie with her likeness. Have not answered yet. I commenced a letter before we started, but did not have time to finish it.
movements.notes: First of three April 2 letters

movements.sigSummary: Writing by candlelight near Fortress Monroe with roll call minutes away, Henry tells his mother he has been "keeping a Journal some time" he means to copy and send home — even as his regiment marches twenty-four miles to York Town at dawn, expecting an onward movement toward Richmond. The rebels have made "a clean sweep of everything," and a peddler who wandered into camp was stripped of his pies and apples in moments. Yet it is the tree toads that make him think of home.
movements.transcription:
April 2, 1862
Hampton — Near Fortress Monroe

Dear Mother:

As I expect Henry Cooper leaves in the morning, I thought I would write a few lines to let you know that I am well. I am writing this letter by candle light, as it is near time for roll call. I cannot write much, or but a few lines. As I am writing I can hear the tree toads. It makes me think of home very much.

3rd. Today is quite mild, we shall have very warm weather before long. I cannot turn around, or go three or four miles but what there are soldiers. I expect we shall make an onward movement towards Richmond before long. Wood is very scarce around here. The rebels have made a clean sweep of everything. Our Regt. will have a good name if they only keep on as they have. Yesterday a peddler came into camp, but he was no sooner in sight, when he was stripped of everything he had — a barrel of pies taken besides a barrel of apples. All those that were in the scrape have been put under arrest. I have nothing more to write this time.

I remain your Aff. Son,

Henry.

P.S. I have been keeping a Journal some time which I forgot to mention. I shall copy it off one of these days and send it home. C. Regt. leaves this place tomorrow morning for York Town, twenty-four miles from here. I expect we shall march it on foot. I shall hand this letter to Cooper. I expect he will mail it in Washington.
movements.notes: Multi-part: Apr 2, continued Apr 3

movements.sigSummary: Writing his brother Charles from a green Hampton, Va. field shared by some twenty-five thousand troops, Henry recounts a crowded two-and-a-half-day boat passage whose steamer ran aground, forcing a transfer to reach shore. Confident after a summer of bayonet drill — "I pity the rebels" — he still confesses he would rather be making sugar this spring than soldiering, and urges Charles not to let out the home sugar bush except to an honest man.
movements.transcription:
April 2, 1862
Hampton, Va.

Dear Brother Charles:

I received your letter and was very glad to hear from you. It is some time since I have written to you. The weather here is quite mild. We are in camp in a large field — green grass all around here. The nights are very cold. There are about twentyfive thousand troops in Camp around here with one brigade. We had rather a crowded time coming on the steam-boat. We were two days and half on the boat. Our steamer ran aground by mistake coming ashore so that we had to go on to another boat to get ashore. The rebels leave their tracks every where they go. They will do all the damage they can if nothing more. I suppose we will keep advancing all the while till the rebels get tired of us. Then I hope the war will close. To tell the truth I would rather be making sugar this Spring than soldiering. I am not the only one, but I shall make the best of every thing.

You wished to know whether we have newspapers. We can have them by paying the small sum of five cents which I do not happen to have. If our Regt. ever comes to bayonet charge, all I have got to say is that I pity the rebels. We have drilled in the bayonet exercise a good deal last Summer. I understand it very well now. Today is very cloudy and rather chilley. I suppose the weather is pretty cold up home. I would not let out the sugar bush unless you can have an honest man. Write all the news.

I remain your aff. Brother

Henry

P.S. If it would be convenient could you send me a fine comb in a letter. I cannot have a chance to buy one here.

Siege of Yorktown. Trench work and bombardment. Confederates evacuate May 4.

movements.sigSummary: Writing from "Camp in field" as heavy musketry sounds off toward Yorktown, Henry tells his brother James he has been keeping a pocket diary — 28 dated entries recording "everything that transpires from day to day." Two days earlier his company double-quicked a mile expecting a fight; a captured rebel in gray overcoat looked on "very sullen." He urges James toward West Point, yet still asks him to mind the cows and horse, hoping to be home next summer.
movements.transcription:
Camp in field
April 6, 1862

Dear James:

I was very glad to receive a few lines from you. Today is very chilly but not very cold. I have seen a great deal more of the country than I thought I would, and I am very likely to see more, but if I ever go around the country again I would rather take a different way than to foot it, but I have stood it pretty well thus far.

The day before yesterday we expected to have a fight. We went on a double quick for about a mile. A good many fell out, but most of our Co. kept together. If we ever go into a fight away goes my knap-sacks, but they are the best friend we have except our guns at night, for it is quite cold here at night.

A rebel prisoner was taken by some of our troops the other day. He was very well dressed — had a gray overcoat, light cap, black pants. He looked very sullen. There are a great many troops around here. If the rebels keep on as they have they will soon get into a place where they will have to fight or surrender. I do not think they have much courage. They are doing themselves more harm than good by holding out as they have.

I forgot to mention that I have been keeping a pocket diary, write down everything that transpires from day to day. I have 28 dates. Take good care of the cows and horse. I shall be home next summer I hope.

If you get into West Point you will probably have an office in the army. I hope you will succeed. I have nothing more to write this time. There was some heavy firing of musketry last night at York Town, or off in that direction. Cooper has not left yet so I shall mail both letters. Write often. I remain your aff. brother,

Henry

P.S. Afternoon. It is raining now. Our tents are made of rubber blankets. I would not object to having a few sleigh rides.

movements.sigSummary: From a nameless "Camp in field" sixteen miles from Hampton, Henry tells his mother how his regiment spent the Sabbath detailed as pioneers — axes, picks, and shovels cutting fresh roads for the artillery through woods the retreating rebels had felled ahead of Yorktown. He records Gen. Gorman's cold counsel to keep cool in action "and not to mind if brother or cousin fell, but to go ahead," then, glimpsing McClellan twice and Virginia trees in blossom, confesses the whole campaign "is all like a dream."
movements.transcription:
April 6th, 1862

Dear Mother:

I received your letter last night and was glad to hear from home. I have to take my chance to write just when I can. Ink is very scarce here. I wrote a letter some time ago but did not have a chance to mail it. I hope to mail this day after tomorrow. I shall write just as often as I can.

Yesterday I had really a hard time. It was the Sabbath, our Regt. was detailed as pioneers with axes, picks and shovels. I used an ax. It was not the work that I did, but it was the marching four or five miles to the place where we were wanted. Between here and York Town the rebels blocked the roads up pretty well (in the woods we had to make new roads for the artillery and troops to march. We expected to have a fight day before yesterday and left Hampton with that intention, but we have not had it yet nor are we likely to. The rebels seem to be retreating everywhere our troops go. I believe there was some fighting though at York Town day before yesterday by the artillery. Have not heard much about it yet. I do not think the rebels will make much of a stand there. There was a great light off in that direction not long since. Some thought that York Town was on fire. We will probably go there before long. Gen. Gorman gave us some very good advice. He told us if we ever came into action to keep cool and not to mind if brother or cousin fell, but to go ahead. We have the best rifles in the service. I do not think there is any probability of our going into action. I do not know what the name of the place that we are in, but I shall call it Camp in field, for that is where we are, about 16 miles from Hampton. We left that place day before yesterday. Gen. McClellan is now at the head of the army out here, or at least out this way. I have seen him twice. He is a young looking man.

The rebels have taken a great deal of pains by throwing up intrenchments along here, but all to no purpose. They were in camp here last winter about two miles from here. Their barracks are very good — much better than we had. In regard to their grub — I do not see why they could not live as well as our troops.

It is very chilly today. The air is very heavy at night. When I march I am always sure to sweat. I have seen several trees in blossom since I left Washington. I should like to be at home and take a sleigh ride. I hope the cows and horses at home will have enough hay and straw. I must confess it is all like a dream, my being here, but if I ever go home I can say that I have seen a good deal of the world, by hard marching.

Write as often as you can. I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

P.S. Always address my letters to Washington and I will be sure to receive them.

movements.letterExcerpt: Your welcome letter I received and very glad was I to hear from you. I am not sure that this letter will go through as there has been a stop put to letter writing, but that was some time ago.
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp sixteen miles from Fortress Monroe after his regiment took the boat from Alexandria, Henry reports the rebels holding York Town but "getting pretty well surrounded," and expects to march there any day for "a little skirmish." He passes along an enslaved man's account that the rebels fled "on a double quick" at word of the Union advance, dismisses them as "a cowardly set," then closes hoping to be home next June, "if the war is over."
movements.transcription:
April 9th, 1862
Camp of the 34th Regt.

Dear Aunt:

Your welcome letter I received and very glad was I to hear from you. I am not sure that this letter will go through as there has been a stop put to letter writing, but that was some time ago.

The weather for some time past has been very pleasant, but for the last two or three days, we have had a drissling rain and it has been quite cold. The weather has not changed yet. We have our rubber blankets for tents.

We are now sixteen miles from Fortress Monroe. Our Regt. and Brigade took the boat at Alexandria. We had very pleasant weather while we were coming except one night it rained. The rebels have possession now of York Town, but they are getting pretty well surrounded and will have to give up before long. I think the rebels are a cowardly set and will run if they see danger ahead. At Hampton the rebels have burnt a great many buildings, only a very few left, but Harpers Ferry is the place where they have been most to work, and where the greatest damage is done. I expect any day we may march to York Town and perhaps have a little skirmish. We are good for them any time. I heard that when the rebels knew that we were on the march for this place they left on a double quick so one of their slaves said.

The rebels have very good barracks, much better than we have had, but they have lost them now. I expect you hear more of the news than I for we do not have any papers except what we receive from home. I received a letter from home not long since. The snow is very deep, six feet in the woods. I expect they will have a freshet this spring. I hope to be home next June — that is if the war is over.

I have nothing more to write this time. Believe me to remain your aff. Nephew,

Henry

movements.sigSummary: At Camp Niles by the Relay House, eighteen-year-old Corporal Alexander frets that the war's "late great victories" may end before he can prove how well he can shoot and use his sabre bayonet: "I should feel rather cheap to come home without having been in one battle at least." He dutifully sends ten dollars home, vowing of his brother's education, "cost money what it may I shall have one."
movements.transcription:
April 11, 1862
Camp Niles, Relay House

My dear Brother:

Pretty near time to answer your letter. Don't you think so? Well, I came to that conclusion some time since, but we have been moving about so much of late that I have barely found time to write a few short letters home.

Well — now for the news. I expect our Regt. will not be guarding this road much longer. Lieut. White said this morning that he thought we should have a chance to see the rebels. I hardly know what to think about it. I hope we shall, but from these late great victories I have been almost led to think that the war is about over. Memphis is certainly done for and New Orleans, Mobile, Yorktown, Norfolk and Savannah will soon be. I don't see what the rebels have to hold on to. Their capital, Richmond, will probably soon be in McClellan's hands. It seems strange that Yorktown, once invested by the forces under Washington and DeRochambeau, should again be invested by American troops. The natural supposition would be that if it ever was again beseiged it would be by foreigners. Who would have thought at that time that these same Southerners from whose cities we were endeavoring to drive out the enemy would ever turn against their Northern brethren. The curse of God it seems to me must be upon their undertaking.

How do home matters progress? How does James get along with his studies at West Point? Do you think he will pass examination? Oh! how mortified I should be if he did not. He must put his "best foot" forward. How much sugar have you received from your sugar maker? I hope he will not prove to be a rascal though Mother seems to think he is.

It will soon be time for Company drill, after which comes dress parade. We have a very fine band of music. Do you remember "Gussy Acorn"? I presume you do. Well, he is a member of the band. His real name is Augustus Hammel. Guess I had better bring my letter to close, as I have not much more time to write. I am very well. Luther also is well. I took a prisoner down to Baltimore the other day. Went down and came back on the cars. I had a pleasant little jaunt. Direct as usual.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander

P.S. We are to have Battallion drill instead of Company. (Battallion drill means Regimental.)

---

April 15, 1862
Relay House

My Dear Mother:

Received your very welcome letter Sunday and was very much pleased to hear from you. What do you now think of the "Rebel Cause"? I think it is pretty near "gone up". There is only one thing that causes me sorrow — i.e. I am afraid I shall never have an opportunity to show the rebels how well I can shoot, and how well I can use my sabre bayonet. It seems a pit to see such good weapons lying idle.

We now have battallion drill and will soon be ready for the field. There are four companies here: two near Baltimore, two at Annapolis Junction and two on the road. All the Companies still do guard duty on the road. Between seventy and eighty men are sent our from here each day. The Companies at Annapolis Junction and near Baltimore also have battallion drill. It is the opinion of some that it will not be long before we will be sent to the field. I should feel rather cheap to come home without having been in one battle at least, but from present appearances I am afraid I shall be obliged to. Nevertheless I have this to comfort me. I have done all they have asked us to do, and we have probably done as hard duty as any Regt. in the field. It seems a pity to keep such a fine Regt. as this on a railroad. How I wish our Regt. had been at Pittsburgh Landing. We would have made the sparks fly I can tell you.

One of the 10th Maine Regt. was killed by the cars the first day we were here. Some of our men went as an escort to the body. They fired three volleys, "the farewell shot", over the grave. Our band was also present. It was a very solemn sight. The band (I do not think I am mistaken) went first, after whom came the escort with arms reversed, then the coffin and lastly those soldiers who chose to go. If the 10th -------- had been here the whole Regt. would have probably been present at the funeral.

Wonder how Mr. Timothy Hoyle is: hope he is better. It would be a public calamity if he should die. I think James owes a great deal to him and his brother. Hope he will "put in" and show himself worthy of the confidence placed in him. It is worth a great struggle. Tell James to "put in" if it is only to spite that little Doolittle. I can never forget what he said. Would like to flog him "first rate" and will when I come home if he says much.

Evening    The Lieut. Colonel drilled the Regt. this afternoon (4 companies). I think we did pretty well. He put us through "right well" (as the people say around here.) It is real fun to hear them talk, "A right smart day, I recon" is a very common expression.

My position in the Company is upon the extreme left; quite an important place. The reason that I am there is because I am the smallest Corporal in the Company. I go by the name, among the other Companies, of "the little Corporal". I don't think I am so very small. Do you?

Wonder what you are doing this evening. Oh! how I should like to be there with you all. How my tongue would fly. I expect to be there in two or three months at the most. Oh how I long for my books. Nevertheless I am content. I expect the pay master will be here soon to pay us off. I must pay that pew tax and for those buffalo robes. Tell James to take extra good care of them.

Our Regt. received marching orders, but General Niles wrote to have them countermanded. Our Colonel has gone to Washington, to prevent this, I expect. I hope we shall move. If we do I think we will go to Fort Corcoran. Good night. The drums are beating for roll call. Good night and pleasant dreams to you all. I sleep upon the soft side of a board and like it.

April 18th. We are to be paid off today. Pretty near time I think as it is nearly four months since we received pay. We will be paid up to the first of March today. We will be mustered in again for pay soon as two months pay will be due us the first of May. I can send home but ten dollars this time as lending that five dollars has "played the dragon" with me. I never thought I was such a fool. I bought a pair of boots last winter (winter — I hardly realise we have had winter) of the sutler and paid four dollars for them. They have proved to be a very good pair. I have them yet and had them tapped the other day. (I pay for the boots out of the money we receive today. On account of lending that five dollars I have the little expenses of six months to pay. I have all my money matters out in "white and Black". The Lieut. has just handed me a letter from you I know. Now for reading it.

We are still under marching orders and I should not be at all surprised if we went to Fortress Monroe. The 10th Maine formerly stationed here is now at Harpers Ferry. One thing is very certain — we will never stay here. Your letters do me real substantial good. I have a very formidable package of them. I received a letter from Willie Savage a day or two since. They seem to be prospering. Luther is quite unwell today. I hope is not going to be sick, if he is I shall take extra good care of him. The ten dollars I send home I give you. Pay the pew tax or do what you please with it.

Your affectionate Son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

---

On same sheet — Dear Brother James:

Am very glad you have at last condescended to write me an anyways decent letter. What good spirit prompted you to do it? I hope you may often have such promptings. You say you will need ninety or one hundred dollars to get an outfit for West Point. You are welcome to all I possess. We shall be paid off again soo and I shall try and send at least twenty dollars to you. You need have no fears for me. If my life and health are with me I shall have an education. Cost money what it may I shall have one.
movements.notes: Multi-day: Apr 11, 15, 18 (to Mother), 18 (to James on same sheet)

movements.letterExcerpt: In Camp within three miles of York Town
movements.sigSummary: Writing his brother Charles from camp three miles outside Yorktown, Henry relays his first secondhand battle reports — a repulsed rebel assault on a Union battery and a Vermont regiment so badly hit one company was left with "only twenty." Carried across eight days, the letter closes with a rebel dawn attack and a sharpshooter shot down. "Nothing livens me up more than to hear the firing cannon," Henry confesses — a green soldier still hungry for the fight he hasn't yet faced.
movements.transcription:
April 18th, 1862
In Camp within three miles of York Town

Dear Charles:

I was very glad to receive a letter from you. I believe I owe you two letters, therefore I shall write a long one this time.

We are beginning to have pretty warm weather now. I find it so when marching with my Knap Sack. A good many have thrown their over coats away, and some threw blankets, shirts, pants, but I have kept mine thus far and mean to. We have no Co. cook, but each one has his ration dealt out to him. A great many would not have it otherwise. Half of the Co. went in for having their rations cooked, the other wanted it cooked. For my part I would rather have a Co. cook, but we all do our cooking, boil our coffee in our tin cups and cook our rations the best way we can. I do not like it at all.

Last Sabbath I worked all day fixing roads. 25 were detailed from our Regt. It was for the purpose to have the artillery and rations to come through. Last night our Regt. was called up into line. I expected as much as could be to have a little skirmishing and have a chance to discharge my piece, but disappointed, but we may have before long. I hear so many stories I do not know hardly what to believe, but as far as I can understand the rebels tryed to capture our battery but were repulsed with some claughter. I think this must be true for a person that was in the action gave the report. One of the Vermont Regts. was in the fight. I heard that out of one of the Co. only twenty- were left, but I do not know how true that is. I also heard that the rebels lay all around dead. I have been keeping a Journal now for some time — have about thirty dates. I shall send you a copy one of these days. Nothing livens me up more than to hear the firing cannon and musketry. The rebels will ketch it before the war is over.

I have received two pair of shoes from the Government, not counting what I received in Albany. I have had bill of clothing but that was not put in what I received in Albany. My clothing and everything that I have received since I left Albany amounts to $20.58. Of course what we do not receive now we have when the war is over — also rations. I believe every Co. has a fund, as far as I understand it.

I get very lonesome sometimes and also very tierd, and I should but wonder, lazy now and then. It is a very idle life for me. All I have to do is to look after myself. I find it difficult to keep clean when marching. Yesterday I had a good wash all over — felt first rate after that. I enjoy pretty good health now. The cannon is fired every half hour at night to let the enemy know, I suppose, where we are. Last night we lay out with our rifles ready for them any time. I should not wonder if you would like soldiering for a while, but you would soon get tired of it. Look out for the Sugar man. I almost wish you were a soldier. Write often. I remain your aff. brother,

Henry

Could you send me a few postage stamps. I have no franked envelopes.

April 24th — I shall have more to write when we get into York Town. I did not have a chance to see the Fort at Fortress Monroe. I saw a steamer that the rebels disabled last spring called the Cheese-box. I saw no very large ships.

Saturday — the 26th: The rebels made an attack this morning quite early, but I think they must have got the worst of it. Our sharp shooters pick off the rebels pretty fast. Lately one of our sharp shooters got wounded pretty bad. There have been several of our men wounded. Rains about all the while here. Makes us quite cold.
movements.notes: Multi-part: Apr 18, 24, 26. Major letter from siege lines.

movements.sigSummary: From the Yorktown siege lines on April 21st, 1862, Henry writes his brother James that the regiment's drums and band have gone silent "for fear that the rebels will find us out and throw shells into our camp," and recounts a driving-rain midnight alarm when the New York 2nd's pickets, attacked in force, refused to be driven in. Between arms inspections and drills, he confesses he often thinks with pleasure of the spring he and James made maple sugar at home.
movements.transcription:
April 21st, 1862 — Monday
Camp near York Town

Dear James:

When I sat down to answer your letter I almost forgot and thought it was Charles that wrote the letter, you have improved so much in writing. I guess you have been practicing some. Keep on and you will be a good pennman.

As I am writing I can hear the rain beat on my tent. We have had a driving rain for some time. By the by, we have new tents, (the whole Regt). They are only made for summer, are not tall enough to stand in. They are made of linnin. We will have to carry them when we march.

York Town is still in possession by the rebels, but we are preparing for them and will give them a good shpping one of these days. The drums are not beat morning nor does the band play for fear that the rebels will find us out and throw shells into our camp. Night before last our Regt. was routed up (driving rain in the bargain) by the heavy firing musketry. It seems the rebels attacked the New York 2nd Regt. Two of their companies were on Picket, and the rebels tryed very hard to drive them in, but did not make out. One of the New York 2nd said there was a thousand of them, but I do not believe it. An order has been read that if the pickets are attacked again the pickets are to fall back on their reserve and then to have reinforcements and drive them back (the rebels).

I have just been cleaning my gun. We have inspection of arms every night at five o'clock and every morning we are obliged to be up at four with guns and drill till day light. It has cleared off some since morning. I would not think much of walking three or four miles to the sugar bush if I was at home, every morning and night for I would be sure of having a good night's rest, but here we are liable to be called up any time, but then there are better days coming. I can lay out all night on the ground and not have a cold. I often think of the time you and I made sugar last spring with pleasure. I thought then it was rather hard, but it is nothing to what I have been through, or may. Nothing more to write this time. Write often.

I remain your aff. brother,

Henry
movements.notes: Written Monday; Henry notes day of week

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp of the 34th Near York Town
movements.sigSummary: Writing from the siege lines near Yorktown, Henry pins down his place in the army — Sedgwick's Division, Gorman's Brigade — and watches a balloon rise each day to spy on the rebel works while McClellan rides past. But the war he describes is quieter: three hours on picket in a dark, rainy night, hearing rebels "pounding and sawing" at their works just beyond sight. Even there, his mind drifts home to the horses, the cattle, and a farm with no one to see to it.
movements.transcription:
April 21st, 1862
Camp of the 34th Near York Town

Dear Mother:

I received your very welcome letter and was glad to hear from home. We belong to Sedgwick's Division, Gorman Brigade. We have had orders to be ready for marching at a moment's notice. Two days rations in our haversacks. All has been still and quite for a day or two. Our Regt. was on picket the night before last. It was a dark rainy night, could hardly see my hand before me. I stood three hours on my post with gun in hand. We could hear the rebels at work, pounding and sawing, probably strengthening their works. How lonesome, dark and dreary, standing on guard in such a night.

I have seen Gen. McClellan several times since we have been here. He is a splendid looking fellow, smiling countenance, rides a fine horse. He has a body guard of about two hundred cavalry. A large balloon has been going up every day to overlook the rebels. We live pretty well now but the cooking does not go right. Our cook is not just exactly the article. I received the fine comb from Charles. I received a paper from Alexander but no letter.

I had four letters to read the other day that came altogether. Plumer would do to hire for a few days but I would not put much confidence in him for a farm. Would it not be well to see about hiring? I fear the farm will suffer on account of no one to see to things. I hope the horses and cattle are well. I worry about these things a good deal. It is all right about the sugar bush. I hope you will not worry about me for I am well and have been since I have been in Virginia and have not taken any cold. It is rather warm here. I wish I could be at home to help you but I can't be everywhere. When I think of the good times I have had at home it seems like a dream. Write often for I like to have a letter from home to read very much.

Your aff. Son,

Henry

April 24th — There is every appearance that we shall have a move before long. We are now cooking by Co. which is a good thing. The Brigade goes on picket tomorrow. How soon after that we shall march is uncertain.

April 26th — Our Co. was on picket yesterday. We were relieved this morning. A little before day there was some firing, probably half an hour brisk. I could see the flash of the cannon — close enough for all practical purposes. They threw some shells — one burst quite near. Write often.
movements.notes: Multi-part: Apr 21, 24, 26

movements.sigSummary: Promoted: their colonel, "a desendent of old revolutionary hero General Green," has been made Brigadier General of Volunteers — and word reaches camp that New Orleans has fallen, "the heaviest blow that has been struck at the rebels since the war commenced." But the letter's heart is Alexander's wounded reply to his mother: "I am astonished and ashamed that you have so poor an opinion of me. I should not be ashamed to die in such a cause."
movements.transcription:
May 1st, 1862
Camp Niles, Relay House

Dear Mother and Brothers:

I am well, Luther is well and all is well. Our Colonel has been promoted to Brigadier General of Volunteers. His name is General Green, a desendent of old revolutionary hero General Green. He certainly is a good officer and a strict disciplinarian. I like him very much. We are still under marching orders but they have been countermanded again. There has been a good deal of excitement in camp today. New Orleans has been captured. It is the heaviest blow that has been struck at the rebels since the war commenced.

You say in your letter Mother that you "repent by this time that you ever went to the war." Why Mother, I am astonished and ashamed that you have so poor an opinion of me. I enlisted to serve three years or during the war. My enlistment was not the act of a moment. I gave the matter days and weeks of consideration and since I have been a soldier I have never for an instant regretted the step I took. On the contrary, I glory in it. I should not be ashamed to die in such a cause. I do not want you to feel that way about it.

One of the prisoners was shot through the leg the other day by one of the sentinels accidentally. It was also reported that one of Co. A's men was shot and instantly killed by one of his friends accidentally. The man who shot him tried to kill himself. There is a good deal of such carelessness in the army.

I will give you an account of what I have spent since I have been in the army:

Sutler — $5.00
Luther — $3.00
Washing — 40¢
Ayes — 50¢
Bond — 27¢
Stems — 25¢
Powers — 10¢
Myers — 10¢
White — 10¢
Bascomb — 10¢
Long — 5¢
Vaughan — 3¢

That is every cent I have spent or loaned in six months. I should not have spent a cent at the sutler's if the rations had been sufficient but they were not. I gave Luther three dollars — he was in need of it. I think I have done pretty well.

Frances — Luther's letter is enclosed. Write often.

Your affectionate Son and Brother,

Alexander
movements.notes: Major letter; emotional and financial detail

movements.letterExcerpt: We have just been paid off for two months. I shall send twenty dollars home. Peter Guyan tapped my boots — one dollar. Sutler — one dollar. Cook — fifty cents. That leaves me three dollars and fifty c...
movements.sigSummary: Newly paid for two months at Fortress Monroe's Camp "Windfield Scott," Henry mails $20 home by express and accounts for every cent that remains — a dollar to tap his boots, fifty cents to the cook, three-fifty to spend as he pleases. Opposite a rebel fort our men raise a tower under daily shelling, and Henry rises before daylight braced for an attack he senses is coming. The Sabbath, he notes, goes unkept like any other day.
movements.transcription:
May 1st, 1862 — Thursday
Fortress Monroe
Camp Windfield Scott

Dear Mother:

We have just been paid off for two months. I shall send twenty dollars home. Peter Guyan tapped my boots — one dollar. Sutler — one dollar. Cook — fifty cents. That leaves me three dollars and fifty cents to spend as I please. Emerson Smith has used all his wages up. I have drawn one pair of shoes and one pair of drawers.

There is a report in camp that there are fifteen thousand prisoners near here. A rebel fort is near by. Our men are building a tower right opposite the rebel fort. Shells are thrown into it every day. There is a great deal of excitement in camp. I think there will be a move before long.

Saturday — I mailed the twenty dollars by express. The express man charged fifty cents. I was on special duty today felling timber. We do that and everything else that comes along. I have been thinking of subscribing for the Plattsburgh paper — it is only ten cents a week. As far as I can see the Sabbath is not kept any more than any other day. I suppose God will not hold us accountable for what we cannot help. We are up before daylight every morning ready for an attack. Nothing more this time.

Your aff. Son,

Henry
movements.notes: Multi-part: May 1 (Thursday), May 3 (Saturday)

movements.letterExcerpt: I enclose twenty dollars by express. I was on picket today. There was heavy cannonading this morning about four o'clock. The rebel fort is to be seen from our camp. Write often.
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp near York Town on May 1st, Henry encloses twenty dollars by express and tells his mother of a rebel fort plainly visible from his lines and heavy cannonading at four that morning. He scrawled the note between turns at picket, signing only "H.H." and closing with a son's plea to "write often."
movements.transcription:
May 1st

Dear Mother:

I enclose twenty dollars by express. I was on picket today. There was heavy cannonading this morning about four o'clock. The rebel fort is to be seen from our camp. Write often.

Your aff. Son,

H.H.
movements.notes: Short note enclosing $20
Battle of Williamsburg. 34th NY engaged in pursuit.
