movements.sigSummary: Inside the abandoned Confederate fortifications at Yorktown — "immense and very strong," sandbags head-high — Henry writes from a captured rebel tent, marveling at the strongest works he has ever seen. He recounts his hardest night of soldiering: an all-night march through driving rain and deep mud, halting every ten paces behind stacked divisions, back to camp by two in the morning. The retreating enemy buried shells underfoot, and some of his men have already been hurt by them.
movements.transcription:
May 6th, 1862
In the Rebels Camp Ground
York Town, Va.

Dear Mother:

The rebels have evacuated York Town. Their fortifications are immense and very strong. I think they are great cowards. Our Regt. went into the rebel intrenchments early Sabbath morning. They had sand bags built up as high as a man's head in some places. Their tents are very good, some of them, much better than ours. I am writing in one of the rebel tents.

We had a night march in a hard rain and deep mud. It was awful. We stopped every ten paces it seemed to me, several divisions being ahead of us. We marched all night and came back to camp about two o'clock in the morning. It was the hardest night I have seen since I have been a soldier.

I expect we shall cross the James River before long. The rebels left shells for us to step on. Some of our men were hurt by them. They are the most cowardly enemy I have ever heard of. I should think they would be ashamed.

Nothing more to write this time. Write often.

Your aff. Son,

Henry
movements.notes: Written from inside rebel fortifications
Battle of Eltham's Landing / West Point. 34th NY engaged.

movements.letterExcerpt: I believe this is the first letter I have written to you since I left home, almost a year ago. I am now at a place called West Point, not West Point where the Military Academy is, but a place on the Y...
movements.sigSummary: Writing his sister Frances for the first time in nearly a year, Henry reports his regiment's crowded boat passage from newly evacuated Yorktown to West Point, Virginia — a landing on the York River, he is careful to note, not the Military Academy — about thirty miles from Richmond. He marvels at the rebels' vast abandoned earthworks and dates the Yorktown bombardment to Wednesday, April 16, then promises once more to send the journal he has kept of the campaign.
movements.transcription:
May 9th, 1862
West Point
Camp Windfield Scott

Dear Frances:

I believe this is the first letter I have written to you since I left home, almost a year ago. I am now at a place called West Point, not West Point where the Military Academy is, but a place on the York River, twenty or thirty miles from York Town and I should think about thirty from Richmond. We left York Town on the seventh on a large boat — the whole Regt. on one boat. We were very much crowded.

York Town has been evacuated by the rebels. Their intrenchments and breastworks are very large and extensive. Our artillery commenced firing on Wednesday the sixteenth of April. I have kept a journal of our doings here and will send you a copy one of these days. It will give you a better idea of what we have been doing than a letter.

Royal Corbin and George are here in the 16th Regt. I saw them the other day. Sid is also here. I was very glad to see them.

Write often. I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: We are now twenty five or thirty miles from Richmond. We came from York Town to this place on one boat, about six hours. The place where Cornwallis surrendered was pointed out to me. It was a great si...
movements.sigSummary: From West Point on the York River, twenty-five to thirty miles from Richmond, Henry is shown the spot where Cornwallis surrendered — "a great sight," the Revolution's ground now ringed again by American troops. Word reaches him of the 16th Regiment's skirmish, one company losing sixteen. Then his thoughts turn back to the farm, his mother's summer, and a newspaper stolen before he could finish it.
movements.transcription:
May 9th, 1862
West Point on the York River

Dear Mother:

We are now twenty five or thirty miles from Richmond. We came from York Town to this place on one boat, about six hours. The place where Cornwallis surrendered was pointed out to me. It was a great sight. The 16th Regt. has been in a skirmish. I heard that one of the companies lost sixteen, several were wounded. George Corbin and Royal shook hands with me. I was very glad to see them.

How do things get along at home? I hope the garden and farm will be attended to. I worry about these things. I think the farm had better be let out on shares. If you could spend the summer at Charlotte it would be very pleasant and much better for you. I hope you will make a visit it will do you so much good. How does Sid come on with his farming. I am afraid he will not make much of a farmer. Silas, I suppose, has a good deal of business by this time.

Write all the news and do not feel anxious if you do not happen to hear from me regularly, for the mail doesn't go very regular. I have not received a paper from home since I left Hampton, and that was stolen before I read half of it. I shall send part of my Journal next time.

Your aff. Son,

Henry
movements.notes: Complete — continues from p40 to p41

movements.sigSummary: At Camp Niles by the Relay House, Alexander tells his anxious mother the railroad will revert to the Company by mid-month and the regiment will soon be discharged — a lieutenant wagering $25 to $1 on it within a month. He reassures her ("We are all in Gods hands") and recounts the band of the Sixtieth answering a heckling Baltimore secessionist with a furious blast of Yankee Doodle, stones gathered to throw if he showed his head again.
movements.transcription:
May 10th, 1862
Camp Niles Relay House

My Dear Mother:

I received your very welcome letter a few days since and immediately wrote one in answer, but did not mail it and on looking it over today I tore it up on acct. of something I stated as certain and have since found it to be a mere rumor.

This railroad will be given up to the Company the fifteenth or twentieth of this month by the Government, and consequently we will no longer be needed here. One of the Lieuts. offered to lay a wager of $25 to $1 (I believe) that our regt. would be discharged within a month. One thing is quite certain, we will not be in service much longer. I am now very anxious to get home as James leaves so soon. I don't mean for you to understand that I am at all sorry I enlisted. I have never for one moment regretted it. I do not wish to return home until this war is over; until this rebellion is crushed and completely crushed. I want to see these Southern braggarts humbled. The Rebels will soon be driven to their "last ditch". I expect there will be great news on Monday. McClellan seems to be pressing pretty hard.

Wonder what sort of weather you are having up there. We seldom have very much warmer weather there in July than we are having here today. We have no drill or inspection here on Saturdays, but are obliged to turn out for dress parade at half after four P.M. How strange it will seem to me when I return home not to be obliged to be present at roll call; not obliged to get a pass when I wish to go anywhere away from the door yard. We are kept in very close, but it does not trouble me at all as I have very little occasion to go outside the camp. One of our men received the sentence of a court-martial yesterday. (He was absent twentyfour hours from camp without leave.) It was this — "That said John Pickle having been found guilty of the charges brought against him be sentenced to lose one half of two months pay (13 dollars)".

Mother I am sorry you worry so much. There is no use in it at all, at all. You must not do it. We are all in Gods hands. He will do as He thinks best. Do you think I have forgotten my Mother, my brothers and sister? No! never, never, never. Forget you indeed — I am astonished, shocked to hear such a thing. — Well, I guess you had the blues when you wrote that, eh? I shall try and write oftener. I have but very little leisure. Our time is so fully occupied with the drill and guard duty. Still I can always find time to write you. Now, Mother, why don't you write me oftener? There were nine days interval between your last two letters. Never fear, Mother, I have not forgotten you. McClellan is giving it to the rebels "right smart" and I expect I shall soon be home.

So you have let out the "plowed land" to Portray, eh? Pretty good plan I guess, only I don't like the pony part of it. Perhaps my fears are groundless. Tell J. and C. to keep a sharp lookout and see that he is not abused. Now Mother don't you let out the cows or garden or any of the land around home. Get a boy by all means and immediately and when you get one get a good one if you do have to pay him higher wages. I will pay him and am only too glad to do it. I shall in all probability be home soon an then you will need the boy no longer. I shall take matters into my own hands and see how nice I can make everything look.

You and I must go and see Grandmother McNiel, and Aunt Jenny. Wonder why she don't answer my last letter. I shall always keep the letter she wrote me. I prize it very much. Wish she would write me another. Grandmother is a real patriot and well worthy of her daughter who has sent two sons to the war.

Secure pasturage, Mother, if you can at Dodds. Don't have anything to do with the "gentleman" who is afraid of a gun. He is a very dangerous fellow, certainly. Wonder if he isn't afraid of a firecracker. Suppose he means to errify people with one of his awfully ferocious looks. If he gets to be very troublesome just put the word "Gunpowder" on your gate and you won't see him again very soon! I don't believe. How does S. P. Hubbell, attorney-at-law, Champlain, get along? Has he got to be justice of the peace yet? Those are two noble patriots, eh? Wonder when they will be ready to get out of their mothers lap?

I have just returned from "dress parade". Tell Charley to add to what I mentioned in my last letter 75 cents for tapping boots, one dollar for the band, 25 cents for a brass drum for our little drummer. We have a splendid band. Their instruments cost over nine hundred dollars. There are probably very few bands in the field superior to "the band of the Sixtieth." They have serenaded (how do you spell it) quite a number in Baltimore, and were very highly praised by the papers. One night while playing in Baltimore a secessionist stuck his head out of a window and began blatting. This made them furious and they immediately struck up with all their might Yankee Doodle. He said no more. They offered the rebel a large sum if he would only come down. As it was they took up stones to hit him if he showed his head again, but the fellow thought it was not quite prudent. A very wise conclusion.

We have battalion drill every day except Saturdays and Sundays. We were drilled in firing yesterday. Each man was supplied with ten rounds of blank cartridges. We made a little noise and smoke. (Drawings of soldiers appear) What am I about, making pictures on my letter. Well, well. I get to thinking and forget what I am about.

You ask me in your letter if I read the 91st Psalm. I do and take great comfort in its precious promises. "God is my refuge and strength; a very present help in trouble." I try to commit all my ways to him. I have not forgotten my promise to you. I love to read the first psalm. Fathers psalm.

Tell James and Charles to write often. Love to all. Do not think I have forgotten you. Do not worry.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander F.

P.S. Look out for pony. Tell James to put in kind regards to Mr. Copeland.
movements.notes: Major letter; financial, military, personal detail

movements.sigSummary: Writing from Camp Alton near West Point, Va., Henry reckons some hundred thousand troops are massed around him and expects the 34th to move on Richmond any day, trusting that "McClellan is working slow but sure." Word reaches him that Alexander's 60th Regt. may be bound for the same place, and he aches to see his brother. Between the lines he is just a farm boy, asking who is working the garden and where the cows are pastured.
movements.transcription:
May 12, 1862
Monday — 34th Regt.
Camp Alton
West Point, Va.

Dear Mother:

I know that you are anxious to hear from me every week and oftener. I shall write a few lines to you just as often as I can. You must not be to anxious about me or Alexander, for it will do no good. I hope you will take good care of your health.

I am very anxious to know where the cows and horse are pastured, but I forgot that vegetation is not so fast up home as it is here. The weather is very warm here, but the nights are cold.

I have not received an answer to the money or from the money that I sent. I expect a letter tomorrow. There is a good deal of card playing going on in out Co. for money. I shall never take a fancy to card playing nor gambling, or anything else. I expect every day we shall move, probably to Richmond. Since I wrote last we have moved three miles from where we were. We are now near a river called the ———. It empties into the York River. I should judge from the looks and from what I have heard, there are about one hundred thousand troops encamped around here. I have heard that the 60th Regt. was on its way for this place. Alexander will get tired of it when he comes to march as much as I have. I shall be very glad to see him. If the war continues as successful as it has lately, seems to me it can not last a great while. McClellan is working slow but sure, which I think is the best way.

Write and let me know who is working the garden. I am very glad that Mrs. Brinkhoff is coming back. It will be much pleasanter for you. What time does James leave for West Point?

The sutler charges 50 cts. for fresh butter — everything else in proportion, but then it costs him a good deal to bring his goods here. He, of course, must make something. I do not go in very deep. I don't care much about it anyway. Write soon.

Your aff. Son

Henry

(On same letter) 13th The weather today is very warm — as warm as it is at home in July. I do not like the South as well as I do the North thus far. The river that we are on is very crooked. Steamboats are passing and going all the while.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander crosses the river and "for the first time planted our feet on the sacred soil of Virginia," writing in haste on his knapsack on the ground at Harpers Ferry. The rebels are not far distant, spies already captured, and a battle is expected — yet he reports himself in excellent health and spirits. In the same breath he tells Mother he has sent James twenty dollars, a brother's promise kept even on the edge of a fight.
movements.transcription:
May 27, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My dear Mother —

I must write you at least two or three words. I am now sitting writing on my knapsack sitting on the ground. We crossed the river this morning and for the first time planted our feet on the sacred soil of Virginia. We are in some expectation of a battle. The rebels are not far distant. We have captured a number of spies. I am in excellent health and spirits. I have sent James 20 dollars. Love to all.

Your affectionate son

Alexander
movements.notes: Short letter; first from Virginia

movements.letterExcerpt: I must write you at least a few lines. We do not know how soon the rebels may attack us. We slept on our arms last night and have done so ever since we have been here. Our batteries opened on the rebe...
movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes his mother from Harpers Ferry having slept on his arms every night since arrival, the regiment called out nearly nightly behind a powerful battery: "It does me good to hear our shells shriek and howl over our heads." As Union guns prepare to shell the town and clear out rebel sharpshooters, the few remaining inhabitants are warned to leave. His verdict on it all, in three words: "Such is war." He signs, for the first time, Corporal Hubbell.
movements.transcription:
May 31st, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother —

I must write you at least a few lines. We do not know how soon the rebels may attack us. We slept on our arms last night and have done so ever since we have been here. Our batteries opened on the rebels strongly yesterday and set them scampering in fine style from some heights they had the boldness to show themselves on. A part of our Regt. was kept in line all last night and several times the whole Regt. was called out. Every night except one since we have been here the Regt. has been called out. We sleep in the open air. Last night we made ourselves a slight shelter to keep off the rain by spreading some tents on boards inclined against a fence. We are stationed behind a powerful battery. If the rebels do attack us, there will be an awful battle. There goes a shell from one of the batteries to keep the rebels awake. It does me good to hear our shells shriek and howl over our heads. We are about to shell the town to prevent the rebel sharpshooters from getting in and picking off our men. The few remaining inhabitants have been warned to leave. Such is war. I have once been out on picket guard. We were called in about three the next day. The rebels had begun throwing shot and shell at our camp. Our batteries replied in fine stile and I understand dismounted a rebel gun and killed several. A rebel deserter came and gave himself up to us. We sent him into Camp. When we were coming in a rebel shot struck within about ten rods of us.

I received your letter and Charles yesterday. Please write often. I do not know when I can write you again. Do not worry. My life is in God's hands. Corporal Luther sends his regards to you all. Remember me to Mrs. Brinkerhoff.

Your affectionate son
(Corporal Hubbell)
Alexander

I am enjoying excellent health and spirits.

movements.sigSummary: Marching while sick himself, Henry gently turns aside his mother's offer to come nurse him at the front — "you would be obliged to be on your feet most of the time, and I am afraid it would bring you down sick." His comrade George Dodds is so wasted "you would not know him," now hospitalized and seeking a discharge, while Henry resolves to "stand it through." He encloses ten dollars and asks who is keeping his money.
movements.transcription:
[**First part of letter missing — page 1 of PDF is blank scan**]

Continuation — June 6, 1862

be very pleasant for me if I should have to go, to be under your care, but I do not think you could stand it. You would be obliged to be on your feet most of the time, and I am afraid it would bring you down sick. There are others better able than you are.

George Dodds has run down so that you would not know him. He is in the hospital. I think he ought to have his discharge. I believe he has applied for it. I have stood the march since I have been sick better than I thought I would. I should be very glad to have a furlough, but I think it would be difficult to get one just now. I shall try to stand it through now. I hope Cyrus and Jayson will be back.

In regard to my having an instrument of music. It would be very pleasant, but I have no way of carrying it, and of course it would be in my way. We are not sure of staying in one place long. I have received no letter from James or Charles in this letter as you wrote.

Please excuse all mistakes and bad spelling. The pen is the best that I can have just now. Tell Frances I shall write when I have a good pen. I have not quite forgotten her yet. I hope James will pass. I shall send ten dollars in the letter and if it is all right send the rest next time. Please let me know who has the keeping of my money. I should like a few postage stamps if it would be convenient to send.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

movements.letterExcerpt: Well here I am at Winchester and have not yet had to shoot at the Rebels, much as I desire it. They took "leg bail" at Harpers Ferry and we have not yet caught up with them. They well merit the degree...
movements.sigSummary: At Winchester, Alexander writes his mother that he still has "not yet had to shoot at the Rebels," who "took 'leg bail'" and fled — earning, he jokes, the title F.F.V., "Free Footed Virginians." He recounts the forty-mile pursuit from Harpers Ferry: knee-deep mud, sleeping in fence corners near Charlestown "where John Brown was hung," eighteen miles in six hours under full kit. Then the surprise that lights him up — running into Albert H. Cook, "the last person I expected to see here."
movements.transcription:
June 8, 1862
Winchester, Virginia

My dear Mother:

Well here I am at Winchester and have not yet had to shoot at the Rebels, much as I desire it. They took "leg bail" at Harpers Ferry and we have not yet caught up with them. They well merit the degree of F.F.V (Free Footed Virginians.) We (our Regt.) are now doing the provost guard of the city. The General of the Rail Road Brigade is trying to get us back again, but I think General Siegel and Stow will make a few objections. If we go back I shall be furious, raving.

Well I suppose you would like to know how I stood the march of about (I believe) forty miles. I stood it "first rate". Marched into the city hall (where we are now quartered) with my Regiment to the tune of "Yankee Doodle". When we were within a few miles of the city quite a number fell out, not being able to keep up. Luther fell out.

We left Harpers Ferry last Tuesday about dark and marched nearly all night, the mud — if I say knee deep I wont much stretch the truth. We halted within a mile or two of Charlestown and rested until daylight. We threw ourselves down by the roadside and in the corners of the fences and slept until morning. It rained almost constantly. Charlestown is quite a large place. John Brown was hung there. We halted the next day about one oclock at Smithsfield and remained there until the next day. It rained all that night and all the next day and in what kind of condition do you think the roads were in? You can guess. We have no tents with us, and very few have rubber blankets, and those who have purchased them themselves. We camped in the open fields. We started early the next morning and did what I call "some tall marching". We reached Winchester a little after twelve A.M., a distance of about eighteen miles. Now dont you think to march that in about six hours is doing pretty well fro a soldier encumbered with his knapsack, haversack, canteen, cartridge box (with forty rounds of cartridges in it) rifle and bayonet. The regulation days march is fifteen miles. We beat every other regiment on the road marching. I hope our other Companies will soon join us.

Afternoon. — Who do you think I have just seen. Guess. Dont believe you can. It was the last person I expected to see here. I never was more astonished in my life. Well — I will tell you. Dont believe you can guess. It was Albert H. Cook, himself. Yes, Cook — Albert Cook. He is a fine looking fellow. I saw last night Lieut. Brinkerhoff Miner. He is about the same old sixpence. They are attached to Banks "Signal Corps". We are now in Banks Division. So Capt. Rich has been cashiered. What a pity. We are under command of Siegel but he is under Banks. Love to all. I hope we shall soon have a chance to charge bayonets on the rebels. Four hundred were brought in prisoners today. I hope James will pass. I feel very anxious.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P.S. It will make it very pleasant to have Cook so near. Write often. Do not wait for me. I shall probably have very few opportunities of writing. Direct to Winchester, Virginia. I received a letter from Henry the day we left the Ferry. (letter head bears photo of Maj. Gen. McClellan)
movements.notes: Major letter; march to Winchester; Albert Cook reunion

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp within five miles of Richmond
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond after the Battle of Fair Oaks, Henry counts himself thankful to have come through unhurt — the regiment lost 123 killed and wounded, his own Company D two killed and ten wounded. Three days sick on quinine, rebel shells whizzing into camp "a caution," he longs for one good meal at home: "even if it wasn't anything but potatoes and salt."
movements.transcription:
June 13th, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Mother:

I received your letter day before yesterday. Very glad to hear from you and know that you are well. How I long to have one good meal at home, even if it wasn't anything but potatoes and salt, anything but hard crackers. I can not bear to look at them. As for fresh meat, I cannot eat it. I often think of what a good time I will have when I am at home. I have not been well for the last three days. Could not take anything but what I would throw up. The Dr. gives quinine and pills, but they have not helped me much. I am better this morning. Do not worry about me.

I suppose you have heard before this time of the Regt. going into battle. As I wrote the day after, the papers state we lost 150, but it was 123 wounded and killed. Our Co. lost two killed and ten wounded. I cannot be too thankful coming out without being injured. Lieut. Scott, I think, has gone home, as he was wounded. He acted very brave. Most of the boys were down on him before, but now they are all for him. Lieut. Ransom has command of the Co. now, as Capt. Reich has been discharged. I wish he was back. Ransom is liked very well.

This morning the rebel battery commenced firing bomb shells into our Camp and grapeshot. A twelve pounder was picked up this morning by one of our boys. The way the balls whiz around here is a caution. We have breastworks built in front of our Camp of logs and dirt thrown up against them. We have good protection from the shells. It is probably Gen. McClellan's intention to storm that battery before long, and then for Richmond.

I wonder how Sid can be so ugly about our cows. I am shure if I was at home seems to me if I was in Sids place I would put up with almost anything, but I suppose our cows are very unruly. They would never jump over Nyes fence, I am sure. I have not received a paper from home for some time, three or four weeks. Give my respects to Mrs. Brinkhoff. Tell her I hope to be home before winter. I do not feel able to write any more just now. I remain your aff. son,

Henry
movements.notes: Battle of Fair Oaks aftermath; casualties

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp within five miles of Richmond
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp five miles from Richmond, Henry gives his brother Charles a firsthand account of the battle of Fair Oaks — the ground shaking, the firing "like a number of men felling trees, only much faster," loading while advancing through woods, and his own forty rounds fired before he ever knew anyone had fallen. A captured secesh tells of Richmond ladies who rode out in carriages to watch Yankees taken, then bore home their own wounded instead. Sick with dysentery, Henry admits he gets lonesome now and then.
movements.transcription:
June 13, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Charles:

I was very glad to hear from you and know that all is going on well at home. The weather here is very warm when it does not rain. I wish we had more of your pleasant weather and less rain, but we have to take it just as it comes. It very often happens that we have to be on picket when it rains.

You must have heard before this of the battle of Fair Oak. It was warm work there for a time. You can have no conception of how exciting it is to be in a battle. No one can except those that have been in. A perfect streak of reed placed all along the line. The firing reminds me very much of a number of men felling trees, only much faster. The ground shakes all around. All I thought of was to keep up in the ranks and load and fire. We very often had to load while advancing. I never knew till after we came out of the woods that any one was wounded or killed. There was a rebel Colonel and Gen. killed that night. Some say that there were three hundred of the rebles killed by our firing. There were two other Regiments engaged at the time besides ours. I did not go over the battle ground afterwards, but the ground was covered with the dead. I fired 40 rounds.

A secesh prisoner said that the road between here and Richmond was lined with carriages with ladies and gents. It was told them that Beauregard was going to capture six thousand Yankees and they came to look at them, but instead of looking at the Yankees they saw their own wounded pass and took the carriages to carry them in. They found it rather hot work. But I must stop, I do not feel well. I have the disentery very bad. I have not received a paper for some time. The secesh have thrown a good many shells over here this morning. One man was killed by a shell this morning at the hospital. I get perfectly disgusted with so much swearing in the Company, but I have to put up with it. I get lonesome now and then. Excuse all mistakes as I do not feel much like writing.

Yours truly,

Henry
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Battle of Fair Oaks firsthand account; Henry fired 40 rounds
Stationed near Front Royal. Picket duty in the Valley.

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp within five miles of Richmond
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp within five miles of Richmond on the first anniversary of his regiment's muster, Henry reckons that fewer than five hundred men are now fit for duty — "a long year it has been to me." Still weak from a week under the doctor's care, he relays a captured rebel's grudging awe at how fast the Yankees could load and fire, and savors how the carriages of ladies who came to watch the Union defeat were instead pressed into carrying off the Confederate wounded.
movements.transcription:
June 16th, 1862
Camp within five miles of Richmond

Dear Aunt:

It is sometime since I have written you but I hope to make up lost time. I have not been well for the last week. Been under the Dr.'s care, but I am better now and hope to be around again. Have not been in the hospital yet. The weather here is very warm most of the time.

It is a year ago yesterday since our Regt. swore in to the United States service. A long year it has been to me. Twelve more months and then our time is up. We may be discharged before that time, the sooner the better. There are not over five hundred men in the Regt. that do duty. It is needless for me to go into particulars about our Regt. going into a fight, as I wrote about it in Nellie's letter. We have had great praise from Gen. Gorman. One of the reble prisoners said he did not know how we could fire so fast, and load. They do not know the Yankees yet, but the are finding us out, to their sorrow.

Saturday, the day we had the fight, one of the rebles said their Gen. told his men to keep up courage as they were going to surmount the Yankees and take them prisoners. He said also that the road between here and Richmond was lined with carriages with ladies and Gents. to see the Yankees, but instead of seeing us, they had to take there own carriages to carry their wounded. It is my belief that they found it rather hot work.

We are having about as hard a time as we will have. Although we are not marching, hard crackers, salt junk, fresh meat I can not eat. The Sutler is sure to be around here pay day, but if there is battle, or any prospect of one, he is off.

We have breast works in front of our camp, but it is all the work of us soldiers as a matter of course.

So Uncle Henry is blessed with a boy. I am glad for his sake. I am sure for my part I would not object to a present of a few hundred, for the boys sake, and perhaps for his own good. He would not feel it much. Now I make motion we try it, but I do not want to have any responsibility. But enough of this for this time. My respects to all my friends. Excuse all mistakes with the hope of doing better next time. Believe me to remain your aff. Nephew.

Henry
movements.notes: One year of service; battle reflections

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your very, very, welcome letter last evening. It did me good to hear from you — real substantial good. I have not heard from you in a long long time. The last letter I received from you was...
movements.sigSummary: Foraging three miles from camp, Alexander climbs cherry trees "bending under their weight," bags a half-dozen fowls, fills his canteen with milk, and dresses chickens by a Virginia pasture — Union rules let him take anything a mile out unless the owner proves his loyalty in writing. "Are you not horrified to think you have a hen roost robbing son?" he teases Mother, arguing those who "precipitated war" deserve the loss.
movements.transcription:
June 17, 1862
Onikers Ferry

My Dear Mother:

I received your very, very, welcome letter last evening. It did me good to hear from you — real substantial good. I have not heard from you in a long long time. The last letter I received from you was at Harpers Ferry a day or tow before we left.

June 18th: I left off writing yesterday and went out on a pass with a squad of "the boys after cherries, and and — fresh or smoked meat. In other words, we went out after plunder. We have the privilege of taking whatever we please outside of a mile from the camp unless the proprietor has a written warrant from the commanding officer certifying that he is a good union man and that his property must not be touched.

Well now about my expedition. We went out to a very flourishing looking place some three miles from Camp and very innocently inquired of a little darkie where their cherries were. "Out in the garden" he replied. To the garden we went and found two immense trees bending under their weight of splendid ripe cherries. Up we went and eat until we could eat no more and then had succeeded in making no perceptable impression on the trees. We then went to the smoke house, but as there was little meat there we took none. We went next to the hen house and bagged a half dozen fowls and then went to the pasture where we filled our canteens with milk and dressed our fowls. The sun was getting low so we started for home. We had started with the intention of bringing home a sheep, but as we came across none on our way back we contented ourselves with what we had got. However, some of "the boys" a little after brought in a sheep and a pig. We made an excellent breakfast off our chickens this morning.

Now, dear Mother, are you not horrified to think you have a hen roost robbing son; are you not shocked. Dont believe you are for I know your good sense will come to your aid. All the provision brought to the large army under Banks is brought on wagons and you must know it is no easy thing to do this. We are now out on detached service and should suffer if we were not allowed to do this. And is it not right that those who precipitated war upon our country should be made to suffer for it.

The day before we left Winchester I went out foraging with a train (of baggage wagons) under command of a Lieut. We took a large quantity of corn, some ham and oats for the horses and from fifty to sixty bushels of wheat. I suppose you would like to know how we came here. A company from each of several regts. in our brigade were detailed to come here, also quite a strong force of cavalry. The

whole commanded by a Major of the Cavalry. We started about dark and reached here in the morning, a distance of about eighteen miles. We are here to prevent the rebels from crossing this ferry and flanking it. We, I understand, to be relieved soon by the cavalry. This ferry is on the Shenandoah River.

I gave you in my former letters a very imperfect account of our doings at Harpers Ferry. When we crossed the river we advanced to Bolivar Heights and formed our line of battle upon it. The right wing was supported by a battery of six guns (rifled) and the left by one of four. A battery supported by infantry was sent out to reconnoitre. They returned towards night. I understand they had quite a brisk time with the rebels. On the third day after our arrival the rebels opened fire on us with their artillery. I was out on picket at the time. The pickets were called in and we marched back to camp. (We did not run). One of the rebel shots struck within about ten rods of us. I suppose they sent that to show us their good will. The rebels did no harm. Their shot all stuck too low. That night we were aroused up about twelve and ordered to fall into line with all our accoutrements on. We soon had the order to "forward march" and took the direction back to the river. I was afraid we were on the retreat and felt as mad as a hornet. We halted a short distance from the ferry and formed our line of battle.

Our regt. was on the extreme right and supported one of the batteries. The next day towards night I went out with a squad back to the Heights to get some knapsacks left there by the pickets. We had not been gone from the hill more than a half or three quarters of an hour when the rebels appeared on the hill. We only went to the foot of the hill. If we had gone on top we should probably have had a few rebel pills thrown at us.

During the forenoon of that day one gun supported by (I believe) one hundred and twenty five sharp shooters from our Regt. went on the hill and had a very brisk time with the rebels. They had a very lively time and some narrow escapes — dodging rebel shells. One shell struck the wheel of the cannon and damaged it considerably. That night the rebels began planting a battery of eleven guns on the hill. Our batteries poured a perfect tempest of shot and shell upon them. They "skedaddled" in fine stile and, I understand, with considerable loss. That night I was roused up by the simultaneous discharge of two of our cannon. I gave my blanket a kick and tumbled out in short order. We were in line ready for the rebels in "no time". Several volleys were fired on the left and I thought for certain that we were to have a good battle, but no, we waited in vain. I have since learned (whether correctly or not I do not know) that the rebel skirmishers were feeling their way along, and were almost on our lines. There was scarce a night but what we were called into line — perhaps several times, sometimes all night. We were often obliged to stay in line nearly all night in a drenching rain. It would do me good to ring Silas and Sids neck, it would. It is quite well that you have sold the old cow. They have been harping about her for the last five or six years.

(Remainder of letter missing) From, Alexander

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp within Five miles of Richmond
movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond on a Sabbath afternoon, Henry confesses to his mother that he has had the dysentery "very bad," unable to do duty for over a week, reporting to the doctor each morning for quinine and pills as sickness spreads through the regiment. Yet he clings to McClellan's siege "starfing them out," even as he admits he is "about disgusted with soldiering" and dreams of home, where he means to sit down and eat nothing but potatoes.
movements.transcription:
June 22, 1862
Camp within Five miles of Richmond
Sabbath afternoon

Dear Mother:

I received your letter this morning, and very glad was I to hear from you. Nothing does me more good than to hear from home. I received the Obs. week ago today. It is very seldom that I receive a paper. I cannot see the reason as the direction is correct. I like the Observer better than any other paper. The New York Herald comes around every morning, but they are 10¢ a paper and I do not buy as I do not have the money and if I had I do not think I should buy them for they cost almost to much.

In my last letter I wrote about my health not being good, nor is it very good now, but I am better than I was. I have not been able to do duty for over a week. I go to the Dr. most every morning. He gives quinine and pills. I have had the disentery very bad. A great many in our Regt. are sick. Our Co. is on picket today, but I did not go as I do not feel able. We have hard bread and salt junk and fresh meat, coffee morning and night, soup for dinner, sometimes rice, beans and vegetable soup. I do not drink coffee, and as for hard bread, I do not eat much of that. It is very seldom that I eat meat. It is what I call pretty tough living. We have potatoes now and then. I can make them go first rate, but we do not have many of them. I shall make up for lost time when I get home. I believe I shall want to sit down and eat nothing but potatoes. The army is provided as well as it can be I suppose. I should like nothing better than to have my discharge, for your sake if nothing more. I have had about enough of it and long to be at home, but you must keep up courage. This war can not last much longer. When we arrive at Richmond they will have to give up. I take a great deal of comfort from the advice you give me in every letter. I know I have your prayers which comforts me very much. I was just thinking what a good dinner I should have if I was at home today, but there are better days coming I hope.

The rebles, from what I see in the New York Herald, are living on half rations and they are getting desperate. Most of them do not like Jeff or Beauregard and would desert if they could. There is a very large force in Richmond, not in Richmond but this side. We can hear their drums night and morning. Yesterday there was quite a skirmish between our pickets and the rebles. I have not heard the particulars yet. Our Regt. was all up in line. We very often are obliged to be up at midnight from their firing. Gen. McClellan is carrying a regular siege at Richmond now, starfing them out. I for one am about disgusted with soldiering, but I shall try to make the best of it. Take good care of your health. Do not go around to much. I am glad you dismissed the boy. He would be a great bother besides the expense. I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

I shall send extracts from my Journal next time and write to Frances.
movements.notes: Health declining; siege of Richmond; war weariness

movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp near Richmond to his brother Charles, Henry recounts a recent bayonet charge in which his regiment "pushed right in head first," halting at the woods' edge to fire low into kneeling rebels before they could volley — by his Colonel's account leaving three hundred dead and wounded. To Charles alone he confesses he is "almost tempted to desert sometimes," held back only by the disgrace and by his mother being all alone.
movements.transcription:
June 22, 1862
Camp near Richmond, Va.

Dear Charles:

I was very glad to hear from you. We are suffering a great deal from the warm weather. Have not had much rain lately. We have a very good spring half a mile from Camp. The water is very cold. Also a very good place to bathe, but not to swim. I sometimes hardly know what to do some days. I get very lonesome — lay around in my tent. I would rather be at home hard at work, be sure of coming home at night and not be routed up, but I shall have to make the best of it.

I gave a description in my last letter about the battle. You may be shure it was very exciting, but I was not frightened for we were pushed right in head first. We came to a bayonet charge just as we came to the woods. The rebles, it seems, got on to their knees. It was their intention when we came on to them to fire into us, but we halted after we had gone some ways and fired into them. We all fired very low. Our Colonel said, from the effects of our fire. Three hundred of the rebles lay dead and wounded. I should not wonder if it was so. I did not go over the field after the fight for I did not feel like it. I saw one rebel who was shot through the head. Our boys went over afterwards and said the ground was covered. I felt to tired myself. I never thought of the danger till after I was out.

I forgot to mention in Mother's letter about Capt. Reich. He had a dishonorable discharge, that is it was read so on dress parade, but I do not take it as such, but so it was read, so do not mention it around. I will just state how it was. On dress parade the Companys were changed by order of the Gen. The Colonel told Capt. to take his Co. in such a place, but he would not, when his sword and belt was taken and he himself put in irons so that he has his discharge. I do not think myself that he was sorry to leave the Co. and the service. I overheard him say to Lieut. Ransom sometime before that he wished he was out of the Company. I for one and most of the Co. wishes that he was back. If you see him tell him I wish he was back again for I miss him very much. I am almost tempted to desert sometimes. I feel so lonesome. If it was not for the name of it, besides Mother being all alone, but I must keep courage a while longer. I must stop for this time. Write often.

Your aff. Brother,

Henry

P.S. I shall be obliged to send this letter without a stamp as they are not to be had. The old Dr. has left that used to frank. Please send me a few stamps. There are not any around here. In the battle our Company was the third from the head.
movements.notes: **CRITICAL** — Fair Oaks bayonet charge; Capt. Reich; tempted to desert

movements.sigSummary: On July 1, 1862, Corporal Alexander F. Hubbell writes his mother from a bough shanty three miles from Strausburgh, electrified by a dispatch read to Generals Sigel and "Slow": Richmond captured after three days' fighting, thirty thousand men "left on the field." He prays Henry has "come out unscathed" and confesses he'll be ashamed to face his brother until he has seen two or three battles of his own.
movements.transcription:
June 30th, 1862
Camp near Sharpsburgh (?)

My Dear Mother:

We have just been mustered in again for pay. On looking over my accounts I feel a little blue. My expenses have been quite heavy. When we left Harpers Ferry we took only our overcoats and blankets in our knapsacks and did not receive the baggage we left until a few days since. How long I wore my shirt I am ashamed to tell you. Only I would say that I threw it away when I took it off. I purchased two shirts and two prs. of socks which cost me three dollars and a half. All my writing materials were completely spoilt by the wet and I have been obliged to supply myself anew from the sutler. A Corporal has often a need of a watch. One day while in Winchester I was sent with a guard of twelve men to the Academy Hospital to guard the sick rebels, some of whom were getting to be pretty strong. I borrowed a watch from one of our company with a cracked crystal. It fell to pieces during they and two hands were knocked off. I was obliged to have it repaired which in Winchester cost three dollars, of which I payed two, etc. etc. etc., all of which count up. When we are paid off I shall be able so far as I can now see to send you at least ten dollars to go to Charlotte with. I feel mad when I think how small it is. A truce to this subject as it is one not very pleasant for me to contemplate.

We are now encamped within about three miles of Strausburgh in a small fine woods. We have made ourselves little shanties of boughs which answer very well to keep of the sun and wind, but when it rains we fasten up a blanket which keeps off the greater portion of the wet.

July 1: July 1! I can hardly realize it. I thought last spring that I should be home by this time, certainly. Well, well, I am content to stay. There is the bugle for drill. The capture of Richmond has just been reported here. I hope it is true. I hope and pray that Henry has again come out unscathed. One of the boys heard the dispatch (to Genls. Siegel and Slow) read. It said that our forces had captured Richmond after three days fighting and that thirty thousand men were left on the field. I only wish our Regiment could have had a share in it. From present appearances I should judge that the whole army in this valley will move on soon. Our Capt. thinks we shall have some fighting soon now that Richmond has been probably captured. He thinks they will try and hold this valley. I shall be ashamed to meet Henry unless I have been in two or three battles.

I am enjoying excellent health. When we are paid off again I hope I shall be able to send home at least twenty dollars. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. Brinkerhoff. I feel very anxious to hear from James.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. Do not forget to remember me to Frances and tell her I hope to see her before long.
movements.notes: Expenses; (false) Richmond capture reported; "ashamed to meet Henry"

movements.sigSummary: Independence Day, 1862, and Alexander marks it from Camp Goodrich near Strausburgh with batteries thundering and the brigade marched down to be harangued by Gen. Cooper. Orders have come to move at a moment's notice — tomorrow, he thinks, on a long march toward somewhere his Orderly guesses is Richmond. Yet beneath the soldier's bravado runs a son's worry: he is anxious for word of James, and gently scolds his mother not to believe "every old fogy" who steers her mail astray.
movements.transcription:
July 4th, 1862
Camp Goodrich
Near Strausburgh, Va.

My Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you a day or two since and was very much disappointed not to hear more definitely from James. I feel very anxious about him. I hope and believe that he will succeed. Please write and let me know as soon as possible.

I received the letter you directed to the 78th Regt. Now, Mother, I shall keep you posted as far as possible as to my whereabouts, ie., ie. and you must not believe everything every old fogy tells you, for they will surely lead you astray. We have had orders to be ready to move at a moment's notice, and I think we shall leave tomorrow. Where we are to go to, I do not know. Our Orderly said to me that he thought we should go to Richmond and I am pretty near of the same opinion. "At any rate" we are to go somewhere, and a prettly long march to.

In the way of celebrating the "fourth" all the batteries have made considerable noise and the brigade marched down to the camp of the first and were harrangued by Gen. Cooper.

Please write often — very often.

Your aff. son

Alexander

movements.sigSummary: Front Royal, Virginia — Alexander marches in safe and sound, the 60th NY pressing on from Camp Goodrich toward Manassas Gap, certain they're bound for Richmond. Beneath the soldier's swagger runs a brother's worry: he begs word of James, threatens to "pull" Frances's ears for her scraps of paper, and dreams that James will succeed so "we shall have one educated soldier in the family."
movements.transcription:
July 8th, 1862
Fort Royal, Va.

My Dear Mother—

Here I am safe and sound. We left Camp Goodrich July 5th at 5 P.M. and reached here at 10 A.M. the next day. We were greatly delayed on the way by the baggage trains of the troops in advance. We leave tomorrow morning at 4 oclock for Manassas Gap. I hope we are going to Richmond and think we are.

Please write often. I feel very anxious to hear from James. I hope he will write me, but I am afraid. He is a poor correspondent. I think a little knapsack drill would do him good. Tell Charles to write. I don't know but I owe him a letter. I have but little opportunity of writing. When will Frances return? I hope she will write me a good long letter. I have had nothing from her but a little scribble on a little scrap of paper for a long time. I shall have to pull her ears when I return. How I should like to see you all, but then, I do not wish to return until this war is over. I hope James will succeed and then we shall have one educated soldier in the family.

Write soon. Remember me to Mrs. B.

Your affectionate son

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Fort Royal; Manassas Gap next; "one educated soldier"

movements.sigSummary: Writing from a camp on the James River after a late-June battle and the army's retreat — "if we call it such" — Henry recounts flinging away his knapsack on the double-quick and watching the regiment's Major lose both feet to a solid shot, faulting the want of judgment that placed them under the rebel batteries. Yet his sister's plans have raised his spirits, and he now burns every letter he receives, slipping ten dollars into the envelope despite the risk.
movements.transcription:
July 8, 1862
Camp near James River

Dear Frances:

I received your welcomed letter yesterday after coming off from fatigue duty. I am glad you are at home again. I only wish I was there, but I must have patience. Time is gliding away gradually — before I know it it will be gone. You must enjoy yourself as well as you can this warm weather. The sun here almost melts a person, more so when we have nothing but rubber blankets for a shelter, which draws the sun down to almost furnace heat.

I am quite delighted with the plans you have been making for my spirits have been raised greatly since the reception of your letter. If they can only be carried out. I should like nothing better than to farm it in Vermont. Aunt Laura made some hints in her last letter about Uncle Henry making a present of a few acres, but it was all in fun I suppose. But if our house and farm can be sold for a reasonable price, I can save enough money to buy a team and go to farming and make Mother's life a good deal easier or more comfortable than it has been.

I have no doubt but what James will succeed for he is a good scholar. I am very anxious to hear from him, but for my part if I get through this, it will be military enough for me. You may be sure I have seen hard times. One night I shall never forget for we were obliged to march about all night in deep mud and rain. I look back and it seems a wonder to me what I have gone through, but thank God I have my health yet.

Our Regt. was in a battle the last of June. I was obliged to throw my knapsack away as we went on the double quick. All our Co. lost their knap-sacks then except Peter Gugan. He managed to find his again. What things we have lost will be made up free of cost so I understand. If you could send me a couple of handkerchiefs it will be all I shall want in regard to clothing as I cannot be loaded down. I can draw shirts and socks from the Government. I have lost all my towels. If you could send me one I shall be much obliged.

In this retreat — if we call it such — I think it will in the end turn out all for the best. Although we have lost a great many men, the rebels have suffered the most. I have great confidence in McClellan. There was one day in which our Regt. was exposed to the rebel batteries. Their shells flew thick and fast around us. The Major from our Regt. had both his feet taken off by a solid shot. It was bad management in having us so near their battery. There is a want of judgement in some of the officers in this army.

I do not know whether you can make out this scroll, but I have to write just as I can. I shall be glad if you could send me some writing paper and pens as I have lost everything. We have all our supplies from the James River. We are under cover of the gun boats. They are a great protection, as yesterday the rebels threw twelve solid shots into a steamboat, but they dare not come very near our boats. There is a great deal I could better tell you about the war than write. You will not doubt see all in the papers before long. All the letters that I receive now I burn. Most that I received before from home I burnt, but those from Aunt L. and Nellie went with my knap-sack. I shall be obliged to stop as the mail goes in a short time.

I hope Lieut. Scott will return for our Co. is running down pretty fast. There is a want of discipline. I hope you will enjoy yourself as well as you can. I should like to have a furlough, but I do not think I can get one. I think it would be pleasant for Mother if you could stay at home at least two or three months for I may be at home by that time, yet I may be obliged to stay my time out. I must hope for the best. I shall send ten dollars in this letter although it is a risk.

Your aff. Brother,

Henry
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Seven Days retreat; lost knapsack; shells; farm plans

movements.sigSummary: Writing from camp near Harrison's Landing after the Seven Days' retreat, Henry recounts the double-quick into the woods, thrown knapsacks, and the bayonet charge where his regiment "fired very low and did great execution" — and the Irish Brigade storming a rebel battery, "a splendid sight, shouting at the top of their voices." Sick with worsening diarrhea, he twice refused McDonald's urging to go to the hospital, unwilling to leave the rest.
movements.transcription:
July 12, 1862
Camp near Haryson's Landing
James River

Dear Mother:

I received two letters from you the other day and was very glad to hear from you and that James had passed his examination. I sent ten dollars in two letters, five in each, but had no way of registering them. I hope you will receive them.

In my last letter to Frances I gave some account of our retreat. I will state some more of the particulars. When the sick were ordered to the hospital, McDonald came to me twice and urged me to go, but I did not feel like leaving the rest and so stayed. The battle commenced the last of June about five o'clock in the afternoon. We were counter-marching for some time before we came to the woods. We were then ordered on the double quick and had to throw our knapsacks. One of our officers, Billings, was sun-struck. I lost my cap in the charge. We came to a bayonet charge just as we entered the woods. Our regiment fired very low and did great execution.

The Irish Brigade charged a rebel battery — it was a splendid sight, shouting at the top of their voices. We lost a great many men, and the battery, ammunition, and provisions. We marched all the next day in a hard rain without a blanket. There are many who shirk the fights. The rebels claim a victory but I think McClellan managed very well. We were not whipped by any means.

Lieut. Webb has invited me to his tent. He is a very fine fellow. I should like very much to get my discharge but it is very difficult. I have now served thirteen months. If I serve my full time I shall receive one hundred dollars bounty and a land warrant.

My diarrhea is very bad. Sherman, who was head doctor, is now in Congress. Walker is head man now. We have a new doctor from New York. I received a letter from Alexander dated June 22nd. He was well, at Middletown. I hope Capt. Rich and Lieut. Scott will return for our company needs them badly.

David Savage wants a secesh bill. I have mailed James's letter to Alexander. Please write often.

Your aff. son,

Henry
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Seven Days battle detail; Irish Brigade charge; McDonald urges hospital; diarrhea

movements.sigSummary: On Pine Mountain near Warrenton, the twenty-year-old corporal watches the sun set behind the Blue Ridge, a bugle floating up, until he "almost forgot I was a soldier" — then imagines the drum beating to arms, the sun glistening on "ten thousand breastplates," and the earth that "will fairly rock." To Frances he confides a quieter ambition: when the war ends, college if he can — "I am determined to make something of myself."
movements.transcription:
July 14th, 1862
Camp on Pine Mountain
Near Warrenton, Va.

My Dear Sister:

"Way down South in Dixie." That is where I am. And a beautiful country too if it were not cursed by the existence of slavery. I am encamped on the summit of a high hill or rather a mountain from which I can see a long distance and the view is very fine. Green fields, meadows, large farms, patches of woods, roads winding here and there, little villages in the distance, and all of this spread out before me like a beautiful painting.

I was sitting on the hill just now watching the sun as it was setting behind the Blue Ridge. The soft notes of the bugle were floating through the air when I almost forgot I was a soldier. I seemed for a moment to be transported to the green fields and quiet scenes of old Clinton County. But then again I thought if the drum should beat to arms tomorrow morning, there will be a different scene. Troops will be forming in line of battle. The sun will be glistening on the bright steel of ten thousand breastplates. The artillery will be wheeled into position and the skirmishers will be thrown out, and then the earth will fairly rock.

But enough of this. Frances, you have returned from Canada, and now I want to have a good long letter from you. I have been looking for one ever since I heard you were at home. I shall have to pull your ears when I come home if you do not write me a good letter soon.

Now I want to tell you something about my plans. If the house can be sold and Uncle Henry's place purchased, I think it would be a good thing. When this war is over I want to go to college if possible. If not I shall go to farming. I must have some object in life and I am determined to make something of myself.

The Signal Corps is encamped about fifty rods from us. Albert Cook is in it. I had a long talk with Lieut. Miner this evening. Please send me some postage stamps as they are hard to get.

Evening. I have just had a cup of coffee with Cook. He is well and in good spirits. I received a letter from Mary Doolittle. Please direct your letters to Washington, D.C., Gen'l Banks Division.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Literary battle scene; Virginia landscape; farm/college plans; Signal Corps; Albert Cook

movements.letterExcerpt: My Dear Mother, Sister and Brother:
movements.sigSummary: Two of her sons have proven themselves, Alexander tells his mother — and the letter shows the cost of that pride. Writing for the first time to Mother, Frances, and Charles at once, he scorns "fireside patriots" Silas and Sid: "brave enough at home, but let them come out here and you would see them whine." Then, the next morning, the First Lieutenant is dead, two more men buried, and Luther lies sick — disease, not battle, thinning the ranks.
movements.transcription:
July 26th, 1862
Camp near Washington, Va.

My Dear Mother, Sister and Brother:

I received your letter yesterday and was glad to hear from you. I also received one from Frances a few days ago which I have not had time to answer. I was very glad to hear that she had returned home and was still in "good spirits."

Now as to Silas and Sid, I have a very poor opinion of such men. They are what I call fireside patriots. They are brave enough at home but let them come out here and you would see them whine. The idea of men at home finding fault while we are doing the fighting! There is a great deal of talk now about drafting. I hope they will draft every man that is able to carry a musket, and I believe they will.

Charles asks me if the military life is as miserable as it is represented. Well, I will give you my opinion. It depends entirely upon the disposition of the individual. If a man enlists and is determined to make the best of it, he will get along very well. But if he enlists and goes to grumbling about everything, he will be miserable. For my part I make the best of everything and am contented.

July 27th. Our First Lieutenant died last night at ten o'clock. It was a heavy blow to us all. He was a Christian Man and died like one. Sergeant Sterns said he "never saw so happy a death." Two of the regiment are being buried this morning. Luther is in the hospital, sick. I am in excellent health and am one of the hardiest men in the company. "Little Doolittle."

I was very glad to hear good news of Henry's conduct. Mother has no reason to blush at conduct of at least two of her sons. Love to all. I will try and give you an account of my adventures in my next. Remember me to Mrs. B.

Yours with affections,

Alex

P.S. I saw Luther this morning. He said he felt better. I hope he will recover soon. He is not dangerously ill.
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — "Fireside patriots"; military life philosophy; 1st Lieut. death; Luther in hospital; two men buried

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your letter with the others and also a paper a few days since. I was feeling very anxious about Henry until I received your paper. A number of the Cadets take the Herald of which I can have...
movements.sigSummary: James, just seventeen, writes brother Charles his first long account of life at West Point's Camp McRae, set on the plain and ringed by six sentinels who call "all is well" through the night. He renders the cadets' hazing with wide-eyed delight — wheelbarrows and an old cannon wheeled out to knock off bayonets; they dragged him about one night but never got his gun. Reading the Herald for word of McClellan, he confesses he was anxious for Henry until news came.
movements.transcription:
July 27th
West Point Military Academy

Dear Charles:

I received your letter with the others and also a paper a few days since. I was feeling very anxious about Henry until I received your paper. A number of the Cadets take the Herald of which I can have the reading when ever I choose, so that I am enabled to keep myself pretty well posted on the movements of McClellan. I saw an account of the fight.

I wish you would send me Henry's and Alex's address. Have you heard from them lately? What do they write? I should like to hear from you often, and in return I will write you of the things going on here, which I think will interest you. I will try and give you a little description of Camp McRae. It is situated on one corner of the plain and is entirely surrounded by shade trees, some of which are not more than three years growth. The camp is surrounded by six sentinels day and night. During the night the hours are called off by the sentinel. First the one at the guard tents gives the number of his post and the hour, the sentinel on the next post takes it up and adds "all is well" and so on in succession all around. The one at the guard tent adds finally "all is well". There are eighteen sentinels detailed for each day. Each sentinel has to walk two hours out of every six of the twenty-four. I have been on guard five times. You have no idea how the Cadets and even the officers of the guard would bother us. I think the latter, however, did it only to see if we understood our orders. Sometimes the Cadets would come out with 1/2 a dozen wheelbarrows, and sometimes with an old cannon. They would knock off our bayonets and get our guns away if they could. They dragged me around one night but could not get my gun away. They took one fellow one night (the most uncouth looking fellow I ever saw) and tied his hands behind him and marched him down through camp. He began to bawl and said "Oh please let me alone I don't know what to do. They thought him decidedly military, but I will go on with my description of the camp. The Corps is divided into four companies; each company has two Cadet Lieutenants and sergeant and two Corporals. The commissioned officers tents are in the rear of the encampment. The shoe black, barber and varnisher tents, back of the officers tents. We had to go down a flight of stone steps and through an underground passage to get to the sink. It is on the side of a hill overlooking the river. No one would ever suspect where it was. I never saw anything so nicely got up. It is kept very neat.

You asked me if I took breakfast on the boat. I did. I forgot to mention it. Mr. Holcomb was aboard of the same boat. I did not know he was aboard until after I had (accidentally) sat down beside him at the table. He was going to New York. We kept together most of the way. Did you receive those clothes I sent? Please write soon.

Your affectionate brother

James

Mr. Holcomb got on at Burlington and took a state room. That's the reason I did not see him before. I had a ticket given me for a berth when I got my passage ticket.

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your letter not long since and was very glad to hear from you. I am rejoiced to know that you have decided to remain at home this summer, or for the rest of the summer, and perhaps the fall...
movements.sigSummary: Henry describes Tuesday's grand review of the Army of the Potomac near the James River — regiments marching in line of battle within sight of the gunboats, the battery firing blanks, an artist on hand whose sketch he expects in Harper's Weekly. Writing to his sister Frances, he confides a quieter wish: that peace might come "just before Sugar time" so he could farm again next spring, though he resigns himself to staying his time out — "there is no such luck for me." He signs off asking her to burn the scribble.
movements.transcription:
July 28th, 1862 - Monday
Camp, near Harisons Landing
James River, Va.

Dear Francis —

I received your letter not long since and was very glad to hear from you. I am rejoiced to know that you have decided to remain at home this summer, or for the rest of the summer, and perhaps the fall months. You no doubt will have a large French class. I should like it very well if peace should be proclaimed just before Sugar time, or in the fore part of next winter, so that I could make arrangements for farming next spring, but there is no such luck for me, as matters and things look now, I am bound to stay my time out. I shall make the best of it.

You have such a good knowledge of French now I have no doubt you could command a good salary almost anywhere.

The weather here is very warm, sultry evenings and nights are the pleasantest part here. Last Tuesday there was a grand review of the Army of the Potomac near the James River within sight of the gunboats. We were marched around in line of battle the same as if we were in battle, only we were not. The battery was also with us and fired blank cartridges. I have no doubt we were sketched by an Artist, as there was a good opportunity to do so. You may perhaps see the sketch in the Harper's Weekly. Papers here are ten cts, such as the New-York Herald and others. The Sutler charges a great deal for his goods, or is very extortionate, but I suppose he has a right, as it is some trouble for him to bring his goods from the river. He makes more than our merchant at home, almost doubles on his goods, but after all a person must indulge a little now and then. When I was sick I do not know what I should have done if it had not been for the Sutler. Reich is head man there yet.

Well here I am on the last page, and I must bring my letter to a close. By the by, how does Sid come on in farming since he is married and works the farm himself. I fancy he does not work much. For my part, I do not intend to run into the fire before I can see my way through — that is, get married. I do not mean to insinuate that Sid will not do well, but he must look out and not hire to much; but I must bring my letter to a close. Please excuse all mistakes as I am oblige to write just as I can. I expect Lieut. Scott must be on his way by this time. James can direct his letters the same as before.

I remain your aff. Brother

Henry

Give my regards to all friends. Burn this scribble — hope to do better next time.
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Grand review of Army of the Potomac; blank cartridges fired; Harper's Weekly artist; Sutler prices; "burn this scribble"

movements.sigSummary: Charles Hubbell enters the collection from the U.S. Barracks at Plattsburgh, where Dr. Foote nearly fails him for near-sightedness until a window-test of the lake shore lets the papers be signed — and Mr. Averill scolds him that he was "too honest." Within days he is appointed 1st Corporal, sleeping in straw-filled ticks on bunks four high, eating boiled pork and bean soup among "a good many hard cases" and a few decent men.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 9, 1862
U.S. Barracks
Plattsburgh, N.Y.

Dear Mother —

As Mr. Averill leaves soon I will send a few lines by him. I was examined by Dr. Foote yesterday & again today. That is my eyes were, nothing else. Some of the fellows were told to strip, but quick as I stood up he caught hold of my eyes & asked me if I did not have something on my eye. I told him no, but that I was a little near sighted. He then told me to look out of the window on the lake shore & tell him what I saw. He was satisfied that I was near sighted. Mr. Averill talked to him, told him that I had two brothers in the Army & one at West Point & that he must pass me. He said he would examine again. This afternoon I was sent for to see the Dr. He told me his instructions were perfect vision. Mr. Averill told him to try me again again. The doctor told me to look out of the window. I did & the doctor said he would sign my papers as I could see pretty well. Mr. Averill told me I was too honest, to tell the Dr. that I was near sighted.

Sept. 15 — I think I had better finish this letter. We have drilled every day since we have been here except the first day & Sunday. I have been to P. village twice. Attended Mr. Youngs church Sunday morning. Pet Stacia & I were shown to the front slip near the door. The Pulpit is between the doors, the seats all facing the doors. We had a fine view of the persons coming into the church — I guess there are about 150 men here now. Mr. Armstrong has appointed me 1st Corporal. I don't know as it is made permanent yet, but I suppose it will be. A Corporal has this advantage, he does not have to stand guard but merely to change the guard, etc. We Non Commissioned officers drill by ourselves & need not drill with the company unless we wish. The drill sargent keeps us ahead of the Co. as we are to drill squads of the men. I have not been on duty yet but expect to be on tomorrow.

The stone barrack is a very comfortable building. There are fireplaces to the different rooms in which we have fires. The bunks are made of rough boards, are broad enough for two to sleep in & are 4 bunks high. The day of our arrival we were told to fill our ticks with straw in the barn. Have two blankets, sleep very well.

We have plenty of pork (boiled), some salt beef, Potatoes, bakers bread, beans. Sometimes, Pork hash & bean soup. This is our diet. Not all of these in one day though.

I have had a good time enough since I have been here. Nearly every man swears. There are a good many hard cases here. There are quite a number of decent men here also.

Have you heard from the boys? I should like to hear about them. How does Frances get along with her French class? How does the farming come on. I don't know when I can have a furlough as we are wanted to drill. When I do get one it can be only for a short one. I wish you would send me an undershirt & shirt by any one coming here. This is all I need. I can get my washing done here.

Affectionate Son

C. F. Hubbell.

movements.sigSummary: At Antietam two days after the bloodiest single day in American history, Alexander writes from "Camp on the battle field" to tell his mother he came through with only "an inconsiderable bruise a little below the right knee by a ball nearly spent." Then the pivot: "I only wish I could report the same of Henry," who is missing. A man of the 34th thinks him a prisoner, not killed, and Alexander builds careful hope. By a September 21 addendum, still no word: "Do not worry."
movements.transcription:
Sept. 19, 1862
Camp on the battle field — Va.
Near Antietam

My Dear Mother —

I presume you will be greatly rejoiced to hear that I came out of the battle of the third safe and sound. I cannot be thankful enough for God's great kindness to me. The only injury I received was an inconsiderable bruise a little below the right knee by a ball nearly spent. I only wish I could report the same of Henry. I saw one of the 34th this morning and he said that he is missing, also that he thought he was quite sure that he was not killed. Thinks he is either a prisoner or missed the Regiment in the confusion (something that very often happens.) I feel very anxious about him, but hope for the best. A large number of our men reported missing have come in. It is very probable he left the field to assist in carrying off some of his wounded comrades. There was as instance of this in our Company. I have strong hopes concerning him and think he will turn up alright. Don't hardly think he was hurt. Our Regiment went into the fight about 200 strong.

Camp below Maryland Heights
Sept. 21st

I have not heard from Henry since writing the above. I hope and think he is yet all right. Do not worry. Our loss was between thirty and forty.

Your affectionate son

Alex F. Hubbell

I will write and give you the particulars of the fight as soon as possible.
movements.notes: **CRITICAL** — ANTIETAM. Alexander safe, bruised knee from ball. HENRY MISSING. 34th NY man says not killed — prisoner or lost in confusion. Regiment went in 200 strong, lost 30-40.
