movements.sigSummary: Charles has enlisted, and James — writing from West Point Academy on Sept 21, 1862 — has only just heard, pressing his mother for details: How did he enlist? Not as a private, he hopes, urging the boy to prove himself and seek promotion. Then the war recedes entirely: his rank in the third section, the prayer book Prof. French handed out, falling into ranks with shoes unblackened. "Ask Frances if she has forgotten me."
movements.transcription:
Sept 21, 1862
West Point Academy

Dear Mother:

You must be very lonely since Charles has left. How did he enlist? I have been expecting a letter every day, but have been disappointed. I hope he did not go as a private, but then if he did, by being on the lookout and proving efficient — which I know he will — he can easily get promoted. I suppose you will say to yourself, "he talks a great deal about getting an office", I suppose I do, but then when a man enlists I think he ought to look out for his own interests. Won't you send me his address and also that of the boys, if there is any place where a letter can be directed, so that it will reach them. Have you heard from Henry and Alex yet? You said in your last letter that you had not heard from them for some time.

You asked me how I stood in my class: I am now in the third section; the whole class is divided into six. They have been trying us for three weeks, and have placed us in the different sections according to our merits. The transfers were read out last night at parade. I am section marcher of the third as my name comes first alphabetically. A man in the third section is regarded as having a very good standing in his class, but I shall try to go up higher, and I think, can. I think if I could have had my choice of the sections, I would have chosen the third. Yes; I know I would.

But it is time for the bible class, and I will finish this after supper.

We had a very interesting class, and became so interested that the first drum beat for parade before we were aware of the lateness of the hour. I came very near getting a late and so did all, as we were obliged to go to our rooms and get our trimmings and get out there before the second drum which beats five minutes after the first. As it was we were obliged to fall in ranks with shoes unblackened, but Mr. Michie, the Cad Lieut, of our company, was very kind and did not look at our shoes. Prof. French gave each of us a prayer book, who was without one, and he also gave us each a book entitled "The Bible and Men of Learning". We cadets, by ourselves, have prayer meetings twice a week. They are attended by quite a number from each of the four classes; the first classmen generally lead the meeting.

But I must close as it is now near ten and at that time every light must be out. I delayed finishing this until late in the evening. Ask Frances if she has forgotten me. P.S. That young Hoyt Uncle Hubbell spoke of was thrown down into the immortals. The "Immortal Section" is the sixth, the lowest.

Your aff. son

James
movements.notes: **MAJOR** — Charles enlisted; James's class standing (third section); Bible class; Prof. French; "Immortal Section"

movements.letterExcerpt: I suppose you will be both surprised and grieved to hear that I am in a hospital. I have had an exhausting diarrhea for several weeks past, which with the severest military duty has brought me pretty ...
movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from the Hospital at Harpers Ferry, brought "pretty low" by weeks of exhausting diarrhea and the severest military duty, yet softens it for his mother before the news she needs: Henry is alive, only slightly wounded in the hand, still with the company. Then the hard ask — could she spare five dollars, "if not, less will do." A loaf of bread bought by kind Orderly Dickinson "will do me a world of good."
movements.transcription:
Sept. 27, 1862
Hospital at Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother —

I suppose you will be both surprised and grieved to hear that I am in a hospital. I have had an exhausting diarrhea for several weeks past, which with the severest military duty has brought me pretty low. I feel much better today and think that with proper care and nourishment I shall get along finely. Orderly Dickinson was down here this morning and purchased some paper and some envelopes and a loaf of bread for me (with his own money). He is very, very, very kind to me. That bread will do me a world of good. I wish you could by some means or token express my gratitude to him. I can never forget his kindness and only hope I may find some means of repaying it. He showed himself every inch a man in the last fight.

I have heard from Henry. He is slightly wounded in the hand, but is still with the company. When I am able I will try and give you some of the particulars of the fight.

I am now, Dear Mother, going to ask a great favor, and it is only the stearnest necessity that makes me do it. Can you send me some money. You know, Mother, what it is to be away from home, sick among strangers and to be without money. I will not try to describe my feelings when I ask for this. You know them all. We shall have four months pay due us the first of Nov. ($52) and I shall be able to return it to you ten fold. Do you suppose you could spare me five dollars, if not, less will do. I will leave you to judge how painful it is for me to ask this of you. If you have not got it to spare do not send it. I do not wish you to deny yourself. I shall try and write often.

Your affectionate son

Alex F. Hubbell

Direct to Washington and I will always get the letter.
movements.notes: **CRITICAL** — Alexander in HOSPITAL at Harpers Ferry. Exhausting diarrhea. Orderly Dickinson's kindness. Henry wounded in hand but with company (FOUND). Asks Mother for $5.

movements.sigSummary: Charles answers his mother from Plattsburgh Barracks with a young man's stubborn optimism: "it may be all for the best." Convinced his wounded brother Henry is a prisoner at Richmond, he reasons the leg wound only kept him from running — and that a prisoner is safer than a soldier. He learned of it at nine the night before, from Alek Douglas, while asking after the 34th regiment. He hopes to come home this week, once the men are mustered in together.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 30/62
Plattsburgh Barracks

Dear Mother —

I received your letter today. I was sorry to hear about Henry. But then it may be all for the best. If he is a prisoner at Richmond as I think he is, he is safer than in our army. I think the wound in his leg prevented his running away. Unless he is exchanged we may not hear from him for sometime. As there is no mail between the south & north it will be some time before we can hear from him.

I shall try & come home this week but it depends upon what time we are mustered into the service. All the men have to be mustered in together.

I did not know anything about Henry till nine ock. last night. Alek Douglas told me. I was inquiring about the 34 regt.

Aff. Son

C. F. Hubbell

I hope you will send newspapers to the boys.
movements.notes: Charles responds to news of Henry's wounding. Thinks Henry is a prisoner at Richmond. Wound in leg prevented escape.

movements.letterExcerpt: It is three weeks yesterday since I left home for this place.
movements.sigSummary: Charles, three weeks a soldier at Plattsburgh Barracks, catalogs his new world like an architect: stone buildings six rooms long, bunks four high, sixteen men packed on an "elevator floor," and the wry confession that he's "only taken my pants off twice since I left home." Then Mother's letter arrives mid-page and the tone breaks: Henry, reported wounded in the thigh and taken prisoner. Charles clings to hope — "I think Henry is with the rebels in Dixie" — because alive beats the alternative.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 30/62
U.S. Plattsburgh Barracks

Dear Alek —

It is three weeks yesterday since I left home for this place.

I was very much concerned last night to hear that Henry was wounded. Alek Douglas told me, said that he thought he was only slightly wounded. I hope that it is true that he is not badly wounded. I hope that you & I will come out of the war all right. But we must take our chances. I mean to take care of myself as well as I can. I have had an easy time so far. Have been on duty as Corporal of the guard once & as Sergeant of the guard once. The privates are on guard every three or four days. They lay pretty thick in the guard house on an elevator floor, 16 sleeping at once packed close together. 21 men are now on duty with 2 corporals & 2 Sergeants. The privates can sleep 4 hours at a time at night.

We have had two men deserts. They had a pass to Plattsburgh village about one mile from here & they went to the village & took the steamer for Albany. We have had any amount of elbow jousting, but I think there will now be a stop put to it. The men do not much mind being shut up here if they can jump the pickets & have a good spree. But there is a new order now which if a picket jumper will be sent to Albany as deserters. Two were sent as such last night.

[page break]

The barracks here are very good stone buildings. There are two separate buildings one for the officers & one for the men. In front of the mens quarters are two verandahs, an upper & lower the the whole length of the building, which is quite long. It is a two story building divided into rooms, 6 bunks long & 4 bunks high. It is 6 rooms long. Some of the rooms have no bunks but have little cots made of rough boards for the sick. There is a doctor here & he has had some patients already, but I have had good health so he has not called on him.

There are two new rough board barracks used by the last reg. here, besides an old wooden building used as a barracks. The bunks are made of rough boards wide enough for two to sleep comfortable. Each one has a straw tick & a blanket. I have only taken my pants off twice since I left home. But I think I shall take them off hereafter. There is a fire place to each room. We had a fire in them before the stoves were put up.

I have been appointed corporal while here & I suppose it will be permanent. The non commissioned officers have been drilling in a squad by themselves.

Since commencing this letter I have received a letter from home. Mother is frightened about Henry. But I think he was wounded in the thigh slightly so that he could not walk well & then taken prisoner. That big Shaw, I guess you know him, over 6 feet high, is enlisted here. He lived in Dudleys farm awhile. He told me that he saw Henrys name in the list of wounded — wounded either in the thigh or his or his forgets which. I wish you could make some enquiries in Henrys Co. There is a man here who had a brother wounded in the battles before Richmond. He was reported missing & no one knew what had become of him. He has just had a letter from his brother in Richmond who is well & says he could as lief be there as with our army. I think Henry is with the rebels in Dixie.

Alek will you write soon & let us know all the news. I suppose I will not like military life as well when I come to camp out, but I have made up my mind to take things as they come. I do not expect to have a very nice time. Forewarned is forearmed you know.

Now Alek remember remember & write often.

Your Aff. Brother
C. F. Hubbell

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles to Alexander — barracks life, Henry wounded in thigh (via Shaw), thinks Henry is prisoner "with the rebels in Dixie." Most detailed description of Plattsburgh Barracks.

movements.sigSummary: Charles returns to Plattsburgh barracks to find double guards posted inside the fences, some with loaded muskets to stop his own regiment from deserting before payday. He sends two pairs of socks home with Alek Douglas, hurried off by his father's injury under a falling timber, and watches men burn $11 on beer the day a $25 check arrives with $67 still owed. He closes still clinging to the hope that his missing brother Henry is only a prisoner.
movements.transcription:
..... 30 .....

Oct. 10, 1862
Plattsburgh

Dear Mother:

As Alek Douglas is to leave for home tonight I send by him two pairs of socks to have the heels run as they will not last any time as they are. My new grey socks have a hole in the heel already. Perhaps the socks at home are better than those I send. If so send them. I think two pairs will be all I will have room for or want to carry, besides those I have on.

Alek D. leaves because his father has been severely hurt by a falling timber. It was not easy for him to get a short furlough. We have double guards posted inside the fences. Part of them have loaded muskets. We received a check for $25 today. There is $67 due us yet including one months pay. The men say they will not leave until they are paid up. But I think they will.

I arrived safely about nine oclock at the barracks the night I left home. Called at Mr. Savages store & at Mrs. R. M. Hubbells. No one at home except Sid & wife when I was. I hope that you will treat the Savages well as they always treated me well. I did not see David S. the other day. I was sorry that I had no time to call at Mr. Savages house. We expected to leave in the morning but I think we will leave Monday.

One of the men told me that he spent $11.00 for beer yesterday treating any one that happened to be on the [?] spot. The grocery is on the grounds. Honesty lasts some of the men no time. Have you heard from Henry? I suppose not as very likely he is a prisoner. Hoping that you & Frances will make the best of things, I will close with this wish.

Your affectionate son, ~~subscriber~~ Charles F. Hubbell
..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles at Plattsburgh on furlough eve — sending socks, father injured by falling timber, "very likely he is a prisoner."

movements.letterExcerpt: We left for this place Monday morning at seven A.M. Arrived here at about 2 A.M. the next morning. On our arrival a large number of men were routed out of their bunks & tents for us to sleep in as the...
movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from Camp Mohawk near Fonda, having marched from Plattsburgh through Whitehall, Saratoga, and Schenectady to join a regiment of 900 men where recruits sleep on straw "like so many pigs" and stealing is rife. He reports he's been appointed Corporal, settles family debts with the Savages, and frets over bounty disputes that nearly stalled the column. He's lost his razor — so he'll let his whiskers grow till he comes home.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 15, 1862
Camp Mohawk

Dear Mother:

We left for this place Monday morning at seven A.M. Arrived here at about 2 A.M. the next morning. On our arrival a large number of men were routed out of their bunks & tents for us to sleep in as there is not sleeping room for the whole of us. A large number of men sent home to sleep last night. The guard have bonfires to warm themselves.

We have 72 tents which will hold 5 or 6 men each & a wood barracks. The barracks is a very rough affair. The bunks will hold four & are covered with straw in which the men lay like so many pigs. The tents have no floors but are covered thick with straw. I slept the first time in a tent last night — slept comfortable. We fare well here — have as much fresh beef three times a day as we wish. The meat is boiled. The men are very fond of onions which they peel themselves & eat raw. The camp is very lively. Large numbers of ladies come here to see friends & sight seeing. We have about 900 men here. We are only a short distance from the village of Fonda which is quite a large place. It is in the country town, I think.

There is some talk of part of us giving up our tents to the men here & we sleep in the hotel at the village. We will know tonight. We have received our new blankets which are large & warm of course, a little heavy. The men are having blankets, boots, socks, shirts, who marked or perused being lost or stolen. There is a good deal of stealing here. There are a good many Dutchman or Germans in this regiment. The men that we found here received a heavy bounty. The towns paying $100 & some a good deal more besides giving a month. Please write me what they are paying in Vermont if you know. Essex pays $100.

On our journey here we had hard crackers & cheese which went well enough, but we could get no water at supper time & could not get out of the cars to get any as the doors were guarded. But finally they gave us some extra. We saw plenty of handkerchiefs waving on the route, to took the ears for Fonda at Whitehall. Passed through Saratoga, Schenectady, etc., but did not see much as it was dark.

I sent a $25 check home by Mr. Marshall. I wish you would show consent the money he gives you & find out if it is good. We will soon have our pay which I wish you would put into Mr. Savages hands at interest. "Will you pay off Mr. Savage, J & R.L. Savage s/o is $16.55. Joel Savage s/o is $27.69. You had

[page break]

better show Mr. Savage the s/o he rendered some time since as it will save him trouble. I sent home by Murray 1 towel, 1 hdkfs. & 1 testament with small book to be left at Savages as I could not carry them.

There is trouble here about bounty again. At Plattsburgh the men said they would not leave till they had all their bounty. But Sunday night in the eating room at supper limit, Col. Armstrong made a speech asking the men if they would go. The reply was a great hurrah to go. The majority were for going so after eating yank'd butter & looking at half raw cork & eating a little bread we left at 7 A.M. the next morning. Our officers say that we shall not leave here till we have all our pay. I believe I am appointed Corporal but none of the officers are named to the men yet, not even the captains. I mean us Plattsburgh fellows.

I wish you would write me. If you write soon, I think we will be here. Have you heard from Henry yet? How do you & Frances get along? I hope you are prospering finely. Please direct your letter to Camp Fonda, Fonda, Montgomery Co. N.Y. It turns out that the men sleet in a barn in the village instead of the hotel. The men are buying revolvers here. I don't know as they will be allowed to carry them. I shall not buy one. I have lost my razor for which I am sorry, but no use crying about spilt milk. Suppose I let my whiskers grow till I come back. I think I will.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

Will you please send me a list of my bad spelling.

..... 30 .....

movements.sigSummary: Alexander breaks a long silence from Harpers Ferry — "It is a long, long time since I last wrote you" — and the reason is a body unraveling: an indisposition that "took a permanent form in the shape of Jaundice," then a cold, then a facial eruption that left his eyes so weak he feared he would lose them. He writes only enough to ease his mother's worry, notes Capt. Ransom's great kindness, and promises a good long letter once his eyes are stronger.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 12th, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother:

It is a long, long time since I last wrote you. I know you must feel very anxious about me, but I do not think you will blame me when you know all. A day or two after I wrote you my last letter we marched shifted our Camp and continued changing until at length we settled down on Bolivar Heights. I have been indisposed for some time and there my indisposition took a permanent form in the shape of Jaundice. I had very little disposition to write and did not wish to until I had something more favorable to write about concerning myself.

We left the Heights a day or two to guard Government property in this place where we now are. To "cap the Climax" I took cold and had my face break out in a way not to be envied. I suffered a great deal with my eyes and was sometimes afraid I should lose them, but they are better now though still very weak. I will write you a good long letter as soon as my eyes are stronger. I received your welcome letter of the 4th inst. last night. Will try and write soon. Capt. Ransom is very, very kind. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,
Alex. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander's first letter since Sept 27 — 46-day gap. Has been too sick to write: jaundice, then cold, then facial eruption affecting eyes. Now at Harpers Ferry guarding government property. Capt. Ransom "very, very kind."

movements.sigSummary: Garrison duty near Alexandria fills this letter with the texture of a soldier's winter: two regiments holding the city, no passing after nine p.m. without the countersign, twelve cold hours at a post with no picket fires allowed. Charles's 153rd guards the convalescent and parole camps and furnishes funeral escorts — one sickly man from Fonda bled at the lungs and died, his company raising $72 to send his body home.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 18th, 1862
Camp near Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter directed to Fonda some days since & have received three since, the last dated Nov. 10th I received on the 15th. We will receive our letters without being delayed, I think, after this. I have recd. two Observers, also for which I am much obliged. The daily newspapers are sold here from 3 to 5 cts. each.

I am much pained that we hear nothing about Henry, but hope that he is a prisoner. I don't think he can be according to the surgeon's account. But we must make the best of whatever comes.

I wrote Jones yesterday & sent Alek's letter to him. Hope he will succeed at West Point, but if he does not it will be nice to have him at home. I do not think

[page break]

I will be at home very soon as the war does not look to me as if it would close this winter. Number of the men expect to go home next spring as they think the war will close by that time. Also a great many wish they had never enlisted. Yet Charles for one. A. Douglas & I are not sorry that we came to the war. But I think we will not go to the front this winter as our regiment is not well drilled & there is plenty of guard duty to be done. Unless a lot of new troops come to take our place we will remain here. There is a resort that we are to go into the city into the barracks now building to stay this winter. I don't know whether it is true.

Two regiments are now guarding the city. All citizens are allowed to come into the city, but none to go out except they have a pass. All soldiers are allowed to go in & out at it is a favorite their camp, but none to come into the city without a pass, after nine p.m. until morning none can pass either way without the countersign. I was glad that the Captains & Lieutenants have to be on guard duty also. I like to see them work. Their business is to pass the men on their post & to look after them once in a while to see that they are doing their duty. We are on 12 hours at a time outside the city. There are 2 or 3 men at a post so that the men can relieve each other. At night we carry our blankets, but it is cold to sleep on the ground & in the open air. No picket fires are allowed, but we find a fire sometimes where we can get warm. We come on duty nearly every day sometimes in the night & other times in the day.

Our Regt. guards the convalescent camp, also the parole camp & furnish a funeral escort for the soldiers that die in the hospitals. So that we have no drill now as there are not men enough. No liquor is allowed to be sold in Alex., but it is done privately — good many bottles of liquor are daily taken from the soldiers in the city & sent to the provost marshals.

A large number of our men are sick, some with one thing & some with another. The hospital here is in a tent. It is full & some are taken to the city. One sickly man enlisted & died not long after coming here. He bled at the lungs. His Co. sent his body home. He was from Fonda. It cost $50, for embalming & $25 for freight, making $45[sic]. His Co. raised $72, nearly every man paying $1.

Two corporals in our Co. have been reduced to the ranks, that is, had their stripes taken off for absences from camp without leave. Another had his stripes cut off for threatening to shoot his Lieut & then he was tied to a telegraph pole till he could behave himself. He was an ugly fellow. Our Co. Corporals are all right for.

I tent with James Lucas, Sam Pelky & a lot of Frenchmen. They all speak good English & are decent men. I was with A. Pouglias[?] some time when we had a change of men to fill up another tent. I heard that I was to go into this tent which was occupied by the worst men in the Co. But Lieut. Col. Frentress[?] made the change instead of someone else & I was put here into the best tent in the street. L. C. Frentress made quite friendly towards me. The men from Fonda do not like him. He is to strict I suppose. Col. Sabastine[?] has not been here since he came from. He has been sick, but is better. The officers boots are a short distance from ours, all in a row. Some of the men cook for them. Each tent has a corporal or sergeant in it. The tent I was in had three corporals so that it was unnecessary for some of us to move. There are a sergeant also with us. As there was no non officer in the at tent a sergeant was put in it & I got into a good place.

Mrs. Ruth Hubbell & sons prosper pecuniarily & otherwise. I think we had better not buy any of their land — so we have more land now that we can manage. And besides we have not more timber enough in all on [?] land I do not think it would be good policy to strip our land of growing timber. You speak of perishable property. I do not think that timber is that kind of property. Those cedars that have been cut ought to be drawn from the first snow. There is where we missed it last winter.

[page break]

Battiste will draw them perhaps, if not he may know someone who will.

That Plummer is a cheat. He owed us three loads at the end of last winter. They were small loads. I should threaten to sue him for trespass if he goes there again.

The weather is now drily, but it has not rained much yet. Over a week since, on Nov. 7 it snowed all day, but it was all gone the next night. I heard that it was more snow that they have had for some years. I think I shall buy me a pair of boots for the mud.

I think you had better dine out Thanksgiving if you are invited. You have lonesome times enough & ought to see company when you can. Frances must be full of business teaching French, etc. Fancy she likes Mr. Simons better than she did Mr. Karns. Has she got into a fight with that French teacher? I hope she will write & tell me all about her class & other things. Reed. her letter, will answer it soon. How is your health? Mine is good & has been good. My cold is better but is in a good place here to catch a new one. I hope that you will try to make yourself as comfortable as possible in every way. Two months & a half pay is now due us, but I do not know when we will be paid. Write soon & all the news.

Aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles's very long first letter from camp near Alexandria. 153rd NY guarding city, convalescent camp, parole camp, funeral escorts. Detailed barracks and camp life. Mathews & Leslie from Henry's Co. in Washington — not seen Henry for some time. "L. La Tube says James Beaumont died not long since of a fever." Rich is Captain, Burdick 1st Lieut. Alek Douglas's pocket book stolen ($26).

movements.sigSummary: Alexander had begged the Colonel to let him slip the ranks, then walked alone by bright moonlight past every guard to find Henry's tent near Georgetown: "Is there a man among you by the name of Hubbell?" A large bearded man stepped out — "Why Dick, is that you?" — and their hands flew together. Writing now from Harpers Ferry, Alexander tells Mother he and Henry fought Antietam a few hundred yards apart, and clings to hope that Henry, wounded and "undoubtedly taken prisoner," still survives.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 19th, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother & Sister:

How I long to see you. Wonder what you are doing today. Miss Fannie I expect is in that cozy room in the old academy (of pleasant memory to me) teaching (teaching the young ideas of how to Charles vous Francis (don't like my spelling do you Miss Fannie?) — and you, Mother, well — I cant imagine what you are about — what do you do with yourself these long days all alone as you are? I should enjoy your pleasant smiles. I am weary — weary of this an ugly day and stir. A little rest would do me oh so much good. Nevertheless, I am content to stay. Our Government is worth any sacrifice.

The war cannot last much longer. Both sides are getting heartily sick of the affair. A vigorous winter campaign on our part will, I think, speedily put an end to the war — and then for home, sweet, sweet, home. And oh — how good it will seem to see you all once more, and shall we all — all — meet again. God grant it. Dear, dear, Henry how I long to see him. I have seen him but twice since I left home. You wished me in one of your letters to tell you all about our first meeting.

About three miles beyond Georgetown, D.C., we passed a large encampment. I hailed a soldier and inquired what troops were encamped there and ascertained that it was Sedgwick's Division. He pointed out the position of the 34th to me. I could not then leave the ranks, but as soon we halted (about two miles beyond) I went to the Colonel and told him I had a brother in one of the regiments we had passed that I had not seen for over a year, and asked permission to go back and see him. The Colonel said he had not the power to grant my request, but said "If you are willing to run the risk, you can go." I said nothing about it. I was willing to run it. It was not dark, but there was a bright moon which gave me sufficient light to see by. I passed all the guards without difficulty. After a considerable search I found the regiment and company. "Is this B company?" I inquired. "Yes." "Is there a man among you by the name of Hubbell?" "Yes." "Hubbell, there is somebody out here that wants to see you." Oh, how my heart bumped. I was in a moment to see my long absent brother. A large bearded man stepped out from one of the tents. It was Henry. The way our two hands flew

[page break]

together was a caution. I laughed — I — well — I was so glad I did not know what to do. You can well imagine Henry's surprise at seeing me. "Why Dick, is that you — really you. I can hardly believe it. How glad I am to see you. Come in my tent and sit down." I soon had quite a crowd of the boys around me and we had a right merry time, I can assure you. It was quite a late hour when I left for Camp.

I saw him again a few days after a little beyond Rockville, by day light. He was a noble looking soldier. He was, I think, undoubtedly taken prisoner at Antietam, and if he yet survives his wound (which from all that I can learn I do not think was dangerous) you will hear from him before long. What do you think, Mother, Henry and I were in the fight at the same time, and the 34th was but a few hundred yards to the left of us. Then I feel like it, Mother, I will try and tell you more of the battle. I have not told you a third.

Please write often, and tell me all bout home affairs. Has the draft taken place yet. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. I am enjoying excellent health. Capt. Ransom is very — very kind.
movements.notes: **THE MEETING STORY.** Alexander narrates finding Henry before Antietam — the dramatic nighttime reunion at the 34th NY camp. "Oh, how my heart bumped." Also believes Henry was "undoubtedly taken prisoner at Antietam." The 34th was "but a few hundred yards to the left of us" at Antietam.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from Harpers Ferry that in the thick of battle, "while the shot and shell were shrieking and whirring around me," he felt "as tho I had a Mother upon her knees praying for me" — God's arm wrapped around him. Days later, on Thanksgiving, he pictures the "old castle," the pony's flying heels, and Grandmother's table while he eats bean soup, boiled pork, and hard tack from a tin plate. The Government still hasn't paid them; he asks, gently, for a little money.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 25th, 1862
Harpers Ferry

My Dear Mother and Sister:

I received your most welcome letter last evening and oh! how much good it has done me. There is nothing, it seems to me, that gives half the joy that a letter from home does. It is one of the strongest links that binds men from vice. My letters are read, and reread and reread before I get another. Please write often, very often. Your letters do me worlds of good. I feel them tho't although I am here among strangers yet I have those who love & care and pray for me; that I am not alone and forgotten in this world. I take great comfort, Mother and Sister, in the thought that you are praying for me, that I may have grace to withstand all the temptations and allurements I am so much exposed to. I felt when in the battle while the shot and shell were shrieking and whirring around me, as tho I had a Mother upon her knees praying for me and I took great comfort in the thought. It seemed as tho God's arm was wrapt around me and I felt that if I fell all would be well with me.

I have just reread your letter. So Mr. A. Whiteside and E. Doolittle are "paying and hoarding substitutes", eh! I hope they will give them the slip just when wanted. Wouldn't it be rich. The miserable, craven hearted cowards deserve it.

Nov. 27. Today is "Thanksgiving" at home. How I wish I was there. Wouldn't I have a jolly time, eh? Rather think I would. Guess the "old castle" would ring a little, and if the sleighing was good wouldn't "pony's" heels fly. What a nice ride we could have, wouldn't we? Wonder what you are about — believe I can guess. You are about starting for church. It is now some after ten a.m. How I should like to hear the "Thanksgiving sermon" with you and then escort you over to Grandmothers for dinner. That a merry, merry time we would have — but God has ordered it otherwise and I must try and be content. You tell me to get up a nice dinner here among ourselves. Such was our intention but Government has not seen fit to pay us off yet and consequently I must content myself with bean soup and boiled pork and "hard tack" today. Good substantial food but a turkey would be much more to my palate, I must confess. I hope, dear Mother, you have changed your mind and will go to Grandmother's for dinner. If I were there I should make you go or rather persuade you.

You ask me if there is anything I need. There is nothing now that I can think

[page break]

of. We are just now in great need of money, but are hoping that Government will pay us off soon. We shall know definitely in a few days. I will then write. If we are not paid off money will be indispensable and Mother, if you can send me a little — and only a little — money, it would be a great comfort to me, and when you write if you will see and then put it in a stamp it will enable me to answer your letters much more readily for it is very difficult to get them here.

Love to all. Your aff. son,

Alexander
movements.notes: Alexander reflects on battle — felt Mother's prayers surrounding him under fire. Thanksgiving: bean soup and hard tack instead of Grandmother's dinner. Whiteside and Doolittle paying for substitutes. Draft criticism.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his sister Frances from Camp near Alexandria, sketching the soldiers' cemetery where the dead lie "as close as possible in straight rows," each grave marked by a white headboard of "durable wood furnished by Government." A Frenchman from his tent has just been buried there, his company unable to raise the dollar apiece to send him home. Charles spends Thanksgiving guarding a bridge and clings to news of Henry he fears is "too good news to be true."
movements.transcription:
Nov. 28, 1862
Camp near Alexandria, Va.

Dear Frances:

I received your & Mothers letter dated Nov. 20th enclosing Luthers. Glad to hear about Henry but am afraid it is too good news to be true. I should think McDonald would have written how he heard about Henry. I hope his information is correct.

You wish to know how I like soldiering. Well, I like it well enough so far, but you must remember I have seen only a small part of a soldiers life. I am afraid of becoming lousy. Several have found them on their clothes in our tent, but I have to keep them off by using unguentum & having clean clothes.

Our regiment is guarding in different places. Sometimes we go to one place & sometimes to another. A certain number of men each day are detailed from each company to guard the city, also to guard the convalescent camp or loose hill as the men have all it. The camp is so called from its being on a hill & the number of them there. We have been guarding the parole camp also, but do not now. The men in the parole camp have no arms at all, but have a guard from another reg. We have had no pay yet & I dont know as we will, have before the 15th of January. The men all say that they have no money & are getting impatient for some. A Frenchman from our tent died not long since. He was a sickly man at home and his come no duty here. His brother in law, wanted to send him home, so the men agreed to give $1 each if the officers would advance the money as the men were out of money, & take it out of their pay. The officers did not do it so he was buried in the soldiers cemetery. In this cemetery they are buried as close as possible in straight rows. Each soldier has a board painted white on which is his name Co. & regiment. The head boards are of durable wood furnished by Government.

I have seen F. Borron, Charles Dodds & several other acquaintances from C. The rest were Frenchmen. C. Dodds looks the same as ever, also looks very healthy. F. Borron looks well, would not go home for anything, as he likes the cavalry service. They all came to our camp to see us. C. Dodds is orderly for an officer in Washington, received $1 a day out of which he pays his board.

Yesterday was Thanksgiving which I spent on guard. We are out of 12 men pleased to guard the bridge over to Johnson (one end of the bridge.) There is a shanty there dug out the side of a hill. We had a good fire obtained by asking for a few sticks from each wagon that passed. I hope you and Mother went to Grandmothers as I think you would have had a good time.

How does Mr. Simons school come on? I hope you will give me all the news that you can. Tell us all about yourself, how you come on teaching, all your trials & troubles, bothers, etc. I don't know where we will stay this winter. We may stay here all winter. I think we will. One regt. besides ours guards the city, together with a remnant of another regiment. We keep the city straight. I like guard duty, all except night guarding. Do you think there will be a draft? We think here that there will be none.

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles to sister Frances (Fannie). Good news about Henry from McDonald seems too good to be true. Regiment guarding different places. Frenchman from tent died. F. Borron in cavalry. Smallpox in regiment — "whole reg. has been vaxxinated." Thanksgiving on guard.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes brother Alek from Camp near Alexandria, Va., still awaiting word that Henry, taken prisoner, will be exchanged and sent home. He itemizes his $67 bounty — $60 state, $28 county, $10 town, $2 enlistment fee — with pay three months overdue. Then the grim detail: four men have shot off their own fingers, thumb, or arm "accidentally," while Charles, who "did not enlist with the expectation of sleeping on a feather bed," guards Alexandria and waits for the war to close.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 4, 1862
Camp near Alexandria, Va.

Dear Alek:

I intended to have written you before & have not much excuse for not doing so, but I did not know as your address was the same & was waiting to hear from home if it was. I did not hear from home till some time after I had been here. The fault was in the mail, but it now comes twice a day. It is over a week since I heard from home. In that letter Mother also that she was afraid you was sick as she had not heard from you for some time. But I hope you are well. She also had heard that Henry was a prisoner & would soon be exchanged & perhaps come home. I have this is good news is true & am very anxious to hear from home to find if it is so.

How do you like being sergeant? Was there not some jealousy among the men on account of your promotion? Capt. Rich is now one of Gen Slough's staff & will be probably till we leave here. Gen. Slough is military governor of Alexandria. We are sorry to have Rich leave us as he understands his duty so well. He commences his new duties today. I think we will stay here this winter. Hope we will. When we leave Capt. Rich returns to us.

Some have the Sibley tents, or large round tents. We have bought floors for them. Some we get out of wood, then we go & chop it & back it to the camp. Our stoves

[page break]

are tunnel shaped & keep us warm so far. The men here are very impatient to see the paymaster as they are out of money. There are three months pay due us. I read in the Herald that the troops are now going to be paid. How long since you have had pay. I received $67 bounty, $60 from the state, $28 from the county, $10 from the town & $2 enlistment fee which makes the $67. I was to receive one fourth of the $10 U.S. bounty & one months pay in advance, but did not. They told us when we enlisted that we would receive it, but afterwards said that we enlisted too late for this bounty. The men at Plattsburgh said they would not leave there till they had all that was promised them. But they did. It was the same at Fonda, but they left there also without it. There are men in our reg. from Fonda that received $200 town bounty besides $4 a month for a year & state bounty besides.

Dec. 8th: I stood up yesterday afternoon to attend battalion drill & then went on guard last night so that I could not finish this till now. I received a letter from home this morning which stated that you had been sick, but are now quite well. Glad to hear that you are well. My health is good & has been since I enlisted with the exception of a cold. There are a good many sick in this Reg. & there has been been several deaths. A good many enlisted for the bounty that were not sound, expecting to be discharged. Two men in our Co. have shot their fingers off accidentally — one shot off his middle finger & the other his fore finger. Another man in the reg. shot his two front fingers off & thumb, another was shot through the arm. He have had one case of small pox here. The whole regiment has been vaccinated. Mine did not work & others did not have it work on them.

We are going to exchange our Austrian rifle muskets for new guns. We have a band taken from the ranks with instruments bought by the men. Also a lot of fifes & drummers. The men here are very anxious for the war to be closed. A good many are home sick. I like soldiering as well as I expected. Did not enlist with the expectation of sleeping on a feather bed. I have talked with soldiers that have been in the service some time & they all said that they would like to go home, that they had had enough of soldiering.

Mother had not heard from McDonald when she wrote, about Henry. McDonald will write to his wife how he obtained his information about Henry. I do hope Henry is safe. Now, Alek, I wish you would write me soon & tell me how your health is & when you think the war will be over. We are guarding the city of Alexandria. We come on guard often. I dont like being on guard nights.

Your Aff. Brother,

C.F.H.
movements.notes: Charles to Alexander. Capt. Rich now on Gen. Slough's staff. Sibley tents. Henry perhaps prisoner & soon exchanged. Mother heard rumor of exchange. Two men shot fingers off accidentally. Exchanging Austrian muskets for new guns. Band instruments. McDonald to write his wife about Henry.

movements.sigSummary: McDonald's story about Henry could not be confirmed: Charles methodically traces the rumor back through Champlain, soldiers' letters, and paroled prisoners, concluding nobody can verify his brother is alive — "he may be a prisoner in some rebel hospital." Writing off guard from Camp near Alexandria, he records frozen creeks, a grave-yard fence burned for warmth, six months' pay owed, and a plea for woolen yarn and darning needles.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 8, 1862
Camp near
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

As I am off guard today I will write to you. Guard duty at the city these cold nights is no fun. We are not allowed any guard fires now. The reason is, I suppose, that the soldiers steal all the wood they can get hold of. Have been burning the grave yard fence. There are three fires, one at each end of the pickets & one in the middle, but we are going to have guard tents put up with stoves in them so that the guard can warm themselves, I hear. There are 2 or 3 men put on in a place so that they can relieve each other. When we go on guard nights we put on our over coats & our blankets. I dont know as I can say put on our overcoats for we have them on nearly all the time. When three men are on a post two can put their blankets together & lay down, but I dont think any one will try it this cold weather.

There is snow on the ground a slight covering & plenty of ice. A creek near us thot running into the Potomac is frozen over solid that we might have good skating if we had any skates. But it will not last long, I think. Food is scarce here. We got out of wood so we went to a fine piece of ashwoods, young trees about as large as my leg, & carried it to camp. It was a pretty large piece of woods, but they came from the convalescent camp in a steady stream all day to hack it & to their camp which is some ways off. Our men & theirs have cut this woods all down. There are 10 or 12 thousand men in the convalescent camp sick, convalescent, & well. The camp is about to be broken up, the well men to return to their regiments, some to return to the hospitals & some to be discharged. This camp we call loose hill.

Capt. Rich is now Aid De Camp to Gen Slough who is military governor of Alexandria. I suppose Rich's employment is till we leave here, but I think from the looks of things we will stay here this winter. The officers are fixing up their tents to well to leave soon.

You wished to know if I was detailed as funeral escort. I was detailed one day, but did not act as there was no death. 26 men were detailed daily as funeral escorts, but there are more detailed now. They went to the provost marshals office where they were told if there were any deaths. The escorts that was to butt of the provost M. office all day if they had nothing else to do, for a funeral might take place any time.

I am glad you have found that memorandum book. When us boys get our pay you will have some figures to put down. I signed an allotment roll at Fonda allotting $10 a month to you. Have it the men signed it. I wrote Jake a few days ago. Received your letter of Dec. 1st, also the Observer. The Observer is like an old friend. I have just seen Ben Bouron & Freeman Houron. Ben is going to Yorktown

[page break]

if he can get a pass, to see his brother Lyman. Ben says it cost him $16 to come here. Will you send me a little woolen yarn & a couple of darning needles if you send me anything. Mrs. Doolittle says he does not have enough to eat. Says he eats when he can cook for himself. Says the men are lazy. Says that each man cooks for himself.

We went down to the city & went through it, but not a thing could we buy as neither of us had a cent of money. There is nearly 6 months pay due Alek & nearly 4 months due me. I dont know when we will be paid. Uncle has poor I guess. The men in our reg. are being trusted by the sutler. I shall not trade with him as he sells to dear. He has good butter, but it is 40 cts. a pound. Some of the men in our tent buy it. Alek says he owes the sutler $11.00 — had to buy as they could not get enough to eat.

We have just received our rubber blankets. I am very glad for they are just what we need. I have been very lucky about getting wet — have not been wet yet. I mean the time very well when not on duty. Riley from Corbeaus has papers sent to him which I read. With a good fire in the stove & a canoe to read I make out first rate. When we are on guard at night we are excused from any duty the next forenoon when we stretch out on the floor, feet to the stove, & try to take a nap, but we are pretty sure to get woke up by the mates. They say that one of the Fonda companies, the Captain I mean, cheated the Government by taking some men of another Co. & putting them with his to fill out his Co. till they had been inspected & drawing the bounty for three men who did not belong in his Co.

I have not been home sick since I have been here. Am glad that I am not a family man as they are the ones who are homesick. I bet Staats says if he ever gets home they will not catch him again — he will not be such a fool as to enlist. The soldiers here all seem to hate the niger. They say it makes them mad to think they are fighting to free the niger. We have a small brass band & a lot of drummers so that we have music mough. Hear it every day at dress parade & guard mounting. I guess you forgot that Alexandria is a large city. I can see and can buy almost anything here. I should not feel anxious about James if he does not succeed at West Point. He will in something else. I wish you would write all about home matters.

[page break — Dec 13 continuation]

Dec. 13, 1862
Camp near Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter last evening. They always come in the evening. Are brought to each man by some one of the Co.

I was very sorry to learn that McDonalds story about Henry was not true. I was afraid when you first wrote of his story that there was some mistake. I still think he may be in or prisoner in some rebel hospital. Probably he was badly wounded. Savagham heard from Mathews that his brother was most likely in a hospital. Bethune belongs to Capt. Rich's old Co. He was not in the battle as he was in the hospital at the time. I saw him in Washington when our reg. was coming here. Also saw him not long since here. He had cut from a newspaper a list of the killed & wounded in his Co. at the battle instances[?]. He showed me the list of killed & wounded. Came here to see Capt. Rich. A stayed here with him a day or two. I did not see him long either time. Both meetings were accidental & he introduced himself. Savagham heard from Mathews, not since if we had heard from Henry. McDonald's report might have started at Champlain. Somebody might have wrote to their friends in the army about him. Mr. Cook might have written Albert & he some one else in Co. B.

[page break]

About horse beef; we do not have any. We have salt beef which I like when the salt is all out. That is, when it is well cooked. Some call it salt horse.

We are not going to North Carolina. I don't think anyone believed we were. The regiment will stay here all winter. We have just had guard tents put up around the city for the guard. There is a fire in each tent & the guard relieve each other. We have also our rubber blankets so that we will be quite comfortable. The guard stays at the city 24 hours. We have boiled fresh beef about four times a week. Each man has a loaf of bread a day which he puts in his haversack. The bread sells in the city for 5 cts. We have boiled rice quite often which I like. It is sweetened a little. A good many of the men dont like it. We have two good cooks now.

I think we will not get our pay till next month. Wish you could send me one dollar. I have sold two dollars for repairing my watch. If that box comes will you send me two pairs of wool socks & two cheap handkerchiefs. They will be plenty. I have 3 prs. of socks but they will wear out before spring. A good many of the men have drawn socks. Some of them were thick & good — others not so. If not convenient dont send them as I can get socks etc. here.

I have not heard from sick yet. I do not like to write letters so Uncle John need not write often. I mean letters to strangers. Has Pollard married Mary Ann Brinkerhoff — you know who I mean. "I. Staats heard so from home. Have you engaged any one to draw those down saw logs. They ought to be drawn the first snow. Neshan will draw them or know of some one.

About James: I hope he will succeed, but if he does not it need be no disgrace. All are not calculated for military men & besides a good many smart men have not succeeded there.

I have seen some paroled prisoners (there is a camp of them not far off), but it would be useless to ask them about Henry as if they saw him they would not notice him as he was not in their Co. We have a good Chaplain. He has only preached to us two short sermons so far. & his sermons ought to be short as the men are drawn up in hollow square & stand. I mean 3 sides of a squad. The Chaplain stands in the 4 side & the officers also. He prays without kneeling. Some of the soldiers sing out of the soldiers hymn book. The Chaplain is quite sick now, caught cold at a soldiers funeral. The Catholics in our Co. attend church every Sunday in the city under the charge of the 1st Lieut. who is a Catholic. I dont know as there is a service anywhere else in the city.

I hope you will write often. You & Frances must make yourselves as comfortable as possible. We do not suffer from the cold as we have good fires. Our tent is a good tight one.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles's longest letter. McDonald's story about Henry "not true." Savagham heard from Mathews — brother most likely in hospital. Bethune in Capt. Rich's old Co. Saw Mathews & Leslie at Washington hospital — not seen Henry. James Beaumont died of fever. Christmas approaching. Horse beef. Paroled prisoners nearby. Chaplain description. Smallpox. Very detailed camp life.
Battle of Fredericksburg. 60th NY in reserve or lightly engaged.
Winter camp near Fairfax Station.

He clings to hope his brother lies in a rebel hospital. Six months unpaid and out of patience, he confesses he would sooner fight the abolitionists than the Southerners.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 21st, 1862
Camp near
Fairfax Station

My Dear Dear Mother & Sister:

I must "hurry up" and write or my fingers will soon be so numb that it will be wholly impossible. How I long to see you and when that will be God only knows. I wrote you a few lines the day before we left the Ferry. Since then we have done no small amount of marching. We went up Loudon Valley to Hillsborough, from there to Leesburg, thim to Fairfax Courthouse, from there to Dumfries, five miles from Aquila Creek and twenty-four from Fredericksburg. The orders were countermanded, I am one, and we marched back to this place, leaving a detachment of the Regts. there and another small force at Bolts ford over Bull Run Creek. We reached here day before yesterday and will probably leave soon.

Please thank Mrs. Hoyle surely for me for her kindness in sending those papers. Tell her that they were the sources of the greatest enjoyment to myself and comrades. The Plattsburgh paper was especially welcome. Say for me that we had the abolitionists quite as badly as does the editor of that sheet, and that we would much prefer fighting them to the Southerners.

You ask me, Mother, about my new duties: I could hardly tell you on paper, that you would understand, only that my responsibilities are much greater. Mother, did you ever receive the letter of two sheets I sent from London Heights telling you of my visit to the Camp of the 34th and all I learned there concerning Henry? I presume you did. I do not remember who they were that said they saw Henry. The boys (a number of them) said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and threw him self down. I think there is a strong probability of his being yet in a rebel hospital.

The first of January there is six months pay due me and I do not see much prospect of my getting it very soon as the treasury department does not seem to be in very good order. I am sorry for I should like to send you some money to get winter necessities. Mother, if you can without inconveniencing and denying yourself send me a little — and only a little — money, it would be a great comfort to me, and when you write if you will see and then put it in a stamp it will enable me to answer your letters much more readily for it is very difficult to get them here.

Love to all. I will try and write again soon. I am enjoying excellent health.

Your affectionate son,

Alex. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander at Fairfax Station after march from Harpers Ferry via Leesburg, Hillsborough, Fairfax Courthouse, Dumfries — "twenty-four from Fredericksburg." Orders countermanded. Visited 34th NY camp — "the boys said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and throw himself down[?]." Believes Henry is prisoner. Pay six months overdue.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander rode the cars free from Fairfax Station to reach Charles's camp near Alexandria on Christmas Day, arriving at 4 p.m. and gone by 11 the next morning — long enough to split butter, currants, and ginger snaps between them. Charles notes his brother looks well but thin on rations, then turns to the tent's quiet truth: of twelve men only three can write, so he pens the others' letters, "what you have a mind to," since they tell him nothing to say.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 26, 1862
Camp near Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I was surprised yesterday to receive a visit from Alek. Day before yesterday Capt. J. B. Ransom visited our Co. He told me then Alek stood in his first place. I asked him if he could let Alek come & see me. He said he couldn't if they did not leave, but said I must come up & see him. I told him I would if I could. His reg. is at Fairfax station, 15 miles from here. The whole army corps is there. I did not think of the railroad as a means of going there & thought of but two ways of my going there on foot — or hire a horse. But I had no money to hire a horse & would have to get a furlough of two days to walk there, so I was afraid I would not see Alek, but he came here on the cars free of expense. He arrived here at 4 p.m. yesterday & left at 11 a.m. today. He looks well, though the eruption he had on his face has not entirely cleared out & also a little whiskers. He is also rather fat. I intend to get a pass & take a railroad ride to see Alek if I can. I gave him half of the butter & currants, some of the g. snaps, a little

[page break]

yarn & a d. needle with the two fingered mittens & a towel as he had nothing to wipe his face with, also a testament. While at Fonda I bought a matt of kid gloves so I have both mittens & gloves. Alek says he does not have enough to eat always. Says he each man cooks for himself. Says he lives on fat pork & hard crackers, though if they have a tin like they fry it on the plate. Also says that he is in a log barracks coffee drinker though they do not get much sugar to put in it. They now have dried apples. He says they live in the open sir as their tents are only large enough to sleep in. Two sleep in a tent.

We went down to the city & went through it, but not a thing could we buy as neither of us had a cent of money. There is nearly 6 months pay due Alek & nearly 4 months due me. I dont know when we will be paid. Uncle has poor I guess. The men in our reg. are being trusted by the sutler. I shall not trade with him as he sells to dear. He has good butter, but it is 40 cts. a pound. Some of the men in our tent buy it. Alek says he owes the sutler $11.00 — had to buy as they could not get enough to eat.

He received the box Dec. 22nd. Alek & I are much obliged. The currants & butter will go well & the snaps have & will go well for a short time. Quite a number of boxes have been received in our Co. & a great many in the reg. One box in our Co. staid 3 or 4 weeks in Washington & some of the eatables are spoiled. Did you pay my charges on the box ? if so how much. Snakes stuff filled up about half of the box. I have sent quite a number of acquaintances since I have been here. Albert Cook has been here. He M.& N.M. there are at the parole camp at Georgetown. Albert looks well, was going to try to get a 20 days furlough to go home. He rode a horse which was one of forty he & Bright took care of, as he told it. I was on guard & did not see much of him. J. Douglas & Albert went into the city. Cyrus Kellogg has been out of the hospital only a short time & is not at the convalescent camp. He has been here several times to see his uncle Norman. The convalescent camp has been moved to about 3 miles from here. There is a shanty there dug out the side of a hill. We had a good fire obtained by asking for a few sticks from each wagon that passed. I hope you and Mother went to Grandmothers as I think you would have had a good time.

Col McMartin said to us the other day that he thought we had no more months here among 800 men that[?] there could be at home among the same number of men. Said we a great deal better off here than we would be at the front in smaller tents. Thought we would stay here this winter. Alek said it made him feel bad to see how comfortable we were & then think of their own camp. Lieut. Burdick came with Capt. Ransom into our Co. I see Burdick quite often. He is a pleasant man. Frances old friend S. Tombe is going to be discharged. He was to be drummer, but has not drummed any. I suppose she remembers what a handsome man he was. Well, he looks the same as ever. Made some particular enquiries about Frances said she went to school when he did & did him a favor when boys were reciting to Mr. Dixon in the teacher class. Tombe became confused & could not answer his question when Frances went on with the lesson as if he had answered right. He told me he was invited to Mrs. Nodiah Moores to a party when C. Walkerton boarded there. Mrs. Vanberton[?] urged him to come & see Charles as he was very polite. He & his brother are both married.

Where does Mrs. Brinkerhoff stay this winter. Has she said you the rent? Mount Vernon is about 8 miles from here. Some of the men have been there. I dont know as I care enough about it to walk there. We had no drill Christmas, nothing but dress parade which we have every day unless it rains. Some of the men went to the Catholic & some to the Episcopal churches on that day. Our 1st Lieut. McGuire is a Catholic & takes a squad of men every Sunday to the Catholic church.

[page break]

At dress parade we have to have shoes blacked, clothes brushed & look as nice as we can. I staid in camp Christmas & at 4 p.m. Alek came. We have 3 men standing on a barrel (each on a barrel) to punish them for having to much of a Christmas. The slave men in Alexandria is a terror to our men. The worst ones are showered. One of our men was on city guard & put down his gun for a few minutes to get a drink when an officer came along & took it his gun. He was shut up in the slave pen & showered.

Washington is about 8 miles from here. It is difficult to get a pass to go there. I think we can get none unless it is on business. How do you & Frances get along? You know I suppose your ears are not jarred by the noise in the stone castle unless it is by the mice. You had better keep money going. It still do you good to take sleigh rides. How does Frances like going to the post office? I wish she would write & tell how the examination went off & all the rest of the news. I hope you still feel well.

Savagham did not write that letter that you read. It was written by Tromby. There are 12 men in our tent & only three can write. Sergeant Welky, Jim Lucas & myself. Those men that cannot write send more letters then I do & receive letters very often. I have written some letters for them. They think as I do that I am not a very rapid letter writer. Some of them all give you a letter to read & tell you to answer it. They dont tell you anything to write so you write what you have a mind to. The majority of the ignorant men are in our tent. I think that the other tents have not so many ignorant men in each tent as there is in ours.

Please write soon & all the news.

Your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell.

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles's Christmas/year-end letter. Visited Alexander at Harpers Ferry before departure. Alexander jaundiced but good spirits. Christmas in camp — shoes blacked, dress parade at 4 PM. Slave men in Alexandria a "terror to our men." Washington 8 miles away. Savagham's letter not written by Tromby[?]. Only 3 men in tent of 12 can write. Charles is letter-writer for illiterate tentmates.
Joined regiment in the field near Fairfax Station.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Alexandria, his company detached for straggler duty, ferrying soldiers back to their regiments by steamboat. The heart is his visit to brother Alek at Fairfax Station, where he found the 60th NY hard up: water drawn from ditches and mudholes, the unit nicknamed "the thieving reg't," Alek six months unpaid and $11 in debt to the sutler. Then he gently corrects his mother, who'd heard Henry was urged not to go into that fight: "every man was obliged to go."
movements.transcription:
Alexandria, Va.
Jan. 2, 1863

Dear Mother:

You see this letter is dated different from my other letters and the reason is our Co. has been detached from the regiment and is stationed in the city near the Potomac. Our duties, I think, will be to take soldiers back near their reg'ts. Two squads from our Co. have taken two different lots of soldiers to Aquia Creek. I expect to go tomorrow as I have not been yet. The men like to go as they go and come on a steamboat. We take one or two days rations with us. One of our Lieuts. goes with the men. We moved day before yesterday, brought our tents and stoves with us. We all like our new quarters better than the old and I think we will stay here some time if the men behave themselves.

Last night there was a heavy wind with rain and it blew down four of our tents leaving the tent I am in and another one standing. The men whose tents were down went into the large d tent which is close to us and staid till morning when they put up their tents. I went to Fairfax Station Jan. 14th to see Alek. Their camp is about one mile from Y. Station in the woods. I staid every night with A. I intended to take the cars at 7 A.M. Alex went with me to the depot, but the cars were gone, so I had to wait till afternoon. I was gone four hours over my time, but nothing was said about it. Alex was well and surprised to see me. His face is scarred with the eruption he had, but it is not bad. Capt. Ransom read me his letter to you. They had just had orders to be ready to march at 12 hours notice with 8 days cooked rations in their haversacks and 8 days rations in the wagons. The men were getting fixed for the winter and hated to leave. Some of the men told me that they had had hard times. They said that the 60th reg't. was called the thieving reg't. That the reg't. left no money behind them, but took all they came across. Alex told me that they did not have enough to eat on a march, but were compelled to buy of the sutler. Told me he had had no pay for six months and he owed the sutler $11.00. They get their water out of a kind of a ditch. The water was riley, but they did not seem to mind it. Said they had often drank out of mudholes in the road on a march. The 60th reg't. forms a part of Gen. Slocum's 12 army corps which is encamped in the woods where I was. The 60th Reg't. is in the 2nd Brigade and 2nd Division. James Luther sends his respects to you and Frances. He looks fat and healthy. The 11th and 12th army corps from the Reserve Grand Division of the army of the Potomac commanded by Gen. Sigel.

I received those two handkerchiefs and say much obliged. Have received the Observer quite often lately. Alex told me he had no postage stamps; said it was the reason he had not written. I have some other. Wish you would send me some. Have borrowed quite a number. I tried to buy some with that dollar Frances sent me, but they wanted U.S. money.

[page break]

You say that Henry was urged not to go into that fight. Perhaps it is not so. When we were called out the roll was called and every man was obliged to go. Mr. Rye says he will pay over and above the appraisal what the land is worth. Does he mean that if they appraise the land below its value, he will make up the balance? If so, what does he call it worth? Mr. Savage has sold several lots at $500 an acre, just over Mrs. Turners. I suppose we had better sell a strip of the garden, but they ought to pay what it is worth. About the sugar bush, if his claim is good he ought to have that strip, but if there is any doubt about it, he can not have it. I don't know how he can come at it.

Have you got fodder enough for this winter? How does Joe get along? Does he do his chores well? I hope Frances will not overwork herself and that you both will try to enjoy yourselves as well as you can. Please write often and I will do so.

Affectionate son,

C. F. Hubbell

I suppose we ought to pay the church tax. But this tax is not for beautifying the church. I paid that tax at the time. This tax has run some time. Has the collector called on you? Have you paid Mr. Copeland anything?

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles detached from regiment, stationed in city near Potomac. Duty: returning soldiers to regiments. Visited Alexander at Fairfax Station Jan 14th[sic — date in letter]. Alexander jaundiced but well. Capt. Ransom's letter enclosed. 60th NY in 2nd Brigade, 2nd Division, 12th Army Corps. Henry "urged not to go into that fight." Mr. Rye claims land value issues.

movements.sigSummary: Orders arrive at evening, and the letter pivots: "We have just received orders to be ready to march in twelve hours and are probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans." Hours earlier Alexander was all bravado, teasing his sister Fannie that nothing beats "a good hunk of raw pork with my hard tack" and shrugging off his destitution: "I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night." movements.transcription:
Jan. 13th, 1863
Camp near Fairfax Station

My dear Mother and Sister:

I received your most welcome and long expected letter yesterday and was quite amused with one portion of it. So you think I had better roast my pork before eating, eh? Well, that will do very well when I am in camp, but when I am on the march, what tastes better than a good hunk of raw pork with my hard tack. You will have to be a soldier to appreciate it as it ought to be. It is really excellent my, Miss Fannie. You are quite shocked that I am in such destitute circumstances. Well, I suppose I am destitute, but then it hardly seems so to me when I compare my present circumstances with those that I have been in. Why, Frances, I have seen the time when I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night.

Evening: We have just received orders to be ready to march in twelve hours and are probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans. Do not be troubled, Mother. We are all in God's hands. He will take care of us. I commend you all to him and know and feel that He will take care of you and me.

Your aff. Son and Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander received letter, amused by Mother's assumption of destitution. "I have seen the time when I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night." Orders to march in 12 hours — "probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans." Commends all to God's hands.

movements.sigSummary: Captain James H. Ransom writes Mrs. Hubbell directly to ease a mother's "trying anxiety," reassuring her that Alexander "never looked so finely and well." He'd applied to send him home on recruiting service, then planned a furlough — until orders came to march at twelve hours' notice with eleven days' rations, destination unknown. A postscript catches the moment Charles arrives in camp to visit, "well and looks finely," before riding out at 7 the next morning.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 14, 1863
12th Army Corps, 2nd Division
2nd Brigade, In camp near
Fairfax Station, Va.

Mrs. F. M. Hubbell:

My Dear Friend:

Your letter to hand making inquiry concerning Alexander's going home. I immediately applied to the commanding officer of the Regiment to have him sent home on recruiting service if any sergeant went from the regiment. The matter was favorably considered by him after reading your letter and an explanation by myself. I thought the request was good for him to go home on duty and thus save expense to himself. If that failed, I was determined to apply for a furlough for him, as our circumstances daily looked more and more like "going into winter quarters" here, I though soon to effect one or the other efforts for him to go home. But yesterday we were ordered to be ready to march at 12 hours notice and with eleven days rations. We do not know where we are to go, of course, some think to join Rosecrans, others think towards Fredericksburg, and others still think we will go back to Harper's Ferry. No one knows exactly; it may be the generals and I don't very much that they know. So you see matters of furlough or recruiting service is all done away with for the present least, by orders to march.

I feel confident that I realize in a certain measure your trying anxiety of mind about your sons, and sympathize most sincerely with you and would be glad to do something to aid in relieving your anxiety. But can at present only assure you that Alexander is very well indeed and never looked so finely and well as at the present time. On Friday last I was down to the 153d Reg't. and say your son Charles, who looked well, too, and is in good health, he says, except a cold. Having many things to attend to in order to be fully ready to march when positively ordered, I write in haste. Please excuse. With much love to yourself and Frances, I am

Your friend,

James H. Ransom

P.S. Since writing the above, Charles arrived in camp to visit us. Is well and looks finely. Will return tomorrow at 7:00 A.M.
movements.notes: Captain Ransom writes to reassure Mother about Alexander. Alexander "never looked so finely and well." Visited Charles at 153rd — Charles also well. Orders to march with 12 hours notice, 11 days rations. Furlough/recruiting service "all done away with." P.S.: Charles arrived in camp; will return tomorrow at 7 AM.
With 153rd NY at DC defenses / Capitol Hill. Limited correspondence.
'Mud March' — Burnside's failed advance. Mired in mud, returned to camp.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from Alexandria the very night the company is paid for two months, with three months still owed — and warns, dryly, that liberty in the city means "we will have some drunken men in our Co. for a few days." He encloses a $20 allotment check, then pleads against worry: "When I am not well I will let you know." A postscript finds him in a stone Episcopal church, the graves around it weather-worn and dated to the 1700s.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 31, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter today and was surprised to learn that you thought I was sick. My health is very good; have got over my cough and hoarseness. Have not missed duty once on account of sickness since I enlisted.

We have just received our pay for two months. Three months pay is now due us. Nearly the whole Co. this evening as soon as paid, which was about 7:00 A.M., went into the city. I guess there will be no roll call tonight as it is pay night, but the men will have a little liberty. I think we will have some drunken men in our Co. for a few days.

Enclosed I send you a $20.00 allotment check. I suppose it will pass as well as money. Tomorrow morning the whole Co. is ordered to fall out with their guns. Nearly the whole Co. will be on duty tomorrow. I will go to Aquia Creek to guard some soldiers from here and some to the convalescent camp to bring them here. I do not go tomorrow to Aquia Creek, but may go to the same. We have a good time here; have straw ticks to sleep on, and eat much to do. Once in a while we have to guard soldiers to Aquia Creek. Can go into the city when we want to, but must look clean, and be here to roll call which we have three times a day, 6:30 A.M., 5 P.M., and 8:30 P.M. At 8 P.M. we have roll call and dress parade. A boy in our Co. about 16 years old, a hard boy, was absent at roll call several nights running. He was sent to the slave pen and showered. He will behave himself now, I guess.

I wish you would not worry about me, Mother. When I am not well I will let you know. I will keep you posted about myself. You will be much happier if you look on the bright side and expect to see Alex and I safe and sound at home some day, than if you fancy we are sick, etc.

I am glad to hear that you and Frances are well again. How you will take the world easy and try to enjoy yourself. I must close as I have no more time. I wish Frances would write. Has she had a letter from C. Fullerton? The newspaper wrapper on the Observer yesterday was written on the outside. Frances had commenced a letter to her cousin on the wrapper. I don't know who the cousin on the wrapper. I don't know who the cousin is, but she received an unexpected letter from the cousin.

Aff. Son

C. F. Hubbell

..... 30 .....

P.S. Feb. 1/63 Today is Sunday and we had no inspection this morning because so many men were on duty. I am not on duty today and I am glad of it because the mud is deep, I have not been to Aquia Creek yet. I received an Observer yesterday and one today. It much obliged. Then I saw Alex he had not received any paper for two or three weeks. Perhaps he does now. Letters and papers for us all come just as well without addressing them to care of any one. Last Sunday I attended church twice. It was the Episcopal church where quite a number of shoulder straps and privates were in attendance. I went in the morning and evening and intend to go this evening. The church is a very old one of stone. In the church yard around it are buried persons who died in 1700s. The grave stones are weather worn. Our men kept coming in all last night, some drunk, of course, but they were quiet. There is a theatre and circus here. How do you get along with Mr. Rye about the land? Please write me all about business matters.

Give my respects to all inquiring friends, as the boys tell me to say when I write for them. As this is written in a hurry, please excuse misspelling, which I wish you would correct.

Aff. Son

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles received pay for two months. Sent $20 allotment check. Whole Co. ordered to fall out with guns tomorrow. Guard duty at Aquia Creek — guarding soldiers. City liberty, no roll call tonight. Boy in Co. (16 years old, hard boy) absent at roll call, sent to slave pen and showered. P.S. Feb 1: Sunday, no inspection. Attended Episcopal church — "very old one of stone... buried persons who died in 1700s." Theater and circus in Alexandria.
Winter/spring camp near Aquia Landing. Drill and supply operations.
