movements.sigSummary: Capt. Ransom has gone home on furlough — "much to my sorrow and the company's" — and Alexander had hoped to go with him, but Gen. Sigel refused to sign his application and sent it on to the War Department, where it may sit forever. Writing from a camp near Stafford House with no fire on a raw February day, he imagines what ten days' leave would bring: "I shall not know whether I am on my head or heals for the space of ten minutes." Rain floods the Virginia roads, and the army can only lie still.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 6, 1863
Camp near Stafford House

My dearest Mother and Sister:

Wonder if it is raining up there today as hard as it is here. It began snowing quite furiously early yesterday morning — settled down into a steady rain — rained hard a good part of yesterday, all last night and is raining hard still. I expect the whole State of Virginia will float away pretty soon. One thing is quite evident — the army will have to lay still quite a little while longer. Capt. Ransom has gone — much to my sorrow and the company's. I had hoped to have gone with him, but Gen Siegel would not sign the furlough and it has gone to the War Department, and it will be some little time before I get it, if I ever do. I went down to the cane with the Capt. If I get this furlough what a time I shall have. I shall not know whether I am on my head or heals for the space of ten minutes. I cannot spare more time than that, for I shall have ten days furlough and shall want all the time possible to see you. You must excuse this short letter for I have no fire and the day is raw and chilly. Luther sends regards. He is well and I am very well. Love to all. Remember me to Mr. and Mrs. Copeland and all they boys.

Your affectionate son

Alexander F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander at Camp near Stafford House after march from Fairfax Station. Capt. Ransom gone — "much to my sorrow and the company's." Furlough application sent to War Department. Rain and mud. Lather sends regards. Short letter — no fire, cold day.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his sister Frances from Alexandria that "Gen. Hooker's army is broken up," noting the Pennsylvania reserves went out 15,000 strong but have only about 2,300 left. He recounts guarding 200 stragglers to Aquia Creek, sleeping four to a steamboat floor with him in the middle for warmth, supping on hard tack and bean soup. Hoping to glimpse brother Alex with the 60th N.Y. nearby, he jokes about his beard and teases that Mother's been "converted into a Greclate."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 13, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Frances:

I received your letter of Feb. 1st. Was glad to hear from you and also glad to read a letter so full of news. I received a letter from D. V. Savage this morning. Will answer it soon. Also one from James yesterday. Have not heard from Alex since I saw him.

Gen. Hooker's army is broken up. It is going south, or a part of it is. The Pennsylvania reserves (which went out 15,000 strong, has only about 2,300 left) come on here and staid a day or two and are now going on down to Washington. The 8th army corps, I hear, has gone to Fortress Monroe. I may see a part of Hooker's army will be retained for the defense of Washington. Last Tuesday I went to Aquia Creek. Left at noon and some stuck Monday afternoon. About eighteen of us — set as guard and took down about 200 stragglers. They call us $200 and a seer. The water was riley, but they did not seem to mind it. Said they had often drunk out of mudholes in the road on a march. There is a Rhode Island Reg't. near us (nine months men who received $500 bounty). Have been here five months, only 4 more to stay. The old soldiers are down at the battery now. The trip down the road was a pleasant one. We could go all over the boat. The stragglers were quiet. Said they did not see what there was a guard on the boat for. There were a great many vessels of all kinds at A. Creek. I heard today that the 60th N.Y. Reg't. is only about 3 miles from there. I may get a chance to see Alex if he stays there long enough. After landing at A. Creek we went to the soldier's Rest and had our supper. It consisted of hard tack, cold fat pork, and bean soup. The soup was very good.

We slept on the floor of the steamboat. I had my rubber blanket and woolen, and four of us slept together, I in the middle, so that I slept warm. The rest of the men had no blankets except rubber. In the morning we set out to the mail steamer and came back to Alexandria. The boat was crowded with officers and privates going home on a ten days furlough. I believe that only Hooker's army have furloughs. One or two men out of a hundred. I saw only one lady on board the boat and she was talking with a soldier that had his communion who was sitting by the stove. I suppose she was some relation.

I was out with the Co. drilling this afternoon. We were ordered to halt as we were marching through a street and Lieut. Knapp stopped and shook hands with Mrs. Burdick. He called for Hubbell and Staats. We stepped out and shook hands with Mrs. B. She leaves for home in three or four days. Invited us to go on and see her. Perhaps we will tonight. A. Douglas and Gokey have been

[page break]

to see and seen her. A. Douglas says they are strong secesh particularly a young lady there. Lieut. Col. Armstrong, Lieut. Knapp, and Douglas were there the other night. I think the people here are secesh but they do not show it.

It is true that I am a bearded fellow. I guess you would not know me if I did not speak. I wonder what Mrs. Burdick thought of my looks. I don't shave for two or three reasons. The main on is, it is a good deal of trouble to shave.

James says he has written me several letters, but directed them all wrong. How is your health? You must take care of yourself, as I try to do of myself. My health is good. Mother must not worry about me if she don't hear just so often. If I am sick at any time I will let her know it. But I hope that I will escape being sick as I have so far. One of our Co. is at Washington sick with the small pox. There are only two besides him that are sick, though not with the small pox. I hope you will write me soon again.

How is your friend Mr. Simonds? You and Mother must take the world easy and enjoy yourselves. So Mother is converted into a Greclate. You must be careful or you will be, too. Ask Mother if she will send me the Tribune once in a while to read, and not for a bed quilt as we have blankets enough. Savagham and I sleep together. He is a short, chunky, Frenchman and we keep each other warm.

Aff. Brother,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles writes to sister Frances. Gen. Hooker's army broken up. Pennsylvania reserves leaving. 60th NY may be retained for defense of Washington. Trip to Aquia Creek — slept on steamboat floor, visited landing. Stragglers. A. Douglas and Gokey have been to see cousin. Savagham and Charles sleep together — "short, chunky, Frenchman." Smallpox in Co. James says he has written several letters but directed them "all wrong."

movements.sigSummary: Alexander reached camp near Aquia Creek Landing safe and sound, six hours before his furlough expired, the journey from Rouse's Point to Washington costing $17.75 and forty-eight hours each way. Now the men are building fortifications. He urges his mother to keep a stout heart: "I believe this war cannot last much longer and trust I shall be home again soon."
movements.transcription:
Camp near Aquia Creek Landing
Feb. 21, 1863

My dear Mother and Sister:

I arrived here safe and sound at about six P.M. yesterday. You pressed me then, that I was but fortyeight hours coming and was here six hours prior to the expiration of my furlough. Found everything here about as I had left it. We are building fortifications. Now as you know how matters and things are going on here, I presume you would like to know something concerning my journey. I went to New York by the N.Y., New Haven railroad. Reached White River Junction that night about two A.M. and remained there until six. Reached New York that day, passing through Springfield, Herts., and Hartford and New Haven, Conn. Crossed the Jersey Ferry and took the first train for Washington which I reached about seven A.M. Friday morning. Left there at twelve M. and reached here as stated. My fare from Rouse's Point to Washington was $17.75. I hope, Mother, you keep up a stout heart. I believe this war cannot last much longer and trust I shall be home again soon.

Love to all, and tell the Capt. I shall write him soon. Luther is well and much pleased with his present.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander
movements.notes: Alexander returned from furlough — arrived safe at 6 PM. Traveled: NY by NY, New Haven railroad → Springfield, Hartford, New Haven, Conn → Jersey Ferry → train to Washington. Fare: Rouse's Point to Washington $17.75. Building fortifications. "I believe this war cannot last much longer and trust I shall be home again soon."

movements.sigSummary: Lieut. Col. Armstrong, after falling out with the regiment's Colonel — now under arrest, Charles hears — has resigned, and came down to bid the company goodbye, promising to carry word home that Charles was all right. A man was buried yesterday, the fourth death here, though Charles assures his mother nearly all are well now. Between snow, mud, and his plea for two dollars toward knee-high boots, he keeps circling back to reaching Aquia Creek to see Alex.
movements.transcription:
Alexandria, Va.
Feb. 22, 1863.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of Feb. 9th and also the Tribune and the Observer. I found the Tribune interesting. I'm sorry that you think I did not receive your letters. I assure you your letters are very welcome. Today is Sunday and we are blockaded by the snow storm. There is about six inches of snow on the ground and it is snowing hard and blowing. I am glad that our men have not to go off today. This snow will all go off at once and make lots of mud which we will have to wade through to go to the distributing camp for the stragglers. A few days since we had a hard snow storm. The snow quickly went off and left us some awful roads to travel. I found then that shoes were not the thing. I wish you would send me two dollars as I want to buy a pair of boots. You can get that $20.00 check cashed and use as much as you are a mind to. I would prefer greenbacks as Uncle Sam's money passes the best here. I bought a pair of boots some time since but after wearing them two or three days sold them as they hurt my feet and will wait until pay day for my pay. We expect to be paid next month. Boots that reach up to the knees or above are all the fashion here among officers and men. The mud dries up very quickly here, but is bad while it lasts. We do not have any as cold weather here as at the North.

I went down to Aquia Creek a few days since and came near going to see Alex. I intend to see him before long if possible. We came back on the mail steamer, which we went on in the evening, and slept there on the floor of the cabin around the store till morning. We started at 9:00 A.M. and arrived here at 1:00 P.M. We do not always get as good a place at that to sleep in. The boat was filled with officers and men going home on a ten days furlough. There were also two sick boys and one man and some more ladies taking care of them. Their mothers, I am sure. A. Douglas has gone to Fortress Monroe with some of our men as a guard, also Lieut. Knapp. They took four days rations with them and we expect them back today. Two or three hundred men have left here nearly every day

[page break]

some time back from the convalescent camp and other camps for their regiments.

Lieut. Col. Armstrong has had some difficulty with our Col. and has resigned. The Col. was restoring under arrest, I hear. Armstrong was down here and bid the Co. goodbye. I told him to tell you I was all right if he saw you. He said he would make it a point to see you. I hear that Capt. Rich will be Major.

Yesterday a man was buried who belonged to this Co. Four have died in this Co., but nearly all the men are well now. How do you and Frances get along? You must both try to enjoy yourselves. I hope Frances will not work too hard teaching French. Would not you both like to make a visit to Charlotte? You wanted to make a visit there last winter with me. I have just overheard that the Adjutant is to be Major, so Capt. Rich will remain as he is. Who is the newest? How did Silas' lecture go off? I have not been to church for some time on account of the weather and being away. Our 1st Lieut. goes to High Mass at the Catholic church, but I think it does not do him much good as he swears hard sometimes. Does Sydney work any this winter or his sister or has he a boy? Has she got along with his officer? I must write slips and send some tomorrow.

I saw one soldier going home on a furlough who said that his Co. drew lots to see who should go. I have not heard from Alex. Do you think he will get a furlough. We have potatoes quite often. We have no dried apples.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles blocked by snow — 6 inches, hard and blowing. Wants $2 for boots. Went to Aquia Creek — stragglers. Trip to see Alexander at Aquia Creek on steamboat. Lieut. Col. Armstrong has difficulty with Col., has resigned. Col. under arrest. Capt. Rich to be Major. Adjutant to be Major. Does Sydney work any — does his sister or he has a boy? Funeral escorts. Dried apples unavailable.

movements.sigSummary: A half-pint of whiskey ration arrives every day, and Alexander gives every drop away — "bound by a resolve I held most sacred in the world, a resolve to my mother." Writing from rain-stalled fortification work at Aquia Landing, where he oversees men raising earthen forts, he relives his recent furlough "all over again in my imagination," frets over a pony's hard ride to Rouse's Point, and tucks a torn dollar bill in the envelope, asking his mother to swap it for a whole one.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 28, 1863
Aquia Landing

My dear Mother and Sister:

It is raining quite furiously here today and as a natural consequence we are not at work on the fortifications, much to my satisfaction. As I told you when I was at home, all I have to do is to oversee the men. We are erecting several forts (of earth) and when they are all completed this will make quite an impregnable position. We have a half-pint of whiskey every day. I do not drink or profess, but give it to the boys. You need have no fear of my ever drinking it. The very smell sickens me and what is more than all, I am bound by a resolve that I held to be most sacred in the world — a resolve to my mother. Well, about my writing — I am living it all over again in my imagination, which you know is quite vivid, and am enjoying it almost as much as when I was there. So you remember, Miss Fannie, hear these presentations: Frenchmen have out of the road, and your humble servant presents rather an undignified appearance whenever that comes into his mind. Wonder how Charley and the big, fat Frenchman get along — wonder if he been him warm still these cold nights? Rich I could see Charley and give him those socks. They will keep his warm.

How do matters and things progress around Champlain? Has pony recovered from his journey to Rouse's Point? I feel very much provoked when I think of that for I should have had ample time to have obtained my ticket and even had time to spare but I taken the care at Champlain, and you, Mother, might have been spared that miserable ride. But time did you get home that night? Tell Willie to take good care of Pony. I will get him a comb and brush as soon as possible. While in New York, when endeavoring to get a bill out of my wallet to pay an omnibus driver, I accidently tore one in two. I send it enclosed. If you

[page break]

can pass it will you send me another? As I wish to return the dollar to the fellow that owned the watch. You know Scott charged me nothing for fixing it. Love to all. Remember me to all the good people of C.

Yours affectionately,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P.S. Regards to the Capt. Luther is well. Send a U.S. note if possible.
movements.notes: Alexander at Aquia Landing. Raining — no work on fortifications. Living on road, reading novels. "Miss Fannie, hear these presentations: Frenchmen have out of the road, and your humble servant presents rather an undignified appearance." Remembers Charley and "the fat Frenchman." Mother has recovered from trip to Rouse's Point. Henry discussion — "I feel very much provoked when I think of that." Wants U.S. note.

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your letter of Feb. 23, also the Observer, in which you said Alex had been home. I was surprised to learn that he had been home. Your letter did not say much about his visit, but I intend t...
movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from Alexandria, March 2, 1863, with a soldier's clear eye: twelve or fifteen women now live with their husbands in the regiment, each couple sharing a tent, the wife drawing rations and washing clothes for pay. He watches one stout woman marching through the mud after her husband — "our men thought she ought to stay at home." Unconvinced the war will end soon, he resolves to "stay my three years."
movements.transcription:
March 2, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of Feb. 23, also the Observer, in which you said Alex had been home. I was surprised to learn that he had been home. Your letter did not say much about his visit, but I intend to go and see him before long to hear about his visit and to get these socks which came just in time.

I went to the Episcopal Church last evening. Heard a very good sermon. There are two or three Methodist churches here that are open. I must go to them. Two or three days since our chaplain made our Co. a visit. He visited each tent and left a few tracts. The men all like him, as he is a cordial man, shakes hands with each one. I have not heard him say anything about religion. I guess the men would rather talk about something else.

I received a letter from Uncle John which I will send in this. Wish you would send it back in your next letter and tell me how to answer it. Did he visit us a year or two since? He is a strong democrat and a little sesesh, I think. I don't like to write to almost strangers.

We were mustered in for pay two days since; expect our pay this month. I have bought me a pair of new boots for $4.25, also sold my watch for $12.00 to be paid at 60 days. The man is not very good, but if he don't pay, I will take the watch back. He is a great spendthrift, has borrowed $5.00 and given $10.00 for it. This man is from Canada. A corporal needs a watch to relieve guard, but I will buy another.

About that land that Mr. Rye claims, I don't know as we can say anything. It is doubtful if we could succeed about the road off our garden. I should not let them have it unless they pay what it is worth. Did Grandfather in his will lay down the boundary between Mr. Rye and us? If he did I do not suppose a surveyor would go by it in settling a dispute.

Lieut. Knapp told me that they had no Champlain officers in Co. H, 60th Reg't.; that both Lieut.'s had resigned. Asked me what sergeant Alex was and I told him that I did not know. There was a soldier shot dead by a citizen and I told him that I did not know. He (the citizen) has been arrested. Have you had a visit from Lieut. Col. Armstrong? I heard today that he was routed out of Plattsburgh. A woman who has just come on to live with her husband here in camp tells the story. I also heard that the friends of some of the soldiers had sued him for that $270. bounty which they did not get. We none of us got it because we enlisted too late. But he promised it to us. I don't believe either of these stories are true. There are twelve or 15 women living with their husbands in our reg't. Each man has a tent for himself and wife. The wife draws

[page break]

rations. She must wash clothes for them, but they must pay her. Today we brought a lot of stragglers from the camp to go to their regiments. I stout woman was marching through the mud after her husband. Our men thought she ought to stay at home.

Have you called on Mrs. Burdick? I wish Frances would write me. How do you and Frances get along? Has Silas made his speech yet? I think he will not make a brilliant speech. Are drygoods very cheap now and groceries? I wish you would send me the Tribune after you have both read it unless you want to keep it for the story. Doesn't Alex want the Observer? The mud here is drying up very fast. After that snow, sleigh rides were taken here.

The war does not look like closing soon to me. I say stay my three years. I will close by asking you to write soon.

Your aff. Son

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles surprised to learn Alexander had been home. Attended Episcopal Church — good sermon. Methodist churches open. Chaplain visited — "shakes hands with each one." Uncle John's letter — "he is a strong democrat and a little sesesh." Boots purchased — $4.25, sold watch for $12 to pay in 60 days. Corporal needs watch to relieve guard. Land dispute with Mr. Rye — boundary/surveyor question. Lieut. Knapp told Charles had Champlain officers visit — called for Hubbell and Staats. Citizen shot soldier; citizen arrested. Lieut. Col. Armstrong routed out of Plattsburgh. Woman living with husband in camp.

movements.sigSummary: New officers gone home and a new captain at the helm — Alexander writes from Aquia Landing that both his Lieutenants have resigned, leaving Lieut. Delany of Co. F as his new Captain, "a most excellent man — one after my own heart." Still building fortifications and "having jolly times," he teases his sister Fannie about a sleigh ride that badly frightened some poor Frenchmen, and promises to forward Cousin Mary McNeil's amusing political letter.
movements.transcription:
March 8, 1863
Aquia Landing

My dear Mother and Sister:

I have written you two letters to your one, nevertheless, I shall write you again and expect the answers will come in due time. How do you get along now? Hope you had any sleigh rides since I left? Be careful, Miss Fannie, the next time you ride out not to scare any more poor Frenchmen as badly as we did those when coming from Cheesje. Poor chaps — wonder if they have recovered yet. Do not fail when you write to let me know how Charley and the fat Frenchman get along — if he still keeps him warm.

We are still building fortifications and are having jolly times. We have a new Captain — Lieut. Delany of Co. F — a most excellent man — one after my own heart. Therefore in directing your letters direct to the care of Capt. Delany. I neglected to tell you that both of our Lieuts. have resigned and gone home.

Goodrich, I received a letter a few days since from cousin Mary McNeil of Goodrich, Mich. It is quite a political dissertation and very amusing. I think I shall enclose it and send it to you. If I do, please put it with my package of old letters. I shall try and answer it today. Love to all.

Yours affectionately,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. You will enjoy Cousin Mary's letter up to "ninety nine."
movements.notes: Short letter. Alexander has written two letters to Mother's one. New Captain — Lieut. Delany of Co. F — "a most excellent man — one after my own heart." Direct letters to care of Capt. Delany. Both Lieutenants have resigned and gone home. Cousin Mary McNeil letter received — "quite a political dissertation and very amusing." P.S.: "You will enjoy Cousin Mary's letter up to 'ninety nine.'"

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Alexandria, anxious that his mother's letters have stopped — three weeks waiting on two borrowed dollars for boots. He recounts a snatched visit to brother Alex at Aquia Creek: "hearty as a buck, big fat face," now third sergeant in the 60th, angling for a furlough he means to spend at home. Beneath the warmth runs unease — Aunt Laura has bought Henry's farm, and the men grumble that Capt. Ransom pocketed their ration money.
movements.transcription:
March 12, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I sit down to write wondering what the reason is that I don't receive a letter. Wrote you nearly three weeks since requesting that you would send me two dollars as I wished to buy a pair of boots. I then borrowed $2.00 and bought the boots and have been looking for a letter with the money, but have received no letter since one dated Feb. 23rd. I think that your letters may have miscarried, if not, it is strange that you don't write.

I went to Aquia Creek Monday and saw Alex. Went on purpose to see him; got there at 3:00 P.M. and staid till after dinner next day. He was surprised to see me; was well and very much pleased with his visit home. I did not think it would cost so much to go home and back. He says it cost him nearly $40.00 to go home. Alex received a letter from Aunt Laura while I was there. She says Aunt has bought Henry's farm and she doesn't know what will become of the homestead; is afraid Cleveland will have it. What do you think about matters at Charlotte? One of Alex's new boots is running down at the heel; the shoemaker is to blame. Alex gave me two pairs of socks he bought. They look like good ones and came just in time. Where did you get them?

The log huts that the 60th reg't. live in are quite comfortable. I did not arrive at a good time to see Alex alone as he was getting ready for inspection and after inspection was on guard so that our private conversation was limited. But I had a good visit and Alex was pleased. He says he is now third sergeant and when their orderly is promoted to Lieut. he will be second sergeant. Luther concurs; he is sergeant so there will be a vacancy. He looks just as he used to, big fat face and hearty as a buck; is anxious to have a furlough and will not fail to call upon you. No furloughs are now granted in that reg't, on account of not making a good advance at inspection, but they are to have another inspection and hope to have furloughs granted again. The men of Capt. Ransom's Co. complain that he took home with him his Co.'s money that he received for rations. I don't know as it is true. I heard some good singing in Alex's tent. The orderly and sergeant Howes and Luther were the singers.

Today the weather is cold, and there is a flurry of snow once in a while. Will you tell me about Alex's visit, what he did, etc? Do you know I think some one is sick or dead over at Charlotte and that you and Frances are there; is the reason why you have not written. I hope that I will receive a letter soon and also that you and Frances are both well.

There have been a number of resignations in our reg. One of the Capts. who used to be a minister has resigned. I heard that Lieut. Burdick is going to do the same thing, but I don't know as he will. I wish you would send me some m. coupons, if convenient. Ron does the pony get along?

Does Richard (pronounced Resham) talk of making a line fence between us this summer? He has plenty of wood of his own to sell off his lot. Who do you think will take the farm next year? How would Resham do? Are you going to have sugar made this year? Where does Mrs. Brinkerhoff live this winter? There, I think I have asked questions enough. Will you write immediately if you have not written as I would like to know how you and Frances are and I would like $2.00 to pay that money that I borrowed.

Hoping that you will take good care of yourself. I remain

Your aff. son

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles visited Alexander at Aquia Creek Monday — Alex well, "very much pleased with his visit home." Alex is now 3rd sergeant, "will be second sergeant" then "promoted to Lieut." Alex looks "just as he used to — big fat face and hearty as a buck." Borrowed $2 for boots. No furloughs granted — another inspection needed. Capt. Ransom's Co. complaint — took home his Co.'s money. Freeman Bowron from Washington visiting. Alex says "it made him feel bad to see how comfortable we were." Does Richard (Resham) talk of selling?

movements.sigSummary: Mother's letter to Charles, with money inside, somehow reached Alexander instead — the postmaster crossing out "60th Regt." for the 153rd, then back again, before settling on the "sixtieth N.Y. Volunteers." Writing from Aquia Landing, where the forts are finished and the daily detail now unloads boats at the wharves, Alex forwards it on, sends Charles two pairs of socks, then turns somber at a paper from Mrs. Hoyle bearing notice of Dana Lyman's death.
movements.transcription:
March 16, 1863
Aquia Landing

My dear Mother and Sister:

How I should like to see you both today — to be seated in your comfortable sitting room and have it snowing "pitchforks" so that we could have a nice cozy visit — something I hardly had while there. How I wish I had had time to visit the Academy while in session. One of the most pleasant points of my visit for me to look back upon is the lecture in the old Academy. Please to tell Mr. Simons, Miss Fannie, that we hope to have an opportunity soon to vindicate our honor before the world, and to show that we have brains and in the right place too.

Now, dear Mother, a very singular circumstance has occurred. The let or you wrote to Charles containing money by some means or other came to me. The letter was directed to 60th Regt., company I. The sixtieth was crossed out, and in place of it, the 153d placed before it. This was also crossed out, and on top of the envelope it was directed by the postmaster to the "sixtieth N.Y. Volunteers." It was very fortunate, was it not, that I got it? I mailed the letter with one from myself to Charles today. Charles was up to see me a day or two since and I gave him two pairs of socks, as you directed. I am glad he has got them. He said they were just what he needed. He has got himself a first rate pair of boots and has paid $4.75 for them. Said he had written you were the age for money and wondered why you did not send it. Said he was afraid that all was not right up there (i.e., you were sick) ... We have finished the forts and now the air is a daily detail to work upon the wharves unloading boats, etc. We are very pleasantly situated, and I hope we shall remain here for some time to come. How are you getting along with that Rye affair? The old rascal will receive his deserts yet!

You will receive a call from Lieut. Ingram are long. He was very much gratified by my visit to his wife. I received a letter from him a few days since. I wish, Mother, if you can, you would send me Albert Cook's address. I should like very much to hear from him. There is a signal station down at the landing and it makes me think of him. Remember me to Mr. and Mrs. Copeland and their children and to all the ladies of C.

I was very much shocked a few days since by receiving a paper from Mrs. Hoyle with a notice of Dana Lyman's death posted upon it. How much her and you in Champlain will miss her. I have not the slightest doubt but what her prayer for her brother's conversion will be answered. Love to all.

Yours affectionately,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander wishes to see Mother — "snowing pitchforks." Charles came up, got boots and socks. Letter sent to Charles with money was redirected by postmaster — "sixtieth" crossed out, "Sixty first N.Y. Volunteers" written. Finished forts, now daily detail on wharves unloading boats. "Very pleasantly situated." Mrs. Hoyle sent paper with notice of Dana Lyman's death.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes home from Alexandria, and tucked between a midnight fire he helped fight with Uncle Sam's new steam engines and a request for two borrowed dollars sits the letter's quiet heart: he has read in the Tribune that mothers can claim a pension for a son who is killed. "Savagham has never been heard from." A list of 400 Union soldiers dead in rebel hospitals is about to be published, and Charles urges his mother to see it.
movements.transcription:
March 19, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

Your letter of March 10th received; glad to hear from you. I have not heard from Alex since I saw him. He is not a good correspondent and I am not one either as I promised to write him and have not done so. Last night I had just come from changing the one o'clock guard when a man fried fire. One sentry ran across the road and pounded on the door of the engine house with his gun crying "Fire." This engine house and the two steam fire engines it contains belong to Uncle Sam. This engine house and the steam fire engines are new engines, just

[page break]

come. Well, as the horses are kept harnessed night and day and fuel in the engines ready for the match, the engines were soon at the fire with steam up ready to commence throwing water. The engine hose was screwed on to the hydrant and a stream of water began to play on the burning houses. I heard that a Captain's wife living in one of the houses had several hundred dollars in money burnt up. The engines prevented the spread of the fire so that only four buildings were burned, thanks to Uncle Sam's engines, which were brought here to protect govt. property. There are only two posts where we have sentries, one at the door where we go into our camp and the other in the city guarding some guns. Two corporals a day are on, each taking half the day and half the night. We are having easy times and I hope we will stay here.

No liquor is allowed to be brought into the city except for hospitals and the private stores of officers. But it is sold slyly still. Some of our men got drunk; they were taken to the provost marshall's office and compelled to maser where they got their liquor. The result was that an Irish woman who sold the whiskey and one of our men were sent to the slave pen for ten days. There is a corporal here by the name of Beardsley who, our orderly says, is a great fool, only he don't know it. Tells about when he taught school so that he was called school master by the serpeant at Plattsburgh. He is a conceited but a good natured fellow. Well, I have received three wrappers from his sister. I did not know that he had a sister till I had received a paper and asked him. I think she may keep sending if she wants to, but I will not send her an entire stranger, any letters. She is careful to put her name on the papers.

I received two Tribunes today; have received two before, so that I have not read all you have sent. I find the Tribune interesting. I also read the Observer a few days since. I saw in the Tribune that mothers can receive a pension for a son that is killed provided that they are dependent or partly dependent on him for support. Savagham has never been heard from.

When do you think the war will end? I hope that we will give the rebels a good thrashing before long. The news is good from Vicksburg if it is true.

My health is very good at present. Alex Douglas complains of a headache for a day or two. Will you send me two dollars immediately if you have not done so, as I borrowed $2.00 about three weeks ago to be paid in about a week which I was not able to do. I hope Frances will write soon. How is her health and yours good? We now ride to the convalescent camp in the cars and bring the stragglers, as we call them, back, in the cars. We go up in the freight cars, no seating and come back with them naked inside and out, — that is, on top of the cars. The stragglers call us $800.00 and a cow, because the soldiers guarding that camp are now nine months men and receive $500.00 bounty. How did Silas' speech go off?

[page break — Mch 20 continuation]

Mch. 20 — I received a letter from Alex this morning enclosing one from you with $3.00. I send you the envelope to show you how it was directed. I suppose the Postmaster at Champlain put on the figures 113th and 60th at the top. Alex was well. You speak of my having wet feet. I have not had wet feet more than once or twice since I enlisted. I wear shoes because they are easier for the feet, I think. Think I shall sell my boots. Twelve of our men have left today for Fortress Monroe as a guard on the boat; took 4 days rations with them.

I don't think the land Mr. Rye claims has any maple trees on it. La Vally I don't think would be a good man. I saw in the Observer that the names of 400 Union soldiers who had died in rebel hospitals was about to be published. I think it would be well to see the list.

..... 30 .....
movements.notes: Charles received letter from March 10. Cyrus Kellogg in squad to Aquia Creek — says Hooker will give two years more "hard fighting." Emerson Smith at convalescent camp. Henry: "I am afraid he was killed." Convalescent camp men in wooden barracks. Deserters in citizen's clothes. Henry Gregory — "too big a heart." Lieut. Burdick more a streak of blue lightning. Continuation March 20: letter from Alex with $3, sent envelope to show misdirection. Alex was well. Our regt. has shoulder scales. Tribune and Observer received. Pennsylvania men received $500 bounty. Church — Methodist, Episcopal.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from Aquia Landing on March 22, 1863, certain the end is near: "I expect, if I live, to be there in the course of ninety days with an honorable discharge in my pocket, and the war over." Between the teasing — Frances writing only "when the fit is upon you," Silas orating about hens and heifers — he recalls his mother boxing his ears during haircuts, calls his own writing "hen's tracks," and asks her to tell Miss Alma Mcyath she will soon fulfill her promise.
movements.transcription:
March 22, 1863
Aquia Landing

My dear Mother and Sister:

To you, Miss Francis, I will first address myself. I received a letter a day or two since from Mother — and none from you, but then you are, I suppose, perfectly excusable, as I believe you generally write upon the inspiration of the moment, or as you say, "when the fit is upon you." Would that these inspirations or "fits" came more often upon you.

Well, has S. P. Hubbell, counsellor-at-law, held forth in the old Academy yet? How he did not say his brother was afraid of a gun. He is certainly a mighty man of valor and a great orator. I have heard him make some wonderful speeches about "the destructiveness of your hens" and "the unruly propensities of your cow and heifer," etc., etc. They were highly entertaining. Did Silas have anything to say about "the hens and heifer" or "who tramped through his oats and grass?" But laying all jesting aside, I hope Silas will do well — and more than well.

How does Mr. Simons and the Misses Crowly prosper? Hope Mr. Simons will soon have a better opinion of the Potomac army.

And now, my dear mother, I will now say a word or two to you. I am just about having my hair cut. It makes me think of the times when you used to box my ears because I would not hold my head still, and tell me that I was perpetual motion. I am half inclined to believe you.

I am very glad Lieut. Ingram has called upon you. I hope you were pleased with him. You tell me, dear Mother, to follow the rules of civilized life as far as possible. Would you insinuate that the U.S. army is an army of barbarians? Shocking! Horrible! I am astonished — shocked to hear such principles confessed and even avowed in the old stone castle. I understand what you mean, Mother, and will try and follow your directions. If you can get an 150 lbs. of sugar for the bush, I think it would be a good plan to let it out. If you see Miss Alma Mcyath, please tell her for me that she will soon have to fulfill her promise for I expect, if I live, to be there in the course of ninety days with an honorable discharge in my pocket, and the war over. How does Mr. "I know" get along? Now, dear mother, you tell me to write you good long letters. You must know this is a difficult thing for me to do. My head and hands fly in all directions and that is one reason why my writing is like hen's tracks or rather goose tracks. My regards to Mr. and Mrs. Copeland and the boys and little girls. Remember me to Mrs. Hoyle and thank as warmly as possible for sending me those papers. They are a blessing to the whole company. Love to all.

Yours affectionately,

Alex F. Hubbell
Company H, 60th NYO

Luther is well. Regards the Captain. He (the Captain) gave me warning of the scolding I may expect from you. I received a letter from him yesterday and am very much obliged.
movements.notes: Alexander addresses Frances directly about writing frequency. Silas Hubbell held forth at Academy — "a mighty man of valor and a great orator." "I am just about having my hair cut. It makes me think of the times when you used to box my ears." Lieut. Ingram has called. Asks Mother to follow "rules of civilized life as far as possible" — shocked at suggestion U.S. army is "an army of barbarians." 150 lbs sugar for the bush. Alma Mcyath — fulfill promise if he lives. Luther well. Regards to Captain.

movements.sigSummary: Mother begged Alexander to write the surgeon for "a place of safety in time of battle," and from Aquia Landing his answer comes back fierce: "Would you have me branded as a coward?" Wherever his regiment goes, he will go. Yet the same hand admits, "Though I love my life as dearly as any one could love it," before turning homeward — to a restored Union, the spring sugar bush, and a certain tailor in Rutland he means to see.
movements.transcription:
March 29, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Mother and Sister:

I received your letter of the 20th inst, a day or two since, and was much displeased with a certain part of it. Why! Mother, I am really astonished that you should say what you did: "Write the surgeon to assign me a place of safety in time of battle!" Haven't Wherever my reg't goes, I will go (God willing). Do you think, Mother, — really think that I could let my company go into battle without my being with them to bear my part of the danger? I am astonished you should counsel such a thing. Now, dear Mother, for my sake do not write the surgeon. Would you have me branded as a coward? Though I love my life as dearly as any one could love it, yet I have too much respect for myself and country to play any such part as that. Should heartless, who have so much at stake, be a whit behind those noble foreigners who are doing so much to save our country from ruin? "No! No!" I know you will say, Mother. A few vigorous and heavy blows dealt soon will, I think, finish this rebellion. You people at the North must give us your support. There is no way of settling this rebellion by the bayonet, and we can, and **will** do it. Oh! what a happy day it will be to me when I can come home, this war over and our glorious Union restored to its former greatness. There is a certain tailor in Rutland I should like then to see.

Well, Mother, so you have let Mr. Clark have the horse and heifer to take care of. A very good idea, I think, and also that of letting out the sugar bush for one hundred and fifty pounds of sugar. 150 lbs. of sugar is a matter not to be despised in these times.

And so, Miss Fannie, you think Silas is in a fair way to take to himself a rib, eh? (one of the Misses Crowley, perhaps.) An extra rib would do him no harm, I think.

There is a very loyal and wealthy widow in Baltimore whom the boys of this Co. thought the Captain thought a great deal of. She is a noble woman and thinks a great deal of the reg't., perhaps partly on account of the Capt. Many a poor soldier has had reason to bless her.

We are expecting our pay next week and will you please write and inform me of the best way of sending my money home? I am now out of stamps. Will you send me two or three? Love to all. Remember me to all my friends, especially to the Capt. I received a long letter from him a day or two since. And please give my regards to Mr. Clark.

Yours with much affection,

Alexander F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander received Mother's letter of 20th. "Why! Mother, I am really astonished that you should say what you did: 'Write the surgeon to assign me a place of safety in time of battle!'" Defends his honor — "Would you have me branded as a coward?" "There is no way of settling this rebellion by the bayonet, and we can, and will do it." Loyal wealthy widow in Baltimore. Expecting pay next week. Mr. Clark caring for horse and heifer. 150 lbs sugar. Silas courting one of the Misses Crowley.

movements.transcription:
March 29, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of Mch. 19th in due time. Am expecting a letter from you tomorrow. I received one from James dated Mch. 22, which I answered. He writes in good spirits. Cyrus Kellogg was in the squad on Friday that we took down to Aquia Creek. He told me to give his regards to my friends. Says his time will be out the 10th of June and that Hooker says he will give the two years men some hard fighting before their time is out. He looks well; he has been in the convalescent camp some time. He inquired about my friends; says he heard from Champlain

[page break]

that James 14 doing well. The men in the convalescent camp live in wooden barracks built this fall. The camp of distribution moved near; it is where we go for the men. Two nights ago our reg't. was called by the long roll and a couple of other reg'ts, lying near. I don't know whether Fort Lyons was any signal fires; at any rate she fired some guns (4) as a signal and the camp was roused. I heard that Lieut. Burdick wore a streak of blue lightning till every man was out of his tent. His men like him for all that. Our Co. being down here escaped all the fun of being routed us. I don't like this having to turn out in the night in such a hurry.

The weather here is quite changeable. Yesterday it rained hard; today there is a cold north wind which keeps us around the fire.

I think that you made a good arrangement about the cow and horse. I suppose you can buy your milk. I read a letter from Champlain which says hay is $2,500 a ton. I guess letting out the farm for grazing will be the best thing you can do. How much did you receive for sugaring last summer? Did Silas find out from that man at the Point about Henry. I am afraid that he was killed. Emerson Smith is at the convalescent camp. Cyrus K. says that Mink and Cook are at Georgetown. I think we will not leave here very soon. We are not very anxious to leave. I have answered Uncle John's letter but did not ask him to write. I don't like to write letters except home letters. That kind of clerks do Jim Morrison and Albert Contreras make? Frances knows how she likes them, I suppose.

There were a lot of deserters here a day or two ago that were going back to their reg'ts. They were dressed in citizen's clothes and were good looking men. One man from our Co. has had a furlough to go to Plattsburgh and has been gone about double his time. I don't know as he will come back. His brother is a soldier in our Co.

Where is Henry Gregory and what is he doing? He is the man with too big a heart as Dr. Coyt said. I am glad you are going to have some maple sugar. Think it is a good bargain if he gives you 150 lbs. and doesn't cut any good wood.

Mch. 30 — I was disappointed this morning in not receiving a letter from home. Have not received any papers for some time. If Alex likes the Tribune you had better send him some of them. I hope you will not send either of us any papers before you have read them through. I sent Alex two Tribunes some time ago.

Our regt. has shoulder scales for the men. It makes the men look better. Last night I went to the Methodist church. It was crowded. Part of the church was filled with soldiers marched there in a body. Had a good sermon. I had rather attend the Episcopal church. As the mail goes out in a few minutes I must close.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles received letter of Mch 19. James letter dated Mch 22 answered. Cyrus Kellogg in squad to Aquia Creek — Hooker will give "two years more hard fighting." Emerson Smith at convalescent camp. "Did Silas find out from that man at the Point about Henry. I am afraid he was killed." Convalescent camp men in wooden barracks. Lieut. Burdick wore a streak of blue lightning. Deserters. Henry Gregory — "too big a heart." Hay $2,500 a ton from Champlain. Continuation Mch 30: no letters received. Not received papers. Methodist church — crowded. Shoulder scales for regiment.

movements.letterExcerpt: I received your and Frances' letter of Mch. 29th in due time. Glad to hear that you both are well. My health is very good.
movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Alexandria that his regiment has just drawn new long Enfield rifles, their iron barrels blacked against rust, and he hopes they won't be ordered to scour them bright. Between target practice and marching three hundred stragglers a day from the convalescent camp, his mind keeps circling Henry: "If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in. I am afraid he was killed."
movements.transcription:
April 11, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your and Frances' letter of Mch. 29th in due time. Glad to hear that you both are well. My health is very good.

Yesterday all the soldiers were mustered that are in the U.S. service. The regiments are to be filled up by a draft. I think Uncle Sam will draft so as to have men enough to soon end this war. I see that we are about attacking Charleston, but I think it will be long before we take it. It is a strong place. Our reg't. has just received new guns. They are long Enfield rifles. These guns have the iron maw all well blacked which prevents their rusting. Our old guns we scoured the black off which made them look better as the barrels were bright, but a great deal more work to keep them clean. I hope that we will not be ordered to brighten our new guns.

The man from our Co. that went home to Plattsburgh on a furlough from our Co. has not come back; goes to Canada, we all think. Another Plattsburgh man has now got a furlough from our Co.

We commenced yesterday to fire at a target. Our reg't. at battalion drill fires blank cartridges. It is afraid our Co. will get behind the reg't. in drilling, but we will have Co. drill soon, I think. Ten men and two sergeants go every afternoon to the convalescent camp for stragglers. They bring them to the soldier's rest where they stay till morning, then take the mail steamer to the creek. Then ten fresh men and a sergeant go with them to the creek. Our men bring two or three hundred stragglers a day from the distributing camp which is close to the convalescent camp. We corporals have an easy time as we don't have to go to the creek or to the distributing camp. We are on duty about three days, but the duty is light. A few days ago I received three Tribunes and the Observer.

I have just seen Freeman Bowron. He came from Washington where his Co. is to see us Champlain boys. Looks very well and says when his three years are out he will reenlist in the regular army. He is orderly sergeant in the cavalry. Says his captain dated his commission as orderly back two months before he got it. If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in. I am afraid he was killed.

I have not heard from Alex for some time. Think Hooker's army will soon march. The weather today is too warm for comfort, but the nights are cold. Need all our blankets at night.

I hear that hay is $20.00 a ton. Your arrangement about the horse and cow was a very good one. Have you had any sugar yet? Seems to me there are not many maples on the strip of land Mr. Rye claims. If the land is not his, he ought not to have it. Mr. Crea claims a corner; he is a hard man, very close.

What does Mr. Copeland think of ministers being drafted? I don't agree with Alex about Silas and Sid. Think they would be very foolish to enlist. I have not got sick of soldiering yet; will not, I think, till the hard times come. Hope our Co. will stay here this summer. Please write all the news. Did you see Charles Dodds? He says he would not stay home for anything. It is too lonesome.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: All soldiers mustered — regiments to be filled up by draft. New Enfield rifles. Old guns scoured. Commenced target fire with blank cartridges. Freeman Bowron from Washington — un-Champlain boys visiting. "If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in. I am afraid he was killed." Hooker's army will soon march. James "not sick of soldiering yet." Hope Co. stays here this summer. "It is too lonesome."

movements.sigSummary: Charles has said three times he fears Henry was killed, but Alexander still hopes: "It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field." Writing from Aquia Landing under marching orders, eight days' rations packed, he calls Mother's fears "groundless and very foolish" — the cruelty of a man who cannot afford to grieve. Gen. Hooker, he says, means to give the two-years men "an opportunity to pay a parting salute to the rebels."
movements.transcription:
April 16, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of the 7 inst. a day or two since and was filled with great wrath when I read your acct. of your trouble with your sugar-maker. I fairly hopped up and down, I was so provoked. If there is such a thing as get satisfaction out of old Rye I will have it if ever I return. Wonder if he can find no better employment than persecuting a helpless woman. Shame on him — though I very much doubt if he has either shame or soul. I cannot find words to express my indignation.

We are now under marching orders and are to take eight days rations in our knapsacks and haversacks. We have five days now packed in our haversacks and will take three more in our knapsacks, when we move. The "Army of the Potomac" was on the move day before yesterday, but I presume we are pretty well stuck in the mud by this time as it has rained furiously all day yesterday. Nevertheless I do not think this will detain them long. General Hooker means to give the two years men an opportunity to pay a parting salute to the rebels. The Army is in fine condition and spirits and please, for my sake, box the ears of the first person you hear say they will not fight. Gen'l. Hooker so far as I know, is in high favor with all the troops.

Your intelligence about Henry fills me with sorrow, though I still hope. It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field and it is upon this that I base my hope that he is yet alive. Your fears that he was wounded are groundless and (excuse me) very foolish. Love to all. Remember me to the Captain and tell him that the company has drawn twenty-eight new rifles. The old ones without bayonets have been turned over, and say to him I am sorry he is not to march and fight with us this summer.

Mrs. Hoyle still sends papers. She is very kind. Upon the wrapper were written some very patriotic sentences in English and Latin. I will delegate Miss Fannie to make a fitting reply — my appreciation of the Latin — my high exalted patriotism — valor and determination to die in the last ditch — ahem! Tell Miss Fan I expect she will do it up brown. Miss Laura's initials were prefixed to the sentences.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander now under marching orders — 8 days rations, 5 in knapsacks. "Army of the Potomac" was moving day before yesterday. Gen. Hooker expects "the two years men an opportunity to pay a parting salute to the rebels." **CRITICAL: Henry intelligence.** "Your intelligence about Henry fills me with sorrow, though I still hope. It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field and it is upon this that I base my hope that he is yet alive. Your fears that he was wounded are groundless and (excuse me) very foolish." Mother told to tell Captain about 28 new rifles. Mrs. Hoyle sends papers — Latin sentences on wrapper.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes home from Aquia Landing, sending forty dollars by express and clearing his debts so the family need send no more — "I do not want you to lay this money up for me," he urges his mother. "Take what little comfort you can with it." A devoted soldier remembering camp under an apple tree and dreaming of showing her the drills at Montreal, he tucks in money for everyone, even worrying whether brother Jim wants for any.
movements.transcription:
April 23, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Mother:

I have sent you today by express forty dollars and enclosed you will find a receipt of seven dollars and ninety cents which Ingram will call and take up which I have no fear he will do. If he does not, all that I shall have to do will be to return the receipt to Frilly and he will refund my money to me again. In all his (Ingram's) dealing with the Co. he has shown himself to be a man of honor. I received a letter from him a short time since. He requested me to do this as he was afraid of trusting his money in the mail. I always liked Ingram from the time I first saw him and would do anything in my power to oblige him. He has been a good friend to me. Ask him about the time when he and I camped under the apple tree and I pulled the pickets off the fence to make a fire. Ask him about the Crimean War. He can tell you some funny stories. A soldier is the man for me anywhere. If ever I come home you must go with me to Montreal and see the soldiers drill.

I received the money you sent me yesterday. I have paid Vaughan so you need not send any more money. Adding this to what little I have sent home before, it makes one hundred and fifty dollars and ninety cents, though the money you have sent me would draw considerably from this amount. Now, Mother, I do not want you to lay this money up for me. I want you to take what little comfort you can with it. Tell Frances to take out for those boots. Wonder if Jim don't want some money. Should hate to have Jim be behind any of the rest of them for want of it. How I should like to see Master James. Received a real good letter from him today. I wrote him today. How I wish I could see him.

I almost forgot to mention that Luther has sent twenty dollars in the same package with mine. Some of the family will call for it. Must be brief for I have another letter to write tonight.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander sent $47 by express and $3 to Frilly. Received money Mother sent. Total home: $150.90. Paid Vaughan. Lieut. Ingram to send money with his. Jim doesn't want money. "How I should like to see Master James." Luther sent $20 in package. Should apply for Henry's back pay and bounty.

movements.sigSummary: A soldier from Henry's old 34th NY regiment passes along a comrade's portrait that pleased Alexander very much: when the boys went off plundering, Henry refused his share, reasoning "if I should take any, I would be as bad as any of you for the partaker is as bad as the thief." Quiet, seldom speaking unless spoken to, yet when bullied he would pitch into his tormentors with a will. Written from Aquia Landing, the note opens with a humbler want — a watch, double-cased.
movements.transcription:
April 24, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Mother:

I mailed a letter to you this morning and forgot to mention a very important matter in it. That is about a watch. Will you get me one? I need one very much. Get one with a double case. Any other would be a nuisance.

I saw one of the 34th yesterday. He inadvertently said something about Henry that pleased me very much. He said that when the boys went off and plundered anything he would not take any of it and would reason in this wise: "You stole that, and if I should take any, I would be as bad as any of you for the partaker is as bad as the thief." He said he was very quiet, seldom spoke to anyone unless spoken to, and a great deal of the time, and was a real good fellow. Sometimes they used to try and bother him, but he would pitch into them with a will and soon make them desist. Said he himself had got some hard knocks. Love to all. Remember me to the Captain and to Mr. and Mrs. Copeland and all the boys.

Your Aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Sutler wrote Frances a short time since. Wants to know if she got the letter. He sends regards. Is fat and husky. Tell Frances if she don't answer it soon, I shall tell her when I come home again. Tell her that I am waiting patiently for the spirit to move her to write me.
movements.notes: Short follow-up — forgot to mention need for a watch. "I saw one of the 34th yesterday. He inadvertently said something about Henry that pleased me very much. He said that when the boys went off and plundered anything he would not take any of it and would reason in this wise: 'You stole that, and if I should take any, I would be as bad as any of you for the partaker is as bad as the thief.'" Henry was "a real good fellow." Sutler wrote Frances.
Chancellorsville Campaign begins. Crossed Rappahannock.

movements.sigSummary: Abram Fry, an artilleryman, swore he had seen Henry's name on a headboard at his grave, but Charles weighs the claim and finds it wanting: "his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now." Still, he concludes there is "not the least doubt that Henry was killed." Snowbound at Alexandria, he asks for two dollars for boots, encloses a $40 allotment check, and notes the 16th N.Y.V. shipping home from Sedgwick's Corps.
movements.transcription:
April 27, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcomed letter of April 17th a few days since. Also one the same day from Mary McNeil. I found the Tribune interesting. I'm sorry that you think I did not receive your letters. I assure you your letters are very welcome. Today is Sunday and we are blockaded by the snow storm. There is about six inches of snow on the ground and it is snowing hard and blowing. I am glad that our men have not to go off today. This snow will all go off at once and make lots of mud which we will have to wade through to go to the distributing camp for the stragglers. A few days since we had a hard snow storm. The snow quickly went off and left us some awful roads to travel. I found then that shoes were not the thing. I wish you would send me two dollars as I want to buy a pair of boots.

You ask me what makes me think Henry was killed. Well, I think so from what you have written me. Think Scott, the tailor, is strong evidence. Right before last I was at the soldier's rest; got a talking with one of the stragglers and he told me he belonged to Co. D, 34 Regt. I asked him about Henry and he did not seem to remember the name, when a soldier close by said he was killed, that he saw the name on a headboard at his grave. This soldier's name is Abram Fry, and he belongs to the last N.Y. artillery. I asked him the stragglers's name. He said the artillery waited after a battle because their sessions carried the shovels, picks, etc. The man belonging to the 34th was hurt at the battle of Antietam, has been in the hospital at Philadelphia ever since. There are only two besides him that are sick, though not with the small pox. I hope you will write me soon again.

I only heard last night that the 60th reg't. was about a mile from Aquia Landing, so I started this morning to see him, but with what success I have just told you. I hope Alex is uninjured. Have been searching to hear about him for two or three days. Two days ago I saw the 16 Reg't. N.Y.V. on board a steamer that stopped here for some old clothes they left here boxed up a year ago. The reg't. was on its way home. discharged as its time was cut out. The men looked hard; that is, they were tanned and clothes very dirty. They belonged to Sedgwick's Corps. Said it on coming out of the woods the first thing they knew the rebs fired a volley into them. This was from the first line of battle which then laid down and the second line fired and laid down in turn, and then the third line fired. Then they had three rebel volleys in a few minutes. They belonged to Sedgwick's Corps.

I saw George Corbin with the 126th Reg't. You say that you want me to go over the battle ground of Antietam. I don't know where this battle field is, and don't know who would go with me that knows where the 34th reg't. fought. As for his Fry, his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now. I think there is not the least doubt that Henry was killed. We would have heard from him long before this if he had been living.

Every day reg'ts. are going home, their time being out. I guess we will stay here all summer. Hope we will for we are having a good time. If the cavalry come on here and the satisfaction of sending us up is in a short time should be blighted. He was so happy in the prospects; said he should begin to count the days soon; dear, dear Henry, my darling boy. Oh, what a pall is over my heart, and must be while I am in this vale of tears. But my pilgrimage is nearly over. Already the loved ones who have gone, are bearing me home.

[page break]

I guess Dan Moore bothers you about this sugar business. Don't you judge Dan rather harshly? If you don't get enough sugar — why, it can't be helped, and let it go. I have finished Vermont's Pride and think it is a good story. Read the Tribune and Observer yesterday and 3 Observers not long previous to this. I think that I receive them all now. Doesn't Alex want some of these papers? Perhaps Mrs. Hoyle forgot to send him any papers. We are having fine warm weather now. The grass is green, flowers are in bloom, and lettuce is fit to eat.

Give my regards to Mrs. E. Hubbell and family when you see them. Enclosed is a $40 allotment check.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles received April 17 letter. Went to Aquia Creek to find whether Alexander came out of fight all right. Got stalling with one of stragglers. **KEY HENRY INTELLIGENCE:** Soldier from Co. D, 34th Regt knew Henry, said he was killed — "he saw the name on a headboard at his grave." Soldier's name is **Abram Fry**, belongs to last N.Y. artillery. He said artillery waited after battle then sessions carried shovels, picks, etc. The man belonging to 34th was hurt at battle of Antietam. In hospital 15 months. "I am afraid he was killed." Scott — thinks he can find more. Troops at the Methodist church — good sermon. "Enclosed is a $40 allotment check."
Battle of Chancellorsville. 60th NY engaged. Jackson's flank attack.

movements.sigSummary: At Chancellorsville the 60th N.Y. lost seventy-three men — nine killed, forty-three wounded, twenty-one missing — yet Alexander writes that he missed the fight entirely, posted to guard the brigade trains while his regiment charged three times and drove the rebels back. Company H's one dead is named plainly: Lester Bond, shot through the forehead. He scorns the Eleventh Corps, which "broke and ran in a most cowardly manner," leaving the 60th unsupported.
movements.transcription:
May 11, 1863
Aquia Landing, Va.

Dear Mother and Sister:

I presume you have long ere this heard of the battle of Chancellorsville in which my regiment was employed. I am sorry to say I was not in the battle, being in command of the guard at the Headquarters trains of the 12th Brigade. I am now relieved from that duty and am again with the reg't. The exact loss of the reg't. is seventy three — nine killed, forty three wounded, and twenty-one missing. Company H lost six men — one killed dead, Lester Bond. He was shot through the forehead and instantly killed while the reg't. was making a bayonet charge. Our orderly was sent Fittingly a few feet in the air, by a rebel shell, but without doing him much damage. The reg't. charged three times upon the rebels, driving them back each time in great disorder. The eleventh corps broke and ran in a most cowardly manner and let the brunt come upon the twelfth. At one time, the 60th and 102nd N.Y. were left unsupported by the rest of the troops and for a long time held the enemy in check.

I received a letter from home today. They are all well. When I sent my money home I asked Mother to send me a watch. She tried to get one, but Scott had none much as I sent. Mother says she received a letter from you saying that you could get one, but we have no money home and so have you. (I sent forty-three dollars and ninety cents). The watch I used very much as you well know, and I must have it. Will you, Charley, if you have but two stamps, write Mother to send the watch without delay. Now Charley, if you do this, you will do me the greatest favor imaginable. Send it as soon as you

[page break]

can, for I need it very, very, very much. Give my regards to all the boys from Champlain.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. We are camping in the same place as when you were here.
movements.notes: **CHANCELLORSVILLE BATTLE REPORT.** "I presume you have long ere this heard of the battle of Chancellorsville." Alexander's regiment engaged — "I am now relieved from that duty and am again with the reg't." The exact loss: "seventy three — nine killed, forty three wounded, and twenty-one missing. Company H lost six men — one killed dead, Lester Bond." Bond shot through forehead and instantly killed. "The trains were but a short distance from the battle field, and I could distinctly hear every shot and even the cheers of the boys when charging. A heavy body of woods prevented my witnessing the battle." 60th made three charges. Mrs. Hoyle acknowledged.

movements.sigSummary: Charles crossed to Aquia Creek to learn whether his brother Alex had come through the fight, only to be turned back by a Provost Marshal who would issue no pass — and never reached the 60th, posted a mile from the landing. He watched the war-worn 16th N.Y.V. ship home from Sedgwick's Corps, describing three rebel volleys in minutes, then confided his dread that Henry was surely killed. He encloses an ambrotype, his coat too large as always.
movements.transcription:
May 13, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I went to Aquia Creek this morning and on my return this afternoon at about 4:00 P.M. found a letter for me that came this morning after I left. Went to the Creek for two reasons; one of them was that I wanted to find out whether Alex came out of the fight all right, and the other reason was that if he had I wanted to see him. Lieut. Knapp told me that he could get me a pass to come back from the Provost M shall at A. Creek. Well, the Lieut. asked the Provost Marshal for a pass, and he replied that it was no way to do business. As he would give me no pass the only way to get back if I stayed would be to wait till our guard came down again and go back with them. But as it was uncertain when the guard would come again I did not want to stay two or three days which I did not, so I came back today with the guard.

I only heard last night that the 60th reg't. was about a mile from Aquia Landing, so I started this morning to see him, but with what success I have just told you. I hope Alex is uninjured. Have been searching to hear about him for two or three days. Two days ago I saw the 16 Regt. N.Y.V. on board a steamer that stopped here for some old clothes they left here boxed up a year ago. The reg't. was on its way home, discharged as its time was cut out. The men looked hard; that is, they were tanned and clothes very dirty. They belonged to Sedgwick's Corps. Said it on coming out of the woods the first thing they knew the rebs fired a volley into them. This was from the first line of battle which then laid down and the second line fired and laid down in turn, and then the third line fired. Then they had three rebel volleys in a few minutes.

I saw George Corbin with the 126th Reg't. You say that you want me to go over the battle ground of Antietam. I don't know where this battle field is, and don't know who would go with me that knows where the 34th reg't. fought. As for his Fry, his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now. I think there is not the least doubt that Henry was killed. We would have heard from him long before this if he had been living.

Every day reg'ts. are going home, their time being out. I guess we will stay here all summer. Hope we will for we are having a good time. If the cavalry come on here and the satisfaction of sending us up is in a

[page break]

short time should be blighted. He was so happy in the prospects; said he should begin to count the days soon; dear, dear Henry, my darling boy. Oh, what a pall is over my heart, and must be while I am in this vale of tears. But my pilgrimage is nearly over. Already the loved ones who have gone, are bearing me home.

Enclosed is my ambrotype taken May 11th. My coat is too large, always was. In this picture gallery I see a woman looking at her picture taken while she was walking a rope from the top of the strate to the top of the building on the opposite side of the street. I have seen her walk it two or three times, once with a very short dress, circus fashion; another time dressed in tights. She had a long balancing pole in her hands, and kneeled down, stood on one leg, the chair one swinging around up very high. The street below was crowded to see her walk the rope.

How come Frances to take three of Mr. Simonds classes? I am afraid she will work herself too hard.

I would not sell your cow if I were you. I bought a watch for $12.25 and have sold it for $16.50 and wait till pay day. Think I shall buy one soon, as it is necessary to have the time. Have $12. still left. I wish you could use what you want of my money and put the rest out at interest. Remember, I want you to use as much as you want of it. You had better pay our new tax out of my money. Ought not to sit in a seat without paying. My health is good. Hope your and Frances' is also. Have had two swims in the Potomac this week.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Charles went to Aquia Creek to find out about Alexander — went to Aquia Creek. Alex told him he was not in the fight, was detailed to guard baggage train. Charles saw 16 Regt NYV going home. **HENRY — DEFINITIVE:** "As for his Fry, his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now. I think there is not the least doubt that Henry was killed." Regiments going home daily. Some may stay all summer. Lieut. ordered corporal to be drilled for being absent. Bought watch for $12.25, sold for $16.50. Ambrotype enclosed — taken May 11th.

movements.sigSummary: Our regiment was pretty roughly handled at Chancellorsville, May 3rd — seventy-three lost, nine killed, forty-three wounded, twenty-one missing — yet what Alexander begs his brother Charley for, again and again, is a watch: without one he must guess the time when relieving his guards. He details Lester Bond shot through the forehead in a bayonet charge, and the 60th and 102nd N.Y. left unsupported, holding the enemy in check while the eleventh corps broke and ran.
movements.transcription:
May 16, 1863
Aquia Landing

Dear Charley:

I received your letter of the 3rd just after we returned from the front and was pleased to hear of your safety. I feared you had been obliged to leave Alexandria as it was reported here that the army had received strong reinforcements from Wash. and Alexandria. I hope you may never be called away from there.

Our reg't. was pretty roughly handled at Chancellorsville, May 3rd. We lost seventy-three, nine killed, forty three wounded and twenty-one missing. Co. H lost six men. Lester Bond (Co. B) was shot through the forehead and instantly killed while the reg't. was making a bayonet charge. Our Orderly was sent Fittingly a few feet in the air, by a rebel shell, but without doing him much damage. The reg't. charged three times upon the rebels, driving them back each time in great disorder. The eleventh corps broke and ran in a most cowardly manner and let the brunt come upon the twelfth. At one time, the 60th and 102nd N.Y. were left unsupported by the rest of the troops and for a long time held the enemy in check.

I received a letter from home today. They are all well. When I sent my money home I asked Mother to send me a watch. She tried to get one, but Scott had none much as I sent. Mother says she received a letter from you saying that you could get one, but you see that will do no good. I have my money home and so have you. (I sent forty-three dollars and ninety cents). The watch I used very much as you well know, and I must have it. Will you, Charley, if you have but two stamps, write Mother to send the watch without delay. Now Charley, if you do this, you will do me the greatest favor imaginable. Send it as soon as you can, for I need it very, very, very much. Give my regards to all the boys from Champlain.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. We are camping in the same place as when you were here.

..... 30 .....

April 13th — I could not mail this letter for want of stamps. About that watch. I wish you would send it as soon as possible. You had better send it by express. The mesh of one gloves me sometimes in a very awkward position. When on guard duty I am obliged to guess at the time my reliefs have been on post. My portfolio with my papers, pens, postage stamps, etc., etc. (on acct of my being on duty) Luther carried in his knapsack were lost in the late battle, owing to the fact that Luther was obliged to throw away his knapsack.

It is reported that the rebels are in full retreat. Our corps suffered severely in the late battles. A large number of reg'ts. have gone and are about going home so that the 10th A.C. is considerably reduced in numbers. If there is truth in the report that Hooker has crossed the river (and I think there is) I think the reason that we are left behind is to keep open the avenue of supplies to the army — though we may be ordered on any moment.

I will endeavor to write soon. My regards to all friends.

Monday Morn. — May 14th —— The rebels commenced shelling the hospitals and the supply and ammunition trains, but did not keep it up long for our cavalry made a charge and captured the two rebel guns (breach loaders). I think I have great reason to thank God for my safe preservation. The same day the trains were moved farther back from the river.

Please let the Capt. know the loss of the company — L. Bond, killed; G. Ploof, wounded; H. Myers, wounded; P. Brookway, ditto; I. Stone, missing; B. Brame, Orderly Sergeant Brookway is still with the company. Luther was uninjured.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alexander writes to Charles from Aquia Landing. Detailed Chancellorsville account. Company L. Bond killed; G. Ploof wounded; H. Myers wounded; P. Brookway wounded (ditto); I. Stone missing; B. Brame, Orderly Sergeant Brookway missing. Luther uninjured. **April 13th addition:** Couldn't mail — rebels shelling hospitals, ammunition trains. Cavalry captured two rebel guns. May 14th: Rebels commenced shelling again — cavalry charge. "Please let the Capt. know the loss of the company." **May 19 addition (Charles's):** Charles received letter — was "very much gratified yesterday to receive a letter from Alexander." Will buy watch.
