movements.sigSummary: On guard duty at Carrol Prison, Charles watched a young lady in broadcloth pants and matching short frock stride past — the superintendent called her "Foster," joked about her breeches, and said women had no business in the army. She'd come to visit Belle Boyd, the confined rebel who flashes a small "secesh" flag at her guards. A soldier's eyewitness brush with two defiant women of the war.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 21st, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I read a letter from you a few days since, also one yesterday from James, which I will enclose with this. I guess a man at Point Lookout will have to be very economical not to be in debt at the end of the course.

A good many regts. have been arriving here from the north lately and going straight to the front. They only stopped long enough to take in rations and then left. A guard from our regt. was at the depot three days to keep the men from straggling from these regts. There were several cavalry regts. There were several new cavalry regts.

Some time since I was on duty at Carrol Prison when I saw something walking in all there. I looked at it sharp for a minute. It was a young lady with broadcloth pants and the same kind of material for the short frock. The superintendent of the prison called her "Foster" and had quite a chat with her. Joked her about her breeches, also told her women had no business to be in the army. She called to see Belle Boyd who is confined there and is a rebel and has small secesh flag which she shows to the guard. The Bloomer doctor is said bold feisty could not be looked nor talked down. She is a unionist and is employed in our army. Quite a number of rebel women are confined in that prison.

It is very uncertain whether we stay here this winter. We may leave any day. Two days since our reg't. was out on general inspection. I got excused that morning by the doctor for this first time, so I missed going on that inspection. Nothing was the matter but a cold. I have bought a vest, price $3.00, so you see I intend to keep warm.

Our 1st Lieut. has within a few days married a lady from Alexandria. They live in a house close to the barracks.

One of our Co. went home with his discharge last night. He had the cabosibles. I think that spells Silas. Is Mr. Boyle going to pay you a cow for yours? I think it will be better for you to buy a cow in the spring unless you are sure you have fodder enough to winter one. But you can't have enough, so you had better buy your milk and butter this winter. What is going on in the quiet village? Does Alex Cash expects to be married or I don't think Sid would move out from the old homestead.

Please write as often as you can. Does the President's new call for men cause any excitement in C?

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **CARROLL PRISON — BELLE BOYD** confined there. "She called to see Belle Boyd who is confined there and is a rebel and has a small secesh flag which she shows to the guard." Young lady in broadcloth pants visited prison superintendent — told her women had no business in army. Bought vest $3. 1st Lieut married lady from Alexandria. Co. member went home with discharge — Silas. Man at Point Lookout. Many regts arriving from north going to front. President's new call for men.
Night Battle of Wauhatchie. 60th NY engaged. Secured supply line to Chattanooga.

movements.letterExcerpt: I rec'd the letter and box brought by Alex, who arrived here the 29th. Am very much obliged for all the nice things you sent which were unaccounted. The dried apples though, I don't know exactly what ...
movements.sigSummary: Charles declines a furlough home for the simplest reason in the war: he has only $1.50 to his name, having sent his pay to Mother in checks. Meanwhile, soldiers around him pack off on furloughs to vote in Tuesday's N.Y. elections. He reports a week's cough now mended, $5 jerked from his vest pocket and lost, five pairs of socks for winter — and, one night, the regiment serenading the Colonel with "Let me kiss him for his mother."
movements.transcription:
Oct. 31, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd the letter and box brought by Alex, who arrived here the 29th. Am very much obliged for all the nice things you sent which were unaccounted. The dried apples though, I don't know exactly what to do with, as I will have to buy sugar for them. I will have plenty of socks for this winter as I now have five pairs.

Yesterday our Lieut. called me to him and asked me if I wanted a furlough. I told him I did not at present. A good many are going home on furlough now so as to vote at the N.Y. elections. But the most are sick furloughs. A good many will leave tonight for home. I have only about $1.50 in money which would be very little to go home with. I can get transportation and have it taken out of my next pay. Also I got transportation part of the way. Last night I saw Capt. Rich. He asked me if I had my word to send home as he was going to C. I told him I was better. For about a week I had a cough and very little appetite and for that time did not do my duty. For two or three days I took cough mixture. I have now been on duty several days and feel all right again.

Today we are to be mustered in for pay. I think I have told you a careless thing I did while we were at Alexandria. I would carry what money I had of in my vest pocket for safe keeping as I would sometimes lose my pocketbook out of my pants at night. Well, I carried a comb and looking glass in the same pocket and in pulling one of these out I suppose I jerked out a five dollar bill. I never found the $5.00 of course, as there are plenty of dishonest soldiers. Also D. said 50¢ charges on the box which is 28¢ apiece for us. I guess Alex's chance for getting into the Invalid Corps is small. I think Alex will not want to be transferred into it.

I will write to James in a few days and send him that letter. What do you think about his prospects? I think Frances will enjoy vacation when it comes, as she has to work so hard. This teaching school would try my temper, I think.

Yesterday I read a letter from Corbeau, in which a mother told her son that she had let out his sheep on double in four years, and is to receive a lb. of wool yr. head yearly besides. That is better than you did with your sheep. We have some fine singers in this reg't. Two or three nights I have heard some our reg't. serenading the Col. It sounded very nice. They sung, "Let me kiss him for his mother" and two or three more songs I do not know the names of. Steais is in the hospital again; complains of his breast.

Today there is a detail of Sergts. and Corporals to go off somewhere with three days rations. I wrote you sometime since that I went to Point Lookout near Fortress Monroe. Well, I happened to look on a map and found that Point Lookout is at the mouth of the Potomac and it near the south of Chesapeake Bay as I wrote you. It is a long ways from there to F. Monroe. I think a good many N.Y. soldiers will be home to vote at the election Tuesday. Moses Cokey will leave tonight for Champlain. I think. Please write as often as you can. I hope you will settle with the Savages immediately. Hoping that you will make yourself comfortable this winter, I will close.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Read letter and box brought by Alex [Douglas]. Dried apples, nice things. Furlough — Lieut asked, declined for now. $1.50 in money, mostly worthless. Cough for about a week. Capt. Rich — visited Alex but missed him. Tribune news is old by time he gets it — 2¢ to send. **POCKET BOOK STOLEN** — $18.78 taken from pocket at dinner; thief returned empty book Sunday evening. Lost all money. Returned old guns, getting new ones. Story about Col. going to Canada.

movements.sigSummary: At Wauhatchie near Chattanooga, Alexander's company held a Cumberland Mountain pass that kept them out of the fight, while four miles off the rebels stormed the brigade at one in the morning, "barely alarmed before they were upon them." Brigade commander Gen. George S. Greene fell seriously, if not mortally, wounded. Pressed by Mother on a discharge, Alexander aches to return to his studies yet admits it would be hard "to leave the rest of the boys to fight it alone."
movements.transcription:
Nov. 1st, 1863
White Side, Georgia

Dear Mother:

Your letter of Oct. 21st rec'd. yesterday. It was the right thing in the right place for I was feeling particularly lonely. We are now holding a pass in the Cumberland Mountains about fifteen miles below Chattanooga. Our coming into this Gap prevented us from being in a fight. The rest of the brigade pushed on and camped about four miles from here. About one or two o'clock (A.M.), the rebels made a furious assault upon the camp, following so closely upon the pickets that the camp was barely alarmed before they were upon them and poured in a withering volley. Reports are so conflicting that I will wait until I can get an authentic acct. which I will give you in my next letter. Suffice it to say the rebs were defeated. Gen'l. George S. Greene, our Brigade commander, was seriously if not mortally wounded. Lieut. Geary, son of Gen'l. Geary, our Division commander, is reported killed and the Gen. himself slightly wounded in the toe.

The rebs yesterday shelled one of our wagon trains, but their practice was bad and did no damage. The other night our pickets were drawn in a short distance, leaving a large fire burning upon their old posts. They had not been gone long before a squad of rebels cavalry dashed upon the fire with loud yells and sabres drawn, expecting, I suppose, to capture the post. Our boys fired upon them when they wheeled about and skedaddled. The pickets have not been molested since.

You will be surprised, I expect, when I tell you I have been in the state of Alabama. Wonder what Aunt Wry would say if she knew my vandal footsteps had pressed the soil of Alabama. Do you suppose she pities us as much as she used to?

You asked me to give you my views fully in regard to a discharge. It would be useless. There is no one, I think, but the chief magistrate of the U.S. has power to grant it. I am anxious to pursue my studies — very anxious — but — well, I don't think you can get a discharge and I will say no more. If you get me one I shall not demur, though it will seem hard to leave the rest of the boys to fight it alone.

Tell Frances to write soon. I want to hear about the books. Tell her I know something about them. I am even with her now. I will write again soon if possible. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alexander

Sid's wife and I will agree very well, I think, for we both think the same of Mrs. Ruth Hubbell.
movements.notes: **WAUHATCHIE — NIGHT BATTLE.** "We are now holding a pass in the Cumberland Mountains about fifteen miles below Chattanooga." Rebels made furious assault on camp — pickets barely alarmed before enemy was upon them. **GEN. GEORGE S. GREENE WOUNDED** — Brigade commander, seriously if not mortally. **LIEUT. GEARY KILLED** — son of Gen'l Geary, Division commander. Gen. Geary himself slightly wounded in toe. Rebels shelled wagon trains. Pickets fired on cavalry. Discharge — views fully; useless to apply, chief magistrate has power. Anxious to pursue studies. Books — "tell her I know something about them."
Encamped at Wauhatchie. Holding the 'Cracker Line' supply route.

movements.letterExcerpt: I rec'd your letter of Nov. 7th yesterday and was glad to hear from you. Mr. Roberts from C. is here visiting his cousin. He says he is going to Meade's army and is to receive $48 a month in the photo...
movements.sigSummary: 1,846 Confederate prisoners arrived near morning, and Charles's regiment — up all night at the Washington depot — marched them with cavalry to the Old Capitol prison, a heavy detail later moving some to Point Lookout. He counts himself lucky to have missed both. Writing his mother from Capitol Hill, he weighs selling the house and notes those who went home to vote had their fare paid by New York's Union party — news that reached him too late.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 19, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd your letter of Nov. 7th yesterday and was glad to hear from you. Mr. Roberts from C. is here visiting his cousin. He says he is going to Meade's army and is to receive $48 a month in the photograph business.

Capt. Rich has got back. I saw his last night at a distance. The other night all our reg't. not on duty were up all night at the depot here waiting for rebel prisoners. They came near morning, 1,846 of them, and our reg't., with some cavalry took them to the Old Capitol prison. Next day there was a heavy detail from our reg't. to take part of them to Point Lookout at the mouth of the Potomac. I was lucky not to be up that night nor yet to go off with the prisoners. A newspaper here said a few days since that all the troops around this place were to be relieved by the Invalid Corps. But for all that I guess we will still stay here this winter. A good many of the I. Corps are on duty in this city now. They are divided into two classes. One class carries rifles and the other carries a sword and colts revolver. Our Co. has gone to N.Y. York on 13 days leave of absence. Major Strain (or Strange) the command while he is gone.

Those who went home to vote, want free, their fare being paid by the Union party of N.Y. I did not know this till too late. I rec'd. two pieces of cheese (it is very good), but have not seen any homeruns or shirts/sleevings; perhaps they are under the currents in the case. At any the apples were sent because our Co. draw from. Have you heard from James lately? How is he getting along and how did he dispose of all his photographs? I think James will get along well enough, but don't expect he will graduate very high. Has Hiram I. got his appointment yet?

If you are offered what the house is worth I think it would be well to sell it. I am glad that you are going to settle with the Savages become the interest runs up fast. How do you direct Alex's letters? I have not written him since I saw him. Do you keep an acct. of the money he sends home? If not, I wish you would be particular about doing so. I sent that Goddard's letter to James, but forgot to tell him to return it to you. I think James will pass the coming examinations well enough and goes to the marks, he has only two months to be marked so he will fall short of 100 reports for all but the two months. You have his reports for all but the two months.

That is Uncle John's visit for! Is it to see about hit share of the estate? Jim Lucas has just told me that Pet Steais is going to get his discharge. A lot of rebel officers from the old Capitol prison were sent to Sandusky, Ohio, two or three days since. I see by today's paper that there is a plot to free them and burn Buffalo and Ogdensburgh. But I guess it will not amount to much.

Give my thanks to those that sent me socks, etc. But do you think it best to trouble so many people about me? Don't forget to take a good many thanks for yourself for that box. Those cookies were first rate and so was that pie.

Please write often. Frances' letter was good, only it was short, but then she is not to blame as she has so much to do.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Mr. Roberts from C. visiting cousin — going to Meade's army, photograph business, $48/month. Capt. Rich got back — 1,846 rebel prisoners at depot, cavalry took them to Old Capitol prison. Heavy detail to Point Lookout. Those who went home to vote — cheese. Selling house/land. Savages settlement. Uncle John's visit. James near exam — 2 months left, fall short of 100. Goddard's letter — return to James. Jim Lucas — Pet Steais discharge. Frances' letter — short.

movements.letterExcerpt: Have you heard from James and Alex lately? James has owed me a letter for some time, but I suppose he is very busy in the reason. My health is good and I hope that I will stand the winter. But we may ...
movements.sigSummary: $18.78 vanished from a soldier's pocketbook: lost beside the knife he'd pulled from the same pocket, then returned with the check intact but the money gone — "they found it without any money in it." From Capitol Hill, Charles encloses a twenty-dollar check for his mother yet must ask her for $2, begging she "not tell all creation." Rumors swirl of orders to Philadelphia, Alexandria, or Chattanooga, and the regiment is trading good guns for new.
movements.transcription:
Have you heard from James and Alex lately? James has owed me a letter for some time, but I suppose he is very busy in the reason. My health is good and I hope that I will stand the winter. But we may not have much of one, but may ride. How is your health and Frances and how does the world go with you both? Hope that you have wood enough to keep warm this cold weather. The weather is warm and pleasant here now. The cold rains are to come.

Nov. 21st — 2:00 P.M. Enclosed is a twenty dollar check. I wish you would use my money freely — as much as you want of it. Our Col. got back last night. They say that he is trying to get our reg't. to Philadelphia, but that we will probably go to Alexandria. Also it is said that Major Strange doesn't like Alexandria. No signs of leaving here yet. I don't think we will go to the front this fall or winter, but to some other place. It has rained all day, but a great many of the men are on passes in this city. Our clothing acct's for 14 months was settled with us yesterday when we got our pay. I rec'd. $2.70 due me for clothes, but some of the men were largely in debt for clothes. We receive $3.50 a month from date of enlistment which is $42 a year. Please write soon.

From your aff. son

C. F. Hubbell

Nov. 23rd — as I was about sending my letter off two days since I put my hand in my pocket to get my check out of my pocketbook, but it was not there. It was lost, and this is the reason that I delayed sending the letter till today. Last night the pocket book was returned to me with the check, but the money was taken out of it. They said they found it without any money in it and that the person that first found it had taken the money. I lost $18.78 in all. I wrote in haste so the mail is going out, but will tell you all about it in my next letter. I must have pulled the pocket book out of my pocket with my knife. If you can send me $2 I will be much obliged. I hope you will not tell all creation about my losing this money. It has not bothered me much. My appetite and sleep are as good as usual. It is now after 1 P.M., and we have just returned our guns. Are to get new ones. I don't know the object of the change as we have very good guns. Are to get more new ones. There is a story here that the Col. has his choice to go to Alexandria or Chattanooga and that he does not want to go to Alexandria. I don't know when he will leave here. I don't know what all the soldier's wives will do, if we go far.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell.

Please let me know soon if you receive the check.
movements.notes: Multi-date letter: Nov 20, 21, 23. Not heard from Alex lately. $20 check enclosed (Nov 21). Col. got back — trying to get reg't to Philadelphia but probably Alexandria. Major Strange doesn't like Alexandria. Clothing acct settled — $2.70 due for clothes; some men largely in debt. **POCKET BOOK STOLEN** — $18.78 taken; money was in it when found Saturday; returned Sunday evening empty. Person who found it first took money. Returned old guns, getting new ones — good guns. Col. may go to Canada — five of Co. on furlough.

movements.sigSummary: Capt. Delaney calls Alexander into his tent to relay a discharge plea from Capt. Ransom — but the surgeon and colonel have no power to grant it. Alexander, with eleven months left to serve, sees the futility plainly: "Secretary Stanton is the man to apply to, or else the President." Writing from muddy Wauhatchie, he humors his mother's hope even as Gen. Geary marches them out under arms in the rain for no purpose but speed.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 21st, 1863
Wauhatchie, East Tennessee

Dear Fannie:

So you defy me, eh! I believe I put a flea in your ear in the last letter I wrote home. Didn't I now! Don't you wish you knew who sent those books? I know, but I'll be bound if I'll tell. How did you like "Harry Lorrequer?" (Ins) Maud the Knight of Dettine worth reading? Please let me know how you like them. I'll just tell you what I think. I think your curiosity is pretty well excited. Am I not right? Enough of this. Now for local matters, etc., etc.

We were ordered to fall in last night under arms with knapsacks packed in ten minutes. We marched over to Division headquarters and a — and marched back again. Interesting, wasn't it? I don't believe General Geary had any other purpose than to see how quickly he could move troops from one part of the line to the other. Other regiments were also ordered out. It was rather a dry joke, considering the rain and mud.

So Professor Bass is flourishing, eh! I like the old chap better than any teacher I ever had. I trust the time is not far distant when I shall be able to battle for drunk and lath on him again. Three years is a pretty big slice off a man's life, isn't it? I shall only have to work all the harder to make up for it. Capt. Delaney called me into his tent the other day and said he had received a letter from Capt. Ransom asking him to use his influence in getting me a discharge. He had talked with the surgeon and colonel, but it was not in their power to do anything in regard to it. I knew this well long ago, but Mother seems averse to giving up the idea. Secretary Stanton is the man to apply to, or else the President.

I have now only about eleven months more to serve, but if Mother wishes for my discharge I shall not oppose her.

Say Frances, I wrote in my last letter for Mother to send me by express some shirts, socks, and a pair of boots and said I could pay for them at the Jan. payment. Now if this will inconvenience you at all, don't send them. If you do send them, direct to Nashville, Tennessee. Be very particular in putting on the Regt. Brigade, Division and Corps. Also put on Army of the Cumberland. Also send me a list of the prices of each and the express charges. Love to all. Please write soon.

Your Aff. Brother,

Alexander

I borrowed this sheet, envelope and stamp.
movements.notes: "Harry Lorrequer" (Lever novel) and "Maud the Knight of Dettine" — books discussion. Ordered to fall in with knapsacks — marched to Division headquarters and back. Gen. Geary — "a dry joke, considering the rain and mud." Professor Bass flourishing. Capt. Delaney — letter from Capt. Ransom asking to use influence for Alexander's discharge. Mother seems averse to giving up the idea. Secretary Stanton is the man to apply to, or else the President. 11 months to serve. Frances — send shirts, socks, boots by express to Nashville, Tenn.

movements.sigSummary: Wounded at the storming of Lookout Mountain, Sergeant Alexander F. Hubbell writes Mother from the General Hospital at Tullahoma: a minie ball in his left side, "rather a close call for my life." Even bleeding, he files Company H's casualties in orderly rank — George Hays killed; himself, Long, Ish, Kelly, and Sidney Rider wounded. The rebs "ran like good fellows," surrendering 1,800 prisoners. "God has been very good to me. I shall soon be back to the regiment."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 1st, 1863
General Hospital
Tullahoma, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I presume you will be surprised to hear from me from this place. Well here I am in the hospital. I was wounded at the storming of Lookout Mountain. I am not seriously hurt. I am wounded in my left side by a minie ball. Rather a close call for my life, I think. I shall soon be back to the regiment. God has been very good to me. Company H lost as follows as near as I can learn: George Hays, killed; Sergeants Hubbell and Long, Corporals Ish and Kelly, Private Sidney Rider, wounded. I am not positive whether Sergt. Long was wounded or not. Latter was all right the last I saw or heard of him. We made a grand bayonet charge at Lookout. The rebs ran like good fellows. He took the whole posse (1800) prisoner. Please write often and direct as usual. I think I shall be with the regt. soon. Love to all.

Your affectionate son

Alexander F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **WOUNDED AT LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN.** "I presume you will be surprised to hear from me from this place. Well here I am in the hospital." Wounded at the storming of Lookout Mountain — minie ball in left side. "Rather a close call for my life, I think." Not seriously hurt; expects to rejoin regiment soon. **CASUALTIES:** George Hays killed; Sergts Hubbell and Long, Corporals Ish and Kelly, Private Sidney Rider wounded; Majo, Doten, Housedean killed. Thomas Small had his leg torn off. "The rebs ran like good fellows." Took whole posse (1,800) prisoner.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Capitol Hill, anxious for word of his brother: "I should like to hear how Alex came out of Hooker's fight, but I don't borrow trouble as it does no good." Around that worry he heaps the small comforts of an easy winter — johnnycakes and butter bought with company savings, milk at ten cents a quart, mashed potatoes and milk gravy for Thanksgiving — and the long, careful saga of a pocket book picked at dinner, its stolen check now traceable through the paymaster.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 1, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

There are no more signs of our leaving this place than the day we were relieved from duty. We on duty but are waiting for marching orders. Some think that we will stay here all winter. Others say that we are going to Alexandria and are waiting till the barracks now being built there are completed. We have a camp fire. We are stringing wires and stuff and that's all the barracks they are building, so I reckon not as I spoke.

guard and dress parade every day and battalion drill in the afternoon. Yesterday there was a stinging cold wind and it made us look blue at drill, but as we drilled on the double quick we did not freeze.

I should like to hear how Alex came out of Hooker's fight, but I don't borrow trouble as it does no good. He may not have been in the fight but may have been detached for other duty. If Meade is successful in this campaign the war will be short. The last ditch men of the rebels will soon have a chance to fight.

I don't know whether I can get a furlough this winter, and if I can, think I had better not take one. It don't pay to go home on a ten days furlough. I have seen some men back from home who said they were glad to get back here. We are having an easy time and ought to get fat. Once in a while we have johnnycakes and butter, the butter bought with Co. savings on rations. We have had baked bread pudding two or three times. Milk is cheap here, ten cents a qt. Milk women come twice a day. How did you pass Thanksgiving? Did you have a good dinner? Our Co. had mashed potatoes and milk gravy for dinner, as much as could eat. It is seldom that we get potatoes.

I must tell you about that pocket book. Don't know but the person that sat next to me at dinner picked my pocket. Still I might have pulled it out of my pocket. I did not expect to lose the check but got another one for it. It lost on Saturday between 10 A.M. and 2 P.M., and on Sunday evening the man returned me the pocket book and check and said there was no money in it when they found it. Perhaps they kept the money, but they said somebody must have found it before they did. There is quite a trade in checks here, the soldiers selling a $20 check for $18, and the buyer getting the full value. The soldiers sign the name of the person to whom it is allotted on the back. I intended to have gone into the city early Monday morning and seen the paymaster, to find out the no. of the check, then me an affidavit before a justice of the peace and have the Adjutant write on to the Treasurer in N.Y. to have payment stopped on it, and get another check. Some time since one of our Co. lost his pocket book with his money, also a check. He did as I have said and the treasurer in N.Y. replied to the Adjutant that if it was not found 3 mo. from date of loss he would on application at the end of that time, send him a certificate entitling him to draw another check.

I have just seen Mr. Steais who came here to see his brother Pet. He looked seedy and the boys thought he was a hard looking fellow. He belongs to the 113th N.Y. and came from the convalescent camp. Said he was going to get his discharge next week, also said he had not been home for 1½ years.

The Tribune news is old by the time I get it and as it costs 2¢ to send it, I think you had better not send it as I can buy the daily papers for 5¢. I rec'd. butter and R. Vinegar. The butter and cheese are gone, but the vinegar I have not touched, though I think that I had better drink it up as it can't be carried. The short-in berries I tried last night. The cook gave me some sugar so they went first rate. James Lucas had quite a lot of them sent to him.

(Incomplete — from Charles)
movements.notes: No signs of leaving Capitol Hill. Camp fire, barracks being built. Half rations — "the whole army is in the same way." Railroad will bring abundance soon. **CO. H LOSSES AT LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN** — per Charles: "Doten and Michael Housedean, killed; Alfred Lemage and Thomas Small, wounded. Thos. Small had his leg torn off." Old Bragg well used up. Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. Half rations. **INCOMPLETE — text cuts off.**

movements.sigSummary: Garrison duty resumed: Charles's regiment took over guarding Carroll Prison again, relieving the Invalid Corps, and now expects to winter in Washington — relief, he notes, that "nobody is sorry" about. He writes with a soldier's dry eye, recalling their nickname as Gen. Slough's "band box regt." for the five-cent collars, and plans to walk two blocks to hear Congress in session. Of his brother Alex, still unheard from, he refuses to "borrow trouble, as that doesn't pay."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 9, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

Our Regt. commenced doing duty this morning again. We now guard Carrol Prison again, relieving the Invalid Corps from that duty. We all now expect to stay here this winter, because we are doing duty again. Sure nobody is sorry, although some have said they wanted to go to the front. I think that it was intended to send us to the front, because we changed our guns for new ones, but for some reason we were not sent. Our regt. was called by some, while in Alexandria, Gen. Slough's band box regt. A good many wear white shirts collars cost five cents each. I think I shall let the collars alone.

The theaters are pretty well attended by our regt., our officers giving a pass till 12 P.M. and the men going to the provost-marshal to get it countersigned by him.

The patrol have out several of our men who had no pass in the Central Guard House. A pass to be good after 8 o'clock has to be signed by the Provost Marshal.

Congress is now in session. I intend to go soon and listen to the proceedings. The Capitol is about two blocks from our barracks so that we have a fine chance to see it. The grounds around the Capitol are large and kept in good order. Iron seats, shape of sofas, are placed all along near the broad stone walks where one can rest in the shade and enjoy himself.

Our Chaplain has formed a union church in this regt. Men of all denominations can belong to it, but I think the majority are Methodists. Last Sunday the sacrament was administered by the Chaplain to our church in the Methodist church close by. A large number were admitted into the church on probation and a good many more, formerly members, were admitted to full communion. One man from each Co. is chosen once in three months to assist the Chaplain. The man chosen on our Co. gave in four names. The Chaplain asked me if I was a member of the church; that was about all he asked me. He is a polite, quiet man and is liked by all the men. I think he is not a very good speaker. Prayer meetings are held every evening. There were quite a few new converts that joined the church on probation. Some members thought they were double I about joined in the same way. A name was read off us joining on full communion. The Chaplain is a Presbyterian, I think.

Have you heard from Alex? I am anxious to hear from him, but don't borrow trouble, as that doesn't pay. How does James get along? I have not heard from him for a long time. I suppose you have his last reports. Hope that Frances is enjoying herself, now that she is out of school. How does Pet Steais get along? I guess he is well enough now he is home, but don't tell that I said it. Must close, and I expect that long letter from Frances that she promised.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Reg't commenced doing duty again — guarding Carroll Prison, relieving Invalid Corps. Expect to stay here this winter. Alexandria visit — Gen. Slough's headquarters. Near barracks. Good many white shirts, collars — $5 each. Theaters attended by officers — pass till 12 PM. Chaplain formed union church — all denominations. Sacrament administered at Methodist. Last Sunday — full communion. Checkers. Have you heard from Alex? "I am anxious to hear from him, but I don't borrow trouble."

movements.letterExcerpt: I presume you have about come to the conclusion that I have left the land of the living or else entirely forgotten you, but it is no such thing. I have not forgotten you, though I would not blame you ...
movements.sigSummary: Climbing Lookout Mountain under enemy fire, Alexander tells his brother Charley the soldier's version: hauling himself up the steep slope by hand, "which you know, in the face of the enemy is not over pleasant." The 60th opened the road to Chattanooga with Hooker, thrashed Longstreet, then made a grand bayonet charge that sent the rebels running and took 1,800 prisoners. His own wound spared him Missionary Ridge and Ringgold — but not the company's toll: Majo, Doten, and Housedean killed.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 13th, 1863
Wauhatchie, East Tennessee

Dear Charley:

I presume you have about come to the conclusion that I have left the land of the living or else entirely forgotten you, but it is no such thing. I have not forgotten you, though I would not blame you for thinking so. I know I have been sadly negligent, but still a great many things have conspired to prevent my writing — the want of materials for the main. I am now writing upon paper I received today. Now for business!

We had a great time coming out here. Were stationed for some time upon the Nashville and Chattanooga railroad, which the 1st Division of our Corps still guards. We (the 2nd Div.) went with Gen. Hooker to open the road to Chattanooga. Five regts. of the Division had a big fight with Longstreet, the night of the 28th of Oct, and thrashed him soundly. I — hours previous we were sent to hold a gap in the mountains on the border of Georgia at a place called Whiteside. So you see we just missed the fight. Three regts of our brigade were engaged. Gen'l Greene, commander of brigade, was wounded. Gen. himself slightly wounded in the toe.

The 60th has been in three fights since then. Our Division was the one chosen to storm Lookout Mountain. I hope you may never be called on to climb such a hill as that. We were often required to halt ourselves on with our hands, which you know, in the face of the enemy is not over pleasant. We sit and look at each other very composedly as we have both learned better manners than to fire at each other. The rebels are very anxious to exchange papers with us, but we have strict orders not to do it. If the settling of the war was left to the soldiers we would do it in short order. Some of the Rebs are pretty nice fellows, much to my surprise.

My wound caused me to miss the fights of Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. The loss of the Co. stands as follows: Lemage, Tees, Rider, Small, Hubbell, wounded; Majo, Doten, Housedean, killed. The last I saw or heard of him. We made a grand bayonet charge at Lookout. The rebs ran like good fellows. He took the whole posse (1800) prisoner.

I shall endeavor to be more punctual in writing hereafter. Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon and I am afraid I would not receive the letter.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander Hubbell
movements.notes: **DETAILED BATTLE NARRATIVE — LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN, MISSIONARY RIDGE, RINGGOLD.** "We were often required to halt ourselves on with our hands, which you know, in the face of the enemy is not over pleasant." 60th has been in THREE fights since Wauhatchie. Division chosen to storm Lookout Mountain. Nashville and Chattanooga railroad. Five regiments fought Longstreet night of Oct 28th — Whiteside. Three regts of brigade engaged. Gen'l Greene wounded. **WOUNDED BY BALL IN SIDE** — "stretched me out in short order." **LOSSES:** Lemage, Tees, Rider, Small, Hubbell wounded; Majo, Doten, Housedean killed. Thomas Small had leg torn off. "Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon."

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from his old camp at Wauhatchie that he has rejoined the regiment and is doing duty, though his side is "still pretty sore" — he had quit the hospital early, telling the surgeon he was ready, his wound having made him miss Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. He sends the loss of Company H: Doten and Michael Housedean killed, Lemage and Thomas Small wounded — Small's "leg torn off." The army is on half rations, "Old Bragg" near used up. He closes by the last of his candle.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 16th, 1863
Wauhatchie, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I am again with the regt. and doing duty. My side is still pretty sore but then I manage to get along first rate. My wound caused me to miss the fights of Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. I did not like the way things worked at the hospital and told the surgeon I was ready to go back to the regt. Two others of the regt. came back with me. We are back again in our old camp and we are pretty hard up for rations. The whole army is in the same way. We are on half rations. The railroad will be open in a few days and we shall have abundance soon.

Old Bragg is pretty well used up and will be wiped out before long, I think. The Regt. was in two battles since I left — Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. Loss of Company H. is as follows: Doten and Michael Housedean, killed; Alfred Lemage and Thomas Small, wounded. Thos. Small had his leg torn off.

I have only a small bit of candle left and must close. Give my regards to Capt. Ransom and let him know the loss of the Co. Love to all. Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon and I am afraid I would lose the letter.

Hoping to see you all soon, I remain

Your Aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Sergt. Long was not hurt.
movements.notes: Side still sore but doing duty. Left hospital — told surgeon he was ready, returned to regt. Two others came back with him. Back in old camp. Half rations — "pretty hard up for rations." **CO. H LOSSES — FINAL LIST:** "Doten and Michael Housedean, killed; Alfred Lemage and Thomas Small, wounded. Thos. Small had his leg torn off." P.S. Sergt. Long was not hurt. Old Bragg will be wiped out before long. Railroad will open in a few days — abundance soon. "Do not write until you hear from me again as we expect to make a move soon." Only a small bit of candle left.

movements.sigSummary: Christmas dinner in camp on Capitol Hill ran to eight turkeys, two kegs of lager, and a bread pudding bought with company funds — though Charles, who dislikes beer, watched the boys get "quite happy" while one drunken Irishman was carried in "as if he had been a dead pig." Marching orders to Harper's Ferry came and were countermanded by morning; Charles, weighing the $1,000 re-enlistment bounty, urges Mother that Alex had better not sign on again.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 3, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I wish you and Frances a happy New Year. Did either of you pass a pleasant New Year's day? I was on guard but passed it well enough. On that day we had boiled flour pudding for supper. It was new business for our cooks and they put the puddings on the bottom of the kettles; one burst and burst the bag; the other two were then raised from the bottom of the kettles by a string tied to them and fastened to the floor above. The pudding was not very good; the raisins were the best part of it. On Christmas we had for dinner 8 turkeys — price $11.50; 2 kegs of lager beer, price $5.50; and a baked bread pudding with raisins in it. The dinner was bought with Co. Funds. I do not like beer so did not drink any. A good many of the boys got quite happy on it.

Christmas morning an Irishman belonging to our Co. was found at the side of the road dead drunk by one of our men. He shouldered him and brought him into camp as if he had been a dead pig. The Irishman says he was having his Christmas.

A good many of the old regts. are reenlisting for three years or the war. They get a 30 days furlough and a large bounty. Their reenlistment is dated from the time they get their furlough and not from next summer when their time is out. In this way the soldier gains several months time. I think Alex had better not reenlist although he can get $1,000 bounty.

Two or three nights since our regt. and the 14th New Hampshire received marching orders with three days rations, but the order was countermanded next day. We were to go to "Hardsburger" or Harper's Ferry and some back in a few days, but they say that if we had once left here we would not have come back. A Brigade from Meade's Army went, so we did not have to go. When we hear about marching orders we don't believe it because it is an old story. We still believe we are going when the knapsacks are on our backs.

Our regt. has done a good deal in the stealing line lately taking turkeys, chickens, etc. A woman came running into our guard house for a guard, saying a soldier stole a turkey and a piece of meat right before her face. Of course she did not get a guard, for the soldier was not going to stay there and be arrested. A guard could not have found him. Most of our regt. are good men but there are some great rascals in it.

Who surveyed the wood land and how much did it cost? I think from what you wrote the surveyors found the true line. Enclosed I send you a letter from Alex that I received about a week since. I forgot to tell you in my other letters that I saw Geo. Dodds some time ago. He came from the hospital to see us Champlainers. He had been sick with a fever and was not then entirely well. Please write soon.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: New Year's Day — on guard. Flour pudding for supper; 2 kegs of lager beer $5.50; baked bread pudding with raisins. Christmas morning an Irishman found drunk at roadside — "he was having his Christmas." Old regts re-enlisting — 30 days furlough and large bounty. 14th New Hampshire received marching orders countermanded. "Hardsburger" or Harper's Ferry. Stealing in regt — turkeys, chickens. Soldier court-martialed for being dirty. Geo. Dodds came from hospital to see Champlainers.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from a Nashville hotel, "on my way to Savannah to join the regt." — and to get there he had to slip out of Chattanooga "clandestinely." "I suppose I am reported at my detachment as a deserter, but this will do me no harm." A sergeant deserting a rear-area post to rejoin the fighting, smuggled through with a detachment of the 18th Corps bound for Sherman. Then the mask slips: "I feel quite sad tonight... Frances would say that I have the blues."
movements.transcription:
Jan. 8, 1864
Lolliecoffer House
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I know you think I am a very naughty boy not to write you oftener, but as I have said before, it is hard for me to write when I get no answers to my letters. This state of things I trust will not last much longer, as I am now on my way to Savannah to join the regt. To accomplish this I was obliged to leave Chattanooga clandestinely. I suppose I am reported at my detachment as a deserted, but this will do me no harm as I shall be able to join the regt. before my report can reach there. I smuggled my way through to this place with a detachment of the 18th Corps on their way to Sherman. Our detachment is still on duty with General Thomas. Some are at Dalton — some on the railroad, etc. I did not like the way things worked and determined to get to the regt. if it took a leg. I reported to the Colonel commanding those barracks and was booked by him for Savannah.

We shall go by the way of New York. A great many of the men will go home when they get into the state. I should like to, but shall not be able. I have not heard from home since I left Savannah. How are the boys? Is James in as good spirits as ever? How many I should like to see them. Much love to Frances and say that I shall endeavor to write her a long, long letter soon. I feel quite sad tonight. I suppose Frances would say that I have the blues. I shall wait until I feel a little more cheerful to finish the letter. Did ever you see a postscript longer than the letter itself before?

April 8th — The mail has come in this morning bringing me a N.Y. Tribune from home. It was mailed March 31st. I hope to get a letter soon. I shall send this off if I can manage to borrow a stamp. O go on guard at half after nine today. Shall be at the fence or stockade.

I shall come home, probably, unless I should fail to pass the medical examination at New York.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **RE-ENLISTED AND LEFT CHATTANOOGA CLANDESTINELY.** Alexander left detachment to rejoin regiment. "I suppose I am reported at my detachment as a deserter, but this will do me no harm as I shall be able to join the regt. before my report can reach there." Smuggled way with 18th Corps detachment to Nashville. On way to Savannah to join regt. Col. Strain arranged reassignment. Shall go by way of New York — medical examination. "I shall come home, probably, unless I should fail to pass the medical examination at New York."

movements.sigSummary: Davis, the regiment's colonel, and his adjutant sit under arrest at Capitol Hill — court-martialed for bucking and gagging the men and for filing the U.S. mark off a government horse, while a false muster at Fonda enrolled the same soldiers in two or three companies to draw bounty for men who never served. Charles tells his mother the men still like Davis and dread losing him. Quieter but historic: Corporal Trombly of his company has won a commission as 2nd Lieutenant in a colored regiment.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 19, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd. your welcome letter of Jan. 11th a few days since and would have answered it before but I have been on guard and we have had general inspection. Am sorry that Alex has reenlisted, but it may be all for the best. You did not say a word about James in your last letter so I infer that he passed the examination. How does he get along? Have not heard from him for a long time. Just before I rec'd. Alex's letter dated in Tennessee, I wrote him. Has he rec'd the letter? I hope Alex will pass a pleasant furlough. Think it would be the best thing he could do to try to improve his penmanship. He can write after copy slates at home; also look over his arithmetic. I wish he would devote himself for a while to these two branches.

Corporal Trombly of our Co. and from the town of Ghash has passed the examining board in this city and has got a commission as 2nd Lieut. in a colored regt. He has reported for duty.

Our regt. is in a queer state. The Col. and Adjutant are under arrest. Ex-Lieut. Colonel Armstrong, our Ex Col., also ex Lieut. Col. Prentoff, also ex-quartermaster, and several others have got to give an account of themselves. It seems there was a fraud in our being mustered at Fonda. Some men belonging to one Co. would go to another Co. to fill it up, the same men being mustered two or three times. The Col. is being tried by a court martial for husking and gagging the men; also for trying to take the mark U.S. off a government horse. Some time since Capt. Spalding was also missed from our regt. for incompetency. In revenge he has preferred charges against our Col. It is he that is making the trouble. The men like Col. Davis and he is a good military officer and would be sorry to lose him. They hope he will not be broke.

In the false muster, bounty was drawn from the state for men that were not in the regt.

Yesterday it rained all day and the mud is deep, but today it is pleasant. Two days since I saw George and Chas. Dodds. They both look healthy. Chas. told me that he had reenlisted. Tell Alex that Mr. Lafountain was here with Chas. Dodds. Lafountain says his brother in your Co. did not reenlist. How many men of your regt. were injured by an accident on the Ogdensburg railroad. Lafountain said that about 4 of your regt. were injured. Is this true? He and Lablue, also Trudell, are in the 6th Cavalry. Lafountain was visiting this city on a five days furlough. Says he will not reenlist.

Perhaps you do not know what bucking and gagging is. A stick is placed in the mouth and tied with a string, the hands are fastened together at the wrist and placed under the knees and over the arms so that the culprit cannot draw his arms up. The man that is bucked sits on the floor and when it is done cannot move. Niggers are punished in this way in the South.

I hope you and Alex will write soon. Will you send me James' letter if you have received any I tely, and I will return it. How does Frances get to school this bad weather? It would be well to hire a sleigh to carry her back and forth to school. Has Mr. Bass a large school this term?

I wrote to Mary McNeill a few days since. I had owed her a letter a long time and before I answered it rec'd another from her. Then I wrote. Enclosed is the letter. Will close by wishing you and Frances a pleasant visit with Alex.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alex has re-enlisted. **COL. AND ADJUTANT UNDER ARREST.** Lieut. Col. Armstrong, ex-Col., also Lieut. Col. Prentoff, ex-quartermaster. Charges against Col. — incompetency. He has preferred charges against our Col. in revenge. Corporal Trombly — passed examining board, 2nd Lieut. in colored regt. **BUCKING AND GAGGING DESCRIBED** — stick in mouth tied with string, hands fastened at wrist, placed under knees. "Niggers are punished in this way in the South." Lafountain — brother in Co. did not re-enlist; injured on Ogdensburg railroad. Alex's letters directed same; Alex will write soon. Mary McNeill — letter owed.

movements.letterExcerpt: I rec'd. your welcome and long looked for letter of Jan. 20 yesterday. Am glad to hear that Alex is enjoying his furlough. Hope that he will continue to have a good time. But I hope that he won't negl...
movements.sigSummary: A guard in Charles's regiment took a $200 bribe to free a prisoner who was recaptured fleeing the city — and now, Charles writes from Capitol Hill, the rumor is the sentry will be shot. He fills the rest with a soldier's wry eye: the most profane man in his company taking communion bread "for the congregation," three comrades who attend church only to see the ladies, and an afternoon spent listening to Congress debate confiscation, Democrat against Republican.
movements.transcription:
Jan. 29, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd. your welcome and long looked for letter of Jan. 20 yesterday. Am glad to hear that Alex is enjoying his furlough. Hope that he will continue to have a good time. But I hope that he won't neglect to give his attention to his penmanship. He is a bad spender. About his bounty, I think he ought to have his $450 town bounty. Do you know how much bounty the state gives? Alex did not answer my questions whether Luther reenlisted and if there were many of his regt. that did not do so. I wish Alex would write me a good and a long letter. Shall not excuse him if he does not. He must not forget to answer the questions. I am sorry that we do not hear from James, but as it does no good to worry or borrow trouble I don't do it.

About Messrs. Savages' acc'ts., it was $16.56. I don't know how they made it out $20. The interest would not make it amount to that, I think. Guess you did not pay them quite $20. While I was at Plattsburgh I made a memoranda of Joel S's. acc't from memory. It was $27.60. The interest will make it more than that. Perhaps Joel will make some discount. It would be well to settle with him immediately. Have you paid your land tax yet? If so, how much was it? I wish you would send me one dollar as we don't expect to be paid till March when 4 months pay will be due us.

The weather is delightful and has been for about a week back. It is so warm in the daytime that we need no fire and we keep the windows up. The mud has dried up which makes it nice for our dress parades. Last evening I attended with a large number of soldiers, a love feast in a church close by. One of the speakers said that he felt the love of God so in his heart that he felt sometimes when walking the streets that he should holler right out and scare some one. He was a soldier of our regt. The most profane man in our Co. when the bread and water was passed around took some of it. When asked about it afterwards he said it was for the congregation. But I guess he wanted to appear good in the eyes of his girl. I know three of our Co. who attend church regularly for the purpose of seeing some ladies.

I am sorry that Sid'ney is having trouble in his family. Hope that you or Frances will not get mixed up in it. I see you heard it from Sid's girl. Guess the girl lied some, or else greatly exaggerated.

A private in our regt. while on guard at the prison for a bribe of $200 let one of the prisoners escape. The prisoner while trying to escape from this city was captured. He swore that he paid $200 to the sentry for letting him escape. The sentry has been confined in prison for a long time and the rumor now is that he is to be shot.

Yesterday I attended Congress. There was a debate in confiscation. I heard one long speech against it by a Democrat and part of one in favor by a Republican. Please write often and all the news. If Frances can find time wish she would write me about her school.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Alex enjoying furlough — hopes he improves penmanship. $450 town bounty discussion — quota may not be full. Savages settlement — $16.56. County bonds at 7% preferred over investment. Chas. Carte visited — saw Champlainers at Biglows. James's abilities — "a great many smart men have failed at West Point." Sid having trouble in family. Love feast — soldier said he felt love of God. Guard bribed $200 to let prisoner escape. **ATTENDED CONGRESS** — debate between Democrat and Republican.

movements.letterExcerpt: I rec'd. Alex's letter of Feb. 9th enclosing one dollar two or three days since. Have been on guard or would have answered it sooner. Since the 14th N.H. regt. left for the front two or three weeks si...
movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Capitol Hill, where his regiment now stands four reliefs deep — two hours on post, the guard never changing because there aren't enough men to relieve it. A week earlier he had marched with a hundred others to Point Lookout, escorting nearly 400 rebel prisoners to a camp of 8,000 penned behind an eight-foot board fence, sentinels pacing a walk near its top. He worries over Alex's bounty and dreads the thought of young James enlisting at all.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 15, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd. Alex's letter of Feb. 9th enclosing one dollar two or three days since. Have been on guard or would have answered it sooner. Since the 14th N.H. regt. left for the front two or three weeks since our regt. have been doing their duty and our own, too. Instead of having three reliefs which makes each relief two hours on post and then four hours off, we now have four reliefs, which makes 2 hours on post and 6 hours off. Then we had three reliefs the guard was changed once every twenty-four hours, but now with four reliefs the guard is not changed, but stays on duty all the time. There are not enough men to change the guard. Of course as all the men are on duty now we have no dress parades. The corporals have a good deal more leisure time than the privates as we do not have to be on duty all the time. I have just come off duty. "As on four days am" was relieved by Jim Lucas who has been promoted again to Corporal.

Over a week since I was down to Point Lookout which is at the mouth of the Potomac. About one hundred of us went there with nearly 400 rebel prisoners. The camp of prisoners there contains about 8000 rebs. It is surrounded by a board fence about 8 feet high, with a walk near the top of the fence for the sentinels to walk their beat. Our Regt. now guard the old Capitol prison and the Carroll Prison which are both close to our barracks. Also guard the railroad depot and the Central Guard House. I don't know how long we will stay here. We may be relieved by the Invalid Corps. I hear that the old Capitol Prison used to be the Capitol of the U.S.

Sergt. Peltier of our Co. went home on furlough two days since. He lives at Kerbo.

How much bounty did Alex get? If Alex does not receive the town bounty it will be cheating him. Sam Underhill was not entitled to it and Alex ought not to have consented, if he did, to divide with Sam. But since the President's new call for troops the quota of the town may not be full, and they may all receive the town bounty. Can you tell me about this?

I don't know whether Alex made a good investment with his money or not. At all events I had rather buy county bonds if they pay 7 percent with my money than to invest it in that bank. My money that is out at 7% is well enough where it is.

Have you paid the land tax yet? If so, how much was it? I rec'd Frances' letter some time since. Tell her I am expecting that long letter that she promised and hope that she won't forget the promise to write. Also that I shall be glad to pay my share towards those furs that she bought for you. They are just the things for our Canada climate and I am glad that she bought them.

I saw Chas. Carte the other day. He was here to see us Champlainers. He said he attended the reenlisted soldiers party at Biglows. Asked me if I knew who he took there. Told him I did not, but guessed Helen Scott. Do you know who she is and who did take her? Have you heard from James lately? It seems too bad for him to go into the army. He might go to school a while and fit himself for a teacher or a month or so. I think as much of James' abilities as ever. A great many smart men have failed at West Point. If James enlisted I hope he will do it where he can get the most bounty. He can go into any regt. he enlists for old enough to be this regt. or Alex's regt. But I hope he will not enlist. Please write soon and all the news. How does Sid get along?

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **TRANSFERRED TO POINT LOOKOUT.** Guard duty at prisoner camp — nearly 400 rebel prisoners, ~8,000 total. Board fence with walk near top for sentinels. Old Capitol Prison and Carroll Prison also guarded. Four reliefs instead of three — on duty all the time. Jim Lucas promoted again to Corporal. Regt left front two or three weeks ago — doing duty for 14th N.H. too. Alex's bounty — town bounty question. Sam Underhill not entitled.
Brief stop at Point Lookout (POW camp) during transfer south.

movements.sigSummary: Sudden orders, written in haste on the coldest day of the winter: Charles tells his mother the regiment leaves Capitol Hill for Alexandria at 7 the next morning, with no one sure whether they march or take a steamboat, or whether the destination is Texas or the Army of the Potomac. He encloses a $20 check and $10.60 in greenbacks, having sold his double-cased watch for $17.50. "I hope you will not worry about us boys. Everything will come out all right."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 17, 1864
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

Military movements are sudden so you must not be surprised to hear that we are to leave this place tomorrow morning at 7 o'clock for Alexandria. It was un-expected, our being relieved from duty last night. Today we received our pay for two months which has been due us some time. It is said that we must report at Alexandria tomorrow at 7:00 A.M. I don't know whether we will go on foot or in a steamboat to Alexandria. Neither do I know whether we will stay there or go to Texas or the Army of the Potomac. Some think we are going to Texas. Our Col. has just come back to the regt, and we are all glad of it as he is a good Col. The men cheered him roundly last night. We are all in good spirits about leaving, although I think the most of us had rather stay here than leave.

Enclosed is a $20 check and $10.60 in greenbacks. Please let me know soon when you receive it. Since last pay day I sold my large double cased watch for $17.50 and have just been paid most of it.

Today it is very cold; the coldest day we have had this winter. Hope it will be warmer tomorrow. The most of the men think we are going to Texas and had rather go there than to go to the other armies.

I am expecting a letter from you. Should like to hear about Jas. and Alex. I think Alex's photograph looks very well. I hope you will not worry about us boys. Everything will come out all right. The best way is to make the best of everything. Please write soon. Must close as I am in haste.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **SUDDEN MARCHING ORDERS — LEAVING FOR ALEXANDRIA.** "Military movements are sudden." Leave tomorrow 7 o'clock for Alexandria. Received 2 months pay. Col. has returned — "men cheered him roundly." Some think going to Texas or Army of the Potomac. Sold large double-cased watch for $17.50. Coldest day of winter. Encloses $20 check and $10.60 in greenbacks. Alex's photograph looks well.

movements.sigSummary: Alex F. Hubbell, in plenty of leisure on a brief transit halt at Nashville, takes a pass into the city and finds Thos. Small in hospital No. 8 — one of his own wounded boys, who lost his leg at Ringgold and now seems "doing well and very cheerful." Even the cars surprise him: comfortable passenger seats instead of the cold freight cars they'd expected. Then, in the same breath, he asks his mother whether Frances and the others have been down to the ravine to slide.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 18, 1864
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you a day or two at on from Louisville, Ky., but you recollect I promised to write you as often as possible — and as I have plenty of leisure at present, I don't know as I can better occupy it than by writing you. You agree with me perfectly, I know.

We left Louisville early yesterday morning and reached here a little before dark last night. Strange to say, we had comfortable passenger cars instead of the cold freight cars we expected. To leave here at three this afternoon. I was out in the city this morning on a pass. I went to hospital No. 8 and saw one of our wounded boys, Thos. Small, who lost his leg at Ringgold. He was doing well and seemed very cheerful.

Luther has spent the greater part of his state bounty — and I don't see as he is any the better for it. Mr. Marshall Dunn said the state bounty yet "please give him five dollars as a reward for his services." He allows the boys to give him what they will. All who have received the bounty have given him five dollars and I would not be "behind hand."

How does Frances and her school flourish? Mrs. Rider and Miss Riley? Have Frances, Miss Averill, and others been down in the ravine to have a slide yet? Tell Frances I shall endeavor to write her soon. All the boys from Champlain are well. Direct your letters in future to Nashville, Tenn., Army of the Cumberland. They will reach me if you direct to Washington, but will come sooner, I think, by directing the other way, to Nashville. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Left Louisville yesterday morning — reached Nashville before dark. **THOS. SMALL VISITED AT HOSPITAL** — lost his leg at Ringgold; doing well, cheerful. Luther spent greater part of state bounty — Marshall Dunn said state bounty yet; $5 reward for services. Direct letters to Nashville, Army of the Cumberland. Boys from Champlain all well. Frances and school — Mrs. Rider, Miss Riley, Miss Averill.
Returned to Stevenson/Bridgeport area. Preparing for Atlanta Campaign.

movements.sigSummary: A rebel cavalry captain Alexander spoke with at Stephenson, Alabama let the Confederate collapse slip in his own words: "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts." On a hushed Sabbath morning — birds singing, the war momentarily still — he and his tent mates refused to build their shanty, certain that soldiers above all needed God's blessing. Across from camp lay the Chickamauga dead, and a defiant reb warned, "wait until the next fight and you will be prisoners."
movements.transcription:
Feb. 21, 1864
Stephenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

It is a most beautiful Sabbath morning. The sun is shining warm and pleasant, the birds are singing, and every thing is hushed to an unusual quiet. It is such a day as is seldom vouchsafed to us soldiers. Nevertheless all are on the alert. The horse thief Morgan is on the move with a force of some eight thousand men and there is no telling upon what particular part he will fall. All the troops stationed here, with the exception of our regt., were under arms last night. All his motions are watched and I am afraid he will find it hard to come upon our troops unprepared.

We reached here night before last and — most wonderful to relate — found a Soldier's Home established here where we were provided with an excellent supper and good sleeping accommodations. Yesterday we established our camp and commenced carrying timber to build our shanties. Today most of us are resting from our labors. My three tent mates and myself had a confab together and came to the conclusion that we would not work upon our shanty today as soldiers above all needed God's blessing — and Sabbath breaking would not be very likely to get it. My tent mates are Corporal Kelly, Oliver Lafountain, and George Bully. Two of them you have seen.

Opposite our camp a large number of soldiers are buried — victims of Chickamauga. After that battle the General Hospital was established here and these men died from the effects of their wounds.

The veterans of 64 attached to the 60th N.Y. had a warm welcome from the old 3rd Brigade when they reached here. (A gentleman attached to the Christian Com., I cannot, just gave me a paper entitled "the Parlor Visitor." So you see I have something good to read today.) The Brigade Band gave them a grand serenade accompanied by lusty cheers from the men of the Brigade present which were promptly responded to by the Veterans. "The Old Sixtieth" is of some account down here, you see.

I have talked with a number of rebs since I came here. They all tell the same story of want and discouragement in the rebel ranks. I was talking with a rebel Capt. of Cavalry yesterday. "Yes," said he in conclusion to what he was saying in regard to the rebel conscription, "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts." One of the rebs told me that it was generally believed in the rebel army that this war will terminate about June. He says Johnson's (formerly Bragg's) army swear that they will not stand in the next battle.

Gen'l. Slocum made a speech here not long since in which he prophesied a speedy termination of the war. There does not seem to be any doubt of the war's terminating this year.

I have done my best to go into minute details. I am afraid you will get sick of it. If you do let me know. Tell Frances I shall certainly write her soon if it be possible. Love to all.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

Gave you heard from James yet? Be particular when you direct your letters to put on the Brigade, Division of Corps, also Army of the Cumberland. The bugles are blowing the dinner call. I must hurry up. One of the rebs said, "You think you took a great many prisoners at the last fight, and so you did, but wait until the next fight and you will be prisoners."
movements.notes: **SOLDIER'S HOME AT STEPHENSON, ALA.** Beautiful Sabbath morning — birds singing. "Horse thief" Morgan on the move — 8,000 men. All troops under arms last night. **VETERANS OF 64** — reached here night before last. Soldier's Home — excellent supper, good sleeping accommodations. Tent mates: Corporal Kelly, Oliver Lafountain, George Bully. Opposite camp — soldiers buried, victims of Chickamauga; General Hospital. **REBEL CAPTAIN CONVERSATION** — "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts." Johnson's (Bragg's) army swear they won't stand in next battle. Gen'l Slocum speech — speedy termination of war. "The Old Sixtieth" paper from Christian Com. Brigade Band serenade.
