movements.sigSummary: At Charleston, Tennessee, Alexander reaches camp after a sixty-mile march and walks the abandoned Confederate forts. He finds guns left unmuzzled and "fit for immediate use," two gun carriages burned, and a pair of enormous rifled guns lying beside the track, ready for cars that never came — Kilpatrick having torn up the railroads first. "The Johnnies must have left here in considerable haste," he tells Mother, with Sherman already off again and no telling when they'll catch him.
movements.transcription:
Feb. 24, 1864
Charleston, S.C.

Dear Mother:

We reached this place yesterday afternoon after a march of some sixty miles. I have not yet been around to see the lions of the place; but shall as soon as possible. The Johnnies must have left here in considerable haste, if I may judge by the appearance of things, for in several of the forts I have passed the guns were left unmuzzled and fit for immediate use. Close to here, they burned the carriages of two guns, but left several others by them unharmed. Two enormous rifled guns lay beside the track ready to be loaded onto cars. I should judge, but I expect Kilpatrick slipped them us on that calculation by tearing up the railroads. They must have left an immense amount of heavy ordnance here. Before writing again I will try and see all things and give you them a minute description.

Sherman is off again and there is no telling when we shall get to him. I presume likely we shall take transports from this place. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. B.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Reached Charleston, S.C. (likely Charleston, Tenn.) after march of 60 miles. Johnnies left in haste — guns left unmuzzled, carriages burned, two enormous rifled guns on track. "I expect Kilpatrick slipped them us on that calculation by tearing up the railroads." Immense ordnance left. Sherman off again — no telling when they'll get to him. Transports from this place likely. Remember me to Mrs. B.

movements.letterExcerpt: Here we are just across the river close to New Orleans. We left Washington Feb. 18th for Alexandria and stayed there in the Soldier's Rest till the 20th when we went aboard the steamship Mississippi b...
movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from Algiers, across the river from New Orleans, after the 153rd New York's steamship Mississippi voyage from Alexandria, entering the river mouth at daylight one Sunday morning to find sugar plantations, orange groves, and darkies tossing oranges that fell short of the boat. His regiment now quarters in a smashed-windowed iron works with no floor but the bare ground. Rumor has it an expedition is fitting out for Mobile.
movements.transcription:
March 1, 1864
Algiers, La.

Dear Mother:

Here we are just across the river close to New Orleans. We left Washington Feb. 18th for Alexandria and stayed there in the Soldier's Rest till the 20th when we went aboard the steamship Mississippi bound for New Orleans. We reached N.O. about sundown, Feb. 28. On the morning of the 4th day about daylight we entered the mouth of the Mississippi River. It was Sunday morning and I passed a pleasant Sabbath on deck of the vessel looking at the beautiful sugar plantations all along both sides of the river. The buildings on a plantation made quite a village. The negro quarters were nice looking small buildings all in rows. We passed orange groves and at one place the darkies threw some oranges at the boat but they did not reach it.

It is a beautiful country along the river but perfectly flat. When we arrived at N.O. we did not land that night but anchored in the river till morning when all the recruits from N. York were landed in N.O., but our regt. was brought to this side of the river which is called Algiers. About 70 of our regt. were detailed to guard the new recruits to a place in the city of N.O. I was part of this guard so had a chance to see N.O. It is a fine city and but little business is now carried on there. The cotton presses (and there are a great many of them) are idle and empty and are used to quarter soldiers in.

Our regt. is quartered in a very large brick building formerly used as an iron works. There is no floor, but the ground, and the windows are nearly all smashed but it will do for warm weather. There is a great change in the weather since yesterday when we arrived here. This morning it is cold and rainy, but yesterday it was quite warm. We do not expect to stay here long, perhaps a month or so. I hear that there is an expedition fitting out for Mobile. I don't know whether we will go there or to Texas. I think we will have to rough it now but that was to be expected. Each man brought his half or a shelter tent from Washington. Two men put their half tents together and slept together. We were glad when our voyage was over. We slept in bunks in the hold, four or five in a bunk. As we slept so close we did not suffer from the cold. We had some rough weather but not a great deal of seasickness. I was not sea sick. Part of the way we used the sails. Our meat and coffee were cooked by steam, also the bean soup. The noon and the meat were boiled in a large barrel which had a steam pipe running down on one side and across the bottom. The steam made the water boil furiously. Coffee was boiled in a large iron tank by steam. We earned our meals, for although we fell in in a long string it was squeeze and mash. Starting on one side we marched around by the coffee tank, thence by the meat board for our meat and hard tack. I got along very well eating hardtack, but it takes me a good deal longer than the rest unless I soak the .

Direct your letters to N.O. The Captain says that is the right way to direct. I am expecting letters from you every day. It is a long time since I heard from you. Should like to hear about James and Alex. Hope you will write often. My health is good. Oranges are in great plenty here at 6¢ each. Apples sold for 10¢ on Sabbath so were we and other things in proportion. Tell the boys to write to me and I will write to them. I still close by hoping to hear that you are all well and that you are taking the world easy.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **LEFT WASHINGTON FOR NEW ORLEANS.** Left Washington Feb. 18 for Alexandria, stayed at Soldier's Rest till 20th, steamship Mississippi to N.O. Reached N.O. about sundown Feb. 28. Passed pleasant Sabbath on deck looking at sugar plantations. **"ALGIERS"** — across river from New Orleans. Quartered in iron works — brick building, no floor, windows nearly all smashed. Expedition fitting out for Mobile or Texas. Sleeping in bunks 4-5 in a bunk. Hardtack and mess, coffee boiled in iron tank by steam. Oranges 6¢ each, apples 10¢. Darkies threw oranges at boat.
With 153rd NY in Louisiana. Red River Campaign area.

movements.letterExcerpt: I came to this place March 3d, which is Gen'l. Banks Head Quarters. On the afternoon of the 2nd the Col sent for me and asked whether I would like to go to N. Orleans as clerk. After looking at my han...
movements.sigSummary: Mother's quiet campaign finally lands her son a desk. Writing from Gen'l. Banks's New Orleans headquarters on March 6, 1864, Charles thanks her plainly — "you are at the bottom of this matter" — after she wrote the Surgeon and Mrs. Strain pressed her husband to detail him as a clerk, the Lieut. Col. having refused to spare "so healthy a man." Safe in a third-story office as his regiment marches toward hard fighting, Charles confesses his copying still falters: "I wish I understood punctuation."
movements.transcription:
March 6, 1864
Department of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Mother:

I came to this place March 3d, which is Gen'l. Banks Head Quarters. On the afternoon of the 2nd the Col sent for me and asked whether I would like to go to N. Orleans as clerk. After looking at my handwriting he asked me if I thought my Capt. would give his consent. I told him I thought he would. He told me to get my Capt. to send in a request to him to detail me and he would do it. I asked him, but he gave me no definite answer. I was then afraid he would not do it. The next morning Lieut. Col. Strain came to me and told me to get ready to go. He said my Capt. wanted A. Douglass to go, but he told him he could not spare so healthy a man. Lieut. Col. Strain told me that you had written the Surgeon and that his (Strain's) wife had written to him several times. That he had been waiting for an opportunity to get me a situation. He is a very pleasant man and you must thank Mrs. Strain for her influence.

Now, Mother, I am much obliged to you, for you are at the bottom of this matter. It is a pleasant place here, a good deal better than being in the field. We are in the third story, where we can get the fresh cool air. There are a good many clerks here and we all mess together. It costs about three dollars a mo. for each of us to buy extras, such as butter, potatoes, etc. One of the older clerks acts as caterer for the mess, that is, draws our gov't. rations and buys the extras. The clerks draw extra pay, but I don't get know how much. About eight clerks are going in a day or two into the field along with the Gen'l.

Our Regt. left Algiers for Franklin, La. the same day that I came here. I took the cars for that place. I think it will see some hard marching before long. The Col. asked me about my health. I told him it was pretty good. He said he meant if I was able to stand a long march. I told him no.

I have received no letters since we left Wash. and there was not one due me at that time. Should like to hear how you all get along. Lieut. Col. Strain told me that I was detached from the regt. — a permanent detachment, — so I suppose that I will not go to the regt. again.

Mch. 11th — A mail steamship leaves here this morning so I will finish this letter. I might have sent this sooner, but was waiting to hear from you. I have rec'd no detail from Head Quarters yet, so am not sure of staying here, but I guess I will stay. My writing is not as good as the other clerks, but I have to improve. My duty is to copy special orders, but I have not done much yet at it yet. If the smallest mistake in spelling or anything else is made, it will not answer but a new copy must be made. I wish I understood punctuation, but I will learn, I suppose. Wish you would correct my bad spelling.

The 153rd is going to Texas, I Believe. The extra pay of the clerks is 40¢ a day which will make my pay about $25 a mo. The 4th of Mch. was a great holiday here when a free state Governor was inaugurated. You must have seen an account of it. 5000 school children sat on the seats and sang together. There was plenty of music and plenty of cannon firing, also musketry firing. In the evening fireworks, music, etc. Two days since the rain poured down and the streets were fairly flooded with water. Please write soon. Love to all.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **CLERK AT GEN. BANKS HEADQUARTERS.** Came to New Orleans March 3rd — Col. Strain sent for him, asked if he'd like to go to N.O. as clerk. After looking at handwriting, Capt. would give consent. Col. Strain — "a very pleasant man and you must thank Mrs. Strain for her influence." 3rd story, fresh cool air. **REGIMENT LEFT FOR FRANKLIN, LA.** — expects hard marching. 153rd going to Texas, he believes. Extra pay 40¢/day — $25/month total. **FREE STATE GOVERNOR INAUGURATED** — 5,000 school children, cannon firing, musketry, fireworks. Streets flooded with rain. Bad spelling acknowledged — "wish you would correct my bad spelling."
Stationed at New Orleans. Preparing for Red River Campaign support.

movements.sigSummary: Rebel deserters from Johnson's and Longstreet's armies paint a doleful picture: rations barely enough for one meal in a day, men determined not to stand at the next fight, and the admission that "the Confederacy was played out and that it was only the pride of the leaders that kept it up." Writing from Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander also appoints his mother and Frances his "business agents in Champlain," trusting the women at home to chase down his bounty money.
movements.transcription:
March 7, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd. your welcome letters of Feb. 14th, 18th, and 22rd and also one enclosed from Frances yesterday. Am sorry to hear that Charley has left Wash. Had hoped he would remain there all summer. I hope he has gone to Texas. I do not think there will be much fighting there. I expect you and Mrs. Bostwick are having dolorous times together, eh? I have written Mrs. Bostwick today — so that she will understand matters and things generally.

Have you heard from James yet? I hope, and I believe, he keeps a stout heart. There is nothing like it. I hope he will get a commission. James is young yet, and the world is wide — there is no reason why he should not retrieve his fortunes.

I hope this war will end soon. There were quite a number of deserters from Johnson's army and from Longstreet's. They give a most dolorous acc't. of the affairs of the so-called Southern Confederacy. They say that Johnson's army is suffering terribly for want of food — that one days rations is scarcely sufficient for one meal, and that the men are determined not to stand at the next fight. They say they never want to be nearer home than they were in the rebel army. Longstreet's men also give a very doleful acc't. They and the 62d Corps are very well acquainted. They asked us if we had not rather be in "the Potomac army than out here." Said they fared very much better while they were under Lee. Said the Confederacy was played out and that it was only the pride of the leaders that kept it up.

One Div. of our Corps will doubtless be sent to the front. I hope it will not be ours. It is said that General Slocum said that if any troops were sent from our Corps to the front it should be the 1st Div., as we had done our share last fall. General Geary, I guess, does not think so, and I am afraid will not rest until he gets us up there. We will doubtless know in a few weeks what we shall do this summer. I hope they will give the men a sound drubbing this summer in Va. I will appoint you and Frances my business agents in Champlain. I do not know that I can give you any more directions. Averill is to get my county bounty and my third of Underhill's. Marshall Dunn will give you my state bounty. Please pay him five dollars for his fee. I think Averill will deal honorably with me. If he plays any rascality it will be very easily proved on him as the receipts for bounty paid at the offices of the Supervisor of the town and the County Clerk will show what amount he received. I shall finish up what I have to say in my letter to Miss Fannie.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Sorry Charley has left Washington — hoped he'd stay all summer. **REBEL DESERTERS FROM LONGSTREET'S AND JOHNSON'S ARMY** — "give a most dolorous acc't of the affairs of the so-called Southern Confederacy." Johnson's army suffering terribly for food — one day's rations scarcely sufficient for one meal. Determined not to stand in next fight. "Said the Confederacy was played out and that it was only the pride of the leaders that kept it up." Longstreet's men also doleful. 62d Corps very well acquainted — asked us if we had not rather be in "the Potomac army." **AVERILL — BOUNTY AND COUNTY BUSINESS.** Marshall Dunn — pay $5 for his fee. County Clerk. Mrs. Bostwick — dolorous times.

movements.sigSummary: He warns his sister Frances against flattery with a mock-pompous flourish — a philosopher so busy walking with his head among the stars that he tumbles into a ditch and breaks his neck. Yet beneath the play runs a soldier's ache: writing from Stevenson, Alabama on March 7, 1864, Alex longs for the day he can lay aside "the terrible title of a 'veteran soldier'" and walk among friends as a citizen — "the proudest day of my life." The brigade band practices nearby, the music grand.
movements.transcription:
Mch. 7th, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Fannie:

So you think I know you would give a thousand worlds to see me — eh? You would like to make me think I am something great, wouldn't you? A fine idea, isn't it? How do you know but what I would get so puffed up that I would not see my boots for six months and perchance, like a certain ancient philosopher who always walked with his head among the stars, might fall into a ditch and break my neck? I warn you to beward of flattery, especially to a young gent who is as susceptible as I am — beward.

So you and Miss Averill have lost your sled rides, eh? Well, I hope it will not be long before the terrible title of a "veteran soldier" will be laid aside by your humble servant and he walk among his friends again in the meek garb of a citizen. Honestly, Frances, it will be the proudest day of my life. You tell Miss A. that when that happy time arrives we will reverse the order and I will draw you both on the sled to the houses. The Brigade band is practicing this afternoon. The music is grand. Have you received the History of the Regt. yet? Please write soon.

Your aff. brother,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Playful letter to Frances. "You would like to make me think I am something great, wouldn't you?" Warns against flattery — "a certain ancient philosopher who always walked with his head among the stars, might fall into a ditch." Hopes to walk among friends again "in the meek garb of a citizen." "It will be the proudest day of my life." Promises when that time comes will reverse the order — draw Frances on sled to houses. Miss Averill lost sled rides. Brigade Band practicing. History of the Regt. — have you received?

movements.sigSummary: Camp at Stevenson, Alabama, and Alexander finally makes good on a long-promised letter to his sister Fannie — though picket duty and an order to guard prisoners at Chattanooga keep interrupting the writing. What he offers her is a word-painting of a beautiful day: distant picket fires, a brass battery glistening on an earthwork, the Brigade band, and Taps, "the last plaintive, soothing call of the bugle." His scorn for the Southern sympathizers back home is just as vivid.
movements.transcription:
March 20, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Fannie:

Here at last is the long expected letter which I have promised so often. Everything has gone on about as usual since I last wrote. We have got our shanty up and a fireplace built and are now quite comfortable. We have had several little starts occasioned by the movements of Morgan.

The other night just as I was about to turn in the orderly came to me and ordered me to provide myself with three days rations and report myself to the Adjutant's office. I did so, and was sent with twenty men to picket about a mile east of camp. Such is a soldier's life. I had promised myself a good night's rest, but who can human calculations. I was ordered today to be ready to go to Chattanooga at half after two to guard prisoners, and this when I had settled myself comfortably to write you, but fortunately for your letter, the order was revoked and your letter will be finished if nothing else turns up. Now, Fannie, I will try and give you a picture.

It is a most beautiful day. The whole country is dotted here and there with the different camps. Away in the distance you see little columns of smoke rising from the fires of the pickets. On a hill at a little distance is a large earth work mounting a brass battery which gleams and glistens brightly in the sun. Close by where I am sitting are headquarters — over which the stars and stripes are proudly floating. At a little distance from headquarters the Brigade band is playing — their instruments gleaming brightly in the sun. Quite a distance from there the drum corps of the different regts. are practicing. It altogether forms a most beautiful picture. I wish that I could paint and in painting could convey to you the different sounds. I would furnish you with many a delicious treat — a view of Seville with all the noise of the drums and bugles, — of Guard Mounting with the soul stirring airs of the Brigade band, — dinner call with its throng, each flourishing a tin cup or plate and each striving to be first at the cook house, — dress parade and its ceremony, — Tattoo and its accompaniment of drums and bugles, and last but not least, — Taps, the last plaintive, soothing call of the bugle which seems to invite all to repose.

I guess you think I am running wild, — eh? Wouldn't blame you at all if you did. I have seen lots of southern women today — and such women! Mother Alice is a queen to these! Pooh! I wish Mr. Bass would come down here and see some of the Southerners he admires so much. He is short many of them would call a "Yankee dough face" — a class of men much despised by them. Oh these Southerners, long legged, long haired, lank, lean, saucy cheeked "sons of guns." Mrs. Bass says, you know, that three Northern men could be beat before one Southern one could. Poor doctrine, I think.

If Marshall Dunn has got that bounty and you have my papers back again, please send me my furlough as I can get nine dollars on it for rations I have not received. You know that we are allowed thirty cents a day for rations. Government has got to shell over the difference.

I have received only one letter so far from home and that was mailed Dec. 23rd — had a great deal to say about "petition" and "discharge" much to my amusement. Please write soon. I hope Culver Bostwick will come along soon. I suppose he is at Elmira now. He will find us very comfortably situated, but does Nathaniel Nichols have to say? How does your school prosper? I hope there are no scenes at the castle now. Guess you are about tired out, so will close.

Your aff. brother,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **THE LONG-PROMISED LETTER TO FRANCES.** Beautiful day — whole country dotted with camps. Columns of smoke from picket fires. Stars and stripes floating from HQ. Brigade band playing, instruments gleaming. **VIVID CAMP SCENE PAINTING** — drums, bugles, dinner call, tin cup and plate, cook house. "Last but not least — Taps." "Yankee dough face" — Southern women despise Northerners who admire them. Mrs. Bass says three Northern men could be beat before one Southern one could. 30¢/day rations. Marshall Dunn — bounty. Culver Bostwick will come along soon — Elmira. Nathaniel Nichols. Morgan's movements — several little starts.
Red River Campaign. Advanced from Franklin to Alexandria.
Red River Campaign. Advanced from Franklin to Alexandria.

movements.sigSummary: A woman steps onto the streetcar track to watch a passing Military Company, panics at the mule too late, and is run down — left under a piece of old carpeting awaiting the coroner: "She was a poor, white woman," Charles writes from Headquarters at New Orleans. He reports the army's Red River victories at Fort DeRussy and Alexandria, then notes Capt. Fox of his regiment dismissed for disloyalty and conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.
movements.transcription:
March 25, 1864
Headquarters Dept. of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Mother:

I have anxiously been expecting a letter for some time, but as yet have rec'd none. Should like to hear about the boys and how you and Frances get along. But I suppose that I will get one after a while. Perhaps there may be a letter for me with the regt. and it has not got in yet.

I am still at these Head Quarters but think I shall not remain here much longer. Have rec'd. no detail yet from these Hd. Qtrs. They tell me my writing is stiff. I think that I can not get to the regt. very readily now and will have to wait a few days. But I am not gone yet, so please direct your letters as above. If I am not here the letter can be forwarded me from this place. If I leave here, I will let you know as soon as I leave. The regt. must have been through some hardships by this time and I have escaped them, so that if I go back to regt. I have profited so much.

A day or two since a woman was killed by the street car. She was standing on the track looking at the Military Co. and did not notice the car coming till the mule was almost on her, and then she was so scared that she ran against the mule, was knocked down, and run over. She was laid on the walk some time waiting for the coroner to come, and was covered with a piece of old carpeting. She was a poor, white woman.

The streets in this city are kept very clean and are well paved. It is a large city and is called the Crescent City because it is built on a bend in the river in the shape of a crescent.

Our army has had two or three victories on the Red River in western Louisiana where it now is, I suppose. You must have, or will, see an account of it. It captured Fort DeRussy, also the town of Alexandria, and has taken a great many prisoners. It is on its way to Texas. — Capt. Fox of our regt. has been dismissed from the service for disloyalty and conduct unbecoming the character of an officer and a gentleman.

The weather for the last few days has been quite cold so that we have kept a fire in the fireplace. The niggers say it is because the whole North has come down here that it is so cold. It costs a good deal to live in this city as everything is very dear. A picayune which is 5¢ is the smallest change that circulates here.

This is called a wicked city and I suppose it is. There are two or three theatres here which are nightly attended. I have not been to one and don't mean to go to them. I hope you don't worry about us boys, but take things as they come, and make the best of them. Should like to know whether James has enlisted. It is a long time since I heard from home, some time before we left Wash. This letter is written in haste, so as to go on the steamer in the morning, so please excuse writing, etc. My health is very good, and I hope that you all are well. Please write often and tell the boys to write to me and I will write to them. From your aff. son, C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Still at HQ but may not remain much longer. Writing stiff — "they tell me my writing is stiff." No detail from HQ yet. Duty — copying special orders, new copy for smallest mistake. **RED RIVER CAMPAIGN NEWS** — Army has had two or three victories on Red River in western Louisiana. Captured Fort DeRussy, town of Alexandria, taken many prisoners. On its way to Texas. **CAPT. FOX DISMISSED** — disloyalty, conduct unbecoming officer and gentleman. **WOMAN KILLED BY STREET CAR** — poor white woman. "Crescent City" — built on bend in river. "Wicked city" — two or three theatres. Weather cold — "niggers say it is because the whole North has come down here." Picayune — 5¢, smallest change. James enlisted?

movements.sigSummary: Warrant renewed — a mere formality — and Alexander holds his old position in the 60th Veterans again. But the real news is in the marching orders: he leaves Stevenson, Alabama in a few days for Chattanooga or Knoxville. Beneath the soldier's business runs a son's ache — no letter came that morning, and he was "very much disappointed." He asks twice for word from home, after his brothers James and Charles, and confesses he is entirely out of stamps, borrowing to send this.
movements.transcription:
April 1st, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

Have had old warrant renewed so that I now hold my old position in the 60th Veterans. It is merely a matter of form. Please preserve this one as you have the other. It is now some time since I heard from you. When the mail came in this morning and no letter for me I was very much disappointed. Please write soon. We have received marching orders and will leave in a few days for Chattanooga or Knoxville, probably.

If you can send the boots direct them the same as the letters. Be careful and put on in care of Capt. Delaney. Love to all. Please write soon. Have you heard from James and Charles?

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Please send me some stamps. I am entirely out and shall have to borrow to send this.
movements.notes: Old warrant renewed — holds old position in 60th Veterans. Merely a matter of form. Received marching orders — leaving in few days for Chattanooga or Knoxville, probably. Very much disappointed — no letter. Asks for boots — send in care of Capt. Delaney. Send stamps. Have you heard from James and Charles?

movements.sigSummary: At Department of the Gulf headquarters in New Orleans, clerk Charles reports $11 in extra pay he insists he hasn't earned — "I have done hardly anything." He sleeps on the office floor of a carpeted, third-story room with a marble mantle and a marble washstand fed by a spigot, knapsack in the corner, while Banks and most of his staff are in the field on the Red River, where the troops "expect to clear the rebels out." Roses are already in bloom in a city park.
movements.transcription:
April 1, 1864
Head Quarters
Department of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Mother:

Although I have rec'd no letter for so long a time, I think I ought to write once in a while as I have been doing. I think the fault must be in the mail. Today I am to receive over $11.00 extra pay. I have not earned it as I have done hardly anything. The extra pay is 40¢ a day and as I came here March 3rd, will receive nearly a month's pay. "Will have to buy me a blouse which will cost about $10.00." This month another clerk is going to be caterer for the mess. Last month we paid $3.10, but this month we pay five. Last month part of the time we did not have butter or sugar so we pay more this month. The clerks here have sent in a petition for commutation of rations and quarters. If it is granted, it will be a good thing for the clerks, as they can then board where they please. Now the pay is not enough for that. A good many of us clerks sleep in the different offices on the floor. Commutation of rations and quarters is receiving the money for rations and a place to live. I wish I was a better writer; don't know whether I will stay here or not; at my rate you had better not say much about it.

Should like very much to hear how you all get along, especially James and Alex. I wonder if James has enlisted. Gen Banks and most of his staff are in the field, and some clerks with them, but part of his staff stay here to attend to business.

Our troops on the Red River are doing very well and we expect to clear the rebels out of western Louisiana and Texas before long. I have not heard a word from the regt. since I left it. Should think if there was any letter for me there that it would be sent me here. If I do not receive a letter soon I shall write there enquiring about it. I am having a good time here, live well, and can sit and read all night in the office if I choose. The office is my home; there in one corner I keep my knapsack and when night comes spread my blankets on the floor and sleep soundly. One clerk always sleeps with me, but I always go to bed first as he spends his evenings in the city somewhere. We have a carpeted room with a marble mantle, also marble washstand with a spigot of water leading to it. We are in the third story. I hope that you all are well. My health is good. Please write often. The weather is not very warm here yet, still flowers are in bloom. I have seen roses and other flowers in bloom in a park in this city. The mail is about a week for the north. It goes out tomorrow morning. Sometimes the mail is oftener.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Still at HQ — no letter for long time. No detail yet from HQ. Extra pay 40¢/day — $25/mo. **GEN. BANKS AND STAFF IN THE FIELD** — Red River. Some clerks with them. "I always go to bed first." Office is his home — keeps knapsack in corner, spreads blankets on floor. Marble mantle, marble washstand with spigot of water. 3rd story. Roses and flowers in bloom — "about a week for the mail to reach the north." **RED RIVER CAMPAIGN** — troops doing very well, expect to clear rebels out of western Louisiana and Texas before long. Wonder if James has enlisted.

movements.sigSummary: Marching orders read at parade leave Alexander stripping for the coming campaign — surplus baggage to the rear, his overcoat sent off, with one grim line: "We shall probably have a hard summer." But his anger burns hotter at home, where twenty-five Champlain men voted against letting soldiers vote: "Whoever did deserves to be blasted with eternal infamy." A 6 P.M. postscript records the mail's arrival and no letter — "I fear all is not right at home."
movements.transcription:
April 6, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

The last letter I rec'd. from home was dated March 14th. I have, I believe rec'd two papers from home since then. I am feeling very anxious about you all. Where is Charles and have you heard from James? I am very anxious to hear from him. Please give me his address as soon as possible, also Charley's, although I suppose his will be the same as usual.

We are under marching orders. An order was read last night at Parade ordering Brigade Commanders to have everything prepared that is necessary for the coming campaign. May God be with us!

Mrs. Hoyle is again sending me papers. Please thank her warmly for me. Say, Mother, please find out if you can who in Champlain voted against soldiers voting. I see there were twenty-five votes cast against it. Whoever did deserves to be (and I may say will be) blasted with eternal infamy. What class of men are more vitally interested in the success of this Gov't. than the soldiers? What liberties would the Northern people enjoy if it were not for the soldiers? I wish they would think of it. If M.M. Bass cast a vote I am sure it was against.

The mail here has not yet come in. I shall not send this until it does. I hope I shall get a letter. You complain that I do not write often enough. I think it is now your turn to complain now. I have very little heart to write when I do not get an answer to my letters.

Everything is moving on here at the usual pace. Our reg't. is relieved from doing picket duty. It is now done by other regt's. of the Brigade. We have sent all our surplus baggage to the rear. I sent my overcoat off yesterday. I do hope I shall get a letter today.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. The 11th & 12th Army Corps have consolidated and now form the Army Corps under command of Gen. Hooker. Gen. Slocum, commands of the 12th Corps, has been assigned to the command of Vicksburg. We shall probably have a hard summer. General Hooker never cusses his men. I hope we shall be able to give the rebels a finishing blow this summer. The mail will not be in till afternoon.

6 P.M. The mail has come in and no letter. I was very much disappointed. I fear all is not right at home. Perhaps I shall get a letter in the morning. I shall wait, I think, until the next mail. I am very much concerned about you all. Please write often.
movements.notes: Under marching orders — everything prepared for coming campaign. "May God be with us!" **20TH ARMY CORPS FORMED** — 11th & 12th Army Corps consolidated under Gen. Hooker. Gen. Slocum assigned to command of Vicksburg. "Shall probably have a hard summer. General Hooker never cusses his men. I hope we shall be able to give the rebels a finishing blow this summer." Mrs. Hoyle sending papers. Soldiers voting in Champlain — Mr. Bass cast a vote against. Picket duty relieved — done by other regts now. Surplus baggage to rear — sent overcoat. 6 P.M. — mail came, no letter — "very much disappointed... I fear all is not right at home."

movements.sigSummary: The 60th NY met two regiments of the Brigade in a game of "Union Base," a kind of game of ball, and beat them badly — soldiers at leisure before active service, with a fiddle and a grand dance on the company street. Alexander catalogues the camp's amusements: a horse race, greased pole, and a greased pig loosed for the contrabands. "A letter of ten pages. Beat it if you can."
movements.transcription:
[First 8 pages missing]

It has been a beautiful warm day. The weather of last month was raw and chilly most of the time. If it was a sample of what you had up there, there must have been very little sugar made during the month of March. From what you say I suppose old Nye is running our bush. It would hardly pay to go to law with him. His heirs will probably be more tractable to settle with than he.

We are enjoying ourselves the best way we can and there is but little lack of way. The great game on the docket now is ball. Two regts. of the Brigade challenged our Regiment to a game of (Union Base) a kind of game of ball. Our regiment beat them badly.

Evening — The boys have got a fiddle and are having a grand dance on the company street. If I understood dancing I should take a turn with them.

Culver Bostwick has not yet appeared, nor any of the recruits for our regiment. They still probably be sent on before long. We will probably be sent on before long. We will probably be on the march before they reach us, though we have not a great way to go before we will find the enemy. It is the opinion of some here that we will not do much more at present than to harass the enemy in order to prevent reinforcing Lee. Everything indicates active service and soon.

You can direct your letters to the same Corps, as usual. When we are thoroughly organized I will give you the address. I feel quite sad tonight. I suppose Frances would say that I have the blues. I shall wait until I feel a little more cheerful to finish the letter. Did ever you see a postscript longer than the letter itself before?

April 8th — The mail has come in this morning bringing me a N.Y. Tribune from home. It was mailed March 31st. I hope to get a letter soon. I shall send this off if I can manage to borrow a stamp. Go on guard at half after nine today. Shall be at the fence or stockade.

We had a great time yesterday. The officers of the Brig. clubbed together and made up a number of purses to the winners in a horse race, sack race, wheelbarrow race, foot race, cook fight, and whoever managed to climb the greased pole. They also had a greased pig expressly for the contrabands to run after. You ought to have seen the little darkies rolling over together on the ground — the greased pig slipping like an eel, from under them. The shell barrow race was performed with a sack over the heads of the competitors with their eyes blindfolded. The sack race was about as amusing as anything I saw there.

I was wonderfully pleased yesterday by the receipt of a Magazine. It was like a shower to a thirsty desert. I hardly know who to thank for it. The address on the Magazine was in your handwriting — on the inside of the cover was "Prospects of S.P. Hubbell" and a little further over Miss Fannie wishes to know if "I will be satisfied with this until she can comply with my favorite advertisement of batter and lard." Now which shall I choose — I am in a quandary and shall leave you to settle it amongst you — giving my most heartfelt thanks to whoever sent it. I hope I may again — and often — have the pleasure of reading "Harpers" in this benighted land.

[Page break]

I want to give you a sentence of a contraband preacher's eloquence, which I doubt not was very edifying to his colored brethren, but which amused me some by its oddity. He was holding forth on the suffering of our Savior. Said he made — "Fess my brederin, day drove a ten penny nail troo his hands and feet — just as true as you are born!" They probably understood the truth presented in this way better than if it had been presented in a more polished manner.

Please write often. Much love to Frances and all friends. I received a letter from Mrs. Reams (Cousin Nell) and she wants to know why you and Frances don't write. I wrote as soon as I received your letter announcing her marriage.

A letter of ten pages. Beat it if you can.

Your affectionate Son,

Alex F. Hubbell.
movements.notes: **10-PAGE LETTER — ONLY 2 PAGES SURVIVE.** **BASEBALL REFERENCE** — "Union Base" game; two regts challenged 60th NY, "our regiment beat them badly." Grand dance on company street — fiddle. Culver Bostwick not yet appeared. Reinforcing Lee prevented — "harass the enemy." April 8th P.S. — horse race, sack race, wheelbarrow race, foot race, cook fight, greased pole. **GREASED PIG.** Shell barrow races — sack over heads. Contrabands run after greased pig. **CONTRABAND PREACHER** — "Fess my brederin, day drove a ten penny nail troo his hands and feet — just as true as you are born!" Magazine received — "Prospects of S.P. Hubbell." Mrs. Reams (Cousin Nell) letter — announcing marriage.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from Department of the Gulf headquarters in New Orleans, copying down the official word on "terrible fighting in Western Louisiana" — a victory "so bloody that we were not able to take advantage of it." The 153d was in it; he doesn't yet know its losses. Then a clerk's drunken death: a head-first pitch over a third-story banister onto the stone pavement. "He never saved nor groaned."
movements.transcription:
April 15, 1864
Head Quarters
Department of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Mother:

Have rec'd no letter yet, but expect one on the steamer due today. I don't know what to think of your long silence. Am afraid sometimes that you are sick, but hope that is not the reason. One week since I saw Sergt. Peltier of our Co. He was home on furlough when the Regt. left the North, and was on the way to join it when I saw him. He said if there were any letters for me with the Regt. he would send them on.

There has been some terrible fighting in Western Louisiana. It is called a victory for us but so bloody that we were not able to take advantage of it. There was a heavy loss on both sides. The 153d was in it, but I haven't heard anything about its loss.

A terrible accident happened here by which one of the clerks lost his life and liquor was the cause of it. He was drunk in the evening, and about twelve o'clock at night after he had spread his mattress on the floor of the office ready to go to bed, he went out on the gallery on the third story in the rear of the building, and accidentally pitched head first over the banister striking the stone pavement in the yard on his head. He never saved nor groaned. One of the clerks in a room close by heard him come staggering along and the next minute heard him fall.

The ladies here, with Mrs. Banks as president, have held a tableaux, etc. for the benefit of the soldiers. The Sanitary Commission receive the funds. The clerks here expect to get commutation of rations and quarters about the 1st of June. If we get it our wages will amount to about sixty dollars a month, everything included. We can then board where we please.

When you write please tell all the news and write long letters. I have not heard from home since the early part of February. Am very anxious to hear how you all get on. I don't know whether I am to stay here or not; have not done much yet. You had better not say much about my being here yet. Penmanship is the only trouble. I have not written Alex yet and I don't know whether James is in the army or not so I can't write him. I had rather not write Alex till I hear from him or home. Please tell the boys to write. I hope Frances has not forgotten me, but will write soon, though I think she is like me — doesn't forget if she doesn't write.

Hoping that you all are well and enjoying life I will close.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Saw Sergt. Heavy loss on both sides. 153rd was in it. **CLERK KILLED BY FALL** — drunk, spread mattress on office floor, went onto gallery on 3rd story, pitched head first over banister striking stone pavement in yard. "He never saved nor groaned." Sanitary Commission tableau — Mrs. Banks as president. Clerks expect commutation of rations — $60/month including everything. Not heard from home since early February. Penmanship only trouble — "I had rather not write than till I hear from him or home."

movements.sigSummary: From his camp at Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander weighs his youngest brother's prospects with a veteran's eye: he doubts the cavalry story and a commission from Gov. Seymour, but is sure James "will surely rise in the service — I do not mean to stripes but straps." He watches Gen. Thomas, "a tremendous large man" with a snow-white beard, review the troops, then pities six Indiana regiments straggling in "poor and haggard." "Few men at the north have any idea of what a soldier has to endure."
movements.transcription:
April 18th, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

I rec'd. your letter of the 4th inst. last evening. I was amazed and vexed at your notion (Bonnett call it anything else) of James. He could not have enlisted, been sent to his reg't., drawn his arms, and been mounted in time to have participated in Kilpatrick's raid, and furthermore I very much doubt his enlisting in the cavalry. I think James is keen enough to look out for himself and do well. As soon as he gets settled he will doubtless write you. I think his chances of getting a commission of Gov. Seymour are rather slim. A person to get a commission has to be very strongly recommended by his commanding officers. He has doubtless enlisted and as soon as he reaches his regt. and corps, he will probably write. If James minds his P's and Q's he will surely rise in the service. I do not mean to stripes but straps. He would be a favorite with the men wherever he might be. You know he used to treat us well when we were little shavers. I hope James will go into the service with spunk to do well, and I believe he will. There are not many much better masters in these days than Uncle Sam. He is sure pay and cash at that.

Am very, very much obliged to you for ordering those boots for me. They will be a great comfort to me. I trust we shall be paid soon. I shall be able, I think, to send home ninety dollars. I shall keep but little with me and if I should be in very great need of more I can send for it. I want to see that five hundred dollars all straight and you paid up. If I should ever come home again I should like at least a thousand dollars to start on.

Now, Mother, I do not want you to be afraid to use my money. My greatest happiness is in seeing you comfortable. How does Frances flourish and is she preceptress of Champlain Academy? When I was home Mr. Bass very pompously told the boys that in Illinois they had strawberries in the middle of April. It is now the middle of April and I have as yet seen no strawberries and I do not think I am likely to in some time, though vegetation is quite forward here — the woods and fields are beginning to look quite green.

I am glad that Mrs. B. is going to live with you in the old Stone Castle. You will not be so entirely alone. You will not have to wait for Frances to come home to disclose your "solemn conclusions" of which you generally have no lack. What have been the "conclusions" since the one of Kilpatrick's raid — or haven't you paper enough to write them? Shall have to employ Frances to record the most important of them for they amuse me vastly.

Gen. Thomas and Hooker were around visiting the troops yesterday. Gen. Thomas is a tremendous large man — very much such a built man as Mr. Burroughs. A good part of his beard is snow white. Gen. Hooker is as fine a looking officer as you could wish to see.

Ball is still the great game. The 78th N.Y. Vet. Vol. have challenged our regt. to a game of ball today and are now playing it out over at the 78th camping ground. We sometimes have grand dances in the company street. I participated in one the other night and had a gay time. As we have no ladies here some of the boys have to act instead. They are distinguished from the gents by having their caps off.

Six new regts. from Indiana passed by here this morning. They had marched from Nashville and looked as if they had passed through a campaign — being poor and haggard — worn out, I might say. They left large numbers on the way unable to march. They will get used to marching after a while. I pitied the poor fellows. Few men at the north have any idea of what a soldier has to endure.

I have no postage stamps and do not know what I shall do to send off this letter. Please send me some as soon as possible and please send some two cent stamps as I should like to send a paper to some of my friends occasionally. Tell Frances if she don't write pretty soon I shall pull her ears. If you have my furlough please send it on. If Marshall Dunn has it it will be sent on soon as the Orderly has written him to send all the furloughs he has immediately. Perhaps Mr. Averill has it. If he has tell him to get it and send it to me! Why doesn't he get my county bounty? I believe they are paying it in county bonds. Please write soon. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

April 19th — I commenced writing this letter some days since but have just been able to borrow a stamp to send it off. I now owe several stamps. I hope you will send me some soon. There is nothing of interest here to write. Everything is going on here about as usual.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes Mother from Stevenson, Alabama, the day his unit is "at length fully organized" into the 20th Army Corps, Army of the Cumberland — and recites the order of battle by heart so she can "give an intelligent answer to any one who may inquire about the Corps." Then the guard drops: though he has tried to call McClellan's removal a good move, "I cannot do it. My heart still yearns toward the man." A soldier confessing the general he still loves.
movements.transcription:
April 22, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

We are at length fully organized and now form the 20th Army Corps, Army of the Cumberland. Direct your letters to 3d Brigade, 2nd Div., 20th Army Corps, Army of the Cumberland.

The third Brigade is composed of seven regt's., the 60th, the 78th, the 102d N.Y. Vets. and the 29th and 111th Penn. Vets. and the 137th and 149th N.Y. Volunteers.

The Corps is divided into four Divisions. We have the same Div. commander as formerly — Gen. John M. Geary. Now, Mother, please to remember what I have told you. It may save you a great deal of needless anxiety and another thing, I want you to be able to give an intelligent answer to any one who may inquire about the Corps. Gen. Hooker commands the Corps. There is a rumor current here that McClellan is about to take command of the Army of the Potomac. I hope it is true. I have tried hard to forget McClellan and think his removal a good move on the part of the Administration, but I cannot do it. My heart still yearns toward the man. I have never had, and am afraid never can have, the confidence in any military officer that I had in him. I do hope he will again take command of the Potomac Army.

I rec'd your letter of the 7th inst. a few days since and am wonderfully pleased about the boots. I went down to the express office this morning to see if they had come. They had not but will probably be here in a few days. Tattoo is now beating so I shall have to stop for tonight.

Apr. 23rd — I rec'd a N.Y. Tribune this morning mailed Apr. 18th. I have rec'd both letters of Charles that you sent, also Aunt Laura's. There is very little of interest to write. I will write again soon. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. I have rec'd eight postage stamps. Why doesn't Charley write me? I have not rec'd a letter from him since I have been in this department — some seven months. I have written him twice since I have been in this place.
movements.notes: **20TH ARMY CORPS FULLY ORGANIZED.** Direct letters to 3d Brigade, 2nd Div., 20th Army Corps, Army of the Cumberland. 3rd Brigade: 60th, 78th, 102d NY Vets, 29th and 111th Penn. Vets, 137th and 149th NY Volunteers. Corps divided into 4 divisions — same Div. commander, Gen. John M. Geary. **RUMOR: McCLELLAN TO COMMAND ARMY OF THE POTOMAC.** "I have tried hard to forget McClellan... My heart still yearns toward the man. I have never had, and am afraid never can have, the confidence in any military officer that I had in him." Gen. Hooker commands Corps. Wonderfully pleased about boots. Rec'd Aunt Laura's letter, Charles's letters.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from New Orleans, relieved by Special Order on April 21st and ordered back to his regiment massed on the Red River, where "another fight" is expected soon. He'll carry the mail to Gen. Banks's headquarters by boat — "a long ride up the Red River which is better than footing it the way the army did." Between reassurances about his brothers, he turns tourist: wooden cisterns tall as houses, sidewalks called banquettes, mule-drawn streetcars run on the honor system.
movements.transcription:
Apr. 23, 1864
Dept. of the Gulf
N. Orleans, La.

Dear Mother:

I was relieved of duty here by Special Order April 21st and ordered to rejoin my Regt at once, but am still here waiting for the boat. I expect to carry the mail to Gen. Banks Hd. Qtrs. in the field, on my way back and if I do will have a state room and subsistence on the boat. "Will have a long ride up the Red River which is better than footing it the way the army did." The army is amassed on the Red River so I will not have far to march to get to the regt. What stuff the Regt. could not carry is left in the city in storehouses. I put my overcoat and dress coat in a box and have put them with the regt's. baggage in this city. Shall carry a knapsack, rubber and woolen blankets, and change of underclothes, also half a shelter tent.

Rec'd. a letter from Alex dated Apr. 10th, Stevenson, Ala. He was well and glad they were doing picket and guard duty there, but were under marching orders. Said that he had rec'd a letter from you saying that I was at these Hd. Qtrs. The army on the Red River expects to have another fight very soon. It is receiving reinforcements.

There is one consolation about my being relieved, which is that I am not the only one that has been relieved. Two men were relieved before I came here. They were both from one regt. but neither of them suited. The man clerk that has just come out cannot write very well. He is not set to work yet but was told to practice writing till he could write better. Should not wonder if he was relieved. I have received $11.60 extra pay for March, but will not receive any for this month. The A.A. General here is very particular about penmanship. You see I have seasoned a long march as far and a fight, so that so much good has been done me by being here. I am in good spirits about going back as I have been expecting to be relieved. Have done nothing lately, but when I first came did a little work.

I was rejoiced to receive your letter of April 8th; was beginning to think something was the matter. Was sorry to learn that you did not know where James was. He does very wrong not to let you know where he is.

Apr. 24th — I leave here today or tomorrow for the regt. Have rec'd. but two letters since I came here, one from you, the other from Alex. Expect to find several when I arrive at the regt. Will write you soon after I get there if I have an opportunity. Where did you get the copies and why did you send that signature? Also say Frances is preceptress of the Academy. She is rising in the world, but I am afraid it is too hard work for her. There is no necessity for her teaching all the time.

There are a great many French here, also many negroes that speak French. In the Constitutional Convention now in session here there is a great deal of debate about publishing the laws in one or two languages. But I think they will decide for the English language only. Some things here are strange to us, for instance, cisterns are made out of wood and are all above ground and stand nearly as high as some houses, so you see they are very prominent. Sidewalks are called banquettes. Street cars are drawn by mules, and there is no conductor, trusting to the honesty of the passengers to put their fare in the box. Some cars have two stories, that is, people ride on top of the car. Cemeteries are different here; most of the people are buried above ground, either in tombs, or in a wall that has holes in it that look like ovens. There are some very fine residences in the suburbs of the city. Trees are trimmed off in different shapes and look very well. A park in this city has a great many beautiful flowers in bloom and it is a pleasant place to take a stroll. The Island of Tortugas on the coast of Florida is a great prison for soldiers. A large fort is being built there and the soldiers condemned to hard labor work on the fort. A good many soldiers in this city are sentenced to the Dry Tortugas, as it is called.

The chief clerk at these Hd. Qtrs. received $4 a day, another clerk that interprets French and German receives $100 a month, the rest receive the same pay — 40¢ a day extra pay. I hope that you will write often and that when James writes you will let me know. I should not be surprised if a long time elapsed before you heard from him as he may be ambitious of making a mark before writing. How do Sid's wife and mother get along? Give my regards to Silas and Sid, also to David Savage. I hope that you will not worry about James or the rest of us, for it does no good and I think we will all get along well enough. Hoping that you are all well, I will close.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: From New Orleans, Charles writes his brother Alex of a clerk who came in drunk at midnight, pitched headlong over a third-story gallery rail to the stone pavement below, and never moved — buried beside a wagon of eight bodies, a clerk's prayer standing in for the absent chaplain, the volleys fired, "and we got into the street car and came home." Relieved of headquarters duty for poor penmanship, he's bound up the Red River to rejoin Banks's army.
movements.transcription:
April 25, 1864
Hd. Qtrs. Dept of the Gulf
New Orleans, La.

Dear Alex:

I rec'd your letter of Apr. 10th yesterday and was very glad to hear from you. Have been waiting to hear from you before I wrote, so that I could have your direction. It is a very long direction. Would you not get your letters as quickly if it was shortened?

I am relieved from duty at these Hd. Qtrs, and ordered to rejoin my regt., but have been waiting the last two or three days for the boat. Will probably go off tomorrow. I am to carry the mail on my way back to Gen. Banks Hd. Qtrs. in the field, as by so doing I will receive subsistence on the boat and a state room. This is better than carrying my rations with me and sleeping anywhere. I will have a long ride up the R. River, which is better than footing it as the army have done. Do you see my being here has done me so much good. There has been a great fight near R. River in which we lost a great many men and I am not sorry I was not in that fight. Another battle is expected soon. The army is amassed on R. River at Grand Encore so then I will ride all the way. My penmanship is not good enough is the reason of my going back to the regt. But I feel well enough about going back as others have failed to suit as well as me. Just before I came two men were relieved and now another new clerk that has come, I think, will be relieved as he does not write very well and he has not been set to work.

A clerk here was killed a short time since. He came in drunk one night about 12 o'clock and after spreading his mattress on the floor of the office where he slept, went out on the gallery on the third story, and as he was about todescend a few steps that led to a lower part of the gallery he pitched headlong over the bannister and struck the stone pavement on his head in the yard below. He never moved. A lot of us soon gathered around to see him. He was in his drawers and shirt as he was just going to bed. All the clerks attended at his burial. He was buried by the hospitals. A wagon from the hospital containing eight bodies followed by another wagon containing a corporal and eight men drove into the cemetery. As the chaplain could not be there that day one of the clerks made a prayer, the volleys were soon fired, and we got into the street car and came home.

I am sorry that James does not let us know where he is. Hope he will come out all right. How do you prosper? Are you in good health? Hope you will try and take good care of yourself. Give my regards to Luther. Have you got your watch yet and does it keep good time? I have rec'd but two letters, yours and Mothers, since I left Washington. Expect to find several with the regt.

The street cars here are drawn by one mule and some of them have two stories, that is, people ride on top of the cars and in it. The honesty of the passengers is trusted to put the fare in the box, as there is no conductor.

The Army on the R. River under Gen. Banks expects to soon drive the rebs out of Louisiana and I think will do it. I will be there to help, if not sick. Did you ever hear anything about the dry Tortugas? It is a small island on the coast of Florida where Uncle Sam is building an immense fort. A great many soldiers are sentenced to hard labor on this island for various crimes. A good many are sent from this city, for five or ten years.

I hope you will prove a better correspondent than you have been so far. Do try and write often and I will answer them. Will close by wishing you good luck.

From your aff. brother,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Relieved from HQ — waiting for boat. Carrying mail to Banks Hd. Qtrs. in field on Red River. Will ride all the way. Penmanship not good enough. **CLERK KILLED — EXPANDED ACCOUNT.** Drunk, 3rd story gallery, pitched over banister, head on stone pavement. "He never moved." Lot of us gathered around, in drawers and shirts. Buried by the hospitals — 8 bodies from hospital in wagon, corporal and 8 men drove into cemetery. Chaplain couldn't be there — one of the clerks made a prayer, volleys fired, got into street car and came home. **GREAT FIGHT NEAR R. RIVER** — lost great many men. Another battle expected soon. Army amassed on Red River at Grand Encore (Ecore). Dry Tortugas — fort, hard labor, 5-10 years. Street cars by mule, no conductor. Have you heard from James?

movements.sigSummary: The Atlanta Campaign opens with a soldier's quiet goodbye. Bound for the front from Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander tells Mother battles are coming within weeks that may "throw completely in the shade" Antietam and Gettysburg: "It is the death struggle of this mighty rebellion." He braces her for the worst, then softens it with talk of letters owed and boots not yet arrived, asking only that she not worry — and sending love, particularly to Frances.
movements.transcription:
Apr. 28, 1864
Stevenson, Ala.

Dear Mother:

We leave here in a day or two — perhaps tomorrow — for the front. The eastern troops in this Department have too good a name for bold unflinching bravery to allow them to lie still while the rest of the Army is fighting. Battles will probably be fought in a few weeks that will not be a whit behind, and perhaps throw completely in the shade the battles of Antietam and Gettysburg. May God be with us and grant victory to our arms. I hope the people at the North will keep a stout heart. The soldiers in the field will do their best to be equal to the emergency. It is the death struggle of this mighty rebellion. I hope, dear Mother, that you will not worry yourself about me. Our Father in Heaven is watching over us all and nothing will happen to us but what is for the best. I hope I shall come safely out of the struggle — if not, I trust that we shall all meet in the better world.

I rec'd your letter of the 18th inst. day before yesterday and should have answered it immediately but several little matters interspersed and prevented my answering until now. Hope you will pardon the delay. I think if you will examine the letters I have written since I have been here you will find that instead of my being in debt it is a little the other way, see but then I shouldn't care to answer to it. I shall write you as often as possible. I have not as yet rec'd. the boots, but expect they will be along in the course of time. I hope I shall get them before we march. If we do not move soon I will endeavor to write you another letter from Stevenson. Love to all, particularly to Frances.

Your aff. son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. Have you heard from James? If not, I do not think you need have cause to worry for he probably is waiting until he gets himself well going so that he will be able to mollify in a measure your regret at his failure. I am glad to hear you think Charles will remain at Hd. Qtrs. I hope he will write me soon. I am a little vexed at him. I have not heard from him for seven or eight months. I have written him twice since I have been here. Enclosed I send a slip from a Louisville paper that you may know our Div. and Div. Commander are up noticed out here. You see that it means we shall be in our share to do. Bridgeport is nine miles from here and is the headquarters of the Div.

movements.letterExcerpt: I arrived here yesterday and am now back with the regt. Went on board of a steamer, Monday, April 25th at N. Orleans, but after staying some time on her she was ordered not to leave so I went on board...
movements.sigSummary: On the Red River above Alexandria, the clerk-turned-soldier finally fired his gun in anger—from behind a breastwork of hardtack boxes—as guerrillas raked the steamer with musketry and a rebel cannon was dismantled by the gunboat. One man was shot dead on board, another wounded, with bullets striking near where Charles crouched. Most haunting: three soldiers who chased cattle ashore never returned. "The boat whistled and waited," but they were gone, supposed shot or taken by guerrillas.
movements.transcription:
May 3rd, 1864
Alexandria, La.

Dear Mother:

I arrived here yesterday and am now back with the regt. Went on board of a steamer, Monday, April 25th at N. Orleans, but after staying some time on her she was ordered not to leave so I went on board of another steamer which left Wednesday afternoon. I carried despatches for Gen. Banks. I occupied a state room with two mail carriers, and we ate at the table with those that paid for a meal. The soldiers on the boat drew their rations and cooked them themselves. The living at the table was nothing extra. We stopped at Port Hudson a short time. The boat was a slow one and it was on the 4th day after we left N. Orleans that we arrived at this place. We ought to have gotten here in two or three days. There were two or three hundred soldiers on board all armed to be prepared for the guerrillas. Only a short time before a steamer on the Mississippi was fired into and two men were killed and 11 wounded. After getting into Red River we were told to report to the gunboat at the mouth of Black River and if necessary a convoy would go with us. On arriving at the mouth of Black River we were told to wait for a convoy which we did one day and night and then as no gunboat was ready to go with us we started without any. There was a great difference in the color of the Red & Black rivers where the Black flows into the Red. The water of the Red is reddish as if mixed with red clay. We passed by some cattle on the shore when the Lieut. Col. commanding ordered the boat to be run ashore and a beef to be shot and dragged on board. One beef was shot and dragged on board with a rope. But three soldiers that went into the woods chasing the cattle after another beef did not come back. The boat whistled and waited for them, but as they did not come back we finally came off without them. It is supposed they were shot or taken prisoners by the guerrillas. This was on the bank of the Red River.

We passed the night at Fort DeRussy and the next morning in convoy with a transport that had three cannon and with a gunboat in the rear we started for this place. When about thirty-five miles from here we had a fight. There was one man shot dead and one wounded on our boat. The rebs had one cannon and the gunboat soon dismantled it. The guerrillas kept up a musketry fire on us some time. As I had my gun I fired it into the woods but did not see any rebs except one who came out of the woods and fired at the gunboat. He had a breastwork on the boat made of boxes of hardtack. As the banks of the river here high we could not see much but those on the hurricane deck had a good view of the rebs. It was there the men were shot on our boat. Two or three bullets came near where I was.

I found four letters for me with the Regt., one from Alex. Alex Douglass sent three to N. Orleans, but as he directed them to the "Provost Marshall" of course I did not receive them. Our Captain thought I was there, and as I did not write to the regt. it was partly on one fault. The regt. look thin in flesh. A. Douglass is not very well. I never saw so much dust as there is here. Then I arrived the regt. were out on a foraging expedition and I never saw such looking men. They were covered with dust half an inch thick when they came in.

I write this sitting on the ground so you must excuse the penmanship. Please write soon. I wish you would send me a newspaper more in a while as there is nothing to read here. Direct your letters to N. Orleans, La., Co. and Regt., of course. The reason why I did not receive the letters you directed to Hd. Qtrs. was because the Co. and Regt. were on the letters.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **ARRIVED AT ALEXANDRIA, LA. — BACK WITH REGIMENT.** Boarded steamer April 25 in N.O. Carried despatches for Gen. Banks. State room with two mail carriers. Soldiers on boat drew rations and cooked themselves. Stopped at Port Hudson — slow boat. **GUERRILLAS FIRED ON STEAMER.** One beef was shot and dragged on board — three soldiers chased cattle into woods, didn't come back. "It is supposed they were shot or taken prisoners by the guerrillas." Passed Fort DeRussy. Next morning — transport with cannon, gunboat in rear. **FIGHT 35 MILES FROM ALEXANDRIA** — one man shot dead, one wounded on boat. Rebs had one cannon — gunboat soon dismantled it. "As I had my gun I fired it into the woods." Three bullets came near where he was. Found 4 letters at regt. Alex Douglass sent 3 to N.O. — didn't receive. Regt. came out on foraging expedition — "never saw such looking men." Dust half inch thick. Writing on ground — "you must excuse the penmanship."

movements.sigSummary: Alexander's first letter from Georgia opens the Atlanta Campaign — "We are close upon the enemy. Our advance came upon them this morning but they fell back." Writing from "Camp somewhere in the State of Georgia," he reckons 35,000 to 40,000 men under Hooker, his regiment on the army's extreme right. The boots his mother sent were too small for his "used up feet," so he sold them and drew government bootees. He signs off as the mail leaves: "Keep a stout heart."
movements.transcription:
May 6, 1864
Camp somewhere in the
State of Georgia

Dear Mother:

I now hasten to write you a few lines to let you know of my welfare. This is my first opportunity of writing you since I left Stevenson. We have been marching hard — very hard for the last few days.

I rec'd the boots when I reached Bridgeport, Ala. I was very much pleased with them, but most unfortunately they proved a little too small for me (as my used up feet will testify) and I have sold them to yours Lafountain from Champlain for $6.50. I have now an excellent pair of Govt. bootees and I find them much better for marching than boots.

The sugar was most excellent and you can well imagine how much I enjoyed it. I am very much obliged to you for sending it. The stripes are very nice indeed.

We are close upon the enemy. Our advance came upon them this morning but they fell back. I hardly think they are in much force. We have between thirty-five and forty thousand men here under Hooker. We are I believe on the extreme right of the army.

I will write you as often as possible. Culver Bostwick is here. He reached the regt. yesterday morning and he wishes me to tell his friends that he would write with me but that he has drawn a new gun and is too busy cleaning it. The mail is going out in a moment and I must close.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Keep a stout heart.
movements.notes: **ATLANTA CAMPAIGN BEGINS.** "Camp somewhere in the State of Georgia." First opportunity to write since leaving Stevenson. Marching hard — "very hard for the last few days." Boots too small — sold to Lafountain for $6.50, now has excellent pair of Govt. bootees. Sugar was excellent. Stripes very nice. **CLOSE UPON THE ENEMY.** Advance came upon them this morning but they fell back. 35,000-40,000 men under Hooker — extreme right of the army. **CULVER BOSTWICK IS HERE** — reached regt. yesterday, drawn new gun, too busy cleaning it. "Keep a stout heart."

movements.sigSummary: Three Hubbell brothers are in combat at once, and Alexander — writing from Camp near Altoona Creek, Georgia, as the mail leaves "in a few minutes" — knows only that James faced "terrible fighting in Va." and prays he and Charley are safe. He reports himself well and just two men of Co. H injured, then asks his mother to find him on the map in Cobb Co. and send stamps. "If there is any one that needs God's help," he writes, "it must be a soldier."
movements.transcription:
May 8th, 1864
Camp near Altoona Creek, Ga.

Dear Mother:

The mail leaves in a few minutes, and I must hasten and have my say for I know you are anxious to hear from your boys in these perilous times. Well, I am happy to say that I am still all right and trust that I shall come out of this campaign so. Culver Bostwick is also well and sends much love to his friends. He has had a chance to try his sharpshooting qualities upon the rebs but with what success I am unable to say — though I expect he made them think a little at least. Of the movements of the army I am unable to inform you. They are so continued I cannot make heads or tails of them. I have rec'd no word from home since I left Bridgeport, Ala., and I feel, oh, so anxious about you all. How you heard from James and was he in that terrible fighting in Va.? I hope and pray he is all right, and Charley. How is he? I see Gen. Banks has moved forward. It is a great comfort to me, Mother, to know that there is One above who knows all things and does all things for the best. It is such a relief to have One to whom we can go and confide all our griefs and trials.

If there is any one that needs God's help I am sure it must be a soldier. I put you all in His hands daily and feel comforted. Give my regards to all friends. With God's help we hope to crush this rebellion this summer. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Luther is well. We have only two men of Co. H injured. Please send me some stamps. I borrowed one of Luther to send this letter. Write often and send the Tribune as often as possible. I believe we are in Cobb Co., Ga, so that if you look us in the map you may know where to find us.
