movements.sigSummary: Buzzard's Roost was a high rocky ridge reachable only through a narrow gap, and Alexander's 3rd Brigade missed Sunday's fight, drawn off to support a cavalry reconnaissance. He describes rebels behind rocks and ledges firing "such a withering fire" that the 1st and 2nd Brigades could only hold long enough to remove their wounded — leaving the dead — then fall back, attacks he judged feints. Reading that the Army of the Potomac had driven the rebs ten miles, Sherman told the troops "let us do likewise."
movements.transcription:
May 10th, 1864
Camp near Buzzard's Roost, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you a few days since but will not write you again that you may not be over anxious about me in these perilous times. The 1st & 2nd brigades of our Div. were engaged with the enemy at this place Sunday. We should have been in but early that morning we (3rd Brig.) were sent out as a support to a Div. of Cavalry on a reconnaissance and did not rejoin our Div. until late in the evening. The firing had just ceased when we came up. Buzzard's Roost is a high rocky ridge and where we are is only accessible by a narrow gap through the high rocky ledge with which its sides are covered. Our men drove the rebels nearly to the crest of the hill when they came upon them in great force posted behind rocks and trees and in the ledges from which they fired upon our men such a withering fire that they were obliged to halt, but managed to hold their ground until all our wounded were removed and, I believe, left the dead, when they fell back to their original position. The Third Div. of our Corps made a similar attempt lower down with like effect. I think both the attacks were but feints to attract the attention of the enemy from other portions of the army. A large force of our army is now in rear of the enemy. I think the Johnnies will have to "up and git" before a great while. Quite a heavy cannonade has been going on this afternoon on the left of our line. We were working all last night building breastworks, as it was feared the enemy might make a break this way and thus get between the two main portions of our army. I think you will hear glorious news from this army before a great while — even before this letter reaches you.

A dispatch was read to the troops today stating that the Army of the Potomac had thrashed the rebs and driven them ten miles and Gen. Sherman added "let us do likewise." I vote and trust we shall drive them ten times ten miles.

Do not be over anxious about me, dear Mother. I am in God's hands. I hope I shall come out of these battles all right. All the boys from our way are well. Culver Bostwick stands the marches like a little hero. The first day he joined us we marched twenty odd miles. It was a pretty good beginning, I thought. Those new boots used up my feet so that I was obliged to march two days in rear of the column and one day was carried in an ambulance. I am happy to say that I am all right now. Our men are busy today strengthening the breastworks. The rebs would find it hard if they attacked us here. We are somewhat isolated from the rest of the army and this is a very important position. That is the reason of our strengthening it so. I will write you all the news as soon as I can find out anything definite.

Please write often. Give my regards to Grandmother and Silas and all friends. Tell Miss Fannie I am patiently awaiting a letter from her. I will write her as soon as I can find opportunity. The cannonade is quite brisk on the left. I expect they are having a big fight. God grant that we have the victory. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Have you heard from James and is Charley still at New Orleans? I have two postage stamps left.
movements.notes: **BATTLE OF BUZZARD'S ROOST (MILL CREEK GAP / ROCKY FACE RIDGE).** 1st & 2nd Brigades engaged at this place Sunday. 3rd Brigade (60th NY) sent out as support to Div. of Cavalry on reconnaissance — did not join Div., firing just ceased when they came up. Buzzard's Roost — "high rocky ridge... accessible by a narrow gap through the high rocky ledge with which its sides are covered." Rebs drove rebels to crest of hill — "they came upon them in great force posted behind rocks and trees and in the ledges from which they fired upon our men such a withering fire that they were obliged to halt, but managed to hold their ground until all our wounded were removed." Believe left dead — "fell back to original position." 3rd Div. of Corps made similar attempt with like effect — "both attacks were but feints to attract the attention of the enemy from other portions of the army." Large force in rear of enemy. "I think the Johnnies will have to 'up and git.'" Heavy cannonade on left this afternoon. Working all last night building breastworks — "the enemy might make a break this way." Dispatch from Army of the Potomac — "had thrashed the rebs and driven them ten miles." Sherman added "let us do likewise."

movements.sigSummary: At Resaca on Sunday the 15th, the troops went in "in a way that I never saw before being formed in solid column," under heavy fire from eleven A.M. until long after dark. Alexander writes his mother that he came through unscathed — and that owing to the ground, a succession of ridges, "not a man of Co. H was hurt." He would rather tell her in person, which he trusts will not be long. The enemy is defeated; they are in close pursuit.
movements.transcription:
May 17th, 1864
Camp South of the Oostanaula River
Georgia

Dear Mother:

I thank God that I am able to inform you that I came out of the battle on Sunday the 15th inst. unscathed. The enemy has been defeated and we are now in close pursuit. The loss of our army is comparatively small, I think. The troops in this fight went in in a way that I never saw before being formed in solid column. We were under a heavy fire from eleven A.M. Sunday, until long after dark, but owing to the nature of the ground (being a succession of ridges) our loss was very slight. I am happy to inform you that not a man of Co. H was hurt. I dislike very much spinning yarns on paper and will wait until I see you, which I trust will not be very long, to tell you all about the fight.

I made a mistake in my last letter in stating that it was Buzzard's Roost that the 2nd Div. attempted to storm. The Ridge is called, I believe, Mills Ridge. Love to all. Please write often. We shall have to march some.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **CAME OUT OF BATTLE SUNDAY THE 15TH UNSCATHED.** "I thank God that I am able to inform you that I came out of the battle on Sunday the 15th inst. unscathed." Enemy defeated — now in close pursuit. Loss of army comparatively small. "The troops in this fight went in in a way that I never saw before being formed in solid column." **HEAVY FIRE FROM 11 A.M. TO LONG AFTER DARK.** Due to nature of ground (succession of ridges) loss very slight. "Not a man of Co. H was hurt." Dislikes "much spinning yarns on paper" — will wait to tell in person. **CORRECTION:** Last letter said Buzzard's Roost — should be Mills Ridge (the Ridge is called Mills Ridge). movements.sigSummary: Mr. Bass has been shot in Champlain, "probably fatally" — Alexander reads it in a paper while resting in Camp near Kingston, Georgia, pursuing Johnson's army. "I think Dodds must have been deranged. Who will now teach the old Academy?" The war at home collides with his own: a brutal comrade picks up a severed rebel leg and shakes it in their faces, and Alexander wants to knock him down with his gun butt. The eastern men, he notes, are learning to respect the Star Corps.
movements.transcription:
May 20th, 1864
Camp near Kingston, Ga.

Dear Fannie:

"At length," I can hear you say, "at length he has found time to write me a letter. Right then, indeed he should, I should think. Not a word has he written since he left on furlough." Now, Miss Fannie, haven't I nursed a right? I will plead guilty to all charges and beg ten thousand pardons, but cannot under existing conditions promise to do any better in future, but will promise to do my best. Now won't you accept my poor apologies and write me a good long letter? You see your silence has brought me to terms.

We are, I suppose you are aware, in close pursuit of Johnson's army. Our advance has had several little brush brushes with the enemy's rear since we started. Yesterday the rebs made a stand where I am now writing. We moved upon them about three P.M. in line of battle, but when we reached here the enemy were found wanting, having again fallen back. Their only object was, I suppose, to check our advance as long as possible. We are resting today awaiting the construction of a bridge which the rebs burned yesterday. You can have little idea how grateful this little rest is to us after being so constantly on the move for the last three weeks. We came late and rise while the stars are shining and march all day under a scorching sun with a load you would think would kill a mule. But then we do not always have such rough times. T

The name of the late battle which we fought, our loss, the loss of the enemy, and all the little particulars I am entirely ignorant of having seen no paper of a date later than the battle. Rumors are in abundance but I have learned not to put much confidence in them. Of the battle all I know is what transpired immediately around me and that is a very small part of a battle. The line of battle was very long and I am thinking it will be a hard thing to settle upon a name for it. The "eastern men are learning to respect the Star Corps (20th)."

I was astonished — shocked yesterday to read in a paper Mr. Hoyle sent that Mr. Bass was shot and probably fatally. Now sad! I think Dodds must have been deranged. Who will now teach the old Academy? Nor Mrs. Bass! His wound I have but little doubt is fatal. I have known men shot through the right lung to liver, but do not recollect of one surviving shot through the left lung. Mr. Bass will have one advantage that we poor fellows do not have out here — that is good nursing and the best medical treatment. One of our men the other day, a brutal fellow, when we were casting over the battle field picked up a rebel leg and foot and shook it in our faces with some disgusting remark. I wanted to knock the fellow down with the butt of my gun.

My paper says halt. I send this letter with my last stamp. The 153rd has been engaged, I see. Charley, I believe, was not there. I rec'd a letter from him a few days since. He was then awaiting the boat to join his regt. Tell Mother to keep a stout heart. All our lives are in God's hands. Love to all.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander

P.S.— Bostwick is a bully soldier. Takes a battle very philosophically and stands the marches first rate. He is a great comfort to me. We mess together. He was somewhat astonished at the mode of proceeding in the late battle. Said he thought they came out in an open field and fought it out. The late battle ground was a perfect wilderness.

movements.letterExcerpt: Camp on the Bank of the Miss. River
movements.sigSummary: James Hubbell walked into Charles's tent on May 23rd, 1864 — the surprise of a younger brother arrived by transport from New Orleans to enlist in his very regiment, where the two will now tent and draw rations together. Charles describes the brutal march from Red River, half a day in line of battle as cavalry skirmished ahead, and a Colonel's news that Richmond had fallen, met with lusty cheering. Along the road he passed Mother's own letters, captured by the rebels and scattered in the mud.
movements.transcription:
May 23rd, 1864
Camp on the Bank of the Miss. River

Dear Mother:

I was much surprised yesterday to see James walking into my tent. He came up from N. Orleans on a transport. He has been in the Camp of Distribution about a week. He enlisted in N.Y. for this regt. It will be pleasant for us both to be in the same regt., together. We will tent and draw rations together and can see each other.

I rejoined the army May 2d and it was March 3d when I left it. By being absent I was saved a long March which I think I could never have stood. We left Alexandria, La., on the march from Red River May 13th and I can tell you I missed this marching more than once. This being obliged to march when you are so tired that you can scarcely move your legs does not suit me. There was no chance to ride because the ambulances were full of sick and one of them were mounted on brokendown skeleton horses. I kept up all the way here till within two miles of this place when I fell out and took my own time. I reached camp about half and hour after the regt. We have rested two or three days since we started. On the way here for half a day we marched in line of battle to meet the rebs, the cavalry skirmishing with them in the front. We halted for a short time while the heavy cannonade was going on and expected every minute to be in a fight, but the rebs skedaddled and we came on. They say we are to take transports on the river to move from here. I hope this is true for I have marched enough for the present. I have rec'd two newspapers lately from Cousin Mary. Alex Douglass is commissary sergt. and received $21 a month. He issues the rations to each company. On our way here we passed parts of our letters that were in the mail that the rebs captured. Your letters were scattered all around. When I rejoined the regt. I wrote you. Did you receive the letter?

James has not shaved since he left West Point and has quite a pair of whiskers. He looks well and healthy. I asked James why he had not written you. He said that he wanted to get to his regt. first. Says that you knew he was going to enlist because he told Alex.

I took a swim in the river today and felt a good deal better after it. The weather is very hot. "We are going to have hats this summer instead of caps." We arrived here yesterday forenoon. Will leave here soon, I think. Hope we will go on boats. Our Col. told his regt. when drawn up in line that he had news that Richmond was taken and he believed it to be authentic. We gave some lusty cheering them. There are rumors here of terrible fighting up north with large loss of life on both sides, but that we were victorious.

Hope you and Frances are well. Please write soon and all the news. Alex Douglass told me that something was the matter with Sid. Either someone was dead, or something burned up, he forgot what it was. What is it?

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Writing under fire from the entrenchments near Dallas, Georgia, Alexander reassures his mother he is "all right thus far" even as bullets whistle overhead — interrupting his own sentence to admire one passing: "there goes one now — b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l." He reports James Thurber and John Rawlins of Co. H wounded, the regiment's loss at twenty-eight with seven killed, and the rebel works so close they can hear the enemy talk. He asks only for postage stamps and a silk handkerchief.
movements.transcription:
May 31st, 1864
Entrenchments near Dallas, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I am happy to inform you that I am all right thus far. God has been very good to me. This is written while we are under fire, the bullets whistling over our heads (there goes one now — b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l) every now and then — not a little oftener. "We have lain rather comfortably healthy." James Thurber and John Rawlins of Co. H have been wounded. Thurber is wounded through the arm and slightly in the shoulder. His wound is not dangerous. Rawlins is wounded through the right side. His wound is severe, but I hope not dangerous. The total loss of this regt. in this big fight is twenty-eight. Seven killed — the remainder wounded. The rebel works are but a very short distance from ours. We can hear them talk quite frequently and distinctly. The Gen'l. will not allow us to go out on the skirmishing line. Says I am always ready to do my duty — but that is no place for me, — the men of the keenest sight are the only ones that are needed there.

Please write often and send me some postage stamps, and will you be kind enough to send me by mail a silk handkerchief. I lost mine the other day and it is almost impossible to get along without one here. I have not rec'd a letter since I left Bridgeport but a number of papers. The letters will be along by and by. This writing to the noise of bullets not very pleasant business. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **WRITING UNDER FIRE.** Entrenchments near Dallas, Ga. H WOUNDED.** Thurber — through arm, slightly in shoulder; Rawlins — right side, not dangerous. Total loss of regt in this big fight: 28 — 7 killed, remainder wounded. movements.sigSummary: James Hubbell has been made Lance Corporal — acting as corporal, drilling the recruits — and Charles reports it with a brother's quiet pride from their shared camp at Morganza Bend on the Mississippi. He enlisted March 9th in New York City as a farmer of Champlain, Clinton Co., never showing his papers from the West Point officers, and drew an $860 bounty. Between the news, Charles cooks his own rations: pancakes of flour, water, and salt, fried heavy but good.
movements.transcription:
June 2, 1864
Camp on the Bank of the
Mississippi River
Morganza Bend,
State of La.

Dear Mother:

Have just heard that a steamer leaves in a short time for New Orleans so will write you a few lines. As I have to get ready for inspection I cannot write much. This morning I had the pleasure of receiving a letter from you dated May 7th, also two newspapers which are very acceptable. Two or three days since I received four letters which were directed to H. Qtrs. N.O. They were dated April 12th, 20th, 26th & May 5d. The letter I rec'd this morning was directed to the regiment and was directed right.

All the men here have built a framework over the tents & have covered the framework with bushes which makes it shady and cool for us. A shelter from the sun is made in the same way for the horses. We do not expect to go out of this department but cannot tell anything about it. I think we will lie in camp till cool weather.

I have got pretty well rested after our march and now have a good appetite. On the march we too tired to have much appetite. Each man in our Co. does his own cooking. We draw all the rations raw. Instead of hard tack for one day we drew flour and last night and this morning I made pancakes. I mixed the flour with water, put in a little salt and fried the cakes in a frying pan. They were heavy, but good. We also have bean soup. It is said that we are to have Co. cooks. I hope we will for it takes about all the time to cook and wash.

James has been made Lance Corporal, that is, acts as corporal. He has to drill with the recruits but don't know how long a time he will have to. It is very pleasant for us to be together. He has his bounty with him and will send it home when he can find an express agent. His trunk he gave away. Says he was about two weeks in Albany at a hotel, paid three dollars a day for board. I guess he never showed his papers from the W.P. officers. James says he told the recruiting officer when asked his place of residence that it was Champlain, Clinton Co., N.Y. He gave his occupation as a farmer. He rec'd $860 bounty and was told that he would receive $975 at his regt. Is he not entitled to Clinton Co. bounty? I think it would be well to inquire about it. He enlisted March 9th in New York City. I hope Alex is all right. Please write soon and give Alex's address. Is his corps the 12th? Is 20th Corps right? Love to all.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Camp on Bank of Mississippi River, Morganza Bend, La. Steamer leaves in short time for N.O. Received letter from Mother dated May 7th, also 2 newspapers and 4 letters directed to Hd. Qtrs. (April 12, 20, 26, May 5). Framework over tents with bushes — shady and cool. Shelter from sun made for horses same way. Will stay in camp till cool weather. Each man does own cooking — draws rations raw. Instead of hard tack, drew flour — made pancakes, fried cakes in frying pan. **JAMES IS LANCE CORPORAL** — "acts as corporal." movements.sigSummary: Six letters from home at once, and Alexander is "jolly" — the mail drought breaks at Marietta as the army rests before chasing the Johnnies, who have "dug out" toward Atlanta. He teases Mother's lurid account of Mr. Bass's shooting — "I have seen thousands of men wounded but hardly ever say anything come up to the pail of blood" — then tallies bounties and loans, hoping to send home over $600. One small ask closes it: please send a silk handkerchief.
movements.transcription:
June 8, 1864
Marietta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I had, oh such a jolly good time this morning. What do you think? I received no less than six letters from home. It did seem so good to hear from you all again. The letters were from April 27th to May 18th inclusive. I am very glad to hear that the Mr. Bass is convalescent. Guess he thinks flirting dangerous business. A man of his age ought to know better. He had a taste of bullets without going to war. I was vastly amused at your account of the matter. I expected when I got your letter I should have a horrible account. So Mr. Bass bled a painfull of blood. Oh, Mother, that is most as bad as the boy and the "hundred foxes." I have seen thousands of men wounded but hardly ever say anything come up to the pail of blood. You will carry off the palm this time certainly.

You will probably hear long ere this reaches you that the Johnnies have "dug out" and fallen back toward Atlanta. We have been resting for the last two days, I suppose in order to bring up supplies. We start on, I believe, after the Rebs in the morning. May God be with us and grant us the victory. I am very glad that you have got my county bounty. Mr. Averill's charges were more moderate than I supposed. You say that my $500 is all taken up and drawing interest. Have you taken out the money I borrowed from you? And does that leave my five hundred clear! I had in Mr. Savage's hands (including what you had deposited before I came home) when I left home four hundred dollars. The State bounty amounted to seventy dollars and the National to $190 making a total of 660 dollars, and now taking out what I owe you — nearly $100, would leave it all right, I think. If I live to be paid I shall be able to send home over $600. The mail is going out immediately so I must close. Culver Bostwick sends much love to his friends. Says he has written ten letters home and has received no answer. Feels always discouraged from writing. "Wished me to tell his friends that he is in the best of spirits." Please send me a silk handkerchief. I need one very much. Love to all.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: **SIX LETTERS FROM HOME — "oh such a jolly good time."** Letters from April 27 to May 18. Glad Mr. Bass convalescent — "he thinks flirting dangerous business." Dodds "a man of his age ought to know better." Bass had taste of bullets without going to war. **"OH, MOTHER, THAT IS MOST AS BAD AS THE BOY AND THE 'HUNDRED FOXES.'"** Mother's account — "a pailful of blood." "I have seen thousands of men wounded but hardly ever say anything come up to the pail of blood." Glad to have county bounty. Averill's charges — $190 making total $650, now taking out what he owes — nearly $100 — would leave all right. $500 in Mr. Savage's hands. "And does that leave my five hundred clear!" If paid shall send home $600. Fallen back toward Atlanta — resting 2 days. Start on after the Rebs in the morning. "May God be with us and grant us the victory." Culver Bostwick sends love — feels discouraged from writing. "Wished me to tell his friends that he is in the best of spirits." Send silk handkerchief.

movements.transcription:
June 13th, 1864
Camp on the Bank of the
Mississippi River —
Morganza, La.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of May 21st a few days since. Am glad that you and Frances are both well. I accidentally saw in a newspaper a short time since that Buzzard's Roost is where Gen. Sherman is encamped. From that I learned that Alex is not in the Army of the Potomac. I am glad of it.

In your letter you spoke of receiving a letter from Alex dated B. Roost, but I supposed that B. Roost was in Va. I have seen no account of Sherman fighting. Newspapers are very acceptable here and I hope that I will receive one from you soon. I send this letter in the express package which contains $400. Twenty dollars of this money is sent by Joseph Martin to his wife. He is a Frenchman from Champlain belonging to our Co. If his wife does not call on you for it, he wants you to let her know that you have received it. Fifty dollars I send and James the balance, which is $330. Think I shall insure it, which with the express charges will cost $2.00 on a hundred. James says he wants his invested in some safe place. Mr. Savage can tell you where it would be a good place to invest. I would as lief let them borrow it if they want it. If you need any of my money I hope you will use it freely at all times. Two or three days since we were paid four months pay, paid up to the 1st of May. James rec'd no pay this pay day, but will next. It is said here that soldiers will receive $16 a month from the 1 of May. Is this true? James has been talking with one of the soldiers that came here with him who told him that the $800 he rec'd was N.Y. bounty. James also rec'd one month's pay, making $873 but he has received. There is due James yet $75, N.Y. State bounty and $242 U.S., which is to be paid at different times. I wish Frances would keep an account of the money each of us sends home and where it is put out. James says he will write in a day or two.

Hoping that you and Frances try to enjoy life I will close. A few days since we went out foraging. Two regts. went with a long wagon train about fifteen miles. We rode out and walked back. When the wagon train came where the corn houses were — plenty — pulled off the side boards of the barns and filled the wagons with corn. The corn had the husks on. The women did not like to see the corn taken. Please write soon.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Received welcome letter of May 21st. Frances and Mother both well. Saw in newspaper Buzzard's Roost — same as Gen. Sherman. Alex is not in Army of the Potomac — in Sherman's army. Glad of it. Letter from Alex dated B. Roost. **JOSEPH MARTIN $400 TO WIFE** — Frenchman from Champlain. $20 of his $400 sent by express — "twenty dollars of this money is sent by Joseph Martin to his wife." Newspapers very acceptable. **JAMES TALKING WITH SOLDIERS** — soldiers said $800 bounty; he rec'd $860. James also rec'd one month's pay making $873. Due: James yet $75 NY State bounty and $242 U.S. — to be paid at different times. Wishes Frances would keep account of money sent home. **FORAGING** — rode out with long wagon train 15 miles. Rode out and walked back. Wagon train came where corn houses were — "plenty pulled off the side boards of the barns and filled the wagons with corn." $828 had the husks on. The women did not like to see the corn taken.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes his mother from a camp near Marietta, Georgia, with the 60th N.Y. Vets, having fought nearly every day and entrenched every night for a week. "The list of killed and wounded in our regt. is beginning to pile up fearfully," he reports, having skirmished the Sabbath from two P.M. until after ten. He twice begs for a silk handkerchief, then leaves his testament: how little the North realizes what the country has cost — it "ought to be prized beyond rubies after this is over."
movements.transcription:
June 20th, 1864
Camp in field near
Marietta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

By the kind providence of God I am permitted to write you again, and inform you that I am still uninjured. We have been fighting nearly every day since I last wrote you and working the greater portion of every night (and sometimes the whole) entrenching ourselves in positions gained the previous day. I shall not attempt to give you any detailed acct. of our proceedings. Suffice it to say that everything thus far is proceeding favorably. During the last week we have driven the enemy from two strong lines of entrenchments and are now burrowing away at him in his third. Yesterday was the Holy Sabbath, and I suppose, was passed by you in quiet and meditation. But far different was it with the 60th N.Y. Vets. We were the advance regt. of the division yesterday, being deployed as skirmishers, and were kept engaged with the enemy from two P.M. until after ten o'clock last night — when we were relieved.

The list of killed and wounded in our regt. is beginning to pile up fearfully. None of the boys from Champlain have been injured. Our Regt. was relieved from the front line this morning by the 2nd, and we now rest a little in the rear of the line of battle but not entirely out of range as the whistle of an occasional bullet plainly tells us. Our batteries are keeping up a pretty steady fire. The skirmish lines are also pretty hotly engaged. The rebel sharpshooters are at present keeping up a pretty lively fire on one of our batteries on the hill just above us, but with not much effect.

Please write often. I will write as often as possible. Keep a stout heart. We are all in God's hands. May He grant us all submission to His will.

Have you heard from James yet? His silence is singular and I think very wrong. The reason of it I think is that he feels his failure keenly and he wishes to make something of a mark in the world before he writes you, so that he may be able to compensate you for your disappointment in his failure. I received your letter of May 21st a few days since, also a N.Y. Tribune and papers from Mrs. Boyle. Please write upon the margin of your papers how you all are as I receive the papers oftener than the letters. The mail seem to be delayed at Chattanooga, I suppose from the difficulty of transportation. Love to all. I hope I will come out of this campaign all right, but if God orders it otherwise may we all meet in heaven. My home and trust is in Jesus our Saviour. Much love to Frances and tell her I shall if possible write her soon.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

How little the people at the North realize how much our country has cost us. It ought to be prized beyond rubies after this is over. I wrote you in my last to send me a little money if you could do so without inconvenience. This letter may reach you before the other — that is the reason I speak of it. If you can send it please do so. Inclose a silk handkerchief. I need one much. I also want you in one of the letters to send me a silk handkerchief. Send it by mail in the form of a package if you can send it without inconvenience.

movements.sigSummary: James Hubbell's first appearance in the collection finds the youngest brother encamped at Morganza, Louisiana, fresh off his single trial of marching — a foraging run that loaded one hundred wagons from a French woman's farm while soldiers were forbidden to take so much as a chicken. He notices everything: negroes speaking French like their masters, sugar mills that yield a spoonful a day. To Frances he turns almost shy — "What do you think of this war?"
movements.transcription:
June 21, 1864
Morganza, La.

Dear Fannie:

We are still encamped on the Mississippi; how long we shall remain here I cannot tell. I heard this morning that it was probable that we should not remain here long. The location is a good one, and if we are to remain in camp this summer I should not object to remaining here.

I have had but one trial of marching. That was out on a foraging expedition for corn. At night I sprawled out on my tent floor feeling that I had done a pretty hard day's work. I stood it pretty well considering I had used my legs so little since I have entered the service. We went to a small town at two great roads and filled our wagons from a French woman's barn. The men are nearly all off to war. Four barns, I think, filled our train of one hundred wagons. They talk about the rebels starving. It cannot be so here. One of our company called at a house and was hospitably entertained with cornbread and syrup, part of which he brought out in his hands. They said they had not seen wheat flour for about two years. There is considerable sugar in the mills along the river but it does not benefit us any. Our allowance is one spoonful per day. Negroes were quite plenty in the town. All spoke French like their masters. In front of some houses there were squads of eight or ten all sitting as radiantly as a negro. We saw numbers of great and little pigs, chickens and vegetable gardens, pretty well filled, all of which tempted our soldiers very much, but foraging was strictly forbidden.

The houses are not built with much style, though they may be very comfortable; they are mostly low wooden buildings. I have seen some very handsome brick houses with beautiful grounds in front. Nearly all have pretty yards in front which seem to be spontaneous. I do not see why brick buildings are not more common. Clay is so abundant on the river and the Mississippi so handy to float the material down. None of the settlements are far back from the river.

James Sweeney has lately come into our regt. as Surgeon. On Friday and I went over to see him. He was such a little faller when he left our place that I hardly remembered him. I think that if either of us are sick he will be a friend worth having. You know in the army a person does not get much care.

Well, I have scribbled over this paper and not said much. Comment vous portez ma vous! What do you think of this war? Do you watch the Army of the Potomac with interest? O, Grant, go ahead and whip the rebels, is the feeling here. An inconvenient place to write has made me scribble and soil this paper. Will you please excuse it.

Your aff. brother,

James
movements.notes: **JAMES'S FIRST LETTER IN THE COLLECTION.** Still on Mississippi — probably won't remain long. Location is good — would not object to remaining. **FORAGING EXPEDITION** — one trial of marching, pretty hard day's work. "I stood it pretty well considering I had used my legs so little since I have entered the service." Small town — filled wagon train of 100 wagons from French woman's barn. French like their masters. **NEGROES** quite plenty in town — "all spoke French like their masters." In front of some houses were squads of 8-10 all sitting as radiantly as a negro. Handsome brick houses — pretty yards in front. Sugar in mills along river — "does not benefit us any." Foraging strictly forbidden. **JAMES SWEENEY** — lately come into regt. as surgeon. Was a little faller when he left our place — "I think that if either of us are sick he will be a friend worth having." "Comment vous portez ma vous?" What do you think of this war? "Do you watch the Army of the Potomac with interest?"

movements.letterExcerpt: As James wrote you yesterday I will write a few lines also and send with him today. We have been waiting to hear from you before we wrote, but as no letter comes will wait no longer.
movements.sigSummary: Dr. James Sweeney, the new Assistant Surgeon, sent a boy to fetch "the two Hubbells" to his tent — the Champlain network reaching all the way to a Louisiana camp. He'd seen Frances three weeks before and was glad of the company; the regiment had gone without a second surgeon since leaving Washington. Charles closes with a bookkeeper's note: $4 freight and $2 insurance on the $400 sent home by express.
movements.transcription:
June 22, 1864
Morganza, La.

Dear Mother:

As James wrote you yesterday I will write a few lines also and send with him today. We have been waiting to hear from you before we wrote, but as no letter comes will wait no longer.

Two or three days since a boy came to us and said that the new doctor wanted to see the two Hubbells. We went there and learned that Doctor James Sweeney was Assistant Surgeon of this Regt. He told us that he saw Frances about three weeks before. He was quite sociable. The Regt. has had but one surgeon since it left Washington till now. On the $400 we sent by express we paid $4 freight and two dollars insurance.
movements.notes: Brief note — James wrote yesterday, Charles adds a few lines. Waiting to hear from home. **DR. JAMES SWEENEY** — new doctor wanted to see the two Hubbells. He told us he saw Frances about 3 weeks before. Sociable. Regt. has had only one surgeon since it left Washington till now. $400 sent by express — paid $4 freight and $2 insurance.
Assault on Kennesaw Mountain.

movements.letterExcerpt: If any additional charge is made please let me know the amount, so I can collect of Martin his share of the freight. He has paid his share of the $5.00 which was 30¢.
movements.sigSummary: James yesterday made his first attempt at doughnuts — frying the grease out of a lot of pork, but with no yeast powder the cakes came out heavy, and sugar at 50¢ at the sutler's was too dear to sweeten them. Charles details a camp economy of dried-apple pies at 50¢ and flour cakes baked in a covered kettle, while word from the chaplain hints they will soon garrison some place near the Mississippi.
movements.transcription:
[Beginning missing]

If any additional charge is made please let me know the amount, so I can collect of Martin his share of the freight. He has paid his share of the $5.00 which was 30¢.

Our Chaplain told me a few days since that he thought that we would not stay here a great while. I don't know where we will go, but probably we will garrison some place near the Mississippi River. Butter are plenty here but they sell very high. Flour they sell from 10 to 12½¢ a pound. Dried apples — 25¢ a lb. Dried apple pies sell at 50¢ each and small short cakes 5¢ each. The pies and flour cakes are made by the men. They are baked in a kettle with a cover.

James yesterday made his first attempt at making doughnuts. He fried the grease out of a lot of pork so that he had plenty of grease. As he put no yeast powder in the dough the cakes were heavy. He wanted sugar or molasses, but sugar costs too much, 50¢ or over at the sutlers. We draw flour once in a while. New York papers sell here for 25¢. I should like to receive some papers from you. How do you and Frances prosper? Have you heard from Alex lately? I have not heard from him nor written to him since I was at N. Orleans. Please write soon.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

From the skirmish line he hears the rebel cheer for Hardee come out "something very like a wail."
movements.transcription:
[Beginning missing]

You see I am going to write you a long letter while I have the chance for we shall probably be "heels over head" in the din and turmoil of the fight in a day or two. The "Johnnies" don't like the way Sherman fights. They say he comes around on the blind side of them and they have to "up and git." One old lady down here expressed great wrath at our proceedings. She said the Yanks came and made three lines of fight in her yard and tipped over a barrel of ashes — she would not have taken two dollars and a half or any sum of money for those "ashes" "And that is not all" she said, "They had a man killed and went off and wouldn't kote him off with them."

(Both)

The first night we came here we (60th) were the skirmishing Regt. of the Brig. and were close to the rebel lines. They seemed to be in a terrible stare. We could hear them talking and shouting and coughing all night long. Once they called out "three cheers for Genl. Hardee" and you thought the setup a — mmh well, I cannot describe it. It was so different from the hearty cheer of our troops. It was something very like a wail — and a sorrowful wriggle. I suppose that old traitor Hardee was passing. If any of the 60th could have clapened an eye on him he would have fared ill, but the woods were too thick. Genls. Hooker and Geary were out on the skirmish line and brought out the 13th N.Y. Battery, but for some reason they did not seem to think it expedient to open on the Rebs and the battery was sent back. The next day they commenced fixing a place for that battery and several others, but we were ordered to another part of the line and the work was suspended. The 14th Corps (Genl. Logan) now holds that part of the line. We are further to the left. The right of our Corps connects with the left of the 15th. The 14th Corps (Genl. "Alonzo") connects with our left, I believe. The feeling of animosity between the eastern and western troops is dying away and we are getting to be pretty good friends. We, the 20th Corps, are known among the western boys as Hookers Regt. or Hookers star men. (You know the badge of the 20th Corps is a star.) Of all Sherman's generals, Hooker, I think, is the most feared by the rebels. They thought he was killed a short time since and great were their rejoicings. He was also reported to us to be killed, and you may be sure I felt pleased when I saw the old fellow riding along as sound as a dollar the next day. It was Genl. Barker that was killed.

You can tell M. H. Cook that the Eastern troops are considerably above par in this department and that old "fighting Joe" is one of the biggest toads in the puddle.

Please thank Mrs. Boyle for the papers she sent me. I got them more regularly than the letters. I was very much pleased with the speech of Genl. McClellan which she sent me. It has the right kind of ring to it. I was very much pleased with the way he spoke of the officers of the regular army who had proved traitors to their country.

I hope James will write me soon. I have written him.

Alex

The ball tore a furrow in his right side and passed through his arm above the elbow — bad but not dangerous, two or three months laid up. movements.transcription:
July 2nd, 1864
In the Field near
Marietta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

Must try and write you a word at least though I am pretty tired as I was up all night working with pick and shovel in the trenches. Our batteries along the whole line opened up on the rebs this morning but everything has settled down again to its usual opening — i.e. — sharp skirmishing and a shot now and then from the batteries. Movements are now being made that will I think, bring matters to a decided issue soon. I hope we shall be able to bring this campaign to a close soon.

Luther was wounded this morning while we were after a log for the top of the breast works. We had just gone up with several men to an old house from which we intended to get the log. When the Capt. (I was at work with the shovels) ordered me with several others to go on and give them a lift in bringing it down, I had just started when a ball whistled close by and was in succession followed by a yell of agony. I ran forward and had gone but a little ways when I met Luther coming back leaning upon one of the men. You may be sure I felt a little queer. To my anxious inquiries Luther replied that he thought he was not much hurt — that he thought that it was only a flesh wound. And so it proved though it was a pretty bad hurt, but not dangerous. The ball tore a furrow in his right side and passed through the fleshy part of his right arm a little above the elbow. He will probably be laid up two or three months. God in his kindness great kindness has as yet preserved me from all harm. Culver Bostwick is also well. (He have just drawn a ration of whiskey. I gave mine to the boys for two hard crackers. I believe Bostwick did the same. We do not draw whiskey every day — only when we have had an unusually hard time. We were up last night, and the night before and — well, I may say we hardly know what an uninterrupted night's rest is. He will know how to appreciate rest if ever we get it. Culver and I are getting worn down bully thin. We suffer terribly from the heat — and — and terrain — if I must say it.

Of army movements I will not attempt to tell you. You can find out pretty much from the papers. James has not yet written me. I hope he has not forgotten his brother Alex. How do all things flourish in Champlain! and what were to be the doings on the Fourth? There is a likelihood of there being considerable powder burned here, though if burning powder makes Fourth of July we have had fourth of July ever since we started. Love to all. Tell Frances I shall wait until there is little firing before I write her, which I hope will be soon.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

Received a letter from Capt. Ransom last night. Will endeavor to write him soon. Please give him my regards. I received the handkerchief some time since, also all the stamps you sent. I get all your letters in the course of time. I am glad that Frances has gone to Charlotte. I hope she will have a pleasant visit. She needed rest. Will she go into school again next term?
movements.notes: In the field near Marietta, Ga. Pretty tired — up all night working with pick and shovel in trenches. Batteries along whole line opened up on rebs — sharp skirmishing and shot from batteries. Settled down again to usual opening — "i.e. — sharp skirmishing and a shot now and then from the batteries." Movements being made — "will bring matters to a decided issue soon." **LUTHER WOUNDED.** "I had just gone up with several men to an old house from which we intended to get the log. When the Capt. (I was at work with the shovels) ordered me with several others to go on and give them a lift in bringing it down." Ball whistled close — "a yell of agony." Luther — "he thought he was not much hurt — that he thought that it was only a flesh wound." Ball tore a furrow in right side — passed through fleshy part of right arm a little above elbow. **NOT DANGEROUS** — laid up two or three months. "God in his kindness great kindness has as yet preserved me from all harm." Culver Bostwick also well. "Culver and I are getting worn down bully thin. We suffer terribly from the heat — and — and terrain — if I must say it."

Days earlier, from a high ridge, the 60th Vets climbed a tree and glimpsed Atlanta itself — spires, chimneys, smoke from its furnaces, forts and rifle pits ringing the city. movements.transcription:
July 8, 1864
In the Field near
Chattahoochee, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of June 20th yesterday and the handkerchief enclosed, for which I am very, very much obliged. I can now wipe the perspiration from my brow with some degree of comfort — before I received the handkerchief I was reduced to the necessity of using a portion of an old rebel meal bag.

Your letter gave me a feeling something akin, I suppose, felt by the Israelites of old when they were described as longing for "the flesh pots of Egypt." I hardly think I shall be at home in time to enjoy the cherries and plums with you, but hope to be before another season rolls around. The fighting will all be done this summer, I think. The eyes of the 60th Vets. have been blest with a sight of the goal (as we suppose) of the campaign — Atlanta. Day before yesterday we were upon a high ridge from which by climbing a tree we could see the city with its tall spires and chimneys — and a great smoke going up — from its numerous furnaces, I suppose. With a glass you could see the windows of the houses and the streets plainly. We could see the forts around the city and lines of rifle pits. The rebs have made a stand again, this side of the river. We are not fighting much at present, only skirmishing and an occasional shot from the batteries. Last night about dusk there was a furious cannonade to the fight of the line, but whether it was accompanied with musketry, we were too distant to tell. I have not heard the cause of it. About midnight the firing of the skirmishers was very sharp, and I expected we should be called up but it settled down again to its usual opening. We are, I understand, about a mile and a halfrom the river. The rebel works are on a ridge close to its banks. They are very strong, I should judge. They have several large earthen forts in the line. We are making the most of our little rest. The officers are hard at work today upon the pay rolls. I suppose we shall not be paid until the campaign is over. It has lasted now over two months. I heard from Luther yesterday. He is doing well.

Is there much excitement up there relative to the Presidential campaign? It occasions very little remark down here. Fremont, I think, will meet little favor with the army. All are awaiting the action of the Democratic convention at Chicago. I see they have postponed the meeting until Aug. 29th. They have shown the right spirit and put the Republicans to shame. Every nerve of the Nation should now be used to strengthen her armies and uphold the administration. It will be time enough to talk politics after the summer's work is done. It will be hard to tell, I think, before that is done who is the right man for President.

I suppose I saw the cannon fired that killed Bishop Polk as our Regt. was close to the batteries at the time. The shot or shell struck him in the breast. If the shell had burst, old Johnston and Hardee would probably ave shared the same fate, as they were close beside him. Please write often. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from within 1¼ miles of Atlanta, his pen jumping as shells burst close: "(There goes another shot.)" "(Another shell made us jump a little just now.)" The war literally breaks into his sentences. He reports the terrific battle of the 20th — the rebs defeated with great loss, their dead and wounded left on the field, none of the Champlain boys hurt, though Captain Delaney took a bad arm wound. "How good God has been to me."
movements.transcription:
July 24, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

How different this Sabbath morning is with you to what it is with us. Instead of the chime of the church bells our ears are saluted with the roar of cannon and bursting shell. (I commenced since one burst close by) and made your humble servant dodge a little, as the pieces flew uncomfortably nigh, so if my writing is unusually bad you will know to what to attribute it — reb shells — not me. (There goes another shot.) "We had a most terrific battle the 20th inst. (Another shell made us jump a little just now.) I wrote you a letter the morning of that day and told you that I thought we should move upon the enemy that day, and we did and met the enemy moving upon us and the battle came off. I will not try to describe the battle to you. I could not do it justice. Suffice it to say that the rebs were defeated with great loss, leaving their dead and a large number of wounded upon the field. None of the boys from Champlain were hurt. Captain Delaney was wounded in the arm, a pretty bad wound but not dangerous. He will not be able to be with us probably for two or three months. The 60th Vets covered themselves with glory. We have the credit of saving the 13th N.Y. Independent Battery. (The rebs are shooting uncomfortably close. I must hurry up and say what I have to say as it is a little dangerous writing out here.) Love to all. You see the rebs have spoiled your letter. Please write often.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. The rebs are shooting very close. We are within 1¼ miles of Atlanta and our long range guns are shelling the city. How good God has been to me.

movements.sigSummary: The cannonade interrupted the long letter Alexander meant to write near Atlanta on July 29, 1864: rebel batteries opened so furiously he fled to the works, where shells blew off one man's arm and killed two battery horses. By Sherman's order the guns stayed silent all day, then at 10 P.M. "the Atlanta Express" sent a shell into the city every five minutes through the night. Sent out to feint an attack while the 15th, 16th and 17th Corps shifted right, his regiment lost two men to the deception.
movements.transcription:
July 29, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of the 11th inst. and paper of the 12th last evening and was much pleased with its contents. They were the right thing in the right place. I am writing this letter upon the paper you sent. It is singular that I receive the papers so much sooner than the letters. You see that the letter was mailed the day previous to the paper and still I received them both at the same time. I wrote you last Sunday and intended writing you a long letter such as you like, but the rebel batteries opened so furiously that I was obliged to desist and seek safety in the works. Their shells did but little damage. One man had his arm blown off, and two battery horses were killed. Our batteries were unusually silent this day, and I understand that it was by special order of Gen'l. Sherman, but about 10 P.M. they opened lustily. The battery we call "the Atlanta Express" sent a shell into the city every five minutes during the night.

We have changed our position since then and are now further to the left of the line. Day before yesterday the 15th, 16th and 17th army corps moved to the right of the line. The cannonading there was very heavy yesterday and I think they had a heavy fight. Our regt. was sent out last night to make a feint as if we intended to attack them here, in order, I understand, to prevent their sending troops to the right. There was "right smart" of shooting done. The rebs opened a heavy fire upon us from their batteries. I am confident they expected a heavy attack. We lost two men. It is tolerably quiet today, a little skirmishing and an occasional shot from the batteries. Please write often.

You asked me how my health is. It is very good and has been generally during the campaign. Never been slightly indisposed only once or twice. I have great reason, I think, for gratitude to God for His great kindness in preserving me thus far. I leave all in His hands and hope for the best. I hope that James and Charles have not forgotten me. I have as yet received no letter from them and have received only one from Charles since I have been in the Department. Love to all. Please write soon.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

Received a letter from Capt. Ransom last night. Will endeavor to write him soon. Please give him my regards. I received the handkerchief some time since, also all the stamps you sent. I got all your letters in the course of time. I am glad that Frances has gone to Charlotte. I hope she will have a pleasant visit. She needed rest. Will she go into school again next term?
movements.notes: Near Atlanta, Ga. Received letter of 11th inst. and paper of 12th. "It is singular that I receive the papers so much sooner than the letters." Writing on paper you sent. Rebel batteries opened so furiously — obliged to seek safety in works. One man had arm blown off, two battery horses killed. **BATTERIES SILENT BY SHERMAN'S ORDER** — about 10 P.M. opened lustily. **"ATLANTA EXPRESS"** — shell into city every five minutes during night. **POSITION CHANGED — further to left.** 15th, 16th, 17th corps moved to right — heavy cannonading, heavy fight. **REGT. SENT FOR FEINT ATTACK** — "right smart" of shooting. Rebs opened heavy fire from batteries. Lost two men. Health very good. James and Charles have not written — received only one letter from Charles since in the Department. Capt. Ransom letter received. Handkerchief received. Frances gone to Charlotte.

Writing from the works near Atlanta on Aug. 2, 1864, Alexander tracks Schofield's 23d Corps sweeping right to strike the Macon and Atlanta railroad. Yet what stings most is silence: "Why does not James write! I would do almost anything for him."
movements.transcription:
Aug. 2, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of July 17th and 18th a day or two since and was pleased to hear that you are all well and considerably surprised to hear the 153d was in Maryland. I knew that Gen'l. Canby's troops were there, but did not suppose that the 153d was among them.

Quite a heavy cannonade has been going on today to the extreme left of the line. The 23d Corps (Gen'l. Schofield) was moving to the right yesterday and the day before. I suppose it is them engaged. The distance is so great that I cannot tell whether or not it is accompanied with musketry. The object of the move is, I think, to strike out the Macon and Atlanta railroad. Our lines, I understand, were within a half mile of the road previous to the 23d Corps going there.

Nothing of special interest has transpired since last I wrote you. Sunday night we commenced constructing a new line of work. We were obliged to work in the night on account of the rebel sharpshooters. They plunged two or three balls into the works the next day but did no damage. Last night while the mail was being distributed (a large crowd always collects around the mail) a rebel sharpshooter, I should think nearly a mile away, sent a ball "spot" into the center of the circle. It made them jump a little but they did not scatter until they had got their letters. The ball passed through a tent in its course. The mail carrier is collecting the mail. I must hurry. I want to write James and Charles, but will not until I learn surely whether they are in Maryland. Why does not James write! I feel quite neglected. There surely cannot be one who has a heartier interest in his welfare than I. I would do almost anything for him. Remember me to Charles and James when you next write, and ask them why they do not write me. Please write often. I have — Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alexander.
movements.notes: Near Atlanta, Ga. Received letters of July 17th and 18th. Surprised to hear 153rd was in Maryland — knew Gen'l. Canby's troops there, didn't suppose 153rd among them. **HEAVY CANNONADE — extreme left.** 23rd Corps (Gen'l. Schofield) moving to right. Object: **STRIKE MACON AND ATLANTA RAILROAD.** Lines within half mile of road. Sunday night constructing new line of work — obliged to work at night on account of rebel sharpshooters. **SHARPSHOOTER HIT THE MAIL** — ball "spot" into center of crowd collecting mail; passed through tent. "It made them jump a little but they did not scatter until they had got their letters." James and Charles haven't written — "Why does not James write!" Feels neglected. "I would do almost anything for him."

movements.sigSummary: Hooker leaves the 20th Corps near Atlanta, and Alexander captures the scene that broke the men's hearts: a Pennsylvania soldier, his leg just shot off by a cannon, calls from the stretcher, "Good bye, General Hooker!" The general dismounts, removes his hat, and shakes the dying man's hand. On the right, fighting drives the enemy a mile and a half, taking a fort and battery and cutting "the only remaining road of the rebels." And still, no stamps: "ain't I a good boy?"
movements.transcription:
[At the top of the letter was written: "My dearest child; Write me immediately."]

Aug. 8, 1864
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of July 25th day before yesterday and your papers, the "Times" and the "Tribune" the day before, also the envelopes and paper enclosed. As I had written you the day I thought I had fulfilled your request of writing you immediately, but like a dutiful son I shall write you again today. Now, "ain't" I a good boy?

You recollect when I last wrote that I mentioned that the armies of McPherson and Schofield were moving to the right. Since then a battle has come off in which our forces were victorious, driving the enemy a mile and a half — taking a fort and a battery, and cutting, I understand, the only remaining road of the rebels. But then I will not weary you with a detailed account of this affair, as you will have seen accounts of it in the papers long before this reaches you.

I regret to inform you that Gen'l. Hooker has left us. He had endeared himself to the whole corps. The day he left he rode along the line bidding the men goodbye. A man from one of the Pennsylvania regts. of our brigade had just had his leg taken off by a cannon shot, was being carried off on a stretcher just at that time. "Good bye, General Hooker!" he sang out. It seemed to have moved the Gen'l. greatly. He got off his horse, took off his hat and went up and shook hands with the poor fellow, making some kind encouraging words at the same time. The 20th Corps will never forget old "Fighting Joe." Major Gen'l. Slocum, our old Corps commander, is now I understand in command of the Corps. We feel somewhat comforted for the loss of Hooker.

I suppose Charles and James are now on the Peninsula with Grant, as the excitement occasioned by the last raid must be nearly over. I hope the report of Charles being ill is not true, but if it is he is where he can get the best medical treatment. I shall try and write them both today. I hope James will try and bear his disappointment like a man. I am afraid it is he instead of Charles that is ill. I suppose Frances is still enjoying her visit at C. Have been expecting a letter from her for some time. She will write soon. I have not a solitary stamp and hardly know what I shall do to end this letter. If you can do so without inconveniencing yourself, please send me some in your next letter. I do not think I have received all the stamps you have sent. I have not received the tea as yet. Culver Bostwick received some some time since. Please write often. Love to all. Give my regards to Mrs. Brikerhoff.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.transcription:
August 8th, 1864

Capt. J. M. Ransom —

Dear Sir:

I received your kind letter of July 10th some days since, but knowing as you do how we soldiers are situated on an active campaign, I trust you will excuse my tardiness in answering. My Mother was right in telling you that I would be very much pleased by the receipt of a letter from you. I was indeed pleased — and sincerely trust they will be less like "angel's visits" in the future.

I have so much to write that I hardly know where to begin — and for that very reason had a good will not to begin at all — but nevertheless I will do my best. Everything seems to be going on here most favorably. The theatre of the most active operations for the last few days has been the extreme right. I will not weary you with a detailed account of its late movements as you will have seen a full acct. of them in the papers long before this reaches you. Suffice it to say that the combined attack of the forces of Howard, (formerly McPherson's) and Schofield was very successful, and that the last remaining railroad to the rebs is severed. I hope we shall be able to bag the Johnnies here, for I am heartily tired of chasing them.

They are bringing us, I understand, a heavy siege train — so I expect the Johnnies are in a pretty tight place. The hardest fighting of the campaign has occurred since we crossed the Chattahoochee and all the Johnnies have to show for it is a long list of casualties that would frighten a man just to look at it. How comforting such a document must be to Jeff Davis & Co. The fight of the 20th of July was an awful one. The rebels threw their men upon us in solid columns and seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. But we were not to be driven. We had come all the way from Chattanooga to see Atlanta and were bound to see it and are now knocking pretty loudly at its doors.

We changed front during the battle no less than three times. I thought matters looked a little "scaly" when I saw the rebs coming up in our rear, but for all that we whipped them. Our regt. and the 147th Penn. have the credit of saving the two Division batteries. The rebs had the use of the guns of Bundy's battery when we came up. Our regt. was the only one of the Brigade that was not broken during the fight. At the fight at Lost Mountain our regt. was the only one of the Brig. that got up to the top of the hill and held the ground. Capt. Delaney was wounded in the fight of the 20th. I have reached nearly the end of my sheets and have not said half what I wish to say. Shall have to leave it to another letter.

Yours truly,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P. H. Brookway has got a commission and is in command of Co. H. Capt. Elliott is now Major and Thomas is Lieut./Col., Goddard is Colonel. We are to be consolidated soon with the 134th N.Y. Hobart is Capt. of Co. I. A good many of the officers will be mustered out when we are consolidated. The surplus non coms are to be reduced. P. H. Brookway has a first Lieut. commission.

movements.sigSummary: Frederick City's hospital sits pleasantly on a hill overlooking the city, but young James writes Mother and Fannie of frustration, not glory: sent from Louisiana to Washington's defenses, dropped into rifle pits, then chasing Early through the Shenandoah while the rebels escaped with a plundered wagon train three miles long. "Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination," he writes — until a blistered foot and want of sleep dropped him from the column.
movements.transcription:
Aug. 15th, 1864
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Mother and Fannie:

It is a long while since I have written you. I think my last letter was from Morganza. Since that time our regt. has seen considerable hardship. We left Louisiana the last of June for the North — this, I think Charlie has written you. As soon as we arrived at Washington D.C. we were sent out to the defenses and placed in the rifle pits. The next morning there was heavy skirmishing near us, but the Rebs retreated and we saw nothing of them. The next day we were sent as a reserve for the 6th Corps and followed the Rebs out to the Shenandoah Valley, the 6th Corps following close and skirmishing, but the Johnnies did not want to fight. We crossed a day and the next we crossed the river and lay in a belt of woods all day expecting a fight, but no, the enemy only wanted to get off with their plunder and keep us off, and they did it. At night we received orders to report at Washington within 24 hours. "Fall in!" ran along the lines and off we marched, many with light eyes and gloomy feelings — the prospect of marching all night does not lighten the feelings of many. Just as we were starting four men came in with a large dressed porker but it was goodly big, for a soldier cannot carry more than his usual load. Pig hitting had gone on pretty briskly that afternoon. Some were fortunate enough to get their pork for supper. Hardtack and coffee was all most of us had to eat. Do you know what hardtack is! Bake a flour and water cake with no salt or saleratus on a griddle till it is hard — throw it on a shelf for three or four days and see what kind of a meal it will make.

We waded the river and with an occasional half hour rest marched until four the next day. I stood it until about eight the next morning and then the want of sleep and food, a blistered foot and fatigue compelled me to fall out. The wagon train soon came along. I put my gun and bundles on one and found I could get along. I kept with this train until we arrived at Chainbridge within the defenses of W. There we consumed. Orders were soon issued to prepare for field service; shoes and clothes were given out, and after a day's rest off we started. Where we went I did not know or care. After several days hard marching the two corps pitched camp about two miles beyond Harper's Ferry. Then came a counter march. Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination, the men in the meantime becoming worn out. At Frederick City I was taken to a hospital where I am now and have been two weeks. I was quite sick but am now pretty well and expect soon to go to a convalescent camp. My sickness was generally unwell and played out. The hospital is pleasantly situated on a hill overlooking the city. Papers are brought in every morning with war and city news. They do not apprehend a draft here — the wards are fast filling out their quotas. Milk is retailed at 16 cents a quart; peaches are selling at 80 cents a bushel. I had a little change and could buy fruit. We get tea four a cent here.

There is a general feeling indignation expressed in these papers that our Generals should not have ascertained the actual force of the enemy and prevented them from coming so near our Capitol. They state that we had twenty thousand troops around Washington, part of them veterans, while the actual forces of the Rebels was 15,000, since ascertained. The fact that the army came up here with that force, harvested, plundered and got off with a wagon train three miles in length is rather irritating to us.

About Charlie's health — he was quite thin and used up when I left; he finds the marches very hard. Charlie is one of the kind that'll go until he cannot go. I do not think that is the way. He remarked that if he was sick he would not have vital energy enough to recover. A good rest and something to eat would set him all right, I think. I hope he has been sent off. Charlie is pretty plucky and won't give up, but I think he ought to favor himself more.

This paper was given me when we arrived at Washington from Louisiana. This I have carried since then which accounts for its being soiled. Our fare here is soft bread or pilot bread, meat twice a day, stewed apples at night.

It seems to me that I should like to come up with the Johnnies and have a good hard fight with them instead of dogging them day and night and then having them get away marching and countermarching, accomplishing nothing, I do not like. What is the news in C? Will they be obliged to draft them in Sept.? Please write soon. Direct as before.

James
movements.notes: Baltimore, Md. (Frederick City hospital). Long while since written — last letter from Morganza. Sent as reserve for 6th Corps — followed rebs to Shenandoah Valley. 6th Corps skirmishing but Johnnies did not want to fight. Crossed river, lay in belt of woods expecting fight — enemy only wanted to get off with plunder. Ordered to report Washington within 24 hours. **NIGHT MARCH — EXHAUSTION.** Four men came in with dressed porker. movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes his mother from the 2d Division Hospital, 20th Corps, near Atlanta, struck down not by a bullet but by "genuine scurvy" — the surgeon telling him he is very young to have it. From his cot he can only hear the war: heavy firing to the right, rebels said to charge the works drunk and "repulsed each time with terrible slaughter." A McClellan man, he feels his politics turning: "I will hoist my colors soon," reckoning he'll be over 21 to cast his first vote this fall.
movements.transcription:
Aug. 22, 1864
2d Div. Hospital — 20th Corps
Near Atlanta, Ga.

Dear Mother:

You perceive that I am again in the hospital. I am not wounded but am afflicted with what the surgeon calls genuine scurvy. He says I am very young to have it. By taking good care of myself and with proper nourishment (vegetables) I think I shall soon be fit for duty.

I received your letter of August 8th yesterday. Dixon brought it down to me. You may be sure I was pleased for I had not heard from you since the 25th of July. I have received several papers since then. You did not send me a Tribune with an acct. of the battle of the 20th. I should like to see it. If you can, please send it or any other paper with an acct. of it.

Nothing of special interest has transpired since I last wrote — yes, there has too, if the report is true. Very heavy artillery and musketry firing was heard a day or two since to the right of the line and the report of the affair is that a heavy battle came off there, the rebels charging and recharging our works, but were repulsed each time with terrible slaughter. Their loss, it is said, is to be counted by the thousand. The rebels are reported to have been very much under the influence of liquor. Reports are so conflicting that I hardly dare write them. Of a battle having taken place I have but little doubt as the firing was very sharp. You must bear in mind that our line is many miles long and we can only judge what is going on by the firing. There are so many rumors afloat that you can hardly tell what is reliable till you see the papers.

Please send papers often and a magazine now and then if convenient. Please write soon and often. Lieut. Brookway has taken charge of my mail and will forward it to me wherever I am. Please send me some stamps. I will use my last when I send this. I found the two stamps I lost. Mrs Frances yet returned? Tell her I received her letter and didn't see my boots for a week after. I will endeavor to write to her soon. I wrote James and Charles a few days since. I hope that they will write me. I think your fears are groundless about their being prisoners. Love to all. F. A. Cook is at Champlain, and he is hot for Lincoln. I will hoist my colors soon. If I live I shall cast a vote this fall. You know I will have been in the service over three years when the election comes off, and according to the laws of the U.S. I shall be of proper age to vote, as no one is received into the U.S. Service under 18. By the muster rolls I shall be over 21.

Your aff. Son

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: 2d Div. Hospital, 20th Corps, near Atlanta. **SCURVY** — "afflicted with what the surgeon calls genuine scurvy. He says I am very young to have it." Needs vegetables. movements.sigSummary: Sheridan's army takes shape around Harper's Ferry, but Charles writes mainly to quiet a worried mother: he is sorry she wasted $5 telegraphing about James, sent thin and with diarrhea to a hospital near Frederick. Safe in the convalescent department as a clerk, he has "flatted in considerably" on all the sugar he can eat. His counsel is hard-won: "You must call no news good news."
movements.transcription:
Aug. 26, 1864
Camp near Harper's Ferry

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you last night dated Aug. 20th, was glad to hear from you, but am very sorry you are so anxious about James and me. James, I think, is all right. When around for a couple of days near Frederick James was sent to the hospital at that place, and Dr. Sweeney told me that he would send me as soon as he could but would not at that time very well. James was thin in flesh and had the diarrhea. If he has been very sick since then the doctors have made him so with their medicine. But I think James is having a good time in some hospital or convalescent camp — that is, a good time compared with marching. I have not heard from James nor have I written him. It is useless to be anxious about him because he has not written. You know, he doesn't seem to care about letter writing. Perhaps he is waiting till he rejoins the regt. As for myself I am well and have been nearly two weeks in the convalescent dept. As there are more clerks here than are necessary I may go back to the regt. any day, and then I may not. There is a good deal of work to do but then we live well. I have flatted in considerably since I have been here because I eat all the sugar I want, for one thing. You have been sending me recipes for the diarrhea, because I suppose as it is an army complaint you think I must have it. I have been troubled very little with it. I know a man with whom it has become chronic, who is a perfect skeleton. He has a good appetite and does duty all the time.

I am sorry you wasted $5 telegraphing about James. Dr. Sweeney told me at the time James was sent to the hospital that he would be sent on to Washington probably, and as I did not know his address I have not written him. James had no chevrons on his coat and I guess in his paper for admission to the Hospital Corporal was not written. I hope you will not worry about us boys, for if there is anything the matter with us you will hear of it. You must call no news good news. I am entirely out of money and postage stamps. When you would send me a couple of dollars and some stamps. You direct the letters me right. I have recd 2 or 3 letters lately from you, also two newspapers. Have not written because I have not had the material or time. We have been on the move nearly all the time, have been here two days. Our Army is composed of the 19th and the 6th Corps — also the 8th — all under the command of General Sheridan who has a large force of cavalry with him. We have not had a sight of the rebs yet, although the cavalry has fought with them some; also a few of the infantry. Please write often. It is not convenient for me to write as I have no place to carry writing materials and not much time, but I will write as often as I can. Give my love to Frances. Also don't forget yourself.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Three of a mother's sons in three hospitals at once — and Alexander, laid up with scurvy, confesses he "did have a hearty laugh" at "your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time." Between jokes about low diet and doctor's medicines, he relays the news: his 20th Corps has fallen back to hold the Chattahoochee line while the rest of the army swings off on a "grand flanking excursion" toward Macon. Camp rumor says the rebels have already left Atlanta.
movements.transcription:
Aug. 30/64
2d Div. Hospital, 20th A.C.

Dear Mother:

Now that I am in a hospital I know you will be anxious to hear from me often and consequently I shall endeavor to be very regular in my correspondence. I am getting along as well as can be expected, though I expect will take some little time to get this scurvy out of my blood. I have very good care taken of me so you need not be troubled on that score.

I received your letter of Aug 16th day before yesterday and am glad to hear that you at home are well, and very, very sorry to hear that James is sick in hospital and Charley likely to be soon. Please excuse me, Mother, but I did have a hearty laugh when I took in the idea of your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time. I suppose you think it is something that should not be laughed at. Well I agree with you on that point — it is not quite so funny as it might be. Low diet and doctor's medicines are not quite as agreeable as some things.

A truce to the blues and now for something lively. Our Corps has fallen back from Atlanta and is now holding a line along the Chattahoochee. The rest of the army I expect has gone on a grand flanking excursion, heading toward Macon. It is reported here today that the rebs have left Atlanta and gone after Sherman. I expect stirring things will happen in a day or two. General Slocum now commands our 6th Corps. 1st Lieut. P. H. Brookway (formerly Orderly Sergt. of Co. H.) now commands our Co. Capt. Delaney, as you are aware, is at home. There is very little of interest to write. I hope the chronic diarrhea will not get hold of James and Charles. It is a terrible disease. Love to all. Please send some stamps.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Wheeler's cavalry tore up the Nashville road, so Alexander's hospital train, two nights and a day out, was forced to stop at Chattanooga, where he writes his mother a tired, brief note: pretty sick yesterday, much better today, soon able to rejoin the regiment.
