movements.transcription:
Sept. 2d, 1864
U. S. General Hospital
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

The evening of the day I wrote you my last letter, I with a large number of other sick and wounded was put on board a hospital train and sent to this place. We were two nights and a day getting here. We should have gone directly to Nashville, but old Wheeler had made a raid and torn up the road so we were obliged to stop here. I do not know how long we shall remain here. Generally as soon as the men are able to hear it they send them on to Nashville. I was pretty sick yesterday and last night, but am very much better today. I shall be able to join the regt. before a great while, I think. Considerable anxiety is felt to know who the Presidential nominee is at the Chicago convention the 29th inst. We will know in a day or two. There is nothing of interest to write. Send your letters to the regt. as usual. Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

"We will know in a day or two." Nothing of interest to write.

movements.sigSummary: 60th N.Y. Vets. were pulled from the front to escort the 20th Corps Paymaster down to Chattanooga — and carried five long-overdue letters to Alexander in U.S. Field Hospital No. 2, where he was fighting "this misnamed scurvy" with a daily drink of lime water. movements.transcription:
Sept. 18, 1864
U. S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Much to my gratification a day or two since the 60th N.Y. Vets. were sent to this place from the front to escort the Paymaster of the 20th Corps down, and of course they brought what mail there was for me at the Regt. (5 letters.) You can rest assured I was well pleased for I had not heard from you in a long, long, time, and I did not dare have the mail sent here for I was liable to be sent off to Nashville or some other place any time. Direct your letters to the regt. as usual. There is too much uncertainty to have them directed here. I am getting along pretty well, but how soon I shall be fit for duty I am unable to say. I may be well soon and it may take a long time to get this misnamed scurvy out of my blood. However I guess I will be all right before long. The man that gives out the medicine has just been around and given me a gay old drink of lime water — something very similar to lemonade. Then I say lime I don't mean lime such as they make mortar of, but limes, a fruit like lemons.

Luther is with the regt. He has been up to see me twice. A number of the boys have been up to see me. It is pleasant to have them here. The regt. is still here unless they have left this morning. I am sorry I shall not be able to draw pay with the regt. this time. Government owes me some two hundred and forty dollars. I may draw a little pay here, sufficient for my wants but no more.

What do the people of C. think of the draft. We all like it down here. There is no way to put down this rebellion but by force of arms. A few more vigorous pushes will shove them into the Atlantic Ocean.

When you speak in your letters of the tomatoes you are having, and the new potatoes, etc., etc. in such abundance, I long to be there to enjoy these good things with you, and I hope I shall before many months roll around. The letters I received from you were of Aug. 24th and 29th. The other letter was from Jack Ingram. I received six stamps in one of your letters which will do for some little time. I received the money and everything you sent except the tea, I think. Perhaps you did not put on enough postage for the tea. Tell Fannie I will try and write her before a great while. Love to all. Remember me to Mrs. B. If any body wants to know my political principles you tell them I am a "war man." That's enough. Please write often.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

I am glad to see the copper heads don't like McClellan. It speaks well for him.

movements.sigSummary: Three years to the day since he swore his oath, Alexander writes from U.S. Hospital No. 2 in Chattanooga — "three long — long — weary years!" — his first time hospitalized sick rather than wounded. He reports a strange affliction: "as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat," with others around him troubled the same way. A postscript betrays his dread: morning papers carry word of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley, and he is anxious to hear from the boys.
movements.transcription:
September 21, 1864
U. S. Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Have you taken a realizing sense that I have now been in the U. S. Service as a soldier three years — three long — long — weary years! Yes — three years ago today I took an oath to serve the United States of America faithfully as a soldier for the term of "three years or the war," and I can conscientiously say that I have with God's help done my best to bear that oath and do my duty as a soldier should do. And now, dear Mother, I want you to join me, (and I know you will) in thanking God for his kind and watchful care over me in preserving me through so many dangers and temptations to which I have been exposed in the past terrible three years of war, and to ask a continuance of his kind care over me during the remainder of my term of service.

When I think of all the things which I have passed my heart is too full to speak. This is the first time since I have been in the service that I have been in a general hospital sick. You know I was in one last fall but then I was wounded and was only a short time from the regt.

Well, I wrote you, only a day or two since, and have nothing of special interest to communicate. I am getting along very well, I think. There is one very singular thing about it — as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat. However it may wear off in time. There are a number here troubled in the same way. Direct your letters to the regt. Give my regards to Mrs. B. Love to all,

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell.

P.S. The morning papers give an acct. of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley. I am very anxious to hear from the boys.

movements.sigSummary: On his three-year anniversary in the service, Alexander Hubbell can manage only "an apology for a letter" — a few dutiful lines penned from U.S. Field Hospital No. 2 at Chattanooga on September 21, 1864. Too unwell to do more, he promises Fannie a long letter "before a great while" and asks only that she write often. "I only write them to let you know I have not forgotten you."
movements.transcription:
Sept. 21, 1864
U.S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Fannie:

I shall now only write an apology for a letter and shall conclude with a promise of a long letter before a great while, and I hope I shall find grace in your eyes. I do not feel very well today, and I trust you will regard this as a sufficient excuse for these few lines. I only write them to let you know I have not forgotten you. Please write me often.

Your aff. Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: James came out of the battle near Winchester two days since unhurt — Charles writes his mother in thanks, four killed and twelve wounded in their company. James, nicely recruited from the hospital, rejoined the regiment that lost 55 wounded and 10 killed; the rebs were whipped and driven to Strasburg, where they are making a stand. Charles, still with the Brigade Commissary, confesses he is "getting fat" on good living while his regiment bleeds.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 21st, 1864
In the field near Strasburg

Dear Mother:

I sit down to write you a few lines, feeling very thankful that James came out of the battle near Winchester two days since unhurt. There were four killed and twelve wounded in our Co. James is looking very well, he got nicely recruited at the hospital. A day or two after Dr. Sweeney wrote James rejoined the regt. Dr. Sweeney is very kind to James and me, and some time since wished me to transfer him to you. I am still with the Brigade Commissary and am getting fat, the result of good living. I have to walk on the march but carry no load.

I rec'd your letter with the $2.00 and stamps, also James rec'd three newspapers with Mr. Hoyle's name on them. James got our Capt. to write to Albany for his state bounty which is twenty-five dollars and ordered it sent to you. He should have had it long since. The letter was sent a few days since. I think the money you invested in the "2d hands" may well pay. It may be well to invest some of our money in the capital of the C. Bank, but will leave you to do as you think best.

We were camped near Berryville two weeks and while there our Regt. drilled twice a day, leaving hardly time to cook. That is the reason James has not written. We lost a good many men in the fight two days since, but whipped the rebs and drove them to this place where they are making a stand, but they will soon have to leave. Our regt. lost 55 wounded and 10 killed. We are now about twelve miles this side of Winchester. Am glad to hear that you and Frances are well. We are pleased to hear from you so often, hope that you will continue to write often.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

(Written on back of this letter — a note from Frances.)
movements.notes: In the field near Strasburg. **BATTLE NEAR WINCHESTER** — two days since, came out unhurt. **4 KILLED, 12 WOUNDED in Co.** James looking very well — nicely recruited. Day or two after Dr. Sweeney wrote, James rejoined regt. Still with Brigade Commissary — "getting fat, the result of good living." Have to walk on march but carry no load. Received letter with $2 and stamps. Also James rec'd 3 newspapers. **JAMES GOT CAPT. TO WRITE ALBANY** for state bounty — $25 — should have had it long since. Mother's investment in "2d hands" may well pay. **CAMPED NEAR BERRYVILLE** two weeks — reason James has not written. Lost good many men in fight two days since — whipped rebs, drove them to this place. **REGT. LOST 55 WOUNDED AND 10 KILLED.** Near Winchester — about 12 miles this side. (Written on back — note from Frances.)

movements.sigSummary: Border-state men and the "Hibernians" will vote McClellan, Alexander tells his sister Fannie from a Chattanooga hospital bed — they would free the slaves only to ship them out of the country, never accept equality. And from three years' service he agrees: "I could never consent to see these black men mingled with our white." Then the soldier-philosopher turns homesick boy, longing for Mother's steamed apple dumplings in the September rain.
movements.transcription:
Sept. 25, 1864
U.S. Field Hospital No. 2
Chattanooga, Tenn.

Dear Fannie:

Now for the long promised letter. You perceive I am still in the same place, but I am unable to say how long I may remain here. I am getting along very well, I think, and will doubtless be able to join the regt. before a very great while. I still continue to be blind at night. The Dr. thinks it will wear off in time. Others tell me I will never get over it, but then I think I shall.

How runs the political excitement in C? Pretty high I expect. It will be a very closely contested election, I think. A good many soldiers will vote for McClellan. A majority of the border state men, I think, will, and a large number of the "Hibernians." They don't like the "nigger" nor any man that favors them. The border men get quite wrathy over the idea of "nigger equality." They say they would rejoice to see the niggers free if they would be sent out of the country, lest to have the nection among them on an equality with the white man they never would agree to it. They say if they would be sent out of the country, they say they have talked with men from all the Northern states and none are willing to have them settle among them. They say the Northern states and none are willing to have them settle there, and are even more hostile to it than they are. "And now," said one, "what are you going to have packed on us what none of you are willing to receive! Never!!!"

I must confess, dear Fannie, that I sympathize strongly with these "border men" in this matter of what they call "nigger equality." I could never consent to see these black men mingled with our white and form a part of the people of the United States. I do not think it was ever the design of Providence that the two races should be mingled and I doubt not the Government will make some wise provision in this case. We have got enough on hand now to put down this rebellion. It will do to talk about this "equality" matter when the war is over.

Have you taken a realizing sense that I am now according to the laws of the United States twenty-one years of age and am privileged to vote at the coming elections. You know I have now been in the U. S. service a little over three years.

Sept. 27 — This morning the weather is quite chilly and threatens rain. It is very much like Sept. weather at home and makes me think of ripe apples and a thousand other good things. I should like tremendously to get hold of one of Mother's steamed apple dumplings. Perhaps before another year rolls round I shall be there to enjoy these good things.

The last letter I received from home was dated in August and I am very anxious to hear from you all, but I dare not have my mail sent here. I may be with the regt. soon. If not I believe I shall risk having it sent here. Continue to direct as before. Give my regards to Mrs. B. and all friends. Give much love to Mother.

Your aff. Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes to Alexander from Harrisonburg, fresh off rejoining the regiment after being cut loose from a too-crowded commissary, and the war reaches him as ledger and labor: a Fresseville recruit drawing $1,202 bounty for one year, rations wagoned ninety miles from Harper's Ferry, cavalry burning barns and grist mills toward Stanton. "A man is no soldier unless he is lousy," he reports — war as housekeeping in a rich valley being eaten bare.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 4, 1864
Harrisonburg

As the mail leaves soon I will write a few lines. I rejoined the regt. the last day of Sept. There were too many clerks there in the commissary so they told two of us to go to our regts. I am quite fat and am in good health. James is very well. I have no gun yet, as I turned in my gun when I left the regt. Expect to have one soon.

A few days since a recruit from Fresseville came to our Co. He rec'd. $1202 bounty. Enlisted for one year. We have been here three days. I don't know which way we will move from here. Have chased the rebs a long way. It is about ninety miles from here to Harper's Ferry. The cavalry have been as far as Stanton and have burned barns and grist mills. We advanced to the next town about 8 miles from here where we got a lot of flour and came back here the next day. The troops have suffered some from want of rations. Rations are wagoned here from Harper's Ferry. On the march the troops we foraged a great deal. Pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc. There is a Provost Marshall to stop such doings but it is done for all that. This is a rich valley — a fine farming country. There are a great many wounded rebs in the hospital here. We have also passed other towns where the rebs were in hospitals. They were sent this way after the fight near Bunker Hill.

Recruits are coming to this army fast. Quite a number have joined our regt. We have burned all the fences for a long ways around this place except where there is a safe guard. These oak rails make a good fire. This is a bad place to camp as water and wood are scarce. Have to go quite a distance for them. Do you know a soldier's daily duty? It is to cook, clean his gun and look over his clothes and pick off the vermin. On a march the soldiers get pretty lousy as they have no kettles to heat water to boil their clothes. It is a common saying that a man is no soldier unless he is lousy. Some of the men think that we are going to Louisiana to spend the winter. I hope not.

Have you rec'd seventy-five dollars from Albany — James' state bounty? James rec'd two or three days since two democratic newspapers (Journal of Commerce). We expect to receive a letter from you next mail. It is some time since we received one.

Charles
movements.notes: Harrisonburg, Shenandoah Valley. **REJOINED REGT. last day of Sept.** Too many clerks in commissary — told to go back. Quite fat and in good health. James very well. About 90 miles from Harper's Ferry. **CAVALRY BURNED BARNS AND GRIST MILLS** as far as Stanton (Staunton). Advanced 8 miles for flour, came back. Troops suffered from want of rations — wagoned from Harper's Ferry. On march, foraged: "pigs, sheep, chickens, apples, butter, etc." Provost Marshall can't stop it. movements.sigSummary: At Harrisonburg in the Shenandoah, James writes his brother Alex after two fights that drove the rebels back — wagons left burning along the night roads — then the pullback to Cedar Creek near Strasburg, burning barns as they went. He fears Alex Douglas, fallen to the rear on a march, has been "boggled by the guerrillas," and recounts a foraging boy nearly hanged as a spy who slipped free mid-battle. At 18 he votes plainly: "I go for old Abe; he is the man."
movements.transcription:
October 4, 1864
Harrisonburg
In the Shenandoah Valley

Dear Alex:

When did I write you last! I know it is a long time since. Do not think because I have not written you that I have forgotten you. We have had two fights of which you have undoubtedly heard, driving the rebels both times. The last pursuit the inhabitants of the towns through which we passed said the Rebs went through there with a rush, and that their army was demoralized. In the road in the pursuit during the night we passed several of their wagons burning. I do not believe that the Johnnies will make another stand here in the valley. You have travelled this road once, I think.

October 12th — Since I commenced this we have fallen back to Cedar Creek near Strasburg — burning barns and forage as we went. Alex Douglas has been boggled by the guerrillas, it is thought. He fell to the rear several days since with one man of our company while on a march and has not been seen or heard of since. The boys in this army have a habit of running through the houses and taking whatever they choose, which I think exasperates the rebels very much, and I cannot but fear for a straggler. This other fellow from our company was one of the greatest house thieves in our regt. Douglas was not any of that. I have heard this thief tell some of his stories. While he was in one house one of the children said, "Ma, there is a Yankee down cellar taking all our preserves and bacon." "Ma, see that Yankee looking in the oven." If they remonstrated with him he would "blackguard" them. I do not pity this fellow much. This running through houses is checked carefully by the officers but cannot always be prevented. Sometime before the battle of Winchester there was a little boy of our brigade gobbled while foraging. He was shot up with rebel deserters. During the fight they were ordered to turn out and help fight; he slipped out with them and made his escape. He said they were going to hang him for a spy.

Last night I received a letter from home. They want to know why we do not write. I have been rather negligent in writing. Charley has written several times but they have not received his letters; the mails have been irregular. Mother says you are quite ill. I hope you are better ere this. I have seen one month in the hospital since I enlisted. I'm all right now. Charley's health is now pretty good. There is some talk about our going to Louisiana. I hope we will not. I do not like the climate.

What are your views on the coming elections? I'm a voter; I go for old Abe; he is the man, I think. Little Mac will probably run strong. This war has lasted nearly four years. I would like to see it ended, and believe it will be soon.

Your aff. brother

James

movements.sigSummary: At Chattanooga the army told Alexander "but, but, but" — a doctor's stammered refusal of the furlough he'd earned, granted instead to a man whose scurvy was "not near so bad." Writing from Hospital No. 3 in Nashville on October 10, 1864, his eyes mending and his regiment beckoning, he tallies the war's politics in miniature: on the hospital car from Chattanooga, thirty-seven men voted Lincoln, five McClellan. "Lincoln seems to be the favored one."
movements.transcription:
Oct. 10th, 1864
U.S.A. Hospital No. 3
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You perceive I have again changed my quarters. I was sent from Chattanooga last Wednesday and reached here Friday morning. The hospital I am now in is a very good one and I am getting along famously. I asked the doctor this morning to let me go to my regiment. He said he would see about it. I think I shall go in a day or two. My eyes are much better.

The political excitement is running high. Lincoln seems to be the favored one. When we were coming from Chattanooga a vote was taken in the car I was in. Thirty-seven voted for Lincoln and five for McClellan. I tried to get a furlough while at Chattanooga but did not succeed. The doctor did not do right, I think. He gave a furlough to a fellow that had the scurvy not near so bad as I did, and when I asked him he said "he would like to but, but, but, etc."

I hope this war will be over before long and then I shall need no furlough. I am anxious to get back to the regt. so I can get hold of the lots of letters there are there for me. I expect there must be a lot. James and Charles have written me. There is little of interest to write. There is to be a flag raised and a political speech to be made at Fort Gillam today. If possible I shall go. Please write often. Love to all. Give my regards to Mrs. B.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: U.S.A. Hospital No. 3, Nashville, Tenn. Sent from Chattanooga last Wednesday. Hospital is very good. Asked doctor to let him go to regiment — said he would see about it. Eyes much better. **LINCOLN SEEMS FAVORED.** "When we were coming from Chattanooga a vote was taken in the car I was in. Thirty-seven voted for Lincoln and five for McClellan." Tried for furlough at Chattanooga — doctor "did not do right." Gave furlough to fellow with scurvy "not near so bad as I did, and when I asked him he said 'he would like to but, but, but, etc.'" War will be over before long — shall need no furlough. movements.sigSummary: At dawn near Strasburg, James woke Charles with a shout — "The Rebs are here!" — and the Battle of Cedar Creek erupted. Charles tells a soldier's story of surprise: breastworks overrun, his brigade scrambling across a ravine as bullets came thick up the hill. James took a flesh wound to the hip and walked five miles to the hospital, a bandage torn from his own drawers. 7 wounded, 2 killed in his company alone.
movements.transcription:
Oct. 22, 1864
Camp near Strasburg, Va.

Dear Mother:

James and I rec'd a lot of newspapers Oct. 18th and were anticipating a good deal of pleasure next day in reading them. Well, next morning I was awakened by a sharp volley of musketry. James exclaimed, "The Rebs are here!" We jumped up and put on our accoutrements and fell in behind our breastworks, but in a few minutes were ordered to pack up. We took our tents down in a jiffy. By that time the rebs were close to us. It was a surprise attack. They got behind our breastworks before we knew it. Our Brigade was ordered to leave our breastworks and form on the other side of a deep ravine. We jumped over the breastworks very quick as the Rebs were firing into us and we were moving up the hill the bullets came very thick. A good many of our men were shot here. James was wounded near this place. A Sergeant of our Co. says that as he was going to the rear with a wounded man he saw James; that James rec'd. a flesh wound in the thigh or hip and walked about five miles to the hospital. Says James had made a bandage of his drawers. He went with James to the hospital and says James is all right. James Lucas was reported killed, but I have since learned that he was taken to the hospital shot through the head and arm. Sergeant Pelkier (pronounced Pelky) from Corbeau of our town was shot through the leg. Alex Douglas has been missing about ten or twelve days. While on the march here, he and another man of our Co. were either captured or killed. It is supposed that they got to the rear and were taken prisoners by guerillas. Every one is very sorry about Douglas as he was very much liked. He and the other man were mounted. James Lucas wrote Mr. Douglas about Alex. Lieut. Col. Strain was wounded in the arm in the fight on the 19th of Oct. Our Regt. had about 50 wounded and 8 killed. Our Co. had 7 wounded and 2 killed.

The Rebs drove us out of our camp in the morning when we lost a great many men, but we rallied and drove them, recapturing all our artillery and all of theirs. We drove them out of our camp and beyond to Fisher's Hill. The Rebs came into our camp by the flank where the 8th Corps lay. I am very thankful that I did not get scratched. I think that I have received all your letters but am sorry that you have not received mine. I wrote two from Harrisburg. Am very sorry about Lucas. He rec'd a letter from home the night before the fight and intended to write the next day. Did you receive a letter from Dr. Sweeney some time since? He inquired of me if you did. Please write soon and send me a few stamps.

From your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes from U.S.A. Hospital No. 3 in Nashville that he refused the oath prescribed in New York's voting law and so lost his chance to vote — yet "could I have voted I should have cast it 'square and fair' for Abraham Lincoln," adding that the majority of soldiers will vote that way. Beneath the politics runs a quieter ache: a son begging his mother to write "a long letter telling me all the news since last August."
movements.transcription:
October 26th, 1864
U.S.A. Hospital No. 3
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You can have no idea how anxious I am to hear from you all and I have at length determined to have a letter directed here. So please, immediately on receipt of this, write me a long letter telling me all the news since last August — the date of the last letter I received from you, and do not fail to send it by return mail. I think I shall be here ten (and perhaps more) days longer.

I would not take the oath prescribed in the New York voting law and have consequently lost my chance of voting. Could I have voted I should have cast it "square and fair" for Abraham Lincoln. The majority of soldiers will vote that way.

Direct your letter simply to Nashville, Tenn. In case I am not here when it arrives I can write to Postmaster and have it sent on.

Love to all.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

movements.sigSummary: Wounded in the left thigh at Cedar Run, James walked several miles to keep from falling into the Johnnies' hands, then rode thirty miles in an army wagon and 120 in a freight car — "that journey was a hard one." He writes Alex from Patterson Park Hospital convinced the Rebs are finished in the Valley, "three times terribly whipped," and means to cast his first vote for Abraham Lincoln.
movements.transcription:
October 29th, 1864
Patterson Park Hospital
Baltimore, Md.

Dear Alex:

I had a letter written and sealed which I carried in my pocket for a long time. I have now determined to add another before I send it to you. I was wounded in the left thigh at Cedar Run. It is nothing but a flesh wound and is doing well. I walked several miles after being hit in order not to fall into the Johnnies hands. They were then driving our forces, but things changed before night. Our forces were driving them full well. Their army was completely demoralized. They threw away everything. We got their wagon train, artillery and almost everything they had. The Johnnies attacked and routed the eighth Corps before daylight. This rather took our force by surprise and compelled them to retreat as they were flanked and the breastworks would be of no use. I do not believe the Rebs will try it again in the Valley — three times terribly whipped.

Our Co. was very much cut up. It was also badly cut up at Winchester, so that there is scarcely anything left of it. Lucas was badly wounded. He is the only one you know in the company. Three fellows assisted me to the hospital which was situated in a barn several miles back. I had gone part of the way myself, but was about played out when they came along. I remained at the Hospital a day and was then sent on here. I had thirty miles to ride in an army wagon to get to a railroad station, and then one hundred and twenty in a freight car. That journey was a hard one.

The hospital here is a very comfortable one and the fare very good. Baltimore seems to be the first great place to which our wounded and sick are sent. They are transferred from here to Philadelphia. You were right when I heard from you last. I hope you have got well ere this. I look for a speedy termination of the war. I think we shall be able to judge a good deal come morning it is after the Presidential election. I shall be able to vote here and shall cast my vote for Abraham Lincoln. I hope he will be elected.

We have not been paid for six months. I think it is about time for the Paymaster to visit us. I do not know how long I will be here but will send you my address; it is Patterson Park Hospital, Baltimore, M.D.

Your affectionate Brother,

James.

movements.letterExcerpt: I read your letter announcing grandmothers death two days since. Was not surprised as she was so old. I suppose Aunt Mary will come North if she can get away.
movements.sigSummary: Grandmother's death reaches Charles in camp at Cedar Creek, where his company is down to its survivors. He hunts for news of the wounded: brother James walked to the hospital, likely a flesh wound; James Lucas lay on the ground all day before an ambulance came; Sgt. Pelkier, shot in the leg, was left in a barn for the rebels but found alive that night. "I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co."
movements.transcription:
Nov. 4, 1864
Camp at Cedar Creek, Va.

Dear Mother:

I read your letter announcing grandmothers death two days since. Was not surprised as she was so old. I suppose Aunt Mary will come North if she can get away.

Have not heard from James nor any of our wounded in the last fight. Two of our Co. who saw him say that his wound is not dangerous. Our Chaplain saw him in the hospital sitting up in bed. He told me James was doing well. I asked the Chaplain if his wound was serious. He said he did not know. I told him that James walked to the hospital. He then said it must be a flesh wound. Our Chaplain is none home sick. The badly wounded were at the hospital at Winchester. The others are forwarded on to the other hospitals. James Lucas, I heard, lay on the ground all day till he was taken up by an ambulance. I did not see him. However that I ought to write his folks, but if you will tell them that he was shot then he head and an arm it will do as well. Our Chaplain told me that he probably would not recover. I do not whether James is at Winchester or been sent on to some other city. The morning of the fight there were no ambulances and if a man could not walk he had to lay on the ground unless some of the soldiers carried him. Segt. Pelkier, of our town, shot in the leg, was carried by some of our Co. & left in a barn to be made prisoner of by the rebs as was supposed, but when we came back that night he was there.

We now drill & have dress parade, regular camp life. Do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. I do not know how long we will stay here, but think not long. De Sweeney was taken prisoner the morning of the fight, but got away from the rebs that night. Did not know what had become of James until that night after dark.

Sunday, 6th: This morning we were called up at 4 oclock & fell into line with our arms. It looked as if they expected an attack, but after standing till daylight we broke ranks & cooked our breakfast. After eating we had Brigade Review & inspection.

I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co.

(Remainder of letter missing) From,

C. F. Hubbell (Charles)
movements.notes: Camp at Cedar Creek, Va. **GRANDMOTHER'S DEATH** announced — letter received. Not surprised — "she was so old." Aunt Mary will come North. Have not heard from James since last fight — wound not dangerous. Chaplain says James walked to hospital. James Lucas shot through head and arm — "I did not see him." Sgt. Pelkier (Pelky) shot through leg. Alex Douglas missing — guerrillas. **CO. NOW NUMBERS ONLY 22.** "In two fights we lost twenty-three men killed and wounded." Lost two in this valley. "In the fight bullets flew all around me but I came out without a scratch." **VOTED FOR LINCOLN.** **"ONLY TWO VOTES FOR LINCOLN IN OUR CO."** De Sweeney was taken prisoner morning of fight — came back that night. "Did not know what had become of James until that night after dark." Sunday 6th — called up at 4 o'clock, stood to arms all day, stood to arms till daylight.
At Nashville. 60th NY consolidated. Preparing for Battle of Nashville.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from winter quarters near Newtown, Virginia, where seven months' pay finally arrives — $108 on December 9th, plus snow six inches deep and rumors of a march past Winchester to guard a railroad. The Thanksgiving turkey ration was so thin that three men in a tent traded it for four hard tacks. Asked by Frances how he looks, he draws himself plainly: mustache and chin whiskers, "quite savage," round-shouldered as ever, shaving only when a razor allows.
movements.transcription:
Nov. 30, 1864
Camp near Newtown, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of Nov. 22nd today containing one dollar & a silk Hdkf. also fine comb. Am sorry that the people of Champlain are in such trouble about the rebs in Canada. Think that the alarm is needless, and you will not be disturbed.

Seven months pay is now due us and we are daily expecting to be paid, but may not be, and that the dollar you sent me will be all I will need, I think. Do you know how much the Hdkf. Alex sent me cost. It is almost too nice for a soldier. I was very much surprised to hear of Alex being home. He is not of age a soldier and therefore not entitled to vote. But am glad that he got the furlough. He was very lucky. I wish he could get into the Invalid Corps. I think that is the best place for him. Am glad to hear from you that James is doing well. I have not heard from him directly, but the Sergt. in our Co. that went to hospital with James, received one from him some time since.

The eighth of Nov, election day, we were called up very early and cooked our breakfast, we then packed up to move and stood to arms till daylight, but did not move and lay under arms all day. Next morning were called up the same way, but did not march till ten oclock, when we reached here after a few hours march. We are in good winter quarters, but some distance from wood & water. Our cabins are quite large & have a stone fireplace & chimney. Have been very busy which is the reason that I have not wrote.

Dec. 9th: Received six months pay last night, one hundred & eight dollars. We signed the pay rolls some days since and I have been waiting for pay before I sent this letter.

Dec. 10th: Last night about six inches of snow fell. They say this morning that our Regt. is going to make about ten miles from here to the other side of Winchester to guard a railroad. He will probably move tomorrow or next day. It is too hard sitting for Thanksgiving we drew turkey for dinner, but the ration for the three in our tent was so small that we annexed it to off for four big hard tacks. Hard tack better. I do not draw enough hard tack. I have bought it at the commissary. There is plenty to do, roll calls, reviews, guard duty, backing wood from the woods, etc. For two Sundays we have had Brigade review; next Sunday, tomorrow, we may be marching, that is our Regt.

Frances wants to know how I look. Well our men say that I never was fatter. I wear mustache & chin whiskers, look quite savage, shave the side of my face every week or two — could oftener but no razor. I do not think I have straightened any since I left home, but am as round shouldered as ever. Was much pleased yesterday to receive a letter from Frances and you, also two Tribunes. You ask if I want a vest — not so, but please send me a pair of No. 8 Rip Skin Boots, one small coarse towel, one small colored Hdkf. Ed better be sent by express, I guess. I will send some more money in a few days. Enclosed is fifty dollars.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Camp near Newtown, Va. Received letter with dollar and silk handkerchief — "also fine comb." Trouble about rebs in Canada — "Think that the alarm is needless." Seven months pay due — daily expecting to be paid. Dollar will be all he needs. "Do you know how much the Hdkf. Alex sent me cost. It is almost too nice for a soldier." Not surprised to hear of Alex being home — he is not of age (soldier age) and therefore not entitled to vote — "But am glad that he got the furlough. He was very lucky. I wish he could get into the Invalid Corps." Best place for him. James doing well. Not heard from him directly, but a Sergt. who went with James to hospital, recd from him some time since. **ELECTION DAY — Nov 8th.** Called up very early, cooked breakfast, stood to arms all day — didn't move. Next morning called up, marched after a few hours. "Did not march till ten oclock, when we reached here after a few hours march." Good winter quarters — "quite large & have a stone fireplace & chimney." "Have been very busy which is the reason that I have not wrote." **DEC 9TH — SIX MONTHS PAY LAST NIGHT — $108.** Signed the pay rolls some days since. **DEC 10TH** — six inches of snow. Regt. going to guard railroad 10 miles from here. **THANKSGIVING** — turkey dinner, but ration for three was so small "we annexed it to off for four big hard tacks." Hard tack better. "I have bought it at the commissary." Plenty to do — roll calls, reviews, guard duty, backing wood from woods, etc. Brigade review next Sunday. **Frances wants to know how he looks** — "I wear mustache & chin whiskers, look quite savage, shave the side of my face every week or two — could oftener but no razor." Lost two teeth in valley. "I do not think I have straightened any since I left home, but am as round shouldered as ever." movements.sigSummary: Hood's army has pushed to the gates of Nashville, and Alexander writes his mother from inside the fortifications, raising breastworks as skirmish fire and artillery crackle around the city. Fort Negley's heavy guns already pound the rebels close by. His confidence never wavers: "Gen. Hood will have to whistle for his supper." Yet he chafes at his posting, wanting his regiment and disgusted that "the officers drink altogether too much whiskey."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 5th, 1864
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

You perceive I am again in Nashville. We left Chattanooga the same day I wrote you my last letter and were two days in getting to this place. We were obliged to move very cautiously as the telegraph wires had been cut and we were not sure but the enemy were in force upon the road. However, we came through without accident. We have been hard at work for the last few days building breastworks, etc., etc. Hood is now in front of the city. No heavy fighting has yet occurred here. Skirmishing and artillery firing is tolerably brisk. The troops here have been and are still hard at work strengthening the fortifications around the city, and I am thinking that Gen. Hood of the bogus Confederacy will have to whistle for his supper so far as getting it out of the storehouse of Nashville is concerned.

I hope it will not be long before I can get to the regiment. I do not like my place here. The officers drink altogether too much whiskey. Fort Negley, close by, is now using its heavy guns upon the rebs.

Please write as often and direct to A. F. Hubbell, Nashville, Tenn. Do not put on economy and rest. Our present duty comes pretty hard on me, but I will soon get inured to it again I expect.

Love to all. Give my regards to Mrs. B., and Grandmothers family. Tell Frances I want to hear all about the "institute" and if she "knows a great deal more" since she attended. Remember me to James and Charles.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Nashville, Tenn. Back in Nashville from Chattanooga — left same day as last letter. **BUILDING BREASTWORKS** — been hard at work for last few days. "Hood is now in front of the city." Skirmishing and artillery firing tolerably brisk. Troops still hard at work strengthening fortifications. **"HOOD OF THE BOGUS CONFEDERACY WILL HAVE TO WHISTLE FOR HIS SUPPER"** — "so far as getting it out of the storehouse of Nashville is concerned." Hope to get to regiment soon — "I do not like my place here." **Officers drink altogether too much whiskey.** **FORT NEGLEY** — close by, now using heavy guns upon the rebs. "Please write as often and direct to A. F. Hubbell, Nashville, Tenn. Do not put on economy and rest."

movements.sigSummary: At Chestnut Hill Hospital his wound has nearly healed, and James is restless to rejoin his regiment — "I feel like getting back again." He recounts the Thanksgiving feast served to the ward: turkey and gravy, oyster soup, cranberry preserves, ice cream, all gone cold because the table was too large. To a mother fretting over Alex, he insists, "You do not know how well a soldier boy can take care of himself."
movements.transcription:
Dec. 9th, 1864
Chestnut Hill Hospital

Dear Mother and Fannie:

I received your letter, papers and package this morning. All were directed Walnut Hill, but they got here nevertheless. The vest is a very nice one, fits very well, and is very comfortable. You took too much trouble with it, considering it is to be worn under a blouse. I carry thread and needles, buttons, pins each, in my pocket book, and find that is the most convenient thing I can carry them in. The handkerchief, I think Miss Avey; my last one went to pieces not long ago. The papers will be doubly acceptable when I get to my Regiment, for there reading is very scarce.

Yesterday a fellow from the 153rd told me that he had heard that the First Brigade of the first Division was now in winter quarters at Newtown. I do not think you need be troubled about Charlie, if he is sick, he will be well taken care of.

I can now walk around very well. My wound has nearly healed. I feel like getting back to my regiment again. You asked what we had for dinner Thanksgiving Day. The dinner was turkey and gravy, oyster soup (I could not eat that) boiled potatoes, bread, cranberry preserves and ice cream. All was cold. It could not be otherwise when the table was so large. Each man had his dinner piled on his plate. Our ward got their dinner about four oclock, being among the last they were obliged to wait for the second table.

To speak of my punctuality in writing. During the campaign I did not carry a knapsack and consequently no writing materials. I could not easily carry a load buckled on my shoulders; instead of that I carried my bundle in a sort of a roll passing over my right shoulder and under my left arm which was far easier.

During the next campaign I am going to carry writing paper folded up and put in the cover of a small book. Think I can easily carry that. You speak of being anxious about Alex. I do not see why you should be if he has only been absent two weeks. You do not know how well a soldier boy can take care of himself. Last night there was news that three tons of mail was sent around by sea to Savannah for Sherman's army.

Enclosed you will find a ring. I made several while on my way last Spring to the regiment, but they got broke in my pocket book. About a furlough; they do not give a single one now because there are so many out. I am so near well that the chances would be small anyway.

Did you see the list of officers wounded in the 153rd? Did Lt. Colonel Strain lose a leg? Some say he did — others that he did not.

James
movements.notes: Chestnut Hill Hospital, Philadelphia. Received letter, papers, package. Directed to Walnut Hill but got here. **COAT DAMAGED — $16** put in Mr. Rich's hands. Keeler called. "We have had such a time in school this week which has resulted in the expelling of two girls — Miss Riley and Pocahontas — it was quite disgraceful." Mr. Webb, Mr. Averill — presented with democratic paper — "said he hoped that I would read it candidly." Mrs. Roe. "Her is grandmother; James Ransom is to take Mrs. Nebb's place." **THANKSGIVING** — "turkey and gravy, oyster soup (I could not eat that) boiled potatoes, bread, cranberry preserves and ice cream. All was cold." Each man had dinner piled on plate — ward got dinner about four o'clock, among last. **CAMPAIGN — DID NOT CARRY KNAPSACK** — carried bundle in sort of roll over right shoulder and under left arm. Far easier. **WOUND NEARLY HEALED.** Feel like getting back to regiment. **WRITING PAPER IN SMALL BOOK** for next campaign. Three tons of mail sent by sea to Savannah for Sherman's army. **RING ENCLOSED** — made several while on way last spring, broke in pocket book. Furloughs — so many out. **DID LT. COL. STRAIN LOSE A LEG?** Some say he did, others say not.

movements.sigSummary: Three days before the Battle of Nashville, with two inches of snow on the ground, Alexander goes beyond the pickets after rails for firewood and drops into the pit of an advanced picket, a colored soldier, to reconnoiter. The man tells him that could he "only les get his eye onto one of dem rebs he would fetch him sure," and Alexander agrees: "These colored soldiers fight well." He waits, heartily sick of Nashville, for Thomas to take the offensive.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 12th, 1864
Nashville, Tenn.

Dear Mother:

Nothing of special interest has transpired here since I last wrote. Since then the weather has been intensely cold. Today the weather is clear, but very keen with about two inches of snow on the ground. Just before the cold weather set in I'd set up in a shanty and fire place and am therefore quite comfortable. I was out this morning beyond the pickets after rails for fire wood, but was not fired at. The firing just to the right was quite sharp. I got into the pit of one of the advanced pickets (a colored soldier) and reconnoitered the ground pretty thoroughly before going out. The colored gentleman told me as if he could "only les get his eye onto one of dem rebs he would fetch him sure" and I rather think he would. These colored soldiers fight well.

There has been very little firing for the last few days. Both sides had all they could attend to in keeping warm. I hardly think the Johnny Rebs will venture to attack us in our present position. I expect Thomas will soon take the offensive. Today's paper seems to think Sherman will be at the coast in a day or two.

I hope we shall be sent on as soon as he gets here. I am heartily sick of my present position. Have the "Raiders" yet appeared in "Northern New York?" The Nashville papers are making considerably fun of the recent fright in Burlington, Vt. Let me hear particulars in your next letter. Is the Militia and Home Guard still kept up and do they still stand guard night and day?

Love to all. Kind regards to Mrs. B. Tell Frances I shall endeavor to write her soon.

Your aff Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. You may direct as usual (Nashville, Tenn.) but be careful and not write contraband intelligence as I may not get the letter. How are Charles and James. Please remember me to them when you write.
movements.notes: Nashville, Tenn. Nothing of special interest — intensely cold. "Just before the cold weather set in I'd set up in a shanty and fire place and am therefore quite comfortable." Out this morning beyond the pickets after rails for fire wood — "but was not fired at." **ADVANCE PICKETS — COLORED SOLDIER.** Got into pit of advance pickets (colored soldier) and reconnoitered the ground pretty thoroughly before going out. **"The colored gentleman told me he if he could 'only les get his eye onto one of dem rebs he would fetch him sure'"** — "and I rather think he would." **"THESE COLORED SOLDIERS FIGHT WELL."** Very little firing for last few days. Both sides keeping warm. "I hardly think the Johnny Rebs will venture to attack us in our present position." Expects **THOMAS WILL SOON TAKE THE OFFENSIVE.** Sherman will be at coast in a day or two. "I am heartily sick of my present position." **"RAIDERS" IN NORTHERN NEW YORK** — Nashville papers making fun of recent fright in Burlington, Vt. Militia and Home Guard still kept up.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes from a snowbound Camp near Newtown, Virginia, to cancel a request: never mind the boots, Mother — he bought a pair of government cavalry boots last night for five dollars, when sutlers want ten to fifteen. He acknowledges fifty dollars sent on the 10th, and asks only for one-fingered mittens, the best kind. Six inches of snow, a hard west wind drifting it across the camp; the weather alone keeps them here, and soon they expect to move down to guard the railroad.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 12, 1864
Camp near Newtown, Va.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you a letter two days since requesting you to send me a pair of boots. Write now to say that I do not want the boots as I bought a pair of government boots last night. My letter of the 10th contained fifty dollars. Please acknowledge as soon as possible.

The law allows four pounds of woolen or cotton goods to be sent by mail. I would like a pair of mittens — mittens with one finger are the best, but given it is hardly worth while to send any. I have a good pair of boots and paid only five dollars for them. Sutlers are selling boots from ten to fifteen dollars. My boots are cavalry boots.

There is about six inches of snow on the ground and it is very cold. A hard west wind is blowing and the snow is drifting. The weather is the cause of our being here now. Expect to move soon, down to the railroad and guarding that will be our duty. Must close as the mail leaves soon.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Camp near Newtown, Va. Wrote requesting boots — now writes to say does not want them. Bought government boots last night — $1, letter of 10th containing fifty dollars. **WANTS MITTENS** — "one finger" style best, but given scarcity, hardly worth sending. Good pair of boots — paid only five dollars. Sutlers selling boots $10-15. **CAVALRY BOOTS.** About six inches of snow — very cold. Hard west wind, snow drifting. Weather is cause of being here. Expect to move soon — down to railroad and guarding. Must close — mail leaves soon.

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother from picket duty at Camp Russell near Newtown, Virginia, the year ending as it began: in the field, on guard, out of stamps. The fall of Savannah drew "rousing cheers" from the brigade, though he reckons brother Alex lucky to have missed that 500-mile march. "I hore the war is nearly over, but have not much faith that it is." He encloses twenty dollars for taxes and bonds, and one weary plea: send postage stamps, for James has none either.
movements.transcription:
Dec. 27thths, 1864
Camp Russell
Near Newtown, Va.

Dear Mother:

I recd. your letter of Dec. 20th two or three days since. Am very, very sorry that you have been so anxious about me, but bad news travels fast, as you heard no bad news it would have been better to have taken it for granted that I was all right.

I wrote James yesterday advising him to be in no hurry about coming back here. Recd. a letter from him a few days since in which he says that he will be back soon here.

Christmas passed off very quietly here, all the men had a ration of whiskey which is now a gill. Enclosed I send twenty dollars. After using all you need of my money to pay taxes, etc., if there is any left you can invest it in the three years V — 30 Bonds. Please write how much the tax is. If the collector calls on you for the tax, you will have to pay five etc. on a dollar, but if you pay him on the day he advertises it will be only one ct. on a dollar for the collectors fee. I hope you will have no trouble in getting your wood drawn & cut. How is Frances going to get through the snow drifts to school. I guess she & you do not like the big snow storms.

I have not written Alex yet. Shall wait till he rejoins his regt. If he was with his regt. he would have had a chance to help take Savannah, but he is lucky that he missed that march of 500 miles. I hore the war is nearly over, but have not much faith that it is. If it lasts James & Alex will be in it, but I will be out next fall.

Not long since De Sweeney called on me at my tent & showed me a letter he had read from you about me. I told him that I had written you two or three days before. Did he write you? He said that I must write oftener. When? On the march last fall De Sweeney did all he could for James & I. Has been a friend. Lt. Col. Strain was the one that got me the class at the commissary & at Banks HQ. Gr. He was very friendly. Have not heard how he is getting along.

I must stop as I have to go on picket in a few minutes. Please send me some postage stamps as I am entirely out. Think James has no stamps.

Your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Camp Russell, near Newtown, Va. Recd letter of Dec 20th. "Am very, very sorry that you have been so anxious about me, but bad news travels fast." Enclosed $20. After taxes, if money left, can invest in three year 7-30 Bonds. **WROTE JAMES** yesterday advising not to hurry about coming back. Recd letter from James — says he will be back soon. **CHRISTMAS** — "all the men had a ration of whiskey which is now a gill." Enclosed $20. Frances going to school through snow drifts. **HAVE NOT WRITTEN ALEX YET** — will wait till he rejoins regt. If he was with regt., would have had chance to help take Savannah — lucky that he missed march of 500 miles. Hore war nearly over — "but have not much faith that it is." If it lasts, James and Alex will be in it. **LAST NIGHT BRIGADE GAVE ROUSING CHEERS** when told of fall of Savannah. **DR. SWEENEY** called at tent — showed letter he had read from Alexander. Told Charles he had written Alexander two or three days before. When? On march last fall "De Sweeney did all he could for James & I." Has been a friend. **LT. COL. STRAIN** — one who got Alexander place at commissary at Banks HQ. Very friendly. Must stop — going on picket. "Please send me some postage stamps as I am entirely out. Think James has no stamps."

movements.sigSummary: Charles writes his mother in haste to catch the night steamer: his regiment left Washington June 5th and landed at Savannah that morning, the war over but his service not. He marvels at a river so well obstructed that piles ran nearly bank to bank past two or three forts, and recalls a swimmer swept toward the open sea before marines rowed out to him. The city "looks deserted," and his three years are up October 17th — though whether he'll be mustered out before then, he cannot say.
movements.transcription:
June 12th, 1865
Savannah, Ga.

Dear Mother:

I write in haste so that this letter will go by the steamer that leaves tonight. Our Regt. left Washington June 5th & landed here this morning. We lay all day yesterday at the mouth of the river waiting for the tide to come in & last night just before dark we came to the city. The river has been very well obstructed. At one place piles were driven all the way across the river except a small opening in the center. Near these piles were two or three forts.

Yesterday while lying at the mouth of the river & while in swimming one of our men was caught by the tide & was rapidly being carried out to sea. A life preserver was thrown him & a boat rowed by marines went to his rescue. He was picked up after being badly scared.

The city looks deserted not much business being done now. I don't know whether our regt. will stay here or go into the interior of the state, but I think it will stay here.

Have you heard from Alex lately, how does he get along? Have you paid Mrs. Joseph Martin twenty dollars as I requested. Please let me know. My three years is on the 17th of Oct. Don't know whether we will be mustered out before that or not.

I hope you and Frances are well & that you will both pass a pleasant summer. Please write soon & tell us all the news. James says he will write next time.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Savannah, Ga. Writing in haste — steamer leaves tonight. **Regt. left Washington June 5th.** Landed Savannah this morning. Lay at mouth of river — **man caught by tide while swimming, nearly carried to sea** — life preserver thrown, rescued by marines. City looks deserted — not much business. "My three years is on the 17th of Oct." Don't know if mustered out before. Joseph Martin $20 — requested.

movements.sigSummary: Chris Greene's leg "hung by a few muscles and these they were obliged to sever with a pocket knife" — two men of the regiment cut it free, carried him from Ringgold, and he later gave each an engraved star. Alexander writes it as history, not horror, in a letter sending $350 home in coupon bonds. He confesses he sold his old watch "to buy bread to keep life in me" — the army did not always feed its sick.
movements.transcription:
June 16, 1865
Near Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

You have doubtless wondered at my long silence. I have been waiting to see if there would not soon be some news of our going home, but I still see no immediate prospects though I presume we will be discharged before a very very long while, as soon as the country gets more settled and the different new State Governs get into smooth working order.

Our corps and division has been broken up. Gen. Geary has issued his farewell order and gone. A large number of veteran regts. formed into a division are commanded by Brevet Major General Bartlette. Our Brig. (3rd) is commanded by Brevet Major General Greene. He was formerly Colonel of our Regt. He was promoted to be a Brigadier and commanded our brigade in the White Star Division a long time. He was wounded in the battle at Wauhatchie, Tenn. and left us then and has not been with us since until now. We like him and are glad at his promotion. His son, Chris Greene (his aide de Camp) was wounded a few weeks after his father at the battle of Ringgold. His leg was taken off by a cannon shot. Two of our Regt. bandaged his leg (it hung by a few muscles and these they were obliged to sever with a pocket knife) and carried him from the field. He presented each of them afterward with a handsome Star with his and their names engraved on them. He is now on the staff of his Father.

We have been paid. I expressed home yesterday three hundred and fifty dollars. Please say fifty to Frances and tell her I regret not being able to buy her before. The money is in fifty dollar coupon bonds. The Paymaster said the money was not invested as well as it could be. Ask Mr. Hoyle what to do with them. Use as much of the money as you want — all of it if you want it. Please write often. I will endeavor to be more prompt in future.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Please send lots of papers, i.e. if you have them. I have been obliged to buy a new watch and consequently could not send home as much as I wish I could. Perhaps I did not tell you I was obliged to sell my other watch to buy bread to keep life in me.
movements.notes: Near Washington, D.C. Long silence — waiting for news of going home. No immediate prospects — "I will still see no immediate prospects though I presume we will be discharged before a very very long while." Corps and division broken up. **GEN. GEARY** issued farewell order and gone. Veteran regts. formed into division commanded by **BREVET MAJ. GEN. GREENE** — "He was formerly Colonel of our Regt." Promoted to Brigadier. Commanded brigade in White Star Division. **WOUNDED AT WAUHATCHIE.** His son **CHRIS GREENE** (aide de camp) — "wounded a few weeks after his father at the battle of Ringgold. His leg was taken off by a cannon shot. Two of our Regt. bandaged his leg (it hung by a few muscles and these they were obliged to sever with a pocket knife) and carried him from the field. He presented each of them afterward with a handsome Star with his and their names engraved on them." Now on staff of his father. **$350 SENT HOME** — fifty dollar coupon bonds. Paymaster said money not well invested. Bought new watch — "I was obliged to sell my other watch to buy bread to keep life in me."

movements.sigSummary: The long wished-for order came at last: on June 26, 1865, near Alexandria, Virginia, the Sixtieth New York Veteran Volunteers were ordered mustered out "immediately," and Alexander writes his sister Fannie to say he is coming home to Ogdensburgh to be discharged and paid off. "That's a happy day that will be, eh, Miss Fannie." Four years on, he marvels that a nation once racked "from its base to its center" now stands "free and united" — by the providence of God.
movements.transcription:
June 27, 1865
Near Alexandria, Va.

Dear Fannie:

I advised in my last letter home that my next should be to you, so here goes. My last letter was dated — I believe — the 16th of June. That's a naughty boy I have been I know you'll say, but I have been waiting for the confirmation of certain rumors and now my dearest Sister, Fannie, I am rejoiced to inform you that last night the long wished for order came to muster the Sixtieth New York Veteran Volunteers out of the United States service immediately. Therefore just as soon as we can make out our papers and get transportation we shall come to Ogdensburgh, and there be discharged and paid off. That's a happy day that will be, eh, Miss Fannie, agreed and a proud one for me. God spare my life to see the time. When I left home nearly four years since our country was racked from its base to its center by one of the most violent and gigantic rebellions recorded on the pages of history. We knew not friends from foes. Treason walked our legislative halls and had command of our armies. Now by the providence of God, after four years of unparalleled struggling we stand a free and united nation, than which in point of honor we have no superior and in point of freedom, no equal.

The mail will leave soon — I must close. Please give much love to Mother and Mrs. Hoff. I received a magazine and some papers from home the other day. I am very much obliged for the magazine. The papers were more than welcome. Please write soon. A letter will come from C. here in two days.

Your aff. brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Please return to Mrs. Bostwick the enclosed letter. Culver was discharged a few days since, and is doubtless at home with his friends by this time.

God spare my life to see the time." **VALEDICTORY** — "When I left home nearly four years since our country was racked from its base to its center by one of the most violent and gigantic rebellions recorded on the pages of history. movements.sigSummary: Savannah, July 13, 1865: in the first peacetime Fourth, Charles watches the city's fire companies parade, "all black but one — the darkeys young and old all turned out," while cotton rolls in from a hundred and sixty miles off. James's nighttime blindness has trailed him here; he sees fine by day but not after dark. Charles and James have expressed home one hundred and thirty dollars and wait, half-hoping, to be discharged before the tomatoes come ripe.
movements.transcription:
July 13th, 1865
Savannah, Ga.

Dear Mother:

The last letter we received from you said, that at Uncle Henry's request you were going to Charlotte. Perhaps that is the reason we have not received my letter or papers from you lately.

I was sorry to hear that you were not in very good health. Hope that it has improved. James & I are in good health. James says that since we came here it troubles him to see at night, but he can see as well as usual in the day time. Since I last wrote you we have moved into the city near the river. We have a good place for a camp. Are now living in board shanties, four men in each. Our Regt. was paid not long since & James & I sent you by express one hundred & thirty dollars. Martin sent seventy dollars with us, so that the express charges would be less. Please let us know whether you have recd. the money. Since any days a good many have been drunk. A man in our Regt. while drunk one night, messed clothes with a woman and then walked down street with her. There were met by some soldiers who after pounding them, robbed each of them.

You speak of hearing from us in Washington. Who did you hear by. Was it Capt. Harry Hummel? There is more business done here now than when we came here. Considerably cotton is being riled and carted. A wagon loaded with cotton came into the city this morning. The driver told me that they had come one hundred & sixty miles with it.

We take a swim in the river quite often. The tide here rises ten or fifteen feet high. The weather is very hot. I nearly melted in church last Sunday. July 4th there was a review of all the troops here. On the Fourth there was a dress parade of each Regt. at eight in the morning, also firing of cannon & ringing of bells. There was a parade of all the fire companies, all black but one. The darkeys young and old all turned out. Yesterday Dr. John Sweeney called on us. He & his brother James are in charge of the Division Hospital. John graduated at the medical school last winter with Ranch Malcolm. Ranch has been assistant surgeon but is not now as his Regt. is discharged. John inquired about you & Frances.

You speak of tomatoes & green corn. I should like to be home to eat some of them, but guess I will not have a chance. He may not be home before our time is out & then we may — it is hard to tell.

I have been quite negligent about writing, but will try & do better. We have a good deal of duty to do. James is on duty so can't write. Please write often & all the news.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell
movements.notes: Savannah, Ga. At Uncle Henry's request, you went to Charlotte. Haven't received letters or papers. Not in very good health — hope improving. **JAMES'S NIGHT BLINDNESS** — "James says that since we came here, troubles him to see at night, but he can see as well as usual in the day time." Moved into city near river. Living in board shanties, 4 men each. **REGT. PAID** — sent $130 by express. Martin has $70. Soldier drunk — "meshed clothes with a woman and then walked down street with her. There were met by some soldiers who after pounding them, robbed each of them." **JULY 4TH** — dress parade, review, firing of cannon & ringing of bells. Parade of all fire companies — **"all black but one. The darkeys young and old all turned out."** **DR. JOHN SWEENEY** called — his brother James in charge of Division Hospital. John graduated medical school with Ranch Malcolm. Ranch was assistant surgeon — now discharged. John inquired about Frances. Tomatoes & green corn — homesick. James on duty, can't write.
Returned to Ogdensburg. Mustered out July 27, 1865.

movements.sigSummary: Alexander writes his shortest letter ever from Camp Wheeler in Ogdensburgh, N.Y. — waiting on a Paymaster who still hasn't come, doubting he'll make it home this week, though he is "very anxious to see you all again." He'll bring Luther down to "our house," and saves the news of "a grand reception" for the tea table. The very paper is borrowed: a printed "Soldier's Letter" poem from a boy who doesn't much like writing.
movements.transcription:
July 27th, 1865
Camp Wheeler
Ogdensburgh, N.Y.

Dear Mother:

We reached here last Sat. and have been waiting for the Paymaster ever since. He has not come yet and I have some doubts whether I shall be able to be home this week. I am very anxious to see you all again. Luther will be down with me and spend a short time at "our house." I got this paper from one of the boys who I guess does not like writing much.

Love to all,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. We had a grand reception. I will tell you all about it at the tea table.

*(Stationery consists of a poem entitled "Soldier's Letter," written in rhyme with fill-in spaces provided for the sender's use.)*
movements.notes: Camp Wheeler, Ogdensburgh, N.Y. **THE HOMECOMING.** "We reached here last Sat. and have been waiting for the Paymaster ever since." Doesn't know if he'll be home this week. "I am very anxious to see you all again." **LUTHER** will come with him — "spend a short time at 'our house.'" I will tell you all about it at the tea table."** Stationery is a printed poem "Soldier's Letter" with fill-in spaces.
